## Understanding digital identity

This chapter covers

How identity supports digital relationships

Why naming matters for authorization

What centralized, federated, and decentralized models are

Tradeoffs among privacy, authenticity, and confidentiality

Why trust and confidence both matter

Imagine you’re a regular at a neighborhood café. Every morning, you walk in and the
barista greets you by name. She remembers your usual order—a double espresso, no

sugar. This recognition isn’t just about knowing your name; it’s about the relationship
you’ve built through repeated interactions.

One day, the café switches to a new self-service kiosk for ordering. The machine doesn't
know you, and it doesn't remember your order. It asks you to sign up, create an account,

and log in. Suddenly, the familiar experience of being recognized is gone, replaced by a
system that knows you only through an identifier and a set of attributes.

[What changed? Your identity at the café was once relational and human, tied to memory,](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-2?potentialInternalRefId=8---book-markup-container)
interaction, and trust. Now, in the digital system, you have been reduced to credentials and

stored preferences. The system recognizes your account, not _you_ . Depending on its
sophistication, the digital system may give the impression it knows you, but its

_personalization_ efforts will often fall short. This scenario illustrates a fundamental question
in digital identity: Are we just a set of attributes, or does identity mean something more?

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

23

As we explore digital identity, we’ll see that it’s not just about logging in or proving who

you are—it’s about how systems recognize, remember, and relate to people, organizations,
and digital entities. And, ultimately, it’s about the relationships we form in digital spaces.

#### 2.1 What is digital identity?

The quickest way to sidetrack any digital identity conversation is to ask, “But what’s

identity?” Identity means different things depending on the context: legal, philosophical,
technical, or social.

Philosophically, there are two broad traditions. Philosopher David Hume thought of
identity as a bundle of attributes. Bundle theory puts attributes into a collection with little

regard to what ties them together. As an example, you might identify an apple as red,
spherical, 12 centimeters in diameter, and crisp. René Descartes thought bundle theory was

mistaken, believing that identity must be tied to some underlying entity. His famous quote,
“I think, therefore I am,” describes his philosophy, called _substance theory_, in a single

memorable phrase.

[While we can’t lose track of these philosophical underpinnings, for our purposes, we will](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-2?potentialInternalRefId=13---book-markup-container)

need a much more functional definition of identity. _Digital identity allows systems to_
_recognize, remember, and relate to people, organizations, things, services, and digital_

_agents._ The ability to recognize, remember, and relate to another entity online is
indispensable for digital interactions.

[Digital identity is foundational to the security, personalization, and functionality of](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-2?potentialInternalRefId=14---book-markup-container)
modern computing systems. Organizations use identity systems to support the specific

kinds of relationships that they need to create with others. For example, it's not unusual for
an organization to use a different identity system for employees than the one they use to

support customers. Each of those relationships has specific needs and thus requires
different systems to support them.

[Identity powers policy-based access control and dynamic authorization. Authorization](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-2?potentialInternalRefId=15---book-markup-container)
depends on who (or what) an entity is, what it does, and its relationships to other entities.

In the context of dynamic authorization, the underlying identity system enables the
authorization system to make decisions about access and permissions by providing the

context for authorization.

[This chapter lays the foundation for understanding digital identity before we explore](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-2?potentialInternalRefId=16---book-markup-container)

authentication in chapter 3 and the basics of authorization in chapter 4. We will examine
the challenges, properties, and models of digital identity, showing how they shape security

and access control.

#### 2.2 The problems of digital identity

The task of recognizing, remembering, and relating to others on the internet is not easy.
Understanding the significant problems that digital identity systems face is important

because it helps us understand why digital identity systems are built the way they are and
where they still fail to completely meet the needs of many digital interactions.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

24

2.2.1 The proximity problem

In the scenario at the start of this chapter, a close, human relationship was replaced by an
experience intermediated by a computer. We all recognize the stark contrast in how the

human and machine-based interactions feel because we’ve all been there. The kiosk may
be located in the coffee shop, but it's just an interface for a system that's located

somewhere else in a place we call "the cloud." The rich visual and conversational interaction
with the barista has been replaced by a transactional experience based on a few specific

pieces of information given to the underlying ordering system. This is the essence of the
proximity problem.

Digital identity systems are far away from the entities they are creating relationships
with and consequently rely on relatively weak signals. They manage the proximity problem

by creating accounts to remember and use authentication mechanisms like usernames and
passwords or biometrics to recognize the entities connecting to them. They also usually

store attributes and other information that they need for context when interacting. These
mechanisms introduce several problems, including user frustration and poor security. We’ll

talk more about these topics in the next chapter when we discuss authentication in detail.

2.2.2 The interoperability problem

The internet was built without an identity layer for humans. Consequently, every
organization has solved the proximity problem in its own way. The result is far from

seamless, resulting in a myriad of user experiences, hundreds of different usernames and
identities, and thousands of online forms that all ask for nearly the same information.

Organizations cope with the interoperability problem using protocols like System for
Cross-domain Identity Management (SCIM, <u>[https://www.​okta.com/​blog/2017/​01/what-is-​](https://www.okta.com/blog/2017/01/what-is-scim)</u>

<u>[scim) for syncing information between systems and OpenID Connect (https://auth0.​](https://www.okta.com/blog/2017/01/what-is-scim)</u>
<u>[com/docs/​protocols/​oidc) for federating identity providers. If you’ve ever used your Google,](https://auth0.com/docs/protocols/oidc)</u>

Facebook, or Apple account to log into another app or service, you’ve used OpenID
Connect. These and other protocols help with interoperability, but they don’t solve the

entire problem.

[The core of this problem is that people have no identity systems of their own and,](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-2?potentialInternalRefId=25---book-markup-container)

consequently, are just visitors in the identity systems of the many organizations with whom
they have relationships. People working on decentralized identity or self-sovereign identity

are hoping to solve this problem. This lack of standing in the digital realm and the problems
it poses are beyond the scope of this book, but in chapter 16, we will look at how

decentralized credentials can result in better authorization decisions.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

25

2.2.3 The flexibility problem

Most identity systems are built to handle specific needs. The schema for the attributes they
store can be limited. For example, if your organization is using Google as your identity

provider, you can only use the attributes that Google chooses. If you want others, you’ll
have to build a system for collecting those as part of the account profile. Solutions for

workforce identity usually allow their schema to be extended, but may still have limitations
for many applications.

Inflexible schemas and limited attributes directly impact authorization systems, which
may need to make decisions based on the context provided by whatever attributes the

identity system provides. This is especially true of dynamic attributes like current location
or work schedule, which may have to be accessed from other systems outside the identity

system.

2.2.4 The privacy problem

The pervasiveness of digital identity systems means that our personally identifying
information (PII) is stored in thousands of systems, some of which are inadequately

secured. Companies often use this information for purposes beyond what it was initially
requested for. The difficulty and expense of running digital identity systems mean that

central identity providers can track access requests and correlate people's activities across
many sites.

Authorization systems can add to this problem by creating authorization logs that leave
a record of access history and require more attributes than are necessary to make a correct

access decision. People concerned about their privacy may lie about self-asserted data,
making access decisions suspect.

[At the same time, dynamic authorization can help with the privacy problem by enforcing](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-2?potentialInternalRefId=32---book-markup-container)
privacy protections so that data is accessed only when necessary and by the right parties.

Privacy is a critical aspect of digital identity, so we’ll discuss it in more detail later in this
chapter.

[Some approaches to privacy, like](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-2?potentialInternalRefId=33---book-markup-container) _self-sovereign identity_ [(SSI) (https://www.​](https://www.manning.com/books/self-sovereign-identity)
<u>[manning.com/​books/self-​sovereign-​identity), aim to give individuals more control over how](https://www.manning.com/books/self-sovereign-identity)</u>

their data is shared and used. We’ll explore these ideas more deeply in chapter 15, when
we discuss decentralized identity and verifiable credentials.

2.2.5 The consent problem

Closely related to the privacy problem is the problem of consent. Many identity systems
lack the means for people to give granular consent. The lack of control over identity data

sharing is often driven by business incentives. The ubiquitous cookie notices that browser
users are forced to endure are a shining example of this. Even when they do allow more

fine-grained consent, organizations make it so difficult that people are likely to just consent
to everything by default.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

26

Authorization systems can make this situation worse by requesting attributes needed for

dynamic authorization behind the scenes without providing people the ability to give
meaningful consent. Flipping that around, when people don’t know how policy decisions

were made, they may have difficulty giving consent to attribute sharing and default to
oversharing to avoid having to repeatedly make a request. Again, SSI was designed to help

with this, and we’ll see in chapter 15 how SSI can aid in solving the consent problem in
authorization systems.

2.2.6 The scale problem

Because digital identities underpin almost every digital interaction, organizations rely on
them to be well-architected and carefully managed. At the same time, getting digital

identity right is difficult. The scale problem arises from needing to manage identity well
across a growing number of services, organizations, and digital interactions. Most

organizations under-resource their identity infrastructure, which often leads to the scale
problem at some point.

The emergence of dynamic authorization and organizations’ increasing reliance on it for
critical operations only adds to the scalability issue. As we've discussed, dynamic

authorization relies on information about the principals and resources referenced in policies.
As organizations adopt a zero-trust model, scrutinizing every access request before

granting authorization, the burden on identity systems intensifies. Without a scalable
identity system, deploying dynamic authorization successfully in your organization is

challenging.

2.2.7 How identity problems affect authorization

The challenges we’ve covered—proximity, interoperability, flexibility, privacy, consent, and

scale—don’t just make identity management difficult. They also directly impact
authorization, making it harder to reliably apply policies, retrieve accurate attributes, or

even correctly identify who (or what) is making a request.

Table 2.1 summarizes these six problems and highlights their direct implications for

dynamic authorization. This connection is crucial: authorization doesn’t exist in isolation.
Every authorization decision depends on what the identity system can provide, and the

quality of those inputs depends on how well these identity challenges have been addressed.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

27

Table 2.1 The six core challenges of digital identity and how they impact authorization. Each problem

complicates identity management and creates risks for dynamic authorization, where timely and accurate

identity data is critical to making good access decisions.

|Problem|Primary Impact|Impact on Authorization|
|---|---|---|
|Proximity|Physical distance and reliance<br>on technical substitutes for<br>human recognition|Poor initial identity proofing leads to<br>weak authorization signals; reliance<br>on insecure authentication<br>mechanisms makes authorization<br>moot|
|Interoperability|No global identity layer for<br>people; every service builds its<br>own silo|Inconsistent attribute quality and<br>trust across systems|
|Flexibility|Fixed schemas that don’t<br>evolve with business needs|Authorization logic can’t get the<br>attributes it needs|
|Privacy|Over-collection, replication, and<br>weak controls on data use|Authorization can fail to protect<br>sensitive information; logs can<br>expose unnecessary data if not well-<br>designed|
|Consent|Coercive or confusing consent<br>requests|Missing consent signals in<br>authorization flows|
|Scale|Growth of users, apps, devices,<br>and policies|Identity systems can’t deliver timely<br>attributes for real-time authorization|

These problems are not just theoretical—they shape how organizations design identity
infrastructure, how they choose to collect and manage attributes, and how much confidence

they can place in each authorization decision. Throughout this book, we’ll see that many of
the design choices in dynamic authorization systems—from policy design to real-time

attribute retrieval—are responses to these identity challenges.

#### 2.3 Identity and digital relationships

We don't build, deploy, and manage identity systems to manage identities. We use them to
support relationships. The real value of an identity system comes from the relationships it

enables—between employers and employees, companies and customers, healthcare
providers and patients, and so on. Each relationship defines which identity attributes are

needed, how they are used, and how they are protected.

2.3.1 Types of digital relationships

Digital relationships aren’t all the same, but they tend to fall into three broad categories:

_Transactional_ relationships center on discrete exchanges—purchasing a
product, submitting a form, or completing a contract.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

28

_Interactional_ relationships, which are longer-lived and richer, accumulate

history and context as interactions unfold over time—like the relationship
you have with your healthcare provider or employer.

_Exploitative_ relationships, where the service derives value directly from
the person’s identity and behavior—often without explicit consent or clear

boundaries—are common in advertising-driven business models.

It’s important to recognize that these are not rigid categories. Relationships often blend

these characteristics— a transactional purchase may evolve into an interactional
relationship over time. Alternatively, an ostensibly interactional relationship may have

exploitative elements hidden beneath the surface, where user behavior is silently collected,
correlated, and monetized. Each digital relationship is unique and context-specific and

evolves over time.

A helpful way to visualize the blended nature of relationships is through the Digital

Relationship Triangle, shown in Figure 2.1. Each corner represents a pure version of one of
these three relationship types. Most real-world relationships land somewhere inside the

triangle, combining aspects of all three.

Figure 2.1 Digital relationships occupy a space where transactional, interactional, and exploitative dynamics

combine in varying degrees. Understanding which type of relationship your system supports is critical for

designing effective identity and authorization policies.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

29

Most of the relationships we create online are transactional. I have a rich relationship with

Amazon that has been in development for over 25 years. Amazon knows a great deal about
me and uses that information to further its goal of selling products and services to me. I

use the relationship to buy the things I need to live and work. But the relationship is, at its
heart, transactional.

On the other hand, I have an interactional relationship with many of my healthcare
providers using their various patient portals. Some of what transpires is transactional when

I use it to schedule appointments or pay my bills. But much of it is interactional, discussing
medical conditions, updates to prescriptions, or questions I have about treatment.

[The type of relationship being supported should shape both the design of the identity](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-2?potentialInternalRefId=57---book-markup-container)
system and the policies that govern access. In a transactional relationship, identity

attributes may be needed only briefly, and the system may retain little history. In
interactional relationships, rich memory is essential—the system needs to retain and

protect the evolving history of interactions. In exploitative relationships, the incentives are
often misaligned with privacy, requiring strong governance and transparency to avoid abuse

or regulatory violations. These distinctions are vital when building authorization policies,
which must align with the true purpose and ethical boundaries of the relationship.

2.3.2 Digital relationship properties

Regardless of their nature, digital identity systems are responsible for supporting three
important properties of digital relationships:

**Integrity** —Ensuring consistent recognition of entities across interactions
to maintain trust

**Lifespan** —Managing the account lifecycle, including account creation,
use, and deletion

**Utility** —Enabling digital relationships by making information about the
entity in the system available for other systems to use

Authentication systems, and their related functions, like account management, are
primarily responsible for the integrity and lifespan of digital relationships. They are

challenging to build, expensive to purchase and maintain, and usually the focus of digital
identity discussions. Good authorization decisions depend on a good authentication system.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

30

AUTHORIZATION DEPENDS ON AUTHENTICATION

Authorization decisions are only as reliable as the identity upon which they rely. If

authentication is weak or easily spoofed, access control policies may mistakenly
grant permissions to the wrong party. In the Target breach we discussed in chapter

1, attackers used stolen credentials from an HVAC vendor to access the network—the
system mistakenly recognized the attacker as a trusted third party. Authorization

failed not because the policy was flawed, but because the identity was
misrepresented.

This is why identity systems must be designed with both authentication and
authorization in mind. The principle of “garbage in, garbage out” applies—faulty or

ambiguous identity input leads to poor authorization decisions. We’ll explore
authentication in detail in chapter 3.

One of the primary ways that identity systems provide utility is by enabling access control
and determining what actions the subject can take. The context of a relationship often

defines the scope of access. For example, a system for managing an employer-employee
relationship will provide utility by ensuring that employees have convenient access to the

tools and information they need to do their jobs without compromising security or privacy.
In a customer-service provider relationship, like the one I mentioned with Amazon, the

identity system is more concerned with storing information about the customer for use in
making purchases, but authorization still plays a role in enabling useful features like wish

list sharing.

Policy-based authorization systems that move authorization out of the code and static

lists expand the role of digital identity systems. By making policy the central focus of
authorization, these systems support the increased use of dynamic authorization in both

product and security.

#### 2.4 Naming and discovery

In 2004, U.S. Senator Ted Kennedy was repeatedly stopped and subjected to additional
screenings at airports. In at least one incident, he was barred from boarding his flight

altogether. The problem? His name matched an entry in the U.S. Transportation Security
Administration’s (TSA’s) No-Fly List, a list of people who are barred from air travel inside or

to and from the United States. At the time, the No-Fly list relied heavily on names alone,
rather than using unique identifiers like passport numbers. Because the TSA’s system

lacked a robust naming scheme and didn’t handle discovery well, Senator Kennedy was
treated as if he were the banned individual.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

31

Naming is one of the most fundamental parts of digital identity and is notoriously

difficult to get right. As the TSA example shows, getting it wrong can have far-reaching
consequences. In the case of Senator Kennedy, he had a pretty good platform—the U.S.

Senate—to fix the problem. Most people aren’t so lucky.

[An important lesson we can learn from this situation is that naming problems often lead](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-2?potentialInternalRefId=72---book-markup-container)

to authorization problems. The failure of the No-Fly list to uniquely identify the correct Ted
Kennedy led to an incorrect denial of service—a fundamental authorization failure caused

by poor naming and discovery processes.

2.4.1 The role of names in digital identity

Names are labels that we give to things so that we don’t have to continually describe them

to each other. In that sense, they’re a kind of shorthand for a person, place, or thing.
Names are often not unique, and we interpret them depending on the context in which we

see them.

We use the word _identifier_ for names that are unique within a certain context, which we

call a _namespace_ . Social security numbers, usernames, email addresses, and database
table names are all examples of identifiers. Digital identity systems need identifiers to

recognize and remember the parties in a relationship. When you type your username in a
login form, you’re reminding the system on the other end who you are.

2.4.2 Tradeoffs in identity naming

When we pick a naming system, there are several tradeoffs we must manage depending on
our goals, and different naming systems prioritize different aspects:

**Human Meaningfulness** —Some use cases require names that are easy
for people to recognize and remember. Examples include email addresses

and usernames.
**Uniqueness and Non-Reusability** —Some systems require non-reusable

identifiers to prevent conflicts and identity takeover. One example is
employee IDs, which should not be reassigned.

**Security Against Impersonation and Forgery** —Some use cases are
sensitive to spoofing and collisions and have differing security needs.

Domain names are a good example where having proper security against
hijacking is vital to their use.

**Decentralized** —Some use cases need names that don’t have to be
managed by a central authority. For example, UUIDs (Universal Unique

Identifiers) are created in such a way that different systems don’t have to
coordinate to be assured that the identifier they’re using is globally

unique.

Different systems must balance these competing concerns to get the best naming system

for their expected use.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

32

2.4.3 Namespaces and their role in identity

As I said earlier, a namespace is the context for a name. But it’s more than just that: A
namespace is a system for structuring names and ensuring their uniqueness within that

context. We can classify namespaces based on how they prevent name collisions:

**Centralized** —A centralized namespace is maintained by a particular

organization, which ensures identifier uniqueness. The primary advantage
is the ease of implementation. But names in centralized namespaces

aren't easily portable. Usernames and employee ID numbers are both
examples of centralized namespaces.

**Hierarchical** —Namespaces are often structured hierarchically. The
Domain Name System (DNS) is a well-known example of a hierarchical

namespace, and that structure is essential to the way domain names
work. Other notable examples of hierarchical namespaces include X.509

certificates and Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP). Hierarchical
namespaces facilitate discovery because the name itself tells you how to

look it up, so long as you know the root. And each node can be granted
local control over the names beneath it without risking collisions.

**Flat** —Flat namespaces have no structure. The chief advantage of flat
namespaces is that names can be used across any context without risk of

collision. There are several ways to do this. In the case of UUIDs,
collisions are avoided algorithmically. Blockchains or other decentralized

data stores can also be used.
**Federated** —A federated namespace is a distributed naming system that

works by sharing the responsibility of assigning names to several
organizations or services. The primary advantage of federated

namespaces is local control with global discovery. Email is probably the
best example of a federated namespace. Each email provider is

responsible for assigning unique names within its domain. Federated
namespaces require governance so that participants in the federation

know how to discover the meaning of names managed by other
participants.

The choice of namespace is strategic, influencing not only how names are managed
internally but also how easily identities can move between systems, how secure naming is

against impersonation, and how easily identities can be discovered when needed for
authorization. A poorly chosen namespace locks identities into silos, increases security

risks, and complicates policy enforcement. In the next section, we’ll explore how the model
for an identity system supports the right namespace.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

33

#### 2.5 Identity system models

Naming and discovery are closely tied to the model of the identity system itself. A

namespace doesn’t exist in isolation—it reflects the underlying architecture of the identity
system that manages it. Whether an organization controls all its own identities, participates

in a federated ecosystem, or allows users to manage their own decentralized identifiers,
each approach shapes how identities are created, authenticated, discovered, and trusted.

Identity system models—centralized, federated, and decentralized—each balance
control, interoperability, and security differently, impacting how identity is managed and

used for authorization. The model choice also impacts the quality and timeliness of identity
attributes, which in turn directly affects authorization decisions. In the sections that follow,

we’ll examine the strengths, limitations, and implications of each model, focusing on how
they influence dynamic authorization.

2.5.1 Centralized identity: single authority, high control

The centralized identity model is the one most of us think of when we think of an identity
system. The identity system your employer uses to manage workforce identity is

centralized, and so is your state-issued driver’s license or ID. Even the loyalty program at
the local supermarket is a centralized identity system. These systems are controlled by a

single entity that provides them and determines how they are used.

Most organizations no longer build their own identity systems, opting to purchase one

instead. These are often cloud services, operated on behalf of the organization. They are
usually architected for a specific purpose, like managing employees.

[One advantage of the centralized identity model is strong control and enforcement.](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-2?potentialInternalRefId=96---book-markup-container)
Because the organization controls the system, they get to make the rules. This allows the

organization to tailor the identity system to their specific needs. The centralized model also
simplifies identity management since governance is kept within the organization. From the

standpoint of authorization, the control that centralized models provide means that they
can usually be more easily configured to provide the attributes needed for authorization

decisions.

[The biggest risk in the centralized model is that it represents a single point of failure—](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-2?potentialInternalRefId=97---book-markup-container)

carefully choosing the system provider is critical to avoid failures that would cripple the
business.

2.5.2 Federated identity: the backbone of modern identity systems

In the federated model, one or more organizations, called _identity providers (IdPs)_, manage
accounts, authentication, and identity attributes. Other organizations, called _relying parties_

_(RP)_, rely on the IdPs for authentication and account services. For this to work, the
interactions between the IdP and the RP are mediated by a protocol.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

34

The common protocols used in federated identity systems include the Security Assertion

Markup Language (SAML), OAuth, and OpenIDConnect (which is based on OAuth). The
details of how these protocols work are beyond the scope of this book, but we will cover

OAuth, which is a federated authorization protocol, more extensively in chapter 12. Each
protocol describes the interactions between the IdP and RP to ensure a technically

trustworthy exchange of assertions about authentication status and attributes.

[Because federated identity allows identity information to be shared across multiple](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-2?potentialInternalRefId=101---book-markup-container)

organizations, they rely on legal agreements called _trust frameworks_ to say how the RP will
use the data and what kind of guarantees the IdP provides.

[For enterprise federation, the IdP is often sharing with the RP so that the RP can provide](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-2?potentialInternalRefId=102---book-markup-container)
a service to the IdP. For example, an employer may act as the IdP for its benefits provider,

the RP in this scenario, allowing employees to easily authenticate to the provider’s system.
SAML is the most commonly used protocol, and the agreements are usually bespoke legal

contracts. In the case of the employer and benefits provider, they will have a well-defined
legal relationship that establishes a trust framework for sharing identity data. You log in at

the benefits provider, and your login credentials are used behind the scenes with your
employer to authenticate you and return the attributes agreed to in the trust framework.

[For online use cases such as single-sign-on (SSO) to a website, the IdP and RP usually](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-2?potentialInternalRefId=103---book-markup-container)
lack a formal agreement. Instead, the RP has agreed to a click-through license that is the

same for everyone. OAuth or OpenID Connect are the most common protocols in this
situation. An example of this is when you use your Google account to sign up for an

account at The Weather Channel. When you authenticate, you’re redirected to Google,
where you log in and Google returns a token with information about you, called _claims_ in

the world of identity, to the Weather Channel.

[There are several advantages to using federated identity. First, the RP doesn’t have to](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-2?potentialInternalRefId=104---book-markup-container)

maintain authentication systems or support onboarding. Second, people find it more
convenient to just sign in with an account that already exists instead of creating a new one.

Finally, because these protocols are widespread, they are well supported by identity
systems and there are many development libraries to choose from.

[The risks of federated identity primarily revolve around the dependence on an external](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-2?potentialInternalRefId=105---book-markup-container)
party for a critical function. This is not as big a risk in enterprise federated use cases like

the benefits provider we discussed earlier, but can be a significant risk for RPs in online use
cases. Consequently, most IdPs are big organizations like Google, Amazon, Facebook, and

Apple that the RP can trust to be reliable. The primary risk for principals is deplatforming: If
you lose your Google account, for example, you also lose access to all the places you've

used it to sign up.

[Another significant risk is the loss of privacy when a federated identity provider (IdP) can](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-2?potentialInternalRefId=106---book-markup-container)

see every site or service a person accesses. This kind of cross-service surveillance may not
be as overtly disruptive as deplatforming, but it creates a persistent record of a person’s

online activity. Over time, that undermines trust—people may begin to hesitate before
engaging online, knowing that their interactions are being silently tracked. Personally, I

always use the email option of federated identity whenever I can to avoid both of these
risks.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

35

The RP’s lack of control over the identity attributes that the IdP shares poses a risk to

authorization systems, where access to the right attributes is often crucial to making good
decisions. This requires authorization systems that rely on decentralized identity models to

have the means of augmenting the data they receive from the IdP with other needed
attributes.

2.5.3 Decentralized identity: shifting control to users

Decentralized identity systems allow users to control and manage their own identity without
relying on a central authority. You’ll also sometimes hear this called _self-sovereign identity_

_(SSI)_ .

In the decentralized identity model, people hold credentials in a cryptographic wallet and

can share them with others when they need to prove something about themselves. This is
the model we use most often in the physical world. You don’t have an account at the local

grocery store that you must log into when you need to prove your age to buy alcohol.
Instead, you show them a government-issued ID that has your birthdate on it. This works

for three reasons:

ID is relatively **_tamper-proof._**

The ID has some means of **_proving it was issued to you,_** like a picture.
The ID was **_issued by someone the grocery store trusts_** to do a good

job of determining people’s birthdates.

Decentralized identity systems use a similar model, where trusted parties issue credentials

to people who hold them in wallets and can present them to RPs who verify them
cryptographically. This process is decentralized because no single organization decides what

credentials exist, which credentials a person should hold, or what credentials an RP must
accept. Anyone can issue a credential for any purpose, hold whatever credentials they like,

and trust whatever credentials they choose.

The primary advantages of the decentralized model lie in the freedoms described in the

previous paragraph. By giving participants choice, decentralized identity models solve the
consent problem and give people the power to manage their privacy more completely.

Organizations can share data without prior agreements. For example, the grocery store has
no agreement with the state that allows it to use the state-issued ID.

[Even so, there’s still a role for trust frameworks. RPs want to know which credentials](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-2?potentialInternalRefId=116---book-markup-container)
they can trust without creating agreements with every credential issuer. These, too, are

decentralized. For example, if a university issues a credential representing a student
transcript and the holder shares it with a potential employer, how do they know it's from a

real university? There are organizations that accredit universities. These bodies can create
trust frameworks for the universities they accredit, and employers can know that the

university is real because of that framework.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

36

Despite the advantages decentralized models have, there are several risks and

limitations. First, as the university transcript example shows, knowing who to trust is more
complicated than in the centralized and federated models. Decentralized systems can be

messy. Second, there are adoption challenges. Most internal use cases can be more easily
solved using a different model, and external use cases have a multi-sided market problem

where issuers are waiting for RPs and RPs are waiting for issuers.

[Decentralized identity models can be the means of solving difficult cross-organization](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-2?potentialInternalRefId=118---book-markup-container)

authorization problems. In chapter 16 we’ll explore a decentralized model that uses
verifiable credentials to provide attributes for authorization decisions.

#### 2.6 Trust and confidence

We use the word _trust_ a lot in identity and authorization discussions—further evidence of

the relational nature of identity. In the chapters that follow, we will distinguish between
_trust_ and _confidence_ to better understand the proper way to solve problems that arise from

these important concepts.

2.6.1 The difference between trust and confidence

In a paper published in the _Handbook of Risk Theory_ (2012), titled “Risk and Trust,”

[(https://philarchive.​org/rec/NICTAR-​2), Philip Nickel and Krist Vaesen define trust as the](https://philarchive.org/rec/NICTAR-2?__cf_chl_tk=pA2W3yBO9Q9Sl8uhIIz7g4Nuto21GudAN5.TaJ2Vtms-1752367087-1.0.1.1-HIj1ERITDfY4RCMlucbSHbmtKFpCX6SOtIl9XThUoeo)
“disposition to willingly rely on another person or entity to perform actions that benefit or

protect oneself or one’s interests in a given domain.” In other words, when we trust
someone, we are vulnerable to their actions. There is a risk that they won’t follow through

or that they’re lying.

In contrast, confidence is based on evidence and firsthand observation. Confidence does

not involve the same degree of risk that trust does because we’re not relying as much on
another party.

[For example, we fly with confidence that the plane will not crash because we’ve flown](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-2?potentialInternalRefId=124---book-markup-container)
before and can find evidence of flight safety. We have confidence that the airline and

government have properly vetted the pilots, flight crew, mechanics, and air traffic
controllers. We don’t have to know how to fly or fix a plane to know these things.

[At the same time, we are vulnerable to that vetting process and the behavior of the](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-2?potentialInternalRefId=125---book-markup-container)
people in those critical positions. Pilots make errors and mechanics miss problems. This

shows that trust and confidence are not a binary proposition. Rather, there’s a spectrum.
Increasing confidence in something allows us to reduce our vulnerability and thus our need

to trust.

2.6.2 Trust and confidence in digital relationships

Because of the proximity problem, both operators and users of digital identity systems are

vulnerable to being deceived by the other. Phishing, at its root, is caused by people trusting
a link, text, or email they shouldn’t have because of false confidence inspired by poorly

designed systems. Because the system doesn’t provide true confidence signals, we teach
people to protect themselves by being less trusting.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

37

There are many risks in a digital identity system:

Is this account compromised?
Have the attributes the IdP returned been verified?

Am I connected to the right website or using the right app?
Does this role have the correct level of access?

Can this account be leveraged to gain access to another?

These and many other questions underlie the level of confidence an identity system

inspires, or the trust it requires.

The tradeoff between confidence and trust relies on several factors. First is the design of

the identity system. As illustrated by the phishing problem, the design of things like email,
SMS, and URLs makes it difficult for people to use their experience wisely. Second, some

confidence-inspiring techniques may be more costly than the use case can support or than
the organization can afford. Finally, how well identity systems are governed and maintained

has an impact on how much confidence we can have in them or how vulnerable we are. For
example, the Target example in chapter 1 was caused by poor authorization practices that

allowed the attackers to assume roles to administer the system using a contractor’s
credentials.

2.6.3 Technical confidence in identity systems

Confidence in identity systems is dependent on technical mechanisms that ensure identity
information is verified, authenticated, and used correctly. Unlike trust, which involves

human or organizational oversight, technical confidence is derived from cryptographic,
procedural, and policy-based controls that limit the risk of identity fraud, impersonation,

and unauthorized access.

One of the most important systems for achieving confidence is the system and processes

for managing accounts. Identity information is not static. Rather, it evolves from the initial
enrollment or signup to updates and use and then to eventual deactivation. Confidence can

be bolstered by a robust process for proofing identity attributes when accounts are
established. We also need to consider whether the attributes have been kept up to date,

whether accounts can be revoked, and whether an account is still valid. Poor management
of account lifecycles leads to mistaken or fraudulent attributes and stale credentials that are

the basis for poor access decisions. The identity lifecycle is critical to maintaining
confidence in digital identities over time. We will explore this topic in greater depth in

chapter 3.

[Another place where confidence is made or broken is the authentication system. Using](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-2?potentialInternalRefId=139---book-markup-container)

stronger authentication mechanisms can provide greater confidence that the entity logging
in is the same one who created the account. Different authentication factors provide

different levels of assurance and protection against hacking and phishing. We will explore
this topic as well in chapter 3.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

38

Attribute verification, or lack of it, plays a particularly important role in the confidence

we place in authorization decisions. No matter how good your authentication system or
authorization policies are, if attributes can be spoofed, then you are at risk. When

attributes are critical, they should be carefully proofed whenever they change to ensure
they are correct. Authorization systems should dynamically evaluate attributes wherever

possible, making sure their record of attributes is up-to-date with the source of truth. Longlived credentials can be a source of out-of-date attributes that lead to unauthorized access.

[Finally, auditing and logging can provide evidence that the identity system is working as](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-2?potentialInternalRefId=141---book-markup-container)
designed. Logs should be systematically checked and used to create reports and feedback

that management, data protection officers, security engineers, and developers can use to
determine their level of confidence in the system.

2.6.4 The limits of technical confidence

Not every risk can be mitigated using technology. For example, even a perfect identity
system can’t protect your organization against an employee with malicious intent,

employee incompetence, or other types of insider threats. Some employees must have
access to vulnerable systems to do their jobs, and you trust them to act according to policy

and industry norms.

Policies are another place where the limits of technically based confidence can be found.

Policy is a result of people defining rules according to some explicit or implicit governing
process. The accounts, authentication, and authorization systems can all be doing their

jobs, but that doesn’t mean that the policies you have in place are sufficient to protect the
business or ensure your customers are secure from hackers, each other, or your

employees. Do policies properly reflect the will of management? Do they properly reflect
regulatory requirements? No technical solution can answer those and similar questions.

[When we hit the limits of technology to provide confidence, we are left to mitigate the](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-2?potentialInternalRefId=145---book-markup-container)
risk we face with either social norms or formal governance. Social norms often play a role

in whether a system is perceived as fair or trustworthy. For example, in ride-sharing
platforms like Uber or Lyft, cultural expectations of reciprocity can influence how ratings are

managed. When drivers are expected to prove their identity attributes but riders are not,
drivers may think the platform is unfair. Using real names is another example. Pseudonyms

like `XX_RIDER23` may inspire less trust by drivers in the rider. Failure to account for these

norms may lead to a system being untrusted even as it provides technical confidence that it

is operating correctly.

[Governance is how rules are made. Governance might include informal policies, a formal](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-2?potentialInternalRefId=146---book-markup-container)

rulebook, government regulations, or even laws. At an organizational level, governance
determines policies and manages tradeoffs with cost, fairness, security, compliance,

operational efficiency, and user experience. As we saw in the discussion on identity models
in section 2.5, governance also plays a role in cross-organization identity transactions,

determining important considerations like who is responsible for authentication, how
attributes can be used, and where liability lies. We will deal with governance in detail in

chapter 18.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

39

Table 2.2 A comparison of technical confidence and trust

|Aspect|Technical Confidence|Trust|
|---|---|---|
|Foundation|Cryptography, software,<br>authentication, policies|Governance, oversight,<br>social norms|
|Scope|Ensures identity validity and<br>policy enforcement|Ensures policies are fair,<br>accountable, and correct|
|Strengths|Objective, measurable,<br>scalable—identity<br>verification and enforcement<br>can be automated with high<br>reliability|Flexible, adaptable, and<br>responsive to human<br>concerns—allows for policy<br>exceptions, ethical<br>oversight, and judgment|
|Weaknesses|Can be circumvented by<br>insider threats, weak<br>policies, or social<br>engineering|Can be subjective, slow, and<br>prone to human error|

Table 2.2 compares the scope, strengths, and weaknesses of technical confidence and trust.

Reading the table should convince you that confidence and trust both play a role in creating
an effective identity system. Where technology provides confidence through evidence and

assurance, governance gives us the ability to mitigate risk and instill trust.

Technical confidence is critical for secure identity systems, but cannot fully replace

human governance. Even the most secure authentication system does not guarantee that a
policy is correct or fair. While we should strive to provide confidence in as many situations

as possible, doing so to the exclusion of trust isn’t possible. The takeaway for dynamic
authorization is that we should combine technical confidence with policy governance to

create both secure and effective access control.

#### 2.7 Privacy, authenticity, and confidentiality

Authorization systems play a big role in protecting privacy, ensuring authenticity, and
providing confidentiality. These three concepts are interrelated, and understanding them

precisely and the tradeoffs between them can help us design authorization systems and
craft policies to correctly authorize access.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

40

2.7.1 Distinguishing privacy from confidentiality

When people talk about privacy informally, they typically mean both privacy and
confidentiality. But we will distinguish between these concepts so that we're clear about

which problems we're solving and what tools to use. The <u>[International Association of](https://iapp.org/resources/glossary/)</u>
<u>[Privacy Professionals (IAPP) glossary](https://iapp.org/resources/glossary/)</u> [(https://iapp.​org/resources/​glossary/) defines four](https://iapp.org/resources/glossary/)

classes of privacy. Two of them, communications privacy and information privacy, are the
most relevant to identity systems. _Communications privacy_ is concerned with protecting the

means of correspondence. _Information privacy_ is concerned with the ability of individuals to
consent to when, how, and to what extent information about them is communicated to

others.

Another way of saying “the means of correspondence” is metadata—all the information

in a communication that makes it possible. So, communications privacy is a metadata
problem. Confidentiality is concerned with the content. Authenticity is knowing with

confidence who the parties to a conversation are—and being able to prove that to others.

[To understand these distinctions better, consider Alice, who visits a virtual health clinic at](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-2?potentialInternalRefId=155---book-markup-container)

`https://ourvirtualhealth.com` for an anonymous consultation. If you’re familiar with TLS

(Transport Layer Security), you’ll know that it creates an encrypted web channel between

Alice’s browser and the server. The content of Alice’s communication is inside encrypted
packets going back and forth. All the metadata, including the URL path, is also encrypted

with the exception of the IP addresses

[s of Alice and the server, along with the domain name of the site she’s visiting. These](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-2?potentialInternalRefId=156---book-markup-container)

have to be clear text to properly route the packets.

[Imagine an eavesdropper, Earl, listening in on the interactions between Alice and](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-2?potentialInternalRefId=157---book-markup-container)

`ourvirtualhealth.com` . Because of TLS, Earl will not know the content of the

correspondence—it is confidential. But because of the unencrypted metadata, he can know

the IP addresses of Alice and the server as well as the domain name. Is Alice’s conversation
private?

[One way to answer this question is to ask another: could Alice repudiate her](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-2?potentialInternalRefId=158---book-markup-container)
conversation with `ourvirtualhealth.com` ? That is, could Earl prove to someone else that

Alice was talking to `ourvirtualhealth.com` ? Earl might be able to reliably identify Alice

using her IP address. For example, I’ve had the same static IP address from my internet

provider for over a decade, so I’m sure it is possible to correlate it with other information
about me. To prove it was Alice, Earl would need to convince someone else of the

_authenticity_ of the link between Alice and her IP address.

2.7.2 Managing tradeoffs

The example in the previous section shows the tradeoff between privacy and authenticity.
When you log into your bank to check your balance, your interaction is confidential, but it is

not private because the bank can prove that you are the other party to the conversation.
Indeed, the bank is legally obligated by anti-money laundering laws to be able to do so.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

41

Given this, you might be tempted to decide that privacy is a hopeless cause since almost

every online conversation is done inside authenticated sessions. The administrators of the
identity platforms know who they’re talking to, and even in pseudonymous interactions may

be able to identify you. This is the entire basis of the online ad industry. To delve deeper
into this threat to communications privacy and its ramifications for society, I recommend

the book _The Age of Surveillance Capitalism,_ by Shoshana Zuboff (PublicAffairs, 2019).

[But all is not lost. Let’s return to our banking example to see why. The bank does keep](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-2?potentialInternalRefId=162---book-markup-container)

logs of what you do and may show them to the proper authorities when required by
regulation. But the record of what you do at the bank should not be available to outsiders

or even employees of the bank without the need to know. Your interactions with the bank
are functionally private—even though you may not have communications privacy, you do

have information privacy, subject to the agreements the bank has with you.

2.7.3 Functional privacy

Functional privacy operationalizes information privacy by ensuring that systems access and

process only the necessary information—nothing more. Functional privacy depends on both
governance and technology to achieve its goals. Governance establishes the rules about

who can access data and under what conditions. For example, the bank may create a rule
that customer transactions are limited to employees with a need-to-know, which would

form the basis for authorization policies. Governance is an important foundation for
dynamic authorization. We’ll cover it in detail in chapter 14.

Policy-Based Access Control (PBAC) is a good technology choice for enforcing these
rules. Here’s why:

PBAC allows fine-grained access to different data and systems to be
limited to only certain people, roles, or situations. For example, a

financial analyst at a hospital may be allowed to confirm a patient’s
insurance coverage without being able to see their health history.

By decoupling authorization from underlying systems, PBAC allows
policies to be managed holistically, tested, and reviewed for correctness.

Many business leaders may be comfortable reading policies to confirm
they conform to rules written in English.

PBAC allows many decisions to be made without having to expose
sensitive information to human operators and reviewers. For example, a

PBAC system could automatically enforce transaction size thresholds,
sending only transactions over certain amounts to a human reviewer.

Well-designed PBAC policies can balance regulatory requirements and
privacy needs, ensuring compliance while minimizing risk.

Regardless of your role—whether as a business leader, security professional, developer, or
policymaker—you must consider privacy, confidentiality, and authenticity when designing

and using digital systems to interact with employees, partners, and customers.

Privacy ensures that individuals retain control over what personal or

sensitive data is shared, with whom, and under what conditions.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

42

Confidentiality protects that data from unauthorized access, ensuring it

remains secure in storage, transit, and processing.
Authenticity guarantees that identities, credentials, and transactions are

legitimate, preventing impersonation, fraud, data manipulation, or
repudiation.

Failing to manage these concerns effectively can lead to data breaches, compliance
violations, loss of customer trust, and operational inefficiencies. At the same time, overly

restrictive policies can drive up costs, frustrate people, and hinder business agility.

Balancing security, compliance, and usability requires that you understand dynamic

authorization. A well-implemented policy-driven authorization model allows you to enforce
privacy and confidentiality while maintaining strong authentication and seamless user

experiences, all without unnecessary overhead or complexity.

#### 2.8 From identity to authentication

Digital identity plays a foundational role in supporting the relationships on which digital
systems rely. Digital identity is not just a technical artifact or a collection of attributes—it is

the bridge that connects systems to people, organizations, and devices, enabling those
systems to recognize, remember, and relate to them over time. Naming and discovery—far

from being just implementation details—are critical to ensuring authorization systems apply
the right policies to the right entities. Well-structured namespaces help support this by

providing clarity, uniqueness, and context. Different identity system models—centralized,
federated, and decentralized—distribute control and responsibility for managing identity and

the attributes that drive policy-based authorization.

No matter how strong our technical decisions are, we must remember that trust—one of

the primary reasons we build identity systems—doesn't come from technology alone. While
identity systems can inspire technical confidence through strong authentication and verified

attributes, true trust requires governance—oversight that ensures the policies, processes,
and outcomes reflect organizational values, regulatory requirements, and social

expectations. Finally, remember that privacy, confidentiality, and authenticity play in
identity and authorization, showing how policy-based authorization (PBAC) can both protect

sensitive data and ensure access decisions respect privacy and regulatory constraints.

[All of these ideas come together at the moment of authentication—the first time a](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-2?potentialInternalRefId=179---book-markup-container)

system asks, “Who are you?” Authentication is where the relationship is renewed, and
where many of the tradeoffs between privacy, usability, and security are made. In the next

chapter, we’ll explore the role of authentication in preserving relationship integrity, the
different methods used to establish confidence, and how the identity lifecycle depends on

strong, well-governed authentication to maintain the trustworthiness of every digital
relationship over time.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

43

#### 2.9 Summary

Digital identity powers digital relationships, allowing systems to

recognize, remember, and relate to people and organizations, forming the
foundation for personalization, security, privacy, and access control.

Namespaces and discovery are critical to authorization. If a system can’t
uniquely name and reliably find identities, policies fail. Structured

namespaces help ensure clarity, uniqueness, and correct policy
application.

Identity system models shape control and trust. Centralized, federated,
and decentralized systems distribute authority differently, impacting

portability, governance, and attribute availability.
Confidence comes from technology; trust comes from governance. Strong

authentication builds confidence, but governance ensures fairness,
compliance, and accountability.

Privacy, confidentiality, and authenticity are tightly linked to digital
identity. Good identity systems and well-crafted authorization policies

minimize unnecessary data exposure while ensuring only the appropriate
parties gain access.
