## Authentication: Who are you?

This chapter covers

Why authentication is crucial to relationship integrity

The phases in the identity lifecycle and why enrollment is often the weak link

How authentication works

The tradeoffs between authentication strength and usability

Properties of a good authentication system

On July 15, 2020, Twitter (now known as X) suffered one of its most high-profile security
breaches. Attackers hijacked the accounts of major public figures, including Elon Musk and

Barack Obama—and even Apple—to hype a cryptocurrency scam. The breach illustrates a
fundamental truth about authentication: it’s only as secure as its weakest link.

The details of how the breach happened offer important insights. The attackers didn’t
use brute force to crack passwords or exploit a bug in Twitter’s software. Instead, they used

social engineering and phishing to trick Twitter employees into giving them legitimate
authentication credentials. By calling Twitter’s IT help desk and pretending to be colleagues,

they convinced employees to reset authentication credentials, giving the attackers access
to Twitter’s internal administrative tools.

[Once inside, the attackers bypassed traditional security controls and took over high-](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-3?potentialInternalRefId=8---book-markup-container)
profile accounts. The near-term fallout was that Twitter had to temporarily lock down all

verified accounts to stop further exploitation; the long-term consequence was a loss of trust
by people with verified accounts and the people who relied on them to be protected from

misinformation.

[We can learn several lessons about authentication from this disaster:](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-3?potentialInternalRefId=9---book-markup-container)

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

45

Strong authentication isn’t just a technical problem but includes process—

governance—too. This is a theme we’ll touch on over and over in this
book.

The use of and strength of multi-factor authentication (MFA) can prevent
some attacks. Just resetting credentials wouldn’t have been sufficient

with good MFA in place. We’ll discuss MFA in detail later in this chapter.
Adopting a zero-trust security model that assumes breach and challenges

people to reassert their credentials when moving from system to system
is a critical practice for modern IT systems. Contingent authorization can

take this a step further, requiring special permissions for highconsequence actions.

Humans remain the weakest link. No matter how secure a system is, if an
attacker can manipulate people into doing their bidding, authentication

fails to stop them. Removing places where humans can override the
system can strengthen your security.

This incident underscores why authentication isn’t just about logging in—it’s about ensuring
the integrity of the relationship that was established when the account was created.

#### 3.1 Terminology

In this chapter, and throughout this book, I’m going to use several terms repeatedly, so it’s

a good idea to define them clearly before we begin:

**Account** —a container for information about an entity. The account holds

attributes, credentials, roles, and other context about the entity.
**Identifier** —a string that uniquely identifies a particular account in the

namespace for a given system.
**Principal** —the entity (such as a person or organization) making a

request.
**Subject** —the entity being referred to in an account, policy, or decision.

You may notice that I didn’t include the word _identity_ in the list. Identity can mean different
things depending on context. In most cases, I find that there is a more precise term, such

as _account, identifier,_ or _principal_ . Using more specific language helps reduce confusion and
makes the discussion clearer.

Figure 3.1 shows the relationships between these terms. As indicated by the dotted line
in the figure, the principal and subject are usually the same, but not always, so it’s a good

idea to be able to distinguish them. For example, a parent who is accessing a system on
behalf of their child would be the principal, while the child is the subject.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

46

Figure 3.1 Relationships among key identity concepts used in authentication and authorization. A principal

(an actor like a user or service) controls an identifier uniquely identifying an account. The account stores

attributes about a subject, which might be the principal itself or another entity the principal manages.

We will define many more terms as we continue our exploration of authorization.

#### 3.2 Authentication preserves relationship integrity

Relationship integrity comes down to technical confidence that the entity that established
the account is the same entity currently using it. The Twitter hack shows how

authentication is necessary to preserve the integrity of the relationship between a system
and the people and services that rely on it. The example also highlights how the

relationships established by the identity system are foundational to the promises and
features that the system makes.

WHY AUTHENTICATION SEEMS LIKE A ONE-WAY STREET

Many people assume that only users authenticate to systems, but authentication is a

two-way street. After all, if we’re trying to preserve relationship integrity, the
authenticity of both parties to the relationship matters. Put more simply: when you

log into a website, how do you know it’s the real site and not an attacker
impersonating it? This is where _cryptographic authentication_ comes in.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

47

Transport Layer Security (TLS) is the protocol that places the little lock in the

address bar of your browser. Websites and applications authenticate themselves
using TLS, which relies on certificates issued by trusted Certificate Authorities (CAs).

The certificate, which can be freely shared, cryptographically links the domain name
of the server to the public key used to authenticate the session. The public key

allows the browser and server to create a confidential communications channel. Your
browser verifies these certificates to ensure you’re connecting to the legitimate

server and shows you the little lock. Clicking on the lock can give you the details of
why the site is trusted.

Like anything, TLS has its weaknesses. TLS can be undermined by misconfigured
certificates, expired CAs, or advanced attacks like man-in-the-middle (MITM)

attacks, where a hacker is able to overcome the certificate’s cryptographic
protections to intercept traffic. Moreover, the lock usually only shows that the key

belongs to the domain name, but people click on the wrong domain name all the
time—that’s the basis of phishing attacks. For example, the name `twitter.com.info`

could have a certificate and show a browser lock. If you’re in a hurry or don’t
understand URLs, you might ignore the `.info` and assume the site is legitimate.

For people, authentication often feels like a one-way process because system
authentication is handled silently by browsers and applications. But authenticating

the system is important too. If you can't trust that you’re talking to the right system,
you may unknowingly authenticate to an attacker, leading to phishing, credential

theft, or session hijacking.

The Twitter attack discussed earlier violated relationship integrity in several ways. It directly

compromised the relationship between Twitter’s administrators and the system itself while
also undermining Twitter’s relationships with the verified account holders whose accounts

were hijacked. Ultimately, the attack harmed the indirect relationships between those
verified account holders and their followers, who trusted Twitter’s assurance that tweets

genuinely represented the intended authors. More broadly, the attack led to brand damage
and loss of customer trust with attendant financial implications.

Figure 3.2 shows the chain reaction that happens when the integrity of just a few
relationships is broken. In this case, the integrity of the relationship that Twitter’s

administrative system had with employees was compromised. This led to a loss of integrity
for verified accounts, which broke the technical confidence that people could place in the

system. Note that their confidence was limited by the design and strength of Twitter’s
internal controls and they were vulnerable in ways they didn’t understand. People were

deceived, leading to financial loss due to the cryptocurrency scam, account lockdowns with
the attendant loss of service, and ultimately, the loss of trust in Twitter to limit the spread

of misinformation.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

48

Figure 3.2 The cascade of consequences triggered by a loss of relationship integrity. Compromised internal

authentication undermines the trusted relationship between administrators and the system, leading to a

broader loss of integrity for verified accounts. As confidence diminishes, individuals are deceived—resulting in

financial loss, account lockouts, and reduced trust in the platform.

Because of the proximity problem, preserving relationship integrity is vital to digital

systems. Strong authentication ensures relationship integrity by verifying that the entity
making a request is truly the account holder. Relationship integrity, established through

reliable authentication, is foundational for making accurate authorization decisions and
maintaining a trustworthy identity lifecycle. The next section will show the role of

authentication throughout the account lifecycle.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

49

#### 3.3 Digital relationship lifecycles

Considering the lifecycle of digital relationships helps ensure that authentication and

authorization remain accurate, secure, and aligned with changes in both other systems and
in the physical world. Without a well-managed lifecycle, your risk of unauthorized access,

orphaned accounts, and policy misalignment increases.

Figure 3.3 shows the phases of the relationship lifecycle. Each phase changes depending

on the type of relationship we’re trying to create and its purpose.

Figure 3.3 Phases in the digital relationship lifecycle. It begins with enrollment, comprising discovery and co
creation, and continues through propagation, use, and eventual termination. The update phase ensures that

changes to the account or its attributes are integrated back into propagation, keeping the relationship

accurate and aligned with current conditions.

3.3.1 Enrollment (discover and co-create)

Enrollment consists of two sub-phases: discovery and co-creating. For many relationships,
the discovery phase is straightforward. For example, employees are told where to create

employee accounts. For others, like a device joining a network, discovery might be
governed by a protocol like Bluetooth.

I use the term _co-create_ rather than just _create_ to emphasize that this is a relationship
and both sides will participate in a ceremony of sorts where information is exchanged. Co
creating a digital relationship happens when identifiers are chosen or assigned, credentials
like passwords or other authentication factors are initialized, and attributes are exchanged.

This process may include identity proofing, credential issuance, and linking the identity to
authoritative sources. We will consider enrollment in more depth in the next section.

3.3.2 Propagate

When a digital relationship is created, updated, or terminated, the changes must be
distributed across relevant systems to ensure that the systems and services that rely on it

have up-to-date information. This may involve synchronizing identity data with directory
services, updating role assignments, or pushing access credentials to federated systems.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

50

Several protocols support propagation. These protocols enable authentication,

authorization, and identity management to remain consistent across an organization’s
infrastructure. Some of the commonly used protocols include SCIM (System for Cross
domain Identity Management), which automates user provisioning and de-provisioning
across multiple systems; LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol), which is a directory

service protocol for querying and managing account data; SAML (Security Assertion Markup
Language), which enables single sign-on (SSO) by passing identity assertions between

identity providers (IdPs) and service providers (SPs); and OpenID Connect (OIDC), which is
an authentication and authorization framework that propagates identity attributes in signed

tokens.

3.3.3 Use

This is the active phase, where identity relationships are verified through authentication,

and authorization governs what actions an identity can perform. During this phase, the
system should continuously verify that the relationship remains valid based on contextual

signals, policies, and real-time risk analysis.

3.3.4 Update

Identity relationships are not static—they evolve as users change roles, update credentials,

or gain new permissions. This process might be simple or complex, depending on what
kinds of functions the relationship is designed to support. One of the most important

update processes in an identity system is account recovery, where a user can rediscover a
lost account or update lost, expired, or forgotten authentication factors. Whenever the

attributes, password, or other information changes, the data connected to the identifier is
updated and then repropagated to ensure that all connected systems reflect the latest

identity state.

Account recovery deserves special mention because it is often the weak link in the

identity life cycle. Consider an authentication system that requires strong authentication
mechanisms but allows email resets. If the authentication system for email isn’t as strong

as that for the most critical piece of the system, then overall authentication is only as
strong as that for email.

3.3.5 Terminate

When an identity relationship is no longer valid, it must be revoked to prevent unauthorized
access. This might happen because an employee leaves the company, a customer closes an

account, or a device terminates a connection. Proper termination ensures that orphaned
accounts and lingering permissions do not create security risks. The General Data

Protection Regulation (GDPR) requires that organizations allow people to request the
deletion of all the information held about them in most cases. Even without that

requirement, it’s often a good idea to close unused accounts to avoid account hijacking due
to stale authentication factors.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

51

The terminate phase of the identity lifecycle is often overlooked, but it’s where many security

issues begin. If not deactivated, dormant accounts—particularly those of former employees,
contractors, or vendors—can be exploited. Always ensure that identity systems support automated

offboarding and regular cleaning of unused identities to prevent unauthorized access.

#### 3.4 Enrollment

_Enrollment_ is the process that establishes a relationship and sets up the mechanisms

necessary for recognizing and remembering the entity described by the account. Since
enrollment is foundational to any digital relationship, let’s dive a little deeper into the

details of how enrollment works.

3.4.1 Self-service vs. admin-driven enrollment

The first important aspect of enrollment to consider is whether enrollment is self-service or

driven by some administrative process. Most of us have hundreds of accounts at various
places online and thus have experienced self-service enrollment more times than we’d like

to remember. In this familiar process, discovery is often prompted by a marketing message,
something the enrollee has read, or a recommendation from a friend.

After finding the right service, the instigator clicks on Create Account and is taken
through a series of steps designed to select an identifier, establish a means of

authentication (usually a password), and collect any needed attributes. Nowadays, almost
every system uses email as the identifier because it’s guaranteed to be unique, saving time

spent checking the person’s choice of identifier for uniqueness and forcing them to choose
another if it’s not.

[Administrative enrollment occurs when a system or administrator initiates and manages](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-3?potentialInternalRefId=60---book-markup-container)
the enrollment process, so discovery is usually straightforward. In non-self-service

enrollments, discovery is dependent on the type of service. This kind of enrollment is
common in enterprise environments, regulated industries, and managed IT systems.

Concrete examples include employee onboarding, contractor or vendor management,
device enrollment in managed IT environments, and cloud service enrollment when new

services are created.

[In administrative enrollment situations, the identifier is often created for the enrollee,](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-3?potentialInternalRefId=61---book-markup-container)

and the administrator chooses initial authentication credentials. These credentials are
usually communicated to the enrollee using an out-of-band process. If these are user

credentials, they usually come with the system-enforced requirement that they be changed
on the first sign-in. But for other kinds of credentials like digital certificates, that isn’t

usually necessary.

[Regardless of type, the result of enrollment is a new relationship anchored by the](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-3?potentialInternalRefId=62---book-markup-container)

identifier, protected by authentication, and containing the attributes and other information
necessary for the relationship to function.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

52

3.4.2 Identity proofing and assurance

The kind of enrollment you use depends on the requirements of the digital relationship
you’re creating. One of the most important aspects is called the _level of assurance_ and is

determined by how strongly you need to be sure of the identity of the entity that you’re
enrolling. The process of verifying an entity during enrollment is called _proofing_ .

NIST Special Publication 800-63-3 defines three levels of assurance (LOAs) based on the
rigor of the proofing process. Table 3.1 summarizes the NIST identity assurance levels.

[Table 3.1 Summary of NIST Identity Assurance Levels (IAL), which define the strength of identity proofing](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-3?potentialInternalRefId=66---book-markup-container)

during enrollment based on the necessary confidence in the claimed identity.

|IAL Level|Description|Enrollment Process Example|
|---|---|---|
|IAL1 (low)|Self-asserted identity; no formal<br>identity proofing.|Signing up for an email account or a<br>social media profile.|
|IAL2<br>(moderate)|Identity verified using trusted<br>documents (e.g., driver’s<br>license); can be remote.|Opening an online bank account with<br>ID and selfie verification.|
|IAL3 (high)|In-person verification with<br>biometrics or cryptographic<br>binding to the identity.|Getting a passport, security<br>clearance, or high-assurance<br>enterprise login.|

Which of these three levels you choose depends on the amount of risk your system can
tolerate. This might be something you decide for yourself but is often driven by regulation.

For example, anti-money-laundering regulations mandate a _Know Your Customer (KYC)_
process that translates, in most cases, to an IAL2 requirement. Consequently, a financial

services institution will likely have customer enrollment processes that are more stringent
than those required when signing up for a social media account.

Identity proofing is usually governed by an organization’s processes and procedures. As
such, the level of assurance is vulnerable to human error and thus outside the realm of

technical confidence. One consequence of this is that proofing processes might be trusted
internally, but are not something that can be easily shared without legal agreements.

Organizations like the <u>[Trust Over IP Foundation](https://trustoverip.org/)</u> [(https://trustoverip.​org/) and](https://trustoverip.org/) <u>[Ayra](https://ayra.forum/)</u>
<u>[Association](https://ayra.forum/)</u> [(https://ayra.forum/) are working to build industry-wide trust frameworks to](https://ayra.forum/)

make this easier and reduce the burden, inconvenience, friction, and cost of identity
proofing, but this is still a work in progress.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

53

3.4.3 Relationship context and boundaries

Enrollment defines the scope of the relationship. Enrollment is foundational to
authentication and proving who someone is with a required level of assurance (LOA). But it

also sets the stage for determining what they can do and under what conditions. For
example, both bank customers and employees may be enrolled and proofed to IAL2, but

their relationship with the bank is fundamentally different. The enrollment process defines
the underlying context of the relationship that provides a foundation for strong

authentication.

I recently created a supplier account with a large tech industry vendor. This account

creation process was administratively controlled. I created an account, linked to me, and
also one for my organization. My account had authentication credentials, but the

organization’s account did not. Only I could perform actions on behalf of the organization
such as submitting invoices. My identity was only proofed to IAL1, but the organization’s

identity proofing involved proving I controlled the domain name for it. Figure 3.4 shows the
relationships for this kind of account.

Figure 3.4 Enrollment relationships between an individual, their organization, and a supplier system. The

individual account is authenticated and proofed to IAL1, while the organization account is established via

domain control. Delegation rights originate from enrollment context and enable the individual to act on behalf

of the organization within the supplier system.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

54

The setup I performed during enrollment was in service of later authentication decisions.

However, the nature of the information collected and the LOA that the enrollment process
established were dictated by the access control needed by the supplier system. For

example, I already had a customer account for this vendor, but this supplier account was
different. There’s no technical reason the same account couldn’t be used, but the company

had decided as a matter of policy to separate them. As the controller of the initial user
account linked to the organization’s account, I was granted default delegation rights that

allowed me to add new users and grant rights to them. Exercising delegation rights was a
matter of authorization, but the attributes (for example, `initial-account` ) recorded during

enrollment provided the required context.

3.4.4 Risk-based boundaries, attribute lifetimes, and re-proofing

The attributes associated with an account change over time. For those determined by the

system itself, they can be updated as they change. But others, provided by the enrollee,
might change without the system’s knowledge or action. Some attributes, formally known

as _traits_, are unlikely to change—these include birthdate and eye color. But others, like
marital status or role inside another organization (think about my relationship to the

supplier account from the last section), often change without any signal that the identity
system can use to trigger an update.

Because of this, many IAL2 and IAL3 systems require reproofing at regular intervals.
Proofed attributes, like those from a driver’s license or state ID, can record information

about the underlying document’s expiration date. This can trigger a need for re-proofing,
but that depends on the organization’s policies and regulatory environment. The birthdate

on your driver’s license is still the same even if the license has expired. In other cases,
some event such as a change in relationship status, role change, detection of fraud, or

change in behavior by an account holder may require reproofing.

3.4.5 The role of credentials and authentication factors

One of the primary purposes of enrollment is to provide the enrollee with authentication

credentials they can use to prove who they are when they come back to the system. Some
of the attributes gathered during enrollment, like email addresses and mobile phone

numbers, are important to get right, so the system often performs automated proofing to
verify these. If the system uses digital certificates or biometrics, these are also recorded

during enrollment. Finally, in both self-service and administrative enrollments, the system
usually assigns initial roles and sets defaults that are helpful later when the enrollee uses

the system.

#### 3.5 Authentication factors

Authentication is how we recognize the rightful account holder, even when they aren’t

physically present. In face-to-face interactions, identity verification is straightforward—a
bank teller can match a customer’s face to their ID, and a security guard can check a badge

against the person holding it. But in digital systems, this is much harder. The proximity
problem—the fact that users authenticate remotely—means systems can’t rely on physical

presence.

When you hear the word _authentication,_ you probably think of passwords. Passwords are

as old as the first timeshare systems, when multiple people started sharing a computer. As
the internet went mainstream and multi-tenanted websites became common, the use of

passwords to authenticate service requestors became common. But passwords are just one
way we can authenticate a request.

[When Alice logs in to her employer’s financial system, the system can’t verify her](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-3?potentialInternalRefId=82---book-markup-container)
identity through physical presence, so it relies on a digital ceremony—commonly called

_logging in_ —to recognize her. The ceremony starts with Alice presenting an identifier, laying
claim to a particular account. The ceremony proceeds with Alice presenting one or more

_authentication factors_ —pieces of evidence that prove she is the legitimate account holder.
Generally speaking, the more factors used, the stronger the authentication process. Note

that the identifier isn’t an authentication factor—it’s a claim by the requester that needs to
be verified.

[Traditionally, authentication is categorized into three](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-3?potentialInternalRefId=83---book-markup-container) _primary factors_ : knowledge,
possession, and inherence. Modern authentication models also consider _contextual factors_

that enhance security without requiring additional user input: behavior, location, and
temporal.

3.5.1 Primary factors

The following sections describe the three primary authentication factors in detail, outlining
their typical uses, strengths, and vulnerabilities.

KNOWLEDGE FACTOR—SOMETHING YOU KNOW, LIKE PASSWORDS

Knowledge factors are the most common—and weakest—authentication factors. These
include passwords, PINs, and security questions. Knowledge factors are vulnerable to

phishing, credential stuffing, and brute-force attacks. They can be lost, shared, or
forgotten. Yet, despite these weaknesses, they are widely used because they are well

understood and supported.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

56

POSSESSION FACTOR—SOMETHING YOU HAVE, LIKE A SMARTPHONE

Possession factors nominally require that the requester physically possess an object. These
objects include smartphones, hardware tokens, smart cards, and security keys. While

possession factors are stronger than knowledge factors, they can still be lost, stolen, or
cloned. In some cases, such as proving you have your phone or email account by receiving

a text or email, they can be phished.

INHERENCE FACTOR—SOMETHING YOU ARE, LIKE BIOMETRICS

_Inherence_ factors use unique biological traits to verify the requester’s claim. These include
things like fingerprints, facial recognition, retina scans, and voice recognition. Most people

have probably used their face or fingerprint to unlock their phone, a prime example of
using an inherence factor. However, storing biometric data remotely, such as in a central

database, introduces significant security, privacy, and trust risks compared to storing it
locally on a device. Unlike a password, if biometric data is stolen or fabricated, you can’t

change your face or fingerprint. Consequently, inherence factors are best used on local
devices in combination with other factors. In addition, the rise of AI-generated _deepfakes_

has provided the means to attack some biometric authentication systems.

3.5.2 Contextual factors

The following sections describe the three contextual authentication factors in detail,

outlining their typical uses, strengths, and limitations.

BEHAVIOR FACTOR—SOMETHING YOU DO, LIKE MOUSE MOVEMENTS

Behavior factors analyze patterns of a person’s behavior rather than static credentials.

These patterns include typing speed, keystroke dynamics, mouse movement, and gait
recognition. You may have been challenged by a CAPTCHA asking you to click a box and

thought, “How is this proving I’m a human?” These challenges can distinguish a human’s
mouse movements from a machine’s—at least for now. They are a good example of a

widely deployed behavior factor.

LOCATION FACTOR—SOMEWHERE YOU ARE LOCATED, LIKE GEOLOCATION

Location factors use things like GPS, IP addresses, or Wi-Fi locations to verify requests.

They can prevent access from unexpected locations or enforce geo-restrictions but are
vulnerable to VPNs and GPS spoofing. Location factors are most effective when used in

combination with one or more primary factors. One application of location factors is
conducting velocity checks to detect impossible travel, where requests originate from

locations that are too distant for travel between them.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

57

TEMPORAL FACTOR—THE TIME YOU’RE IN, SUCH AS THE CURRENT LOCAL TIME

Temporal factors assess whether an authentication request occurs at an appropriate time.
They can identify logins at unusual hours or detect anomalies in session timing. Like other

contextual factors, they are most effective when combined with other primary factors. AIbased systems have made it easier to identify anomalous access times.

3.5.3 Authentication factors

The primary factors can be used alone or in combination with other factors. The contextual

factors are rarely used alone. We’ll see in later chapters that contextual factors can also be
used in a more fine-grained manner in dynamic authorization. Consequently, knowledge,

possession, and inherence factors are used for direct authentication, and behavior, location,
and temporal factors are typically used for risk-based authentication, strengthening security

dynamically.

Each of these factors uniquely contributes to a system’s ability to distinguish between

legitimate requests and attacks. Let’s explore how they can be used to create
authentication systems that provide the needed security.

#### 3.6 Authentication methods

When Alice lays claim to a particular account, there are four primary methods the system

can use to authenticate that it’s really her. All these methods use some kind of identifier
that represents the claim Alice is making. These are the four methods, in increasing order

of strength:

Identifier-only

Token-based
Identifier with authentication factors

Challenge-response

Let’s explore each of these. In the descriptions in each section, we’ll follow Alice as she

authenticates using different authentication methods and see how they differ. In the
figures, assume that the authentication service is part of, or is working with, some other

service that Alice wants to interact with.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

58

3.6.1 Identifier-only

In an identifier-only authentication scenario, Alice returns the same identifier with each
request, thereby laying claim to an account or session. Identifier-only authentication might

sound like an oxymoron. The idea of authenticating someone using just an identifier seems
impossible, but that’s exactly what browser cookies are. Browser cookies are an identifier

created by a website that’s stored in the browser and meant to be returned to the website
the next time the user visits. This is how sessions are maintained between individual

browser clicks since HTTP, the protocol underlying the web, is stateless and can’t maintain
sessions on its own. Figure 3.5 shows the interactions between Alice and an identifier-only

authentication service.

Figure 3.5 Identifier-only authentication flow. When Alice first visits, the authentication service creates and

stores an identifier (such as a session cookie) and returns it to her client. For subsequent requests, Alice’s

client presents this identifier to indicate her relationship with the system. No additional authentication

factors are used. This approach relies entirely on the secrecy of the identifier, making it vulnerable to

interception, guessing, or reuse if not properly secured with transport encryption and randomness.

Upon Alice’s initial visit, the service returns an identifier to Alice, that she resends each

time she returns. Identifier-only authentication treats the identifier as a shared secret; it’s
only secure when you can be reasonably sure that the identifier is not easily guessed or

stolen. Consequently, public identifiers, like email addresses, don’t work. This is the primary
disadvantage of identifier-only authentication. Anyone who can guess or intercept the

identifier can hijack the relationship and impersonate the requester. This is one reason TLS
is vital for secure web interactions. TLS encrypts the channel to maintain the confidentiality

of the communications, including any identifiers that are exchanged in the HTTP headers.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

59

3.6.2 Token-based

Token-based authentication is a special case of identifier-only authentication that I
distinguish primarily by whether the token (which is also acting as the identifier) is issued

only after an initial authentication using some stronger authentication method. If you look
at figure 3.6 and compare it to figure 3.5, you’ll see that the flow now includes an initial

registration step to enroll Alice and an authentication step to authenticate her for a given
session.

Figure 3.6 Token-based authentication flow. Alice begins by registering with the authentication service, which

stores her identifier along with one or more authentication factors. During login, she presents her identifier

and authentication factors. If verified, the service issues a cryptographically verifiable token that represents

her authenticated session. For subsequent requests, Alice presents only the token (identifier), which the

service uses to link the request to her previously authenticated session. This method enhances usability by

eliminating the need to reenter credentials, but it depends on the token being securely stored and

transmitted to prevent hijacking.

Compared with identifier-only authentication, token-based authentication offers more
security by enrolling the requester, subject to any level of identity proofing, and then

authenticating them before issuing the token.

Given the definition of token-based authentication, you might realize that websites can

use cookies to implement tokens for session management. Even so, many cookies, most
related to surveillance-based web advertising, are not authenticated. For example, in a

[scan I did of www.allrecipes.​com](http://www.allreceipes.com/) (chosen randomly), I found more than half (30 out of 58)
were from third parties; that is, they were not from the website itself.

[Token-based authentication is widely used. The OAuth 2.0 protocol, for example (which](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-3?potentialInternalRefId=119---book-markup-container)
we’ll discuss in detail in chapter 12), uses authenticated tokens. OAuth 2.0 is the basis of

the OpenID Connect protocols that are used in social login systems that implement singlesign-on using a social networking account like those from Google, Facebook, and X. Token
based authentication is also often used in delegated authentication flows.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

60

[3.6.3 Identifier with authentication factors](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-3?potentialInternalRefId=120---book-markup-container)

Identifier with authentication factors is the most commonly used authentication method.
Let’s examine how authentication factors are used together to prove control over an

identifier and its associated account.

When Alice logs in, she provides an identifier to signal which account she is claiming.

She also presents one or more authentication factors to prove that the identifier belongs to
her. These factors may be provided simultaneously along with the identifier or as part of a

workflow, a process known as _progressive disclosure_ .

_[Multi-factor](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-3?potentialInternalRefId=123---book-markup-container)_ authentication, where two or more factors are combined, is now quite

common, although it is often optional. Passwords are usually combined with a possession
factor in the form of a one-time password (OTP) to make it harder for an attacker to gain

access to Alice’s account using a stolen, guessed, or phished password. OTPs are
possession factors because they depend on Alice having access to the means by which the

OTP is either delivered to her or generated. OTPs can take the form of SMS or email
messages with a PIN, a push notification on an app, or a code from an authentication app

such as Authy or Microsoft Authenticator. Figure 3.7 shows the flow for authentication using
an identifier and authentication factors.

Figure 3.7 Identifier with authentication factors flow. During registration, Alice provides an identifier (such as

a username or email) and one or more authentication factors (like a password or biometric). The

authentication service securely stores these. At login, Alice is prompted for her identifier and corresponding

authentication factors. The service verifies both before granting or denying access. This is the most common

authentication pattern and serves as the foundation for multi-factor authentication, where the combination of

factors enhances security by requiring control over multiple types of evidence.

When registering, Alice provides an identifier, chooses a password, and, usually, chooses

what additional authentication factors she wants to use. The authentication service binds
these authentication factors to the identifier, storing them securely. Alice must provide

these each time she logs in.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

61

3.6.4 Challenge-response

In challenge-response, after Alice provides an identifier to indicate which account she’s
claiming, the system sends back a challenge, and Alice must send back the correct

response to prove she has control over a secret. Unlike a password, which is static, the
challenge and response are usually derived in real time, allowing Alice to prove control over

some secret without revealing it.

A _CAPTCHA_ is a kind of challenge-response authentication method, although it’s not

usually used to prove that a specific requester knows a specific secret—rather, it’s a
challenge where the response is supposed to prove the requester is human. Still, it meets

the description from the preceding paragraph in that both the challenge and response are
derived in real-time.

[The strength of challenge-response systems is that they use artifacts derived in real-](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-3?potentialInternalRefId=129---book-markup-container)
time, making it nearly impossible to reuse the response, even if it’s intercepted. This

strategy protects against phishing and replay attacks, so it is often used in cryptographic
protocols, device authentication, and phishing-resistant flows.

A replay attack occurs when an attacker captures a valid authentication message—like
a one-time code sent via SMS—and reuses it to gain unauthorized access. If the system doesn’t verify

that the message is associated with a unique challenge, it may accept the replayed code. Challengeresponse protocols prevent this by ensuring each authentication request has a distinct, non-reusable

challenge.

To see how this can work, imagine that the authentication service is using public-private

key cryptography to create the responses as shown in figure 3.8. Compare figure 3.8 with
figure 3.7 and you’ll notice the flows are quite different.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

62

Figure 3.8 Challenge-response authentication flow using public-key cryptography. Alice registers by providing

an identifier and a public key. At login, the service sends a challenge that Alice signs with her private key. The

service verifies the signature using the stored public key, confirming her identity without exposing the private

key. This method offers strong resistance to phishing and replay attacks.

During registration, Alice provides an identifier and a public key, which the authentication
service stores. When Alice wants to authenticate, she provides only her identifier, and the

service sends back a challenge. This can be any string depending on the specific protocol.
Alice uses the private key that pairs with the public key she registered with the service to

cryptographically sign the challenge and sends it back. The service can use her public key
to verify the signature and know that Alice controls the private key matching the public key

they’ve stored.

Note that Alice never shares her secret (the private key) with anyone. Because of how

public-private cryptography works, she proves possession without ever having to reveal it.
The authentication service can send a unique challenge each time Alice logs in, making the

response impossible to replay and resistant to phishing since, even if intercepted, the
attacker can’t use it.

Public-key cryptography is critical to how many of the most important processes in digital
identity systems work. If you are unsure about the principles of public key cryptography, I

recommend Chapter 9 of my book Learning Digital Identity (O’Reilly Media, 2023) for a developerlevel primer on the subject.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

63

Passkeys, as specified by the FIDO Alliance, are the best, easiest-to-deploy challenge
response system available. One benefit of passkeys is the WebAuthn protocol, which
integrates passkeys with browsers and JavaScript applications, making them nearly

impossible to phish. If you’re not familiar with passkeys, you can try them out at
<u>[www.passkeys.​io. The biggest drawback to passkeys is that they are unfamiliar to many](http://www.passkeys.io/)</u>

users, but they are being deployed as options for authentication by many online services,
including Google, Apple, Amazon, and others.

Other examples of strong, challenge-response systems in common use include SSH key
authentication to servers and smart cards or USB keys for enterprise logins. These and

passkeys are all based on public-private key cryptography.

[Digital certificates, based on public-key infrastructure (PKI) package an identifier and](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-3?potentialInternalRefId=140---book-markup-container)

public key together in a certificate that’s been issued by a certificate authority. You are
probably familiar with these from TLS since they’re used to link the public key used to

encrypt HTTPS traffic with an identifier in the form of a domain name. But they can also
include attributes about the identifier, and the issuer can (for a fee) conduct more thorough

identity proofing than is commonly done for certificates used in TLS. This makes them very
flexible because they don’t necessarily require pre-registration for the requester to prove

they are in control of an identifier. So long as the authentication service trusts the
certificate issuer, certificates can provide a rich set of attributes about the identifier without

registration.

#### 3.7 Attack models for authentication

There are many attack vectors for authentication, and covering them in detail is beyond the
scope of this book, but we should talk about them briefly before comparing different

authentication methods. We’ve mentioned a few, like phishing, already. Table 3.2 provides a
concise description of common attack models and risks for different authentication methods

along with suggested mitigation strategies.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

64

Table 3.2 Common attack models targeting authentication systems and the methods they exploit. This table

details each attack type, highlights the most vulnerable authentication methods, and suggests strategies for

mitigation to improve resilience and reduce risk.

|Attack Type|Description|Vulnerable Methods|Mitigation<br>Strategies|
|---|---|---|---|
|Phishing|Trick user into revealing<br>credentials via fake<br>login pages or<br>messages.|Passwords, OTP via<br>SMS or email|Passkeys,<br>FIDO2/WebAuthn,<br>phishing-resistant<br>MFA, user training|
|Credential<br>Stuffing|Use stolen<br>username/password<br>combos from other<br>breaches.|Password-based logins|MFA, rate limiting,<br>breached password<br>detection|
|Replay<br>Attacks|Intercept and reuse<br>authentication<br>messages or tokens.|OTPs, bearer tokens|Challenge-response<br>protocols, short<br>token lifetimes, TLS|
|Man-in-the-<br>Middle|Intercept<br>communication<br>between user and<br>service.|All methods if TLS is<br>not enforced or<br>implemented end-to-<br>end|TLS with certificate<br>validation, mutual<br>TLS, signed<br>challenges|
|SIM<br>Swapping|Hijack a phone number<br>to intercept SMS OTPs.|SMS-based 2FA|App-based<br>authenticators,<br>hardware tokens|
|MFA Fatigue<br>Attacks|Send repeated push<br>notifications to annoy<br>user into accepting an<br>auth request.|Push-based MFA|Rate limiting,<br>number matching,<br>intelligent<br>notification controls|
|Session<br>Hijacking|Steal session token<br>from browser or<br>memory to impersonate<br>a user.|Token-based<br>authentication|Token binding,<br>session expiration,<br>re-auth for sensitive<br>actions|

You’ll see how these attack methods come into play as we discuss authentication strength

in the next two sections.

3.7.1 Authentication assurance levels

A common way to compare authentication strength is to use NIST’s authentication

assurance levels (AAL) from NIST SP 800-63B, the same document where we found the
identity assurance levels given in table 3.1. Table 3.3 shows the NIST AALs.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

Table 3.3 NIST’s Authentication Assurance Levels (AAL) categorize the strength of authentication mechanisms

based on their resistance to common attacks and their ability to establish trust. This table summarizes each

level, ranging from basic single-factor authentication to hardware-backed, cryptographically secure methods

that are suitable for high-risk environments.

|AAL Level|Description|Example authentication<br>process|
|---|---|---|
|AAL1 (low)|Requires single-factor<br>authentication. No requirement for<br>resistance to eavesdropping or<br>replay attacks.|Password-only login to a news<br>website or basic SaaS app.|
|AAL2 (moderate)|Requires multi-factor<br>authentication. At least one factor<br>must be resistant to replay attacks<br>(for example, OTP, cryptographic<br>token).|Password + OTP from an<br>authenticator app or SMS.|
|AAL3 (high)|Requires hardware-based<br>authenticator that is resistant to<br>phishing, impersonation, and<br>replay. Authentication must use<br>proof of possession of a<br>cryptographic key.|Smart card + PIN; or FIDO2<br>security key that signs a<br>challenge during login.|

The NIST classification is widely used in United States federal IT systems and regulated
industries like healthcare and financial services. While HIPAA (a federal law regulating

healthcare records) doesn’t explicitly mandate AALs, many healthcare vendors reference it
as a concise way to assess identity system-related risk. Similarly, financial institutions

regularly use NIST AALs to align their practices with federal guidance on protecting
customer data and preventing fraud. You’ll often see AALs referenced in authentication

system vendor literature to describe the strength of their authentication options. Globally,
many governments and standards bodies use frameworks that are inspired by or align with

NIST AALs.

3.7.2 Authentication strength and usability

While the NIST AAL system is widely used, I like to use the strength-and-usability pyramid

shown in Figure 3.9. The pyramid shows commonly used authentication methods, from
weakest at the bottom to strongest at the top. Interestingly, stronger methods are almost

always more usable.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

66

Figure 3.9 The strength and usability pyramid for authentication methods. As you ascend the pyramid,

authentication mechanisms become more resistant to phishing, replay attacks, and credential theft—though

some may require a more technical setup or infrastructure. Passwords, located at the base, offer poor security

and usability, while challenge-response methods like passkeys and PKI provide high assurance with an

improved user experience. Multi-factor approaches (MFA) are positioned across the middle tiers, balancing

security and usability by combining various types of factors.

I’ve left identifier-only authentication off the pyramid due to security concerns that limit its
applications, despite its great usability. Token-based authentication could be placed at any

level on the pyramid because its strength primarily depends on the initial authentication
method used to issue the token.

Let’s discuss the levels in the pyramid from bottom to top:

Passwords—on their own—provide poor security because of credential

stuffing attacks, and their usability suffers from the need to register,
remember, and recover them.

One-time passwords sent via SMS or email provide better security than
passwords alone, but their usability is reduced because users must often

switch apps and manually enter the code. As shown in table 3.2, their
security can be compromised using phishing or SIM swapping.

One-time passwords from an authentication app are more secure because
they’re harder to intercept, but they still require switching apps and

manually transferring the code. Phishing remains the most common
attack vector in this context.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

67

Push notifications to an app are also hard to intercept and offer increased

usability because, while you still switch apps, you don’t need to transfer a
code. Hackers bypass push notifications by using credential stuffing

combined with MFA fatigue.
Passkeys are the first level of the pyramid that is phishing-resistant.

Because they resist phishing, passkeys are more secure than other
authentication methods. Additionally, they are not vulnerable to MFA

fatigue. The most common threats involve lost devices with weak security
or malware infections that can expose the key store. Usability remains

high because the underlying protocols handle generating and registering
the key, storing it, and using it to respond to challenges.

PKI may be more trustworthy than passkeys if the certificate issuer
performs identity proofing. Similar to passkeys, the main threat is a lost

device or a virus infection. However, the process of applying for and
setting up certificates is generally not easy for non-technical people.

After studying figure 3.9, you might wonder, “Why don’t we just use PKI for everything?”
Besides usability, the biggest problem with using PKI for workaday authentication problems

is its cost. Good certificates cost money because the issuer is doing work to verify that the
certificate is valid and, potentially, providing identity proofing. User certificates were

proposed in the 1990s, and some browsers still support them, but they have never been
widely used.

The bottom line is that there’s no reason not to use passkeys everywhere for everything.
They are secure, affordable, and easy to use. The most likely attacks involve lost devices

with inadequate device security or a virus infection that can expose the key store. These
issues can be mitigated with good device hygiene. If your organization isn’t already using

them, that should be the first thing you address before worrying about authorization or
zero-trust, because it’s the quickest way to make your services easier to use and more

secure at the same time.

#### 3.8 Connecting authentication and authorization

Authentication and authorization are deeply connected and often discussed in tandem. But
they serve very different purposes. As we’ve discussed, the identity relationship formed

during enrollment is validated for each interaction during authentication. Due to the
proximity problem, authentication must continually verify the participants in any digital

interaction.

As we discovered in the preceding section, selecting and configuring an authentication

system has a big impact on its strength and usability. When authentication is weak,
authorization decisions are based on a shaky foundation where attackers are potentially

impersonating others. An attacker might pose as Alice, gaining access to anything she has
permissions for if the authentication process is too weak to confirm she’s really making the

request.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

68

3.8.1 Identity as context

When Alice authenticates, the system not only validates the identifier but also gains a
relationship context—all the information recorded about Alice since her enrollment. This can

include contextual elements such as:

Attributes (for example, department, clearance level, subscription tier)

Roles (for example, admin, contributor, viewer)
Group memberships

Device posture and location
Recent behavior or signals of compromise

Preferences or other information gleaned from Alice’s actions.

All this context can be used to inform access decisions. Thus, establishing that the original

enrollee is the current requester is vital to making correct authorization decisions.

WHAT IS DEVICE POSTURE?

_Device posture_ refers to the current trustworthiness of the device involved in an
authentication or access request. Device posture is not just a single signal or a fixed

property; it is a combined assessment based on multiple device-related attributes
evaluated at the moment of access. These attributes typically answer questions like

these:

Is the device managed by the organization?

Is it compliant with required security controls (OS version, encryption,
screen lock)?

Is it healthy (not jailbroken, rooted, or reporting malware)?
Is it connecting from an expected environment (network, geography,

time)?
Is its security state recently attested, or is the information stale?

In zero-trust architectures, device posture is considered a primary context signal.
Authentication not only confirms who is making a request but also assesses the

device and the conditions. A valid identity from a non-compliant or unknown device
may authenticate successfully but can still be denied access to sensitive resources.

Throughout this book, when we refer to policies that require a managed, trusted, or
healthy device, we rely on device posture as an input signal. The specific signals and

thresholds are determined by each organization, but the core idea remains the
same: Access decisions depend on not only identity but also the state of the device

asserting that identity.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

69

3.8.2 Looking ahead

In the next chapter, we’ll shift our focus from identifying relationships to defining and
enforcing their capabilities. We’ll explore how authorization models and policies make

decisions based on the identity and attributes established through authentication.

#### 3.9 Summary

Authentication ensures the integrity of digital relationships by verifying

that the entity interacting with the system is the same one that originally
established the account.

Relationship integrity is central to system trust; when authentication fails,
it can compromise not only direct relationships but also those that

depend on them indirectly.
The identity relationship lifecycle includes enrollment, propagation, use,

update, and termination—each phase plays a role in maintaining secure,
accurate access.

Enrollment establishes the account and binds it to attributes and
authentication credentials; weak enrollment processes can undermine

even strong authentication systems.
Authentication relies on a combination of factors—knowledge, possession,

inherence, behavior, location, and temporal context—to determine if an
account holder is legitimate.

Authentication methods vary in strength and usability, from simple
identifier-only approaches to cryptographic challenge-response protocols

that resist phishing and replay.
Strong authentication methods use multi-factor or challenge-response

techniques to better protect against common attack models like phishing,
credential stuffing, and session hijacking.

Authentication sets the stage for authorization by validating the account
and its context, allowing access decisions to reflect the true nature of the

digital relationship.
Without strong authentication, authorization policies are applied to

potentially false identities, creating risk and undermining the security of
the entire system.
