## Authorization: What can you do?

This chapter covers

A look at why authentication isn’t enough—and why authorization deserves focused
attention

The PARC model for breaking down access decisions

Core terminology that underpins modern authorization systems, from roles and

attributes to policies and entitlements

A tour of the authorization reference architecture and how its components work
together

Real-world deployment patterns for enforcing and evaluating policies in centralized
and distributed systems

In 2023, the U.S. Federal Trade Commission (FTC) filed a complaint against Ring, the
popular home security company owned by Amazon. The allegations were startling:

employees and third-party contractors had unrestricted access to customers’ private video
feeds—sometimes without their knowledge or consent. In a particularly egregious case, one

employee viewed thousands of videos of female customers in their bedrooms and
bathrooms over several months before being discovered.

_What went wrong?_ From a traditional access control standpoint, the individuals involved
were all authenticated. They had usernames and passwords. They were Ring employees or

authorized contractors. The system knew who they were.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

71

But that wasn’t the issue. The real failure lay in authorization—the system lacked

controls to determine what these authenticated users were allowed to do. There were no
meaningful limits on who could view customer video feeds, no contextual checks, and no

policy-based enforcement. The system trusted too much.

[The fallout was significant: regulatory scrutiny, damaged brand trust, and a $5.8 million](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-4?potentialInternalRefId=9---book-markup-container)

settlement. However, the technical lesson is timeless: Authentication is necessary, but not
sufficient. Authorization is what truly protects sensitive data and resources.

[As we begin our exploration of authorization in earnest, the Ring case serves as a](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-4?potentialInternalRefId=10---book-markup-container)
cautionary tale. It reminds us that verifying someone’s identity is only the starting point.

The real challenge—and where many systems falter—lies in determining what that person is
allowed to do in a given context, at a given time, on a given resource.

#### 4.1 Authorization deserves its own focus

In Chapter 3, we explored the evolution of authentication—from passwords and security

questions to biometrics and multi-factor authentication. That discussion culminated with
passkeys, a modern, phishing-resistant alternative to traditional methods of authentication

that promises to finally break the Internet’s dependency on passwords, solving many of the
user experience and security problems that passwords have created. With passkeys, the

essential building blocks of secure, user-friendly authentication are finally in place. The
remaining work will focus on deployment, interoperability, and user adoption. In many

ways, authentication has reached a strategic plateau: it’s now about operationalizing
passkeys everywhere.

Authorization, on the other hand, is just beginning to receive the attention it deserves.
While authentication answers the question, “Who are you?” authorization poses a more

challenging question: “What should you be allowed to do?” Moreover, whereas
authentication is typically a point-in-time event, authorization is continuous, contextual,

and often decentralized, making it a more difficult—and more consequential—problem to
solve.

[Most systems today rely on brittle combinations of roles, hardcoded rules, and](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-4?potentialInternalRefId=14---book-markup-container)
permissions scattered across codebases. There’s no standardized equivalent to passkeys for

authorization. No universal model. No easy button. This makes authorization a
fundamentally harder, broader, and more business-critical problem—one that touches every

interaction, every resource, and every compliance boundary.

[While authentication has matured into a well-understood and increasingly standardized](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-4?potentialInternalRefId=15---book-markup-container)

process, authorization is still rapidly evolving. It’s more than just the next step after
authentication; it presents a rich, multidimensional challenge that permeates every layer of

modern systems. Here’s why authorization deserves our focused attention:

**It’s contextual** . Unlike authentication, which is often a point-in-time

decision, authorization is continuous and situational. What a user can do
may depend on time of day, device used, location, or other dynamic

factors.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

72

**It’s complex** . Real-world access control is rarely a simple yes or no.

Policies might need to account for team membership, project roles, data
classification levels, legal jurisdictions, or dozens of other variables.

**It’s distributed** . In modern architectures, access decisions are made
across services, platforms, and APIs. Centralized, consistent authorization

logic becomes crucial to maintaining control and visibility.
**It’s critical to security and compliance** . Misconfigured access controls

are among the most common and damaging security failures. Whether
it’s unauthorized data exposure or violations of regulations like HIPAA or

GDPR, the root cause is often poor authorization design.
**It shapes user experience and functionality** . Authorization isn’t just

a safeguard—it defines the contours of what users can see and do. Get it
wrong, and users are blocked from getting work done or exposed to more

than they should be. Beyond the user experience, authorization also
frequently drives the user interface.

In short, authorization is more than a technical concern—it’s foundational to modern
software design, security posture, resiliency, and regulatory compliance.. As identity

systems mature, it’s authorization that increasingly defines trust.

#### 4.2 From relationships to access control

As discussed in chapter 2, digital identity is best understood not as a static profile or a set
of credentials but as a relationship between two entities—for example, a student and a

university, a contractor and a client organization, or a customer and a service provider.
Identity systems exist to facilitate, mediate, and enforce the terms of these relationships.

Authentication, as we saw in chapter 3, validates that relationship at a moment in time,
proving that the entity interacting with the system is indeed one that’s recognized in that

relationship.

Authorization makes the relationship actionable and enforceable. It defines how a

system determines what the authenticated entity can do, under what conditions, and with
what data or resources. Access control is where identity becomes operational, turned into

decisions that the system can enforce.

[Here are a few examples that illustrate this transformation:](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-4?potentialInternalRefId=25---book-markup-container)

Polly, a project manager, authenticates using her enterprise credentials.
Her account includes a role that indicates she is a manager. The system

authorizes her to view project dashboards and assign tasks—not simply
because she authenticated, but because of her role within the

organization.
Carl, a call center agent, logs in with a passkey. A policy checks whether

it’s between 9 AM and 5 PM—his assigned shift. Even though he’s
authenticated, access to sensitive customer data is conditional on time.

The system combines his identity with contextual data—his shift hours—
to drive the authorization decision.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

73

Sally, a university student, signs in using SSO from her laptop. During

enrollment, the MAC address of her device was recorded. A policy checks
whether the request comes from a registered device. Access is granted

not only based on her authentication but also because her session
originates from a trusted device.

In each case, identity provides a contextual anchor; however, it’s authorization that applies
that context to determine whether access should be granted. The richness of the identity

relationship—roles, attributes, schedules, devices—feeds into decisions about what
someone can do, when, and under what circumstances.

This relational view highlights why authorization deserves its own discipline. It is not just
about securing resources; it is about governing interactions between entities, grounded in

the terms of their relationships and mediated by policy. This perspective reframes
authorization not as an afterthought to authentication but rather as the primary mechanism

by which digital relationships are honored—or denied—in real time.

#### 4.3 Speaking authorization: key concepts and terms

In the previous section, we saw how authorization operationalizes identity relationships,
turning them into real-time decisions about who can do what. To do this effectively, we

need a shared language.

Let’s begin by clarifying a common source of confusion: access control versus

authorization.

_Access control_ is the discipline or strategy focused on managing access to

systems, data, or resources. It includes all the policies, rules, and
mechanisms that determine who can access what, when, and under what

conditions.
_Authorization_, by contrast, is the mechanism that enforces access

decisions based on identity, attributes, and policy. It serves as the aspect
of access control that addresses this question: Should this action be

allowed right now, under these conditions?

Put simply, access control defines the strategy, while authorization is the method of

enforcement.

4.3.1 The PARC model

To help us discuss the various components of an authorization decision consistently, we will

use a mental model called PARC, which stands for _p_ rincipal, _a_ ction, _r_ esource, and
_c_ onditions. In any access decision, someone (a _principal_ ) is trying to do something (an

_action_ ) to something (a _resource_ )—but only if the right _conditions_ are met. Together, these
elements provide a common, widely applicable framework for thinking about and discussing

access decisions. PARC offers a structured way to analyze policies and authorization
requests, making them easier to analyze, test, and manage.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

74

The _principal_ is the entity that makes the request. Examples of principals include a

person, a service account, or an IoT device. Principals often have attributes that can be
referenced in a policy, such as their department, clearance level, role, or group

membership.

[The](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-4?potentialInternalRefId=40---book-markup-container) _action_ refers to the operation that the principal wants to perform. Common actions

include `read`, `write`, `update`, and `delete` . They are often specific to the application or

service that executes the request. For instance, a photo-sharing application might include

actions like `ShareWithFriend`, `ShareWithGroup`, or `ApplyPhotoFilter` . In APIs, actions

typically represent the verbs associated with the API endpoints.

[The](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-4?potentialInternalRefId=41---book-markup-container) _resource_ is the object or entity on which the action is performed. Examples include
generic resources like a database row or document, but they can also include application
specific objects such as an `account`, `invoice`, or `photo` . Resources are often organized

hierarchically, with these groups also qualifying as resources. For instance, an action might

apply to all the photos in a particular folder. Like principals, resources can have attributes—
such as `owner`, `classification`, or `status` —which can be referenced in the policy. Again,

these attributes are usually application-specific.

[The](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-4?potentialInternalRefId=42---book-markup-container) _condition_ is the context in which access is permitted or denied. Conditions might

include factors such as time, location, device trust, risk score, or workload identity.
_Workload identity_ refers to the identity of the service or process making the request on

behalf of the principal. For example, an API policy might require that the calling service’s
identity include a tag like `env=production` or that it runs in a secure enclave. Conditions

are typically the most dynamic aspect of the PARC model and can depend on attributes of
the principal, the resource, or the environment—or combinations of these elements.

[Most authorization systems use these four elements, either explicitly or implicitly, when](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-4?potentialInternalRefId=43---book-markup-container)
evaluating policies to make access decisions. They enable policy languages to express rich,

contextual rules while keeping complex policies understandable and maintainable.

4.3.2 Understanding the language of access

Now that we’ve established the PARC model, let’s take a closer look at the vocabulary

commonly used in access control and authorization. These terms appear in policy
languages, IAM platforms, and system documentation, but they’re not always used

consistently. In this section, we’ll define them precisely and explain how they relate to one
another, and to the decisions that systems make about access. A clear understanding of

these terms will help you design better policies, reason about authorization systems, and
communicate more effectively across technical and business roles.

The following is a list of words, in addition to those defined in the last section, that we’ll
use frequently in our discussion of authorization.

**Entity** —a structured object within the authorization system that
participates in policies. Entities include principals such as users, devices,

or services, as well as resources like documents, records, or applications.
Each entity can have attributes that influence policy decisions.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

75

**Subject** —in chapter 2, we defined _subject_ as the “entity being referred to

in an account, policy, or decision.” In this book, I will avoid using the
word _subject_ to minimize confusion, as it could refer to either the

principal or the resource depending on the context. Some historical
systems use subject instead of principal, and I will highlight those

instances when necessary.
**Group** —a collection of entities that can be referenced collectively in a

policy. Groups simplify access management by allowing shared rules to be
applied to multiple users or resources simultaneously. For example, all

members of the `Customer-CustCo-Users` group might be allowed to view

documents owned by CustCo.

**Namespace** —a prefix that organizes and clarifies entities and actions.
Namespaces prevent collisions and help specify to which domain or

system a particular entity or policy belongs. For example,
`PhotoApp::User` and `BillingApp::User` represent distinct entity types

within separate domains.
**Policy** —a declarative rule or a set of rules that determines whether

access should be granted. Policies describe who can do what under which
conditions and serve as the primary means of expressing access logic in

modern systems.
**Role** —a named collection of permissions that represents a function or job

responsibility. Examples include descriptors such as `admin`, `editor`, and

`billingReviewer` . Roles are generally assigned to principals or groups to

simplify management and consolidate related capabilities. If you’re
confusing roles and groups, keep in mind that all roles can be considered

groups, but not all groups are roles.
**Attribute** —refers to a characteristic of a principal, resource, or

environment that informs access decisions. A principal may possess
attributes such as department, job title, or clearance level. A resource

may be labeled with attributes like owner, classification level, or
publication status. Environmental attributes could include location, time

of access, or risk score. They are fundamental to context-aware and
attribute-based fine-grained access models.

**Permission** —a specific right to perform an action on a resource.
Permissions can be directly assigned, derived from a policy, or bundled

into roles. Examples include the ability to edit an invoice, view a
dashboard, or delete a customer record.

**Entitlement** —the effective set of permissions that a principal holds at a
specific point in time, determined by roles, attributes, and policies.

Entitlements can be calculated dynamically during a request or
precomputed for auditing, enforcement, or optimization. Entitlements are

not the same as roles. Roles have entitlements associated with them that
are inherited by anyone who is assigned that role.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

76

**Authorization Request** —a structured query to the authorization system

that asks: “Is this principal allowed to perform this action on this
resource, under these conditions?”

**Authorization Response** —the result of evaluating an authorization
request. It typically returns `allow` or `deny,` and may include metadata

that provides additional information, such as the reasoning used or the
policies that determined the decision.

**Satisfied Policies** are the set of policies whose conditions match the
context of the authorization request. These policies are considered during

evaluation and can influence the decision. However, not all satisfying
policies ultimately determine the outcome.

**Determining Policies** —the specific policies that directly influenced the
outcome of an authorization decision. These are the rules that caused the

system to return either `allow` or `deny` . Determining policies are a subset

of satisfying policies—they not only matched the request, but also played

a decisive role in producing the result.

These terms may seem somewhat dry at first glance, but they form the foundation for

everything that follows. Figure 4.1 shows the relationships between some of these terms.
Whether you’re writing policies, designing a system, or simply trying to understand how

someone gained access to something they shouldn’t have, having a clear and shared
vocabulary makes a significant difference.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

77

Figure 4.1 Relationships among key authorization terms. Principals, actions, and resources form the core of

access decisions and are enriched with attributes, roles, and group memberships. All entities exist within

namespaces and can be either principals or resources. The diagram also shows the legacy term subject as an

older equivalent of principal and illustrates how actions operate on resources based on contextual and

identity-based properties.

Using clear terminology allows teams to discuss authorization consistently and precisely,

which becomes even more crucial as systems grow in complexity. With our language
established, we can examine how these concepts come together in a typical authorization

architecture. Let's consider who makes the decisions, where they are enforced, and how
everything interconnects.

#### 4.4 Authorization reference architecture

To truly grasp how modern authorization systems are constructed, it’s beneficial to look

back at one of the earliest and most comprehensive efforts to shape their architecture:
XACML, which stands for the eXtensible Access Control Markup Language.

Back in the early 2000s, OASIS introduced XACML, and it was more than just a policy
language—it established a comprehensive model for making and enforcing access control

decisions! It really helped clarify the separation of concerns that many of our modern
systems still adhere to today. Specifically, XACML provided us with a clear architecture that

revolves around these four key components:

**Policy Enforcement Point (PEP)** —where access is intercepted and

checked
**Policy Decision Point (PDP)** —where policies are evaluated to reach a

decision

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

78

**Policy Administration Point (PAP)** —where policies are created and

managed
**Policy Information Point (PIP)** —a source of contextual data and

attributes

Although XACML—which uses verbose XML and can be quite complex to implement—hasn’t

become widely adopted in modern systems, its architectural model has made a significant
impact and has become a reference architecture for authorization systems.

WHAT IS A REFERENCE ARCHITECTURE?

_A reference architecture_ is a standardized, high-level design blueprint that outlines
the essential components, roles, and relationships in a specific type of system. It

does not prescribe a single implementation but instead provides a template or bestpractice guide for structuring systems to address a particular class of problems.

Reference architectures possess several important properties:

**Abstract yet actionable** : It identifies the necessary components (for example,

Policy Enforcement Point, Policy Decision Point) and explains their interactions,
illustrating their importance without dictating specific tools or code.

**Reusable across domains** : A reference architecture can be used in various
contexts (for example, cloud platforms, internal apps, APIs), offering a consistent

language for teams to design, build, and evaluate systems.

**Guides implementation** : It assists architects, engineers, and decision-makers in

aligning on how to break down responsibilities, reduce duplication, and enforce
consistent security or functional patterns.

Reference architectures provide a solid mental model that helps us discuss, analyze,
and understand IT systems.

Figure 4.2 illustrates the authorization reference architecture that we will use to discuss
authorization systems throughout the book. The terminology in this reference architecture

is widely used, and references to it can be found in system documentation, blog posts, and
even sales literature. Nowadays, we can see this clear separation of enforcement, decision
making, policy management, and attribute retrieval in systems like AWS Verified
Permissions, Open Policy Agent (OPA), and Aserto’s Topaz.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

79

Figure 4.2 Authorization reference architecture showing how access decisions are made. The Policy

Enforcement Point (PEP) intercepts Alice’s request to ACMEProject and sends it to the Policy Decision Point

(PDP). The PDP evaluates the request using policies from the Policy Administration Point (PAP), managed by

Carol, and retrieves context from the Policy Information Point (PIP), which sources attributes from systems

like identity providers, time servers, and network telemetry. The PDP returns a decision, which the PEP

enforces in real time.

In this section, we will explore how this reference architecture works, why it matters, and
how it relates to both legacy systems and today’s cloud-native applications.

4.4.1 How access decisions are made

Let’s say Alice is a project manager at ACME Corp. One evening, she logs into ACMEProject,
the company’s internal dashboard for project tracking and reporting, as shown in figure 4.2.

Managers like Alice use ACMEProject to review team progress, assign tasks, and generate
reports before key meetings. She clicks on the tab labeled Team Reports, hoping to review

progress updates before a morning meeting.

Alice opens the dashboard from her laptop at home and clicks on the Team Reports tab,

hoping to review her team’s weekly performance summary. That simple click kicks off a
sophisticated process behind the scenes.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

80

[The Policy Enforcement Point (PEP)—in this case, embedded in the application—](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-4?potentialInternalRefId=83---book-markup-container)

intercepts the request. It recognizes that Alice is trying to view a report, which is a
protected resource, and it needs to know: Is she allowed to do that right now, from this

device, in this context?

[The PEP sends the request to the Policy Decision Point (PDP), which is responsible for](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-4?potentialInternalRefId=84---book-markup-container)

evaluating access requests. The PDP reviews the key facts:

The principal is Alice.

The action is `view` .

The resource is a team report.

The conditions include the current time (9:17 PM), her device (companyissued laptop), and her network (home, not corporate).

But the PDP needs more information to make an informed decision. It turns to the Policy
Information Point (PIP). The PIP retrieves Alice’s attributes from the company’s identity

system: she’s in the Project Managers group, her current session originates from a
registered device, and her access to reports is typically allowed between 7 AM and 8 PM.

Now the PDP has what it needs. It checks the policies:

✅ Alice is in the right role.

✅ She’s using a trusted device.
❌ But it’s outside of approved hours.

The PDP returns a `deny` decision to the PEP, including the specific policy that prompted the

denial. Using the information about the decision, the application can display a helpful

message: “Access to team reports is restricted outside of working hours.”

To Alice, the system simply told her no. However, behind the scenes, that decision

resulted from a carefully orchestrated, policy-driven process involving the PEP, PDP, and PIP
—each playing a clear, well-defined role.

[This flow—intercept, evaluate, enrich, decide, enforce—lies at the heart of any effective,](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-4?potentialInternalRefId=96---book-markup-container)
policy-driven authorization system. It transforms identity and context into trustworthy, real
time decisions on which systems can rely.

4.4.2 Where policies come from

Meet Carol. She’s a security administrator at ACME Corp, responsible for defining and

managing access policies across the company’s internal systems. While Alice, a project
manager at ACME, reviews team dashboards and updates project timelines, Carol works

behind the scenes to ensure that only the right people can do the right things under the
right conditions.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

81

Carol doesn’t embed authorization logic into the application code. Instead, she writes

policies in a centralized management system—the Policy Administration Point (PAP) as
shown in figure 4.2. Here, policies are created, reviewed, versioned, and deployed much

like code. It’s also where policy changes can be tested and rolled out using familiar
software development workflows.

[Let’s say Carol wants to ensure that only users in the Project Managers group can access](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-4?potentialInternalRefId=100---book-markup-container)
the Team Reports section of ACMEProject—and only during working hours. She writes a

policy that captures this logic in a structured, declarative format using a language such as
Cedar. Here’s the policy Carol defined that denied Carol access outside work hours:

permit(

principal in Group::"ProjectManagers",

action == Action::"view",

resource in Report::"TeamReports"

) when {

context.time >= "07:00" && context.time <= "20:00"

};

Alice, as we noted in the previous section, is in the Project Managers group. This policy
applies directly to her—it determines whether her request to access team reports is allowed

based on the time and device she’s using.

Instead of pushing this change directly into production, Carol treats it like any other

software artifact. She commits the policy to version control, where it can be reviewed by a
teammate, tested against known scenarios, and audited as part of ACME Corp’s change

management process. The PAP encompasses all this functionality.

[Carol’s work in the PAP transforms evolving business rules into secure, versioned policy](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-4?potentialInternalRefId=104---book-markup-container)

logic that governs what users like Alice can do. This process supports agility without
sacrificing control.

[Once approved, the policy is deployed to production and used by the Policy Decision](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-4?potentialInternalRefId=105---book-markup-container)
Point (PDP), which employs it to evaluate real-time authorization requests, such as the one

Alice triggered earlier. Depending on the deployment model, the policy may take effect
immediately in a centralized PDP or after a short delay in distributed systems where PDPs

periodically pull updates or rely on cached policies.

[At ACME, managing authorization policies like software artifacts—written in a declarative](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-4?potentialInternalRefId=106---book-markup-container)

language, stored in version control, and reviewed through code workflows—has
transformed how access is governed. Policies are no longer hidden inside application logic

or buried in configuration files. They’re externalized, testable, auditable, and traceable—
making access control more reliable and adaptable to change.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

#### 4.5 Architecture patterns in practice

It’s one thing to define components like the PEP, PDP, and PIP on a whiteboard. It’s another

to figure out where they actually reside in a working system. At ACME Corp, as in most
real-world environments, the deployment of these components depends on factors such as

architecture, performance, trust boundaries, and organizational structure.

Let’s explore a few common patterns and how they come together in practice.

4.5.1 Embedded PEPs in applications and gateways

The Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) can be deployed in various ways, depending on where
enforcement is most effective within the system.

Figure 4.3 shows the PEP embedded directly in the application code. This is often the
most straightforward approach. For instance, when Alice clicks the Team Reports tab in

ACMEProject, the backend performs an inline access check by calling the PDP before
returning data. This check, initiated at the moment a sensitive action is requested, serves

as the application’s PEP, enforcing a policy decision.

Figure 4.3 The Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) embedded in application code. In this model, the PEP is

implemented directly within the ACMEProject backend, allowing it to evaluate access decisions with full

visibility into the application’s internal state and context.

Figure 4.4 shows the PEP situated in an API gateway, positioned before ACMEProject and
other internal services. Many organizations use gateways like Kong, AWS API Gateway, or

Envoy to centralize access control for multiple services. This approach enables uniform
policy enforcement with minimal changes to application code. Additionally, it provides

benefits such as centralized logging, auditing, and easier rollout of policy updates across
services.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

83

Figure 4.4 The Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) deployed in an API gateway. In this model, the PEP sits in front

of ACMEProject, intercepting and evaluating access requests before they reach the application. This approach

centralizes enforcement and simplifies policy updates across multiple services.

Figure 4.5 shows the PEP deployed in a sidecar container alongside the application
container within the same pod. This pattern, common in service mesh environments like

Istio, enables fine-grained control over service-to-service communication without modifying
the app itself. While Alice is shown accessing ACMEProject from outside, this sidecar pattern

also applies to internal microservice-to-microservice requests, ensuring that authorization
decisions are consistently enforced across components.

Figure 4.5 The Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) deployed as a sidecar. In this model, the PEP runs alongside

the application, typically within the same container or virtual machine (VM). This approach ensures that

policies are enforced locally at the service level, without altering the core application architecture.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

84

A service mesh is an infrastructure layer that manages how microservices communicate

with one another, handling tasks like routing, load balancing, service discovery, and security without
requiring changes to the services themselves. Rather than bake these responsibilities into

application code, the service mesh injects sidecar proxies alongside each service instance. These
proxies intercept all inbound and outbound traffic, enabling the mesh to enforce policies, encrypt

communication, and collect telemetry data transparently.

Each PEP deployment option shown in figures 4.3, 4.4, and 4.5 offers distinct trade-offs

concerning flexibility, operational complexity, and enforcement consistency. Table 4.1
summarizes these differences to help you evaluate which pattern best fits a given system.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

85

the necessity for centralized policy decisions.

|Deployment<br>model|Pros|Cons|Best used when?|
|---|---|---|---|
|Embedded in<br>application|Fine-grained control<br>Access to full<br>application context<br>Simple for single-<br>service apps|Repetition across<br>apps<br>Harder to update<br>uniformly|You need contextual<br>logic tied closely to<br>app behavior. When the PEP is embedded in application code, developers gain access to the full context of
the request, which facilitates fine-grained, dynamic access decisions. This is useful for apps

like ACMEProject, where access to specific UI elements or resource attributes may depend
on user roles, project assignments, or workflow status. However, this approach can result in

duplicated logic across services and makes centralizing policy updates more challenging.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

86

By contrast, placing the PEP in an API gateway provides a centralized enforcement point

for all incoming requests. This approach simplifies updates, standardizes checks across
services, and enables consistent logging and auditing—without altering application code.

However, API gateways operate at the perimeter of the system, which limits their ability to
make deeply contextual decisions that depend on the internal application state.

[Finally, deploying the PEP in a sidecar container, as seen in service mesh architectures,](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-4?potentialInternalRefId=124---book-markup-container)
enables policies to be enforced at the infrastructure level for all inbound and outbound

service traffic. This pattern facilitates microservice-to-microservice authorization and is
ideal for zero trust architectures; however, it introduces complexity regarding proxy

management, policy synchronization, and ensures that fresh context is available locally.

[No single option is best—each has its place. Many organizations use a combination of](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-4?potentialInternalRefId=125---book-markup-container)

these models, incorporating coarse-grained checks at the gateway with more contextual
logic in the app or mesh. The key is to understand your system’s trust boundaries,

performance requirements, and policy lifecycle needs.

4.5.2 Centralized PDPs

The Policy Decision Point (PDP) is the component responsible for evaluating access requests

against a defined set of policies. At ACME Corp, several internal applications—including
ACMEProject, ACMEHR, and ACMEFinance—use a centralized PDP to manage authorization

decisions. As illustrated in figure 4.6, each application has its own Policy Enforcement Point
(PEP), which forwards requests to the shared PDP.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

87

Figure 4.6 Centralized authorization architecture at ACME Corp. Multiple application-specific PEPs send

access requests to a shared PDP, which evaluates them using policies authored and managed by Carol in the

PAP. This approach centralizes decision-making and simplifies policy updates, but it introduces potential

availability concerns.

This centralized architecture offers a single source of truth for authorization logic. When
Carol, ACME’s security administrator, updates a policy via the Policy Administration Point

(PAP), the PDP immediately begins using the new rules to evaluate access requests across
all connected applications. This streamlines policy management, enhances consistency, and

centralizes logging and auditing.

However, there’s a trade-off. Since all PEPs rely on the same PDP, any latency, failure, or

unavailability in the decision service can degrade the performance of all dependent
systems. In high-scale or latency-sensitive environments, this dependency might be a

concern, requiring careful design for availability, caching, or fallback strategies.

4.5.3 Distributing authorization decisions

As ACME Corp’s systems become more distributed, the limitations of a centralized PDP may

become more pronounced. Applications that require low latency, high availability, or
localized decision-making often benefit from a distributed authorization model. In this

model, each application or service includes its own authorization client—a bundled
component that manages authorization requests locally by integrating the Policy

Enforcement Point (PEP), Policy Decision Point (PDP), and a local entity cache. This setup is
illustrated in figure 4.7.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

88

Figure 4.7 Distributed authorization architecture at ACME Corp. Each service includes an authorization client

—a bundled component that contains the PEP, PDP, and an entity cache. The client may be deployed as a

sidecar (ACMEFinance), as a library within application code (ACMEProject), or integrated into an API gateway

(ACMEHR). Policies are authored and managed by Carol via the Policy Administration Point (PAP) and then

distributed to each client. Contextual data is retrieved from shared Policy Information Points (PIPs), such as

identity stores, time servers, and network telemetry, and is cached inside the client.

These authorization clients can be deployed in the same ways that the PEP was deployed,

depending on the architecture of the service. At ACME Corp, they appear as:

Integrated into an API gateway (for example, ACMEHR)

A library embedded directly into the application (for example,
ACMEProject)

A sidecar container running alongside the app in a pod (for example,
ACMEFinance)

Regardless of the deployment model, the authorization client is responsible for intercepting
requests, evaluating them against the policy, and enforcing the outcome—all performed

locally and with minimal latency.

Carol still authors policies centrally in the Policy Administration Point (PAP). These are

distributed to each PDP as part of a versioned policy management workflow.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

89

[The PDP needs more than just the policy to evaluate requests effectively; it also needs](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-4?potentialInternalRefId=140---book-markup-container)

contextual data: attributes about the principal (such as Alice’s role or department), the
resource (for example, classification or ownership), and the environment (including time of

day or network risk level). This data is retrieved from Policy Information Points (PIPs),
which may include identity providers, databases, time servers, or telemetry services.

[To avoid fetching this data with every request, each authorization client maintains an](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-4?potentialInternalRefId=141---book-markup-container)
entity cache—a local store of attributes for principals and resources. These caches are

periodically refreshed from the PIPs, allowing the PDP to make decisions quickly and
independently.

[This distributed approach enhances resilience, performance, and scalability. It also aligns](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-4?potentialInternalRefId=142---book-markup-container)
well with modern deployment models, such as microservices, edge computing, and zero

trust. The trade-off is increased operational complexity: caches must remain fresh, policy
synchronization needs to be reliable, and the behavior of PDPs must stay consistent across

deployments.

FIELD GUIDE: DESIGNING AN AUTHORIZATION ARCHITECTURE

When choosing how to structure authorization in your systems, keep these guiding

questions in mind:

Where should enforcement happen? At the edge (API gateway)? In the

app? Between services (sidecar)?

Choose based on trust boundaries and granularity of

control.

How close should decision-making be to the application?

Centralized PDPs offer consistency and auditability.
Distributed PDPs reduce latency and improve resilience.

What context is needed to make decisions?

Identify required attributes: user roles, resource

ownership, environment conditions.
Plan where that context lives and how it gets to the

PDP (real-time or cached?).

How will policies be authored and deployed?

Use version control and CI/CD for policies.
Prefer declarative, testable formats (policy-as-code).

What needs to be logged and audited?

Centralize logs where possible.

Use a consistent schema.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

90

How will you handle outages and staleness?

Design for graceful degradation: cache policies and
context where needed.

Monitor for drift between distributed components.

There’s no single correct deployment, but there is a correct fit for each use case. Align

architectural decisions with your system’s goals for security, speed, scale, and simplicity.

4.5.4 Choosing the right pattern

There is no one-size-fits-all architecture. At ACME Corp, centralized PDPs are employed for

internal business applications where consistency and auditability are crucial. In contrast,
distributed PDPs—embedded within authorization clients—power latency-sensitive services

like ACMEFinance and ACMEProject, where local decision-making is essential. PEPs are
strategically placed in application code, API gateways, or service mesh sidecars, depending

on performance, visibility, and trust boundary requirements.

The goal isn’t to rigidly follow a single model but rather to select the right balance of

performance, reliability, observability, and control for each system. Whether centralized or
distributed, embedded or sidecar-based, the core pattern remains the same: intercept the

request, enrich it with context, evaluate it against policy, and enforce the decision.

[Whether centralized or distributed, embedded or external, these patterns are shaped by](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-4?potentialInternalRefId=166---book-markup-container)

a deeper principle: the separation of concerns in authorization architecture. Understanding
why this separation exists is as crucial as understanding how the components fit together.

4.5.5 Why this separation matters

At first glance, separating enforcement, decision-making, policy management, and data
sourcing may seem like overengineering. Wouldn’t it be easier to simply check permissions

directly in the app?

The problem is that’s what most systems did for decades. And it worked—until it didn’t.

[As systems became more distributed, dynamic, and regulated, embedding access logic in](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-4?potentialInternalRefId=170---book-markup-container)
application code or relying on hardcoded role checks became a liability. This approach led to

brittle, fragmented systems where authorization rules were duplicated across services,
making them difficult to update and nearly impossible to audit.

[The architecture we’ve explored—separating the Policy Enforcement Point (PEP), Policy](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-4?potentialInternalRefId=171---book-markup-container)
Decision Point (PDP), Policy Administration Point (PAP), and Policy Information Point (PIP)—

emerged to address precisely those challenges.

[Here’s why this separation matters:](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-4?potentialInternalRefId=172---book-markup-container)

Maintainability: Policies can be updated independently of application code.
When Carol updates the access rules for ACMEProject, developers don’t

need to deploy new builds or touch code at all.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

91

Consistency: The same policy can be applied consistently across multiple

applications and services, ensuring uniform behavior and minimizing drift.
Transparency: Authorization decisions can be traced back to specific

policies and contextual data, which enhances auditability and trust.
Scalability: The ability to distribute PDPs and entity caches allows

systems to grow without encountering a single bottleneck or central point
of failure.

Security: Keeping access control logic distinct from business logic limits
the blast radius of bugs, reduces attack surfaces, and supports defense
in-depth.

In short, separating these concerns transforms authorization from a code-level detail into a

platform capability. It converts access control into something that can be reasoned about,
tested, managed, and governed, just like any other critical part of the system.

#### 4.6 From architecture to models

While authorization is ultimately a yes-or-no decision, it also represents the system-level

expression of relationships, roles, responsibilities, and context. In this chapter, we explored
what makes authorization distinct from authentication, introduced the PARC model, and

examined the architecture that supports dynamic, policy-based access control. Whether
decisions are centralized for consistency or distributed for performance, the pattern

remains the same: intercept the request, enrich it with context, evaluate it against policy,
and enforce the result.

With that foundation in place, we’re ready to explore how systems define who gets
access to what. In the next chapter, we will examine the most common authorization

models—from access control lists to roles to attributes—and how each one influences the
design, enforcement, and understanding of policies.

#### 4.7 Summary

Authorization defines what an authenticated principal can do, under which

conditions, and with what resources. This discipline is separate from
authentication and plays a crucial role in security, compliance, and user

experience.
Authorization not only protects resources but also governs interactions

between entities based on the terms of their digital relationships.
The PARC model— _p_ rincipal, _a_ ction, _r_ esource, and _c_ onditions—offers a

clear and flexible framework for describing access decisions.
Terms like policy, role, attribute, and entitlement form the foundation of

modern authorization systems and foster a shared understanding across
teams.

The authorization reference architecture delineates the responsibilities of
enforcement, decision-making, policy management, and context retrieval,

thereby enhancing system maintainability, auditability, and security.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

Deployment patterns vary depending on system architecture; PEPs, PDPs,

and entity caches can be embedded, centralized, or distributed based on
performance, trust boundaries, and operational requirements.

Separating concerns among PEPs, PDPs, PAPs, and PIPs allows systems to
scale, maintain consistency, and respond flexibly to evolving business and

regulatory needs.
