## Static authorization models

This chapter covers

Distinguishing static versus dynamic authorization models

Managing permissions with Access Control Lists (ACLs)

Assigning access through Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)

Mapping ACLs and RBAC to the reference architecture components

Evaluating the strengths and limitations of static models

Identifying where ACLs and RBAC still make sense in modern systems

When ACME Corp launched its first SaaS product, authorization was an afterthought. With a

handful of developers and a few early customers, it was easy to hardcode access to the
admin dashboard and restrict sensitive features to known team members. Everyone had

access to staging environments, and customer data was stored in separate folders,
protected more by convention than by control.

As the company grew—from a scrappy startup to a fast-scaling enterprise—its access
control needs became more complex. Contractors needed limited access to customer

support tools. Sales reps required region-based access to accounts. Engineering teams
asked for staging environments with access scoped by project. Support teams needed the

ability to debug customer issues without compromising security. And Finance needed a
better understanding of access for regulatory compliance.

[In the absence of a structured system, developers responded the only way they could:](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-5?potentialInternalRefId=9---book-markup-container)
by adding custom if-then conditionals. These conditionals crept into APIs, databases, and

front-end logic. Some were based on email domains, others on team assignments in a
database, and still others on temporary configuration flags.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

94

What started as a few simple checks grew into a sprawling web of undocumented logic.

Access decisions varied across services, and exceptions became the norm. When auditors
finally arrived to assess compliance, no one could provide a clear answer to a simple

question: who has access to what, and why?

[ACME Corp’s journey is far from unique. Most organizations begin with basic access](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-5?potentialInternalRefId=11---book-markup-container)

controls and scale their way into complexity. The good news? Established models exist that
provide structure, repeatability, and control—models that can tame the sprawl and support

the growth of any digital system.

In practice, most organizations don’t rely on a single access control model; they often use a

mix, sometimes by design, sometimes by necessity. Access rules may be based on roles in one
system, attributes in another, and relationships in yet another. Some decisions are enforced by

centralized policy engines, while others are hardcoded for historical reasons or dictated by the
constraints of SaaS applications. Understanding these models isn’t about picking the “right” one, but

rather knowing how to work across all of them.

We categorize these models as either static or dynamic, based on how they evaluate

authorization decisions. Static models rely on predefined rules tied to identities or roles.
They are easy to understand and efficient to evaluate, but they don’t account for changing

conditions, relationships, or context at runtime. Dynamic models, on the other hand,
incorporate attributes, context, and policies that can adapt to the moment, making them

more flexible but also more complex.

This chapter discusses two foundational static authorization models: Access Control Lists

(ACLs) and Role-Based Access Control (RBAC). These models are deeply embedded in the
infrastructure of modern systems and continue to play a critical role in many real-world

environments. The next chapter will explore dynamic authorization models that evaluate
access based on context, environmental conditions, and entity relationships.

You’ll often see models such as ACL, RBAC, and ABAC described as access control models.
That’s the traditional term, particularly in security and operating system contexts. In this book, we

refer to them as authorization models to emphasize their role in determining which actions are
allowed—especially in the context of externalized, policy-driven systems. The underlying concepts

remain the same; the shift in terminology reflects a broader view of how modern systems make
access decisions.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

95

#### 5.1 Access Control Lists (ACL)

Access Control Lists are one of the earliest and most straightforward methods for managing

authorization. They attach permissions directly to resources, specifying which users or
groups can perform certain actions. This approach is simple and intuitive, and remains

widely used in file systems, network shares, and legacy applications. But as organizations
grow and access needs become more dynamic, the limitations of ACLs quickly become

evident.

To see how ACLs work in practice, consider a familiar scenario. At ACME Corp, Alice

manages the marketing team and maintains a shared folder of campaign plans on the
company’s internal file server. She wants her team to be able to read the documents but

not edit them. Meanwhile, Bob, a fellow manager in Product, is collaborating with marketing
on a new launch and needs both read and write access to the campaign plans.

[To manage this strategy, Alice creates the folder and sets its permissions. She doesn’t](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-5?potentialInternalRefId=21---book-markup-container)
know it, but she’s created an Access Control List (ACL):

Alice: read, write
Marketing team: read

Bob: read, write
Everyone else: no access

Each time someone tries to open the folder or a file inside it, the system checks the ACL to
decide whether to allow the requested action. Access is determined by the list attached to

the folder, not by a centralized policy or the principal’s organizational role. As the
permissions that Alice has set demonstrate, that list can reference organizations, not just

individuals.

Just like a bouncer checking names at the door of a private party, an ACL serves as a

guest list associated with the resource. The list doesn’t care who you are within the broader
organization; it only matters whether your name is on the list and what type of access

you’ve been granted. Alice might be the head of marketing, but if her name isn’t on the
ACL, she won’t get in.

[Access Control Lists (ACLs) are a foundational authorization model where permissions](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-5?potentialInternalRefId=28---book-markup-container)
are assigned directly to the resources being protected. Each resource—whether a file,

database record, or network share—has an associated list that specifies which principals
can access it and what operations they’re allowed to perform.

[An ACL is essentially a table attached to a resource, where each entry includes:](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-5?potentialInternalRefId=29---book-markup-container)

Principal: the user or group the rule applies to

Permissions: the actions that the principal is allowed (or denied) to
perform

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

96

This model is _resource-centric_ —access control logic is stored with the resource itself, rather

than being maintained in a centralized policy or identity system. When a principal tries to
perform an action, the system checks the ACL on the resource to determine if that action is

permitted.

Figure 5.1 illustrates this model: a shared folder containing marketing campaign plans is

protected by an ACL that lists Alice, Bob, and the Marketing team, along with their
respective permissions. The ACL is evaluated at the time of access based solely on what is

listed for each principal.

Figure 5.1 An Access Control List (ACL) attached to a shared resource. The ACL specifies which principals—

such as Alice, Bob, and the Marketing group—are authorized to access the “Marketing Campaign Plans”

folder and outlines the actions they are allowed to perform.

When Alice tries to write to the folder, she’s allowed. Similarly, when Bob tries to read from
the folder, he’s allowed. However, Carol, who is not on the Marketing team, is not allowed

to read from the folder.

ACLs are well-suited to environments where resource ownership is clear and relatively

static or where the permission set is pre-determined and fixed. They remain widely used in
operating systems, file systems, and legacy applications where simple, direct access control

is sufficient.

UNIX PERMISSIONS: A SIMPLIFIED ACL

Before modern access control systems evolved, Unix provided one of the earliest and
most widely adopted forms of resource-based access control. Although it doesn’t use

the term _Access Control List,_ the Unix file permission model is conceptually a very
simple form of an ACL.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

97

5.1.1 How ACLs work

As shown in the previous section, Access Control Lists attach permissions directly to the
resource they protect. This could be a file, a database record, a network share, a cloud

storage object, or even a REST API endpoint. The ACL for ACME Corp’s Marketing Campaign
Plans folder, for instance, lists specific principals—Alice, Bob, and the Marketing team—

alongside the actions each is allowed to perform. When someone attempts to access the
folder, the system simply checks the list.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

98

Here’s how it works in practice: imagine Bob from the Product team tries to open a

folder containing marketing plans. The system locates the ACL attached to the folder and
checks for an entry for Bob. If the list shows that Bob is allowed to read and write, the

action proceeds. If there’s no matching entry or the entry denies the requested action,
access is blocked. For example, in figure 5.1, Bob is allowed to read but not write; there’s

an entry for Bob, but if he tries to do anything other than read the folder, the action will be
denied.

[Similarly, imagine that Doug, a member of the Marketing team, tries to access a](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-5?potentialInternalRefId=54---book-markup-container)
document in the folder. Even though he is not explicitly mentioned, his membership in a

group, the Marketing team, allows him to read or write documents. The decision depends
entirely on whether the ACL explicitly authorizes the principal’s action on that resource.

[Most ACL systems follow this basic pattern, though implementation details may vary:](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-5?potentialInternalRefId=55---book-markup-container)

Some support both Allow and Deny entries, which may be evaluated

sequentially or give precedence to deny rules.
Others permit entries for groups or wildcards, providing broader

permissions without listing every individual.
Advanced implementations, such as Windows NTFS, support inheritance,

where child resources or subordinate objects inherit permissions from
parent folders or containers. This introduces a hierarchical structure to

ACLs, enabling more efficient access management across nested
resources.

ACLs are typically evaluated at authorization time, just before a resource is accessed—
whether that means opening a file, retrieving a database record, or executing a command.

The system performs a synchronous, binary check: does the ACL for this resource allow this
principal to perform this action?

What unifies all ACL-based systems is their resource-centric logic. Each decision depends
solely on the identity of the requestor and the list of permissions attached to the resource,

not on external attributes or policies. This makes ACLs fast and easy to reason about
locally, but increasingly difficult to manage at scale.

5.1.2 Mapping ACLs onto the authorization reference architecture

Even though ACLs are one of the oldest authorization models, they still map cleanly onto
the components of the reference architecture introduced in chapter 4. Because ACLs are

often embedded directly in the resource or application, the architecture is usually tightly
coupled, but the roles of enforcement, decision-making, and data sourcing are still present.

Table 5.1 shows how each of the four core components—PEP, PDP, PAP, and PIP—is typically
realized in an ACL-based system.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

99

Table 5.1 Mapping ACLs onto the authorization reference architecture. Each component has a place in ACL
based systems, even if they’re not always separated in practice.

|Component|What it does|How ACLs implement it|
|---|---|---|
|Policy Enforcement Point<br>(PEP)|Intercepts access requests<br>and enforces the decision|Typically, the application or<br>resource itself (for example,<br>file system, database, service)|
|Policy Decision Point<br>(PDP)|Determines whether the<br>requested action is allowed|Usually, embedded logic that<br>checks the ACL attached to<br>the resource|
|Policy Administration<br>Point (PAP)|Manages and stores roles,<br>permissions, and<br>assignments|Often local to each resource<br>(for example, filesystem<br>metadata, in-resource access<br>list, or admin interface)|
|Policy Information Point<br>(PIP)|Supplies user and role data<br>to the PDP at runtime|Commonly derived from the<br>identity context passed to the<br>system (for example, OS user<br>ID, authenticated principal)|

In most ACL-based systems, these components are not explicitly separated. The resource
often acts as both PAP and PDP—storing its own access list and enforcing decisions based

on it. The PIP is minimal, usually just resolving the current user’s identity or group
membership. While simple and efficient, this tight coupling can make ACLs difficult to scale

across distributed systems or centralize for governance.

5.1.3 Strengths and limitations of ACLs

Access Control Lists have stood the test of time for a reason: they’re simple, direct, and

easy to understand. Because ACLs attach permissions directly to the resource, it’s usually
clear who can access what. That clarity can be valuable in small environments or systems

with a strong ownership model.

However, this simplicity comes at a cost. As the number of users and resources grows,

managing permissions individually becomes unmanageable. Table 5.2 summarizes the most
common strengths and limitations of ACLs. This comparison highlights why ACLs remain

appealing in some contexts but are problematic in others, especially as systems scale and
require more adaptive access decisions.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

100

Table 5.2 Strengths and limitations of Access Control Lists (ACLs)

|Strengths|Limitations|
|---|---|
|Easy to understand and implement|Becomes difficult to manage in large,<br>complex environments|
|Permissions are local and transparent|No centralized or global view of access|
|Fine-grained control on individual resources|Hard to apply consistent policies across<br>many resources|
|Fast to evaluate at runtime|High administrative overhead in dynamic<br>environments|
|Familiar and widely supported in legacy<br>systems|Not well-suited to modern, scalable access<br>control|
|Predictable and deterministic access<br>decisions|Inflexible—doesn’t support contextual or<br>conditional access|

In short, ACLs work well when access control needs are relatively static, local, and clear,

especially in systems that support inheritance or hierarchical scoping to reduce repetitive
configuration. However, as systems evolve—supporting multiple users, teams, tenants, or

compliance constraints—organizations quickly discover that managing permissions in this
manner becomes brittle and error-prone.

Importantly, ACLs evaluate access solely based on the principal’s identity (or their group
membership) and the permissions listed in the ACL. They do not consider additional

context, such as time of day, device posture, network zone, or other environmental signals.
This simplicity makes them efficient and predictable, but it also makes them inflexible in

environments where access decisions must adapt to changing conditions.

[These limitations often lead organizations to adopt more flexible access control models—](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-5?potentialInternalRefId=71---book-markup-container)

ones that can express broader policies, adapt to dynamic context, and scale more
effectively as complexity grows.

5.1.4 Where ACLs still make sense

Despite their limitations, ACLs remain widely used in real systems, and for good reason. In
the right context, their simplicity and directness can be strengths, not weaknesses. ACLs

are especially well-suited to environments where:

The set of resources is clearly defined and comparatively stable.

The number of principals is small or bounded.
Ownership and access boundaries are clear.

Policy complexity is low.

Many common tools and platforms still use ACLs as their primary or default authorization

model:

Operating systems such as Unix and Windows use ACLs to manage access

to files, directories, and devices.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

101

Network storage systems (e.g., NFS, SMB) use ACLs to control access to

shared drives and folders.
Databases like PostgreSQL and MySQL use ACL-style grant statements to

assign privileges to users and roles for specific tables or schemas.
Messaging platforms such as RabbitMQ and Kafka often use ACLs to

control who can publish to or consume from specific topics or queues.
Cloud services like Google Cloud Storage and Azure Files continue to

provide ACL-based models for fine-grained permissions on storage
objects, even while also supporting more advanced IAM policies.

ACLs also work well in single-user or small-team applications, where adding a full role or
policy engine would introduce more complexity than it’s worth. In such cases, ACLs provide

transparency, speed, and direct control.

Ultimately, ACLs are not obsolete; they’re just specialized. When used in the appropriate

context, they provide a solid foundation for access control, particularly in systems where
the overhead of more dynamic models isn’t justified.

5.1.5 When ACLs fall short

As organizations grow, their systems and associated access control needs become more
complex. Managing access on a per-resource, per-principal basis doesn’t scale well when

there are hundreds or thousands of users and resources with nuanced access scenarios.
Adding or removing access for even a single person can require updating multiple separate

lists. More importantly, it becomes challenging to maintain visibility and control—especially
when auditing access decisions is a regulatory, accreditation, or security requirement.

Without a unified approach to manage and reason about access, ensuring compliance and
demonstrating that the right people have the right access at the right time becomes nearly

impossible.

More importantly, ACLs lack a method to express why someone has access. They record

what someone can do with a specific resource, but they do not provide the business
rationale for that access. For example, is Doug permitted to edit the campaign folder

because he’s on the marketing team, or due to a temporary collaboration? The ACL doesn’t
say—it only lists permissions.

[These challenges create pressure to adopt access control models that accommodate](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-5?potentialInternalRefId=89---book-markup-container)
organizational complexity while remaining manageable. One widely accepted approach is

role-based access control (RBAC), which introduces the concept of roles—bundles of
permissions tied to job functions or responsibilities. Roles enable more consistent

assignment and management of access, even as systems and teams expand.

[In the next section, we’ll explore RBAC in detail, including how it helps organizations](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-5?potentialInternalRefId=90---book-markup-container)

simplify access management while preserving alignment with business logic.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

102

#### 5.2 Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)

After struggling to manage a tangle of ACLs and hardcoded exceptions, ACME Corp’s

identity team decided it was time for a more structured approach to authorization. Their
first step was to define a handful of roles that accurately reflected the company’s

operational structure. Roles such as `customer-support`, `support-lead`, `engineer`, and

`senior-engineer` became the building blocks of access across the organization.

Instead of assigning permissions directly to users or adding names to lists on each
resource, ACME began assigning permissions to roles and roles to people. Now, when a new

support rep joins the team, granting access to tools and data is as simple as assigning the
`customer-support` role. If someone changes jobs, their access changes when their role

changes—there's no need to hunt down every ACL they are listed on.

[Figure 5.2 shows how ACME Corp uses RBAC to assign users to roles, assign roles to](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-5?potentialInternalRefId=94---book-markup-container)

permissions, and define role hierarchies that reflect organizational structure.

Figure 5.2 Users are assigned to roles like engineer, senior-engineer, or support-lead, which define

what permissions they receive. Some roles inherit from others, allowing access to be layered and managed

through organizational structure.

RBAC didn’t eliminate all complexity, but it created a layer of abstraction and consistency
that facilitated the company's growth. It also provided auditors with something they had

never had before: a clear, centralized picture of who could do what and why.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

103

As shown in figure 5.2, RBAC introduces a level of indirection that makes authorization

easier to understand and manage. By assigning permissions to roles instead of individual
users, organizations can centralize access logic and align it with their internal structure.

Role hierarchies further reduce duplication and facilitate the expression of progressive
levels of responsibility. Though RBAC does not eliminate complexity, it offers a scalable

foundation, especially when linked to identity lifecycle events such as hiring, promotions, or
role changes.

[In Access Control Lists (ACLs), permissions are attached directly to the resource, listing](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-5?potentialInternalRefId=98---book-markup-container)
the specific principals allowed to perform certain actions. In Role-Based Access Control

(RBAC), the model shifts: permissions are no longer granted to individual principals or
teams for specific resources but to _roles_ —that is, named collections of permissions that

reflect job functions or organizational responsibilities. Principals are then assigned to one or
more roles, gaining access indirectly through those assignments. This separation between

identity and permission makes it easier to manage access at scale and keeps authorization
logic aligned with the organization’s structure.

[Rather than maintain separate access rules for each user, an RBAC system defines a set](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-5?potentialInternalRefId=99---book-markup-container)
of roles that reflect real-world job functions—such as `engineer`, `customer-support`, or

`support-lead` —and assigns permissions to those roles. Users are then granted one or more

roles based on their responsibilities. This approach simplifies change management: when a

user changes roles, their access is updated automatically.

[RBAC also supports role hierarchies, where one role can inherit the permissions of](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-5?potentialInternalRefId=100---book-markup-container)

another. This is useful for modeling organizational seniority or layered responsibilities. For
instance, the `senior-engineer` role might inherit permissions from the `engineer` role and

add elevated privileges, such as deploying code to production. Role inheritance provides
greater control of, and visibility into, access decisions by reducing the number of roles

principals have.

5.2.1 How RBAC works

At runtime, an RBAC system determines whether a user is allowed to perform a particular

action by evaluating their assigned roles and the permissions associated with those roles.
The system doesn’t check whether the user has direct access to the resource—it checks

whether one of their roles grants the necessary permission.

When a user makes a request, the system typically performs the following steps:

1. Identify the user (principal) making the request.
2. Determine the roles assigned to that user.

3. Retrieve the permissions associated with those roles.
4. Check whether any of those permissions permits the requested action.

If the requested action is among the permissions granted by one or more of the user’s
roles, the request is allowed. Otherwise, it’s denied.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

104

As mentioned earlier, RBAC systems often include role hierarchies, where one role

inherits the permissions of another. In these cases, the evaluation logic must resolve
inherited roles and combine all relevant permissions before making a decision.

[RBAC systems may also enforce separation of duty (SoD) constraints, which prevent](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-5?potentialInternalRefId=110---book-markup-container)
users from holding conflicting roles. For instance, we don’t want one person to have both

the `payment-initiator` and the `payment-approver` roles. These constraints help limit the

risk of fraud or abuse, especially in regulated or high-stakes environments.

[Table 5.3 shows how ACME Corp makes authorization decisions using the roles and](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-5?potentialInternalRefId=111---book-markup-container)
permissions defined in figure 5.2. Each decision is based not on individual user-to-resource

mappings, but on whether the user’s assigned role(s)—and any inherited roles—contain the
required permission.

[Table 5.3 Sample authorization decisions using RBAC. This table presents scenarios related to the RBAC](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-5?potentialInternalRefId=112---book-markup-container)

permissions shown in figure 5.2. Each decision is based on the roles assigned to a principal and the

permissions granted through those roles or their inherited roles.

|Scenario|Principal|Requested<br>Action|Decision|Reason|
|---|---|---|---|---|
|Can Bob<br>approve a code<br>check-in?|Bob|approve-code-<br>check-in|✅ Allowed|Bob has theengineer<br>role, which includes this<br>permission.|
|Can Alice<br>approve a code<br>check-in?|Alice|approve-code-<br>check-in|✅ Allowed|senior-engineer<br>inherits fromengineer,<br>so Alice inherits the<br>permission.|
|Can Alice<br>deploy to<br>production?|Alice|deploy-to-<br>production|✅ Allowed|senior-engineer grants<br>this permission directly.|
|Can Bob deploy<br>to production?|Bob|deploy-to-<br>production|❌ Denied|engineer does not grant<br>this permission.|
|Can Carol view<br>tickets?|Carol|view-tickets|✅ Allowed|support-lead inherits<br>fromcustomer-support,<br>which grants this<br>permission.|
|Can Carol<br>delete tickets?|Carol|delete-tickets|✅ Allowed|support-lead grants this<br>permission directly.|
|Can Bob delete<br>tickets?|Bob|delete-tickets|❌ Denied|engineer has no ticketing<br>roles; no permission<br>granted.|

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

105

As the scenarios in table 5.3 illustrate, RBAC enables consistent and predictable

authorization decisions by abstracting permissions through roles. Instead of scattering
authorization logic across individual services or hardcoding rules in applications,

organizations can depend on a centralized role structure that reflects how work is
organized. While RBAC doesn’t support dynamic conditions like time of day or device

posture, its simplicity and alignment with organizational structure make it a dependable
choice in many environments, especially when paired with well-governed role definitions

and assignment processes.

ARE GROUPS THE SAME AS ROLES?

At first glance, groups and roles may look interchangeable—they both represent

collections of users, and both can be used to assign permissions. But while they’re
closely related, they serve different purposes and come from different parts of the

system architecture.

Groups are collections of identifiers that are used to organize identity; for instance,

assigning users to various departments or teams in an identity provider such as
LDAP or Active Directory.

Roles are designed to express authorization logic: which actions someone can
perform and in what context.

In practice, groups and roles often interact. A group like engineering might map
directly to a role, such as engineer, or it might be used to dynamically determine role

assignment. Some systems even treat groups as roles, blurring the line entirely.

RBAC adds more structure than simple group-based access:

Roles link to permission sets, while groups usually do not.
RBAC supports role hierarchies and separation of duty constraints.

Roles often have governance processes, while groups are more often
managed informally.

Bottom line: all roles are groups, but not all groups are roles. Groups might be used
to assign roles, but they aren’t roles themselves. RBAC builds on the idea of

grouping to introduce a more formal, policy-aligned way of managing access.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

106

5.2.2 Mapping RBAC onto the authorization reference architecture

RBAC naturally aligns with the authorization reference architecture introduced in chapter 4.
While the core ideas remain the same—evaluate a request, decide whether it’s allowed, and

enforce the outcome—the way each component is implemented can vary widely depending
on the scale and maturity of the system.

Table 5.4 shows how the core components of the architecture—PEP, PDP, PAP, and PIP—
are generally realized in an RBAC model. In smaller systems, these components are often

closely integrated with the application that enforces access, evaluates permissions, and
retrieves role assignments within the same codebase. In larger or more mature

environments, RBAC responsibilities may be externalized into shared libraries or centralized
services, or integrated with enterprise identity systems.

[Table 5.4 Mapping RBAC onto the authorization reference architecture. Each architectural component plays a](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-5?potentialInternalRefId=127---book-markup-container)

unique role in authorization. This table illustrates how RBAC systems generally implement each component,

along with notes on common variations.

|Component|What it does|How RBAC implements it|
|---|---|---|
|Policy Enforcement Point<br>(PEP)|Intercepts access requests<br>and enforces the decision|Usually embedded in<br>application code, API gateway,<br>or middleware|
|Policy Decision Point<br>(PDP)|Determines whether the<br>requested action is allowed|Often, a function or module<br>that checks whether the user’s<br>role includes the required<br>permission; may be<br>embedded, shared as a<br>library, or centralized as a<br>service|
|Policy Administration<br>Point (PAP)|Manages and stores roles,<br>permissions, and<br>assignments|Roles and mappings stored in<br>a database, LDAP/AD<br>directory, config files, or<br>managed through an admin UI<br>or an infrastructure-as-code<br>(IaC) system like Terraform|
|Policy Information Point<br>(PIP)|Supplies user and role data<br>to the PDP at runtime|Role data often comes from<br>identity provider, database<br>lookup, or session context|

RBAC’s simplicity and architectural versatility aren’t just a convenience—they’re one of the

reasons RBAC has endured. By cleanly separating concerns, RBAC enables the evolution
from tightly coupled, application-level logic to enterprise-grade, externalized authorization

services without altering the core model. Whether permissions are enforced inline or roles
are defined using infrastructure as code, the RBAC pattern remains recognizable,

adaptable, and effective.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

107

5.2.3 Strengths and limitations of RBAC

RBAC has remained one of the most widely used authorization models for good reason: it
offers a balance of structure, clarity, and operational efficiency. By aligning access with

organizational roles, it supports scalable management and improves both auditability and
communication across teams. However, like any model, RBAC has its tradeoffs. It works

best in environments with relatively stable responsibilities and clear functional boundaries—
and is less effective when access needs are dynamic, contextual, or highly individualized.

Table 5.5 summarizes the most common strengths and limitations of RBAC in practice.

Table 5.5 Strengths and limitations of role-based access control. RBAC offers clarity and manageability,

especially in structured environments. But it can struggle with exceptions, fine-grained needs, and dynamic

|conditions.|Col2|
|---|---|
|**Strengths**|**Limitations**|
|Maps access to roles rather than just<br>organizational structure|Struggles in fast-changing or highly<br>dynamic organizations|
|Easy to understand and communicate|Can become complex with too many<br>narrowly scoped roles|
|Centralizes permission management via<br>roles|Hard to manage exceptions and one-off<br>access needs|
|Scales well for onboarding and job changes|Requires manual updates when<br>responsibilities don’t align cleanly with roles|
|Supports separation of duty constraints|Doesn’t support runtime context like time,<br>location, or device|
|Roles can be versioned and managed as<br>code|Lacks fine-grained control over specific<br>resources|

As the table shows, RBAC shines in environments where responsibilities are well-defined

and relatively stable. It offers a clear mental model that aligns with how organizations
operate, making access control easier to manage, explain, and audit. The indirection

through roles simplifies onboarding and offboarding and supports governance features like
separation of duty constraints.

However, RBAC has its limitations. It doesn’t consider dynamic factors such as the time
of day, network location, or device posture. When access requirements do not align neatly

with predefined roles, organizations may create overly granular roles or depend on
exceptions—both of which undermine the clarity that RBAC is intended to provide. While

roles can be managed in a declarative manner using infrastructure as code, RBAC remains
fundamentally a static model. As systems become more complex, many organizations

discover that they require more adaptive and fine-grained approaches.

5.2.4 Where RBAC still makes sense

Despite its limitations, RBAC remains a reliable choice in many settings. Its structure and

predictability are especially beneficial when roles and responsibilities are stable and when
access needs closely align with organizational boundaries.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

108

RBAC works well in:

Enterprise systems with clearly defined job roles—such as `finance-`

`analyst`, `hr-admin`, `or sales-manager,` as long as fine-grained

authorization isn’t required.
Internal tools used by employees whose access needs are linked to their

job functions and remain consistent over time.
Regulated environments, where auditability and separation of duty

constraints are critical.
Identity platforms and IAM tools that consider RBAC a foundational

capability are often employed to manage access to SaaS applications.
Infrastructure systems, where roles like `db-admin` or `cloud-ops` align

clearly with operational responsibilities and can be managed as code.

RBAC serves as a practical foundation for organizations that are starting to formalize their

approach to authorization. It offers structure without requiring a complete policy engine or
a transition to attribute- or relationship-based models. For many teams, particularly those

with limited authorization needs or a small number of applications, RBAC strikes the right
balance of simplicity and control.

5.2.5 Where RBAC falls short

RBAC offers clarity and structure, but as access needs become more dynamic, its
limitations are increasingly difficult to overlook. One of the most common signs that RBAC

is no longer sufficient is role explosion—the proliferation of narrowly scoped roles created to
accommodate edge cases and special conditions. Instead of a clean, stable set of job
aligned roles, teams find themselves managing dozens or even hundreds of variations such
as `regional-sales-north`, `regional-sales-east`, or `support-temp-tier1`, each with

slightly different permissions.

As mentioned earlier, another challenge is contextual access. RBAC lacks a native way to

account for conditions such as time of day, device security posture, or network zone. If a
user should only have access during business hours or only from a corporate device, RBAC

alone can’t express that. Such decisions require dynamic evaluation—something RBAC was
never designed to handle.

[RBAC also falls short in multi-tenant or collaborative environments, where access may](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-5?potentialInternalRefId=146---book-markup-container)
depend on not just who a person is but also their relationship to a resource, such as

ownership, sharing, or team membership. In these situations, roles often become too broad
or unclear to capture the nuances of access control unless the identity system is also split

up by tenant.

[None of this means that RBAC is broken; it simply wasn’t designed to handle these](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-5?potentialInternalRefId=147---book-markup-container)

scenarios. As organizations grow in scale and complexity, many find themselves layering in
other models—like the dynamic ones introduced in the next chapter—or adopting policy
based systems that provide the flexibility RBAC lacks.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

109

#### 5.3 Beyond static authorization

ACLs and RBAC both offer structure, clarity, and simplicity—but only up to a point. As

systems become more interconnected and access decisions rely increasingly on context,
relationships, and runtime conditions, static models start to strain under the weight of

complexity. The more exceptions you need to handle, the harder it becomes to understand
who has access to what—and why.

In many modern systems, a user’s access can’t be determined solely by their job title or
inclusion on a list. It may depend on factors such as the time of day, the security posture of

their device, their relationship to a specific resource, or whether they meet regulatory or
contractual requirements. These factors are dynamic, requiring dynamic models.

[The next chapter explores three models: Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC),](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-5?potentialInternalRefId=151---book-markup-container)
Relationship-Based Access Control (ReBAC), and Policy-Based Access Control (PBAC). These

approaches offer greater flexibility, expressiveness, and scalability—though at the cost of
increased complexity. Together, they establish the foundation for modern, policy-driven

authorization systems that can meet the demands of today’s applications.

#### 5.4 Summary

Static authorization models evaluate access based on predefined lists or
assignments and are efficient to evaluate at runtime.

Access Control Lists (ACLs) attach permissions directly to resources,
making them simple and transparent but difficult to manage at scale.

Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) introduces roles as an intermediary,
aligning access with organizational structure and improving

manageability.
Both ACLs and RBAC map onto the standard authorization reference

architecture, though often with tightly coupled or application-embedded
components.

RBAC supports additional governance features, like separation of duty
constraints and role hierarchies, but lacks support for dynamic context.

Static models remain widely used and appropriate in systems with stable
responsibilities and clearly bounded access needs.

As systems grow more dynamic and complex, static models struggle to
adapt, creating a need for more expressive, context-aware approaches.

## Dynamic authorization models

This chapter covers

How authorization evolved from simple role-based controls to dynamic, contextaware authorization

When and why to use relationship-based access control (ReBAC) for collaborative
systems

How attribute-based access control (ABAC) enables fine-grained, real-time decisions

How policy-based access control (PBAC) unifies roles, attributes, and relationships

The tradeoffs and strengths of each model, and how to choose the right
combination for your system

At first, ACME Corp’s switch to Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) seemed like a major
breakthrough. After years of scattered Access Control Lists and inconsistent permissions,

establishing a clear set of roles—customer support, sales manager, engineer, senior
engineer—brought much-needed order to their internal systems. Onboarding got faster.

Audits got cleaner. Developers could finally reason about access without digging through
nested conditionals. But that clarity didn’t last.

As the company expanded into global markets and adopted more collaborative, multitenant services, cracks began to emerge. Roles multiplied, permissions drifted, and

employees—especially those who wore multiple hats—began to complain.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

111

Alice, now a senior engineer, spent increasing amounts of time on cross-functional

project work. She constantly bumped into permissions she didn’t have—even though, on
paper, she was clearly the right person for the job. The system was secure, but it got in the

way of Alice doing her job. “I don’t need access to everything,” she told the identity team,
“just the stuff I’ve been assigned to.”

[Bob, managing field operations in three different regions, faced a different frustration.](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-6?potentialInternalRefId=9---book-markup-container)
“I’m in the sales-manager role,” he said, “but I only need access to my own region’s

accounts. Why do I either have too little or too much?”

[Meanwhile, Carol—who had stepped into a security administrator role—was observing all](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-6?potentialInternalRefId=10---book-markup-container)

of this from a different perspective. Her dashboards showed sprawling role definitions and
audit logs filled with role-based exceptions. Permissions were being assigned informally by

adding users to increasingly specific roles. Most concerning, access policies were beginning
to diverge across systems once more. What had once been a straightforward model had

now become a patchwork. It was clear that ACME Corp’s access requirements had outgrown
static authorization.

[The team didn’t want to abandon RBAC entirely. Still, they needed a more expressive](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-6?potentialInternalRefId=11---book-markup-container)
model—one that could adapt to context, capture relationships, and support fine-grained

rules reflecting how people actually worked. That’s when they started adopting dynamic
authorization models.

[In their new Customer Collaboration platform, they implemented Relationship-Based](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-6?potentialInternalRefId=12---book-markup-container)
Access Control (ReBAC). Instead of relying on team-wide roles, access was granted based

on whether a user was assigned as a viewer, editor, or owner of a document. Alice was now
able to access project files she was involved in, even when those projects spanned different

departments.

[Within their internal systems, they began using Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC)](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-6?potentialInternalRefId=13---book-markup-container)

to define permissions that took into account region, clearance, and time of day. Bob’s
access to customer data was now governed by his assigned region and the sensitivity of the

record rather than a one-size-fits-all role.

[For Carol, the change meant fewer exceptions, increased visibility, and greater](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-6?potentialInternalRefId=14---book-markup-container)

confidence that the company’s access controls aligned with both business needs and
security policies.

[Dynamic models didn’t replace RBAC at ACME Corp—they complemented it. Where roles](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-6?potentialInternalRefId=15---book-markup-container)
still made sense, they stayed. But now, access decisions could reflect the context,

relationships, and conditions that mattered most.

[What changed was how ACME Corp thought about authorization. Instead of hardcoding](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-6?potentialInternalRefId=16---book-markup-container)

access logic or tying it rigidly to static roles, they started writing policies—declarative rules
that outlined who should be allowed to do what under specific conditions. These policies

became the main layer connecting employee, customer, and contractor data with resource
metadata and organizational context.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

112

In some systems, policies were defined in code, using attribute-based rules that

considered roles, departments, clearance levels, and request context—an approach often
associated with ABAC. In others, policies worked with data stored in a relationship graph—

granting or denying access based on connections between people and resources. This datacentric approach, often implemented using ReBAC, enabled flexible delegation,

collaboration, and real-time access checks that reflected how the business actually worked.

[Together, these approaches merged into a larger shift: a transition to policy-based](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-6?potentialInternalRefId=18---book-markup-container)

access control (PBAC). Whether implemented in code or driven by live relationship data,
policies provided ACME with a single, consistent, yet dynamic way to express and enforce

authorization logic across their expanding ecosystem.

#### 6.1 Relationship-based access control

In traditional access control models, such as ACLs and RBAC, access decisions are typically
based on static lists or assigned roles. But in collaborative, multi-tenant environments—like

shared documents, issue tracking platforms, and customer portals—access often depends
on relationships between people and resources. That’s where Relationship-Based Access

Control (ReBAC) shines.

ReBAC grants permissions based on relationships between entities. Rather than ask,

“Does this role grant permission?” ReBAC systems ask, “Does principal A have relation B to
resource C?” These relationships could include owner, viewer, manager, or more complex

indirect connections, such as “manager of the owner.” This model is particularly well-suited
for systems where access is dependent on social, organizational, or collaborative structures.

[If this strategy seems abstract, think about how authorization works in Google Docs.](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-6?potentialInternalRefId=22---book-markup-container)
When you share a document with a colleague, you can decide whether they are a viewer,

commenter, or editor. You don’t assign them a role in a central system—you give access
based on your relationship with that document. Under the hood, Google uses a ReBAC

system called Zanzibar to enforce this model. <u>[Zanzibar](https://research.google/pubs/zanzibar-googles-consistent-global-authorization-system/)</u> [(https://research.​google/pubs/​](https://research.google/pubs/zanzibar-googles-consistent-global-authorization-system/)
<u>[zanzibar-​googles-consistent-​global-authorization-​system/) is a highly scalable authorization](https://research.google/pubs/zanzibar-googles-consistent-global-authorization-system/)</u>

system that determines access through a graph of relationships among users, resources,
and permissions. It supports authorization for various Google products, including Docs,

Drive, Calendar, and more.

[Zanzibar has sparked a wave of modern ReBAC systems—from open-source projects like](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-6?potentialInternalRefId=23---book-markup-container)

<u>[Authzed](https://authzed.com/)</u> [(https://authzed.​com) and OpenFGA](https://authzed.com/) [(https://openfga.​dev) to enterprise solutions](https://openfga.dev/)
built by companies like Airbnb, Carta, and Intuit. What they all have in common is a graph
based method for access control: principals and resources are represented as nodes, with
the connections between them defining permissions and justifications.

[ACME Corp adopted ReBAC as part of a new Customer Collaboration Platform designed](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-6?potentialInternalRefId=24---book-markup-container)
to enhance how employees and customers work together. This system manages access to

content like support tickets, deployment plans, and other shared documents. Employees
such as support engineers, solution architects, and account managers interact directly with

customers and need to control who can see what based on their relationships.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

113

To support this model, ACME represents employees, customers, and documents as nodes

in a graph, and defines edges based on roles and responsibilities. For example:

Jack and Kate are ACME Corp customers.

Bob is a support engineer assigned to ticket #456 as an editor.
Bob is one of Kate’s support engineers.

Alice, Jack’s solution architect, owns a deployment plan that Jack can
view.

Carol manages Alice and Bob.
The graph also captures semantic relationships between resource types,

like tickets, project plans, and other documents.

Figure 6.1 provides a snapshot of this relationship graph, illustrating employees, customers,

and resources along with the relationships that govern access.

Figure 6.1 A relationship graph used by ACME Corp’s Customer Collaboration platform. Employees like Bob

and Alice are linked to customer accounts through roles such as support engineer and solution architect.

Access to resources like support tickets and deployment plans is controlled by these relationships, allowing

for dynamic, fine-grained authorization decisions based on who is connected to what and how.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

114

ReBAC systems determine access by traversing this type of graph. Instead of assigning

permissions directly, they verify whether a path exists between a principal and a resource
that meets a policy condition, such as viewer of a document, owner of a ticket, or manager

of an owner. These paths can be short and straightforward or more complex, involving
multiple relationship hops to represent business logic. This graph model makes it easier to

manage delegated access, shared ownership, and team-based collaboration across
organizational boundaries.

In the following subsection, we’ll examine how ReBAC systems evaluate access at
runtime and how policies use relationship paths to define rules.

6.1.1 How ReBAC works

Relationship-based access control (ReBAC) grants access based on the connections between
entities, rather than just their identities or associated attributes. Instead of checking to see

if a person holds a specific role or can claim certain attributes, ReBAC systems assess the
relationship between the principal and the resource they want to access.

This is especially effective in systems where collaboration and delegation are key. You’ve
already seen how ACME Corp’s Customer Collaboration platform uses ReBAC to simplify

access to documents, tickets, and deployment artifacts. Now let’s take a closer look at how
that system works.

[Broadly speaking, a ReBAC system has three parts:](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-6?potentialInternalRefId=39---book-markup-container)

_Static rules_ define uniform access logic.

The _authorization service_ enforces those rules across all applications.
The _relationship graph_ provides data—connections between people,

teams, and resources—that the system uses to decide whether to
approve a request.

Importantly, the logic of a ReBAC system changes much less often than the rules change in
other authorization models. Static authorization rules are written once and rarely updated.

What does change are the relationships themselves: who owns a resource, who manages
whom, and who has been granted viewer access. That makes ReBAC flexible without

needing to change the underlying logic.

Figure 6.2 shows how ACME’s platform evaluates access to documents in the Customer

Collaboration system. When an employee tries to open a document, the authorization client
sends a request to the central authorization service, which evaluates that request using

rules and the current state of the relationship graph.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

115

Figure 6.2 Relationship-based authorization using graph traversal and policy evaluation. Access is determined

by analyzing relationships between principals and resources.

ACME has written a number of static rules for the authorization service that govern access
by both employees and customers. Here are some examples:

permit view when principal has "viewer" or "owner" relationship to resource

permit view, update when principal has "editor" relationship to resource

permit all when principal has "owner" relationship to resource

permit all when principal is "manager" of an "owner" of the resource

These rules cover most access scenarios. Referring to the graph in figure 6.1:

Alice, a solution architect, has full access to and can share the

_deployment plan_ she owns.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

116

Bob, a support engineer, can change _support ticket #456_ because he’s

the ticket’s editor.
Carol can delete _support ticket #456_ because she’s the owner.

Carol, Alice’s manager, can access the _deployment plan_ because _Alice_
_owns it_ —a transitive rule that depends on the static policy and dynamic

graph.

This final example is worth noting. Carol’s access depends on the chain of manager →

owner → resource. If Alice is removed as the owner of the resource, Carol’s access will also
disappear. There’s no need to explicitly revoke permissions.

Rules that `permit all` are not limited to viewing or editing. In ACME’s system, `all`

includes:

Updating or deleting the resource
Granting or revoking others’ access

Assigning ownership

As I’ve mentioned, the rules remain fixed: they don’t change daily. What changes is the

data—the graph of relationships that the system evaluates against. _That graph is the policy._
Whether access is granted depends not on rewriting the logic but on updating the

relationships. If Carol is assigned as a manager of the Customer Success team, she gains
access to what her team owns. If she’s removed from that relationship, she loses it. This

dynamic assessment, based on a static set of rules, enables fine-grained, flexible access
decisions without overly complicating the authorization logic.

This approach offers remarkable flexibility because it makes controlling access simple.
Anyone with the right permissions can shape policy just by managing relationships.

Assigning a new owner to a document, giving a team editing rights, or designating a
customer contact as a collaborator—all these actions become policy updates. There’s no

need to write or deploy new code; the same interface used to change access is used to
update relationships. This makes ReBAC uniquely powerful: product managers, solutions

architects, support engineers, and even customers themselves can safely participate in
shaping access, all within guardrails set by a small set of clear, consistent rules.

[In short, ReBAC allows ACME’s Collaboration platform to scale access control without](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-6?potentialInternalRefId=60---book-markup-container)
constant policy churn. A few well-defined rules are combined with a constantly changing

graph of people and resources, resulting in clear, explainable, and flexible access decisions.

6.1.2 Mapping ReBAC onto the authorization reference architecture

Like ACLs and RBAC, relationship-based access control (ReBAC) fits cleanly into the

authorization reference architecture described in chapter 4. What sets ReBAC apart is how
each component functions, particularly the relationship between rules, data, and the user

interface that modifies them.

Table 6.1 explains how each component of the architecture is usually implemented in a

ReBAC system.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

Table 6.1 Mapping ReBAC onto the authorization reference architecture. Each component is present in ReBAC

systems, though often realized differently than in ACL or RBAC models.

|Component|What It Does|How ReBAC Implements It|
|---|---|---|
|Policy Enforcement Point<br>(PEP)|Intercepts access requests<br>and enforces the decision|Often embedded in the<br>application or gateway;<br>enforces access based on PDP<br>outcome|
|Policy Decision Point<br>(PDP)|Determines whether the<br>requested action is allowed|Authorization engine evaluates<br>static rules against the current<br>state of the relationship graph|
|Policy Administration<br>Point (PAP)|Manages and stores roles,<br>permissions, and<br>assignments|Relationship graph updated<br>via app UI (for example, share<br>dialogs, team assignments)|
|Policy Information Point<br>(PIP)|Supplies user and role data<br>to the PDP at runtime|Combines relationship graph<br>queries with data from the<br>identity system or session<br>context|

In ReBAC systems, the Policy Administration Point (PAP) often shows up in an unexpected—
but powerful—form: the user interface. Figure 6.3 shows a user interface element, modeled

after Google Doc’s sharing interface, in the Customer Collaboration platform, with Bob
sharing the support ticket with Kate.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

118

Figure 6.3 The user interface for the application provides users with the ability to affect access to documents

by allowing them to change the relationship graph. In this figure, Bob is sharing “support ticket #456” with

Kate, making her a Viewer.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

119

Because the relationship graph is the primary source of policy data, any UI element that

allows a person to change those relationships is effectively participating in policy
administration. When an account manager shares a document with a customer or a team

lead adds a new engineer to a project space, they’re updating the graph—and thereby
changing the outcome of future authorization decisions. These actions don’t require writing

code or modifying a policy file; they’re made through contextual UI components that reflect
the resource currently being viewed. This tight coupling between user intent, interface, and

authorization data makes ReBAC uniquely flexible and delegatable. Anyone can be a policy
editor—not by crafting rules, but by shaping relationships. Additionally, a graph

management tool will likely be available, enabling administrators to access the graph for
debugging, auditing, and other global activities.

The Policy Information Point (PIP), by contrast, supplies the decision engine with the
data it needs to evaluate access. In a ReBAC system, that includes the relationship graph

but may also involve other sources—such as the identity provider—to answer questions like
“who is this principal?” or “what customer does this employee work with?”

6.1.3 Strengths and limitations of ReBAC

ReBAC offers a powerful model for managing access in complex, collaborative systems. _Its_
_main idea—that relationships influence access choices—makes it especially useful for_

_systems where authorization depends on social, organizational, or ownership structures_
_that often change._ Rather than embed access rules in fixed roles or code policies, ReBAC

relies on a relationship graph as the source of truth. If a principal is connected to a
resource via an authorized path, access is granted.

By treating data as policy, ReBAC enables teams to delegate policy authoring to the
people closest to the work. Permissions are granted and revoked through intuitive UI

actions—such as inviting a teammate, assigning ownership, or sharing a workspace—
without involving centralized administrators. This makes ReBAC highly scalable and

adaptable to change, especially in areas where resource boundaries and team structures
often shift. On the other hand, delegating policy authority to individuals requires trusting

them to make informed decisions. This informs the use cases where ReBAC makes sense.

[But ReBAC has its tradeoffs. In large or densely connected graphs, it can be difficult to](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-6?potentialInternalRefId=72---book-markup-container)

see the impact of a single change on access. Debugging who has access—and why—may
require tracing complex relationship paths, often with specialized tools. And while

relationship data works well for collaboration and delegation, it doesn’t support contextaware access decisions, such as time-of-day restrictions or device posture. Other models

better manage those conditions.

[Table 6.2 summarizes the most common strengths and limitations of ReBAC in practice.](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-6?potentialInternalRefId=73---book-markup-container)

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

120

Table 6.2 Strengths and limitations of relationship-based access control

|Strengths|Limitations|
|---|---|
|Aligns access decisions with real-world<br>relationships|Not well suited to conditional or contextual<br>access (for example, time or device)|
|Empowers employees to manage access via<br>intuitive UI|Requires robust graph management and<br>path-tracing capabilities|
|Avoids role explosion by encoding policy in<br>relationship data|Can be difficult to debug in large or<br>complex graphs|
|Supports fine-grained delegation without<br>central approval|Access logic can be hard to audit without<br>visibility into the full graph|
|Enables consistent access control across<br>shared, multi-tenant systems|Assumes the relationship model is well<br>designed and maintained|
|Makes it easy for non-technical staff to be<br>policy authors|May require custom tooling for<br>administration and governance|

As the table shows, ReBAC delivers clear advantages in collaborative, relationship-rich
environments, offering intuitive delegation, decentralized policy management, and

alignment with how teams actually work. But it also demands strong modeling discipline
and operational tooling to avoid unintended access or confusion. The key to using ReBAC

effectively is knowing when relationships provide the right foundation—and when other
models, like ABAC, are better suited to capture dynamic conditions or nuanced business

logic. ReBAC is most powerful when it complements, rather than replaces, other approaches
in a layered authorization strategy.

6.1.4 Where ReBAC makes sense

ReBAC performs well in environments where access decisions depend on human or
organizational relationships. It naturally suits collaborative platforms that involve sharing,

delegation, or scoped teamwork, such as document management systems, developer
portals, customer support tools, ticketing systems, or learning management systems. In

these settings, permissions are often determined less by job titles or security groups and
more by questions like this: Who owns the resource? Who’s part of the project? Who needs

to contribute? ReBAC reflects how people typically think about access: through
relationships.

At ACME Corp, ReBAC became a critical part of the company’s Customer Collaboration
platform. This system facilitates complex, dynamic interactions between internal employees

—such as solution architects, support engineers, and account managers—and external
customers. Access to shared workspaces is determined by account ownership and

management chains: employees can grant access to collaborators, and managers
automatically inherit access to their reports’ accounts. These patterns are difficult to

represent clearly with static roles or fragile attribute rules. ReBAC allows ACME to express
them using a few simple rules and a shared graph, making access both flexible and easy to

understand.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

121

The true power of ReBAC becomes evident as systems grow and evolve. Business teams

can handle access themselves using familiar UI actions. Permissions adapt to the structure
of the graph, automatically adjusting as relationships change. Governance teams still

maintain visibility and control, but without needing to be involved in every decision. ReBAC
allows policies to evolve with the organization, making it an ideal foundation for systems

centered on collaboration and trust.

6.1.5 When ReBAC falls short

ReBAC systems are powerful, but they aren’t always the best choice, especially when

access depends on runtime context or complex business conditions. If permissions need to
change based on the time of day, device security posture, geographic location, or other

transient signals, ReBAC can’t evaluate those factors on its own. Trying to embed such logic
into the relationship graph can lead to an explosion of relationship types or edges that are

hard to validate and understand. Overloading the graph with every condition doesn’t just
make it more complex—it can also obscure the original intent behind access decisions.

Operational challenges also emerge. In dynamic systems, entities and relationships are
often created and removed, making lifecycle management essential. Because access logic is

embedded in the graph's structure, even minor changes can have unintended
consequences, especially in complex systems where relationship pathways aren’t obvious.

While ReBAC allows teams to author policies through user-friendly interfaces, that same
flexibility can complicate governance and auditing without specialized tools. Organizations

adopting ReBAC should invest in guardrails, training, and simulation tools to keep the
system safe and predictable.

[ReBAC works well when access is based on how people naturally collaborate. However,](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-6?potentialInternalRefId=83---book-markup-container)
when access depends on what a person is doing—not just who they’re connected to—other

models, such as ABAC, might be a better choice.

#### 6.2 Attribute-based access control

As ACME Corp grew, its internal systems and the teams using them needed increasingly
fine-grained, context-aware access controls. Engineering required secure deployment

pipelines that allowed changes only under specific conditions. Finance systems stored
confidential reports that needed clearance-based restrictions. HR systems had to expose

sensitive records to managers, but only in certain situations. Relying solely on roles or
relationships was not sufficient. Access often depended on the attributes of the person

making the request, the resource being accessed, and the conditions under which the
request occurred.

Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) provided ACME with the flexibility it needed.
ABAC makes decisions based on attributes, including named values linked to the principal

(such as department or clearance), the resource (like classification or owner), the
environment (for example, time or network risk), or the request itself (such as action type).

Instead of tying access directly to roles or relationships, ABAC employs policies that are
evaluated using these attributes at the time of the decision.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

122

[This model proved useful across the organization:](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-6?potentialInternalRefId=87---book-markup-container)

Engineering used ABAC to control access to production deployment tools.
Engineers with high clearance and using a company-managed device

could deploy during business hours. Outside those hours, they also
needed to be on call.

Finance systems required that only employees in the finance department
with the necessary clearance could view sensitive quarterly reports. Even

then, they could only see those from their region.
HR enforced policies that limited access to employee records based on

attributes such as data sensitivity, request purpose, and regulatory flags.
For example, a policy might permit access to compensation data only

when the request is for approved audit purposes and the requester has
proper clearance.

Figure 6.4 illustrates a simple example of ABAC in use. Alice and Bob are both in the
finance department and work from the same location. However, only Alice has the clearance

needed to view the Q2 Financial Data. The policy that enforces this—stored as code—
permits access only if the principal’s department matches the resource’s owner, the

clearance level is high, and the access happens before a specified time of day.

Figure 6.4 Attribute-based authorization with principal, resource, and environment attributes. Access

decisions are based on evaluating policies in the context of attributes from multiple sources. Alice’s

attributes meet the policy conditions, so access is granted. Bob’s do not, so access is denied.

_ABAC is powerful because it treats authorization as a dynamic decision: given this set of_
_attributes and current conditions, should access be granted?_ This flexibility makes it an

excellent choice for systems where conditions and constraints are as important as identity.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

123

6.2.1 How ABAC works

Let’s explore figure 6.4 more deeply to see how ABAC makes authorization decisions. When
Alice and Bob each try to access a sensitive financial document, their requests are routed to

an authorization client, which queries a central policy engine. That engine evaluates a
policy using attributes from three sources: the principal (Alice or Bob), the resource (the

Q2 Financial Data), and the environment (the time, network risk level, and request type).
In this example, the policy grants access only if the requesting principal belongs to the

same department as the resource owner and has “high” clearance and the request occurs
before 6 p.m. Because Alice meets all of these criteria, her request is permitted. Bob, who

has “low” clearance, is denied.

This example highlights a key aspect of ABAC: policies are static, but evaluated

dynamically based on current attributes. The rules themselves—written in a policy language
—don’t change from one request to the next. What changes are the attribute values.

Different times, network conditions, or HR system assignments can produce different
results. Policies function like code. Attributes serve as their inputs.

[In practice, ABAC systems evaluate many policies across a variety of contexts, not just a](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-6?potentialInternalRefId=97---book-markup-container)
single one, as shown in figure 6.4. A policy engine might retrieve relevant policies from

multiple policy stores—some scoped to an application, and others global to the
organization. Attributes are collected from a wide range of systems: identity platforms, HR

systems, device management services, resource metadata stores, and environmental
sensors. Each request can trigger the evaluation of multiple policies, each containing fine
grained logic to match a wide range of conditions.

[In real-life systems, deciding whether to grant access can involve evaluating dozens of](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-6?potentialInternalRefId=98---book-markup-container)

policies for a single request. Policies can be layered: some might establish baseline
requirements—such as device management or geo-fencing—while others relate to specific

actions, departments, or sensitivity levels. The final decision results from the combined
impact of all evaluated policies.

[To make this description more concrete, table 6.3 presents an attribute evaluation](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-6?potentialInternalRefId=99---book-markup-container)
matrix for ACME Corp’s deployment system. It shows how various combinations of

attributes—such as clearance level, device status, time of day, and on-call status—might
impact the outcome of a deployment access request.

|Scenario|clearance_level|device_managed|hour_of_day|on_call|Decision|
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
|Alice<br>deploying<br>at 10 pm,<br>on call|high|true<br>|22|true|✅ Allow|
|Alice<br>deploying<br>at 10 pm,<br>not on<br>call|high|true|22|false|❌ Deny|
