This matrix captures the layered logic of ACME’s ABAC policy: all requests must originate

from a managed device; during business hours, engineers with high clearance are
permitted; outside business hours, the requester must also be on call. Although simplified

for illustration, this pattern demonstrates how ABAC enables access to be both flexible and
precise, adapting to context while remaining grounded in clear policy logic. This makes

ABAC ideal for organizations with decentralized teams and diverse systems: each team or
application can define policies suited to their needs while still conforming to broader

organizational standards.

6.2.2 Mapping ABAC onto the authorization reference architecture

ABAC maps naturally onto the authorization reference architecture described in chapter 4.

The Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) is typically integrated into the application or a system
like an API gateway, reverse proxy, or backend service. Its role is to intercept requests and

call the policy engine to determine if access should be granted. From the caller’s
perspective, authorization happens in real time and is closely tied to the specific action

being performed.

Table 6.4 summarizes how the four core components—PEP, PDP, PAP, and PIP—are

usually realized in ABAC systems.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

125

Table 6.4 Mapping ABAC onto the authorization reference architecture

|Component|What It Does|How ABAC Implements It|
|---|---|---|
|Policy Enforcement Point<br>(PEP)|Intercepts access requests<br>and enforces the decision|Typically integrated into the<br>application, API gateway, or<br>middleware layer that<br>intercepts requests and<br>queries the PDP|
|Policy Decision Point<br>(PDP)|Determines whether the<br>requested action is allowed|A policy engine (like Cedar,<br>Open Policy Agent, or a<br>homegrown system) that<br>evaluates code-like policies<br>against the current attributes|
|Policy Administration<br>Point (PAP)|Manages and stores roles,<br>permissions, and<br>assignments|Maintained as code, often<br>versioned alongside<br>application code or kept in<br>centralized policy stores. IDEs<br>or CI/CD tools may be used to<br>manage changes|
|Policy Information Point<br>(PIP)|Supplies user and role data<br>to the PDP at runtime|Pulls attributes from identity<br>providers, HR systems,<br>resource metadata, device<br>management platforms, and<br>contextual signal providers<br>(e.g., time, risk, location)|

The Policy Decision Point (PDP) is usually implemented as a policy engine that evaluates
policies. Unlike RBAC, where decisions rely on simple role-to-permission mappings, ABAC

policies are more expressive: they’re code-like logic that references input attributes. The
PDP receives the request, fetches the relevant attributes, retrieves the relevant policies,

and evaluates them to return an allow or deny decision.

In practice, ABAC PDPs must balance flexibility with performance. Because policies can

number in the hundreds or thousands, efficient retrieval and indexing are essential. Many
systems tag policies with metadata—such as relevant resource types, actions, or attribute

filters—to limit the evaluation scope. Caching frequently used attributes or precomputing
decisions for common scenarios can also boost responsiveness. At scale, organizations

often deploy distributed PDPs close to enforcement points to reduce latency while
synchronizing them with a central policy store to maintain consistency. These

improvements guarantee that dynamic authorization decisions stay fast, reliable, and
auditable in production environments.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

126

Those policies originate from the Policy Administration Point (PAP), which in ABAC

systems is usually a centralized configuration store or policy management system. Policies
might reside in source-controlled files (such as Rego, Cedar, or JSON files), be deployed

through CI/CD pipelines, or be managed with specialized tooling. Because these policies are
based on logic rather than data, they are created by developers, policy engineers, or

platform teams—individuals with both domain knowledge and coding skills.

[The Policy Information Point (PIP) is essential for ABAC. It provides the dynamic](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-6?potentialInternalRefId=109---book-markup-container)

attributes needed to evaluate each access request, such as the principal’s department,
security clearance, or device posture, as well as resource properties like sensitivity or

project affiliation. These attributes often originate from multiple systems: an identity
provider (IdP) for user details, mobile device management (MDM) systems for device

status, cloud metadata APIs for resource context, and external sources for signals like time
of day or risk scores. In some designs, the PIP is a standalone component responsible for

collecting and supplying these attributes to the PDP. In others, attribute resolution occurs
directly within the PDP or is delegated to the application. ABAC relies on the freshness and

accuracy of these attributes, making attribute management and trust a fundamental
challenge in production environments.

6.2.3 Strengths and limitations of ABAC

ABAC provides a powerful and flexible model for making access decisions based on realtime context. By using _attributes_ —structured facts about the principal, resource, action,

and environment—ABAC enables fine-grained and dynamic authorization without
embedding logic directly into the application. Contrast this with RBAC, where everyone with

the same role has the same access. This approach is particularly valuable in environments
where access depends not just on who someone is, but on what they’re doing, when they’re

doing it, and under what conditions.

One of ABAC’s core strengths is its ability to express complex policies in a centralized

and maintainable way. Instead of creating numerous roles or custom access rules,
organizations can develop reusable policies that reference attributes like clearance level,

department, device status, or geolocation. As we’ve seen, policies can be layered and
composed to reflect detailed requirements. Policies automatically adapt as input attributes

change, allowing access decisions to be both accurate and resilient without manual
updates.

[For example, ABAC is well-suited for financial systems, where access to data must](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-6?potentialInternalRefId=113---book-markup-container)
consider regulatory controls, time-based restrictions, and employee status. For instance,

ACME Corp’s finance team manages quarterly reports that are classified as confidential and
region-specific, as shown in figure 6.4. Analysts with high clearance can access these

reports during business hours, but outside those hours, access is limited to employees who
are actively on call. Policies like these evaluate attributes from multiple sources—such as

clearance level, department, region, and current shift status—to make access decisions in
real time. Instead of manually defining roles for every possible scenario, ACME encodes

these conditions as attribute-driven policies, providing precision and agility while easing the
administrative burden.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

127

[However, that same flexibility brings new challenges. ABAC systems need to reliably](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-6?potentialInternalRefId=114---book-markup-container)

retrieve and assess attributes from multiple sources, often in real-time. Policies—being
code-like—can become difficult to write, manage, or debug without proper tools. Since

decisions depend on a combination of inputs and logic, it can be hard to understand why
access was granted or denied without good logging and tools to analyze logs. Table 6.5

highlights some of the most common strengths and limitations of ABAC in practice.

[Table 6.5 Strengths and limitations of attribute-based authorization (ABAC)](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-6?potentialInternalRefId=115---book-markup-container)

|Strengths|Limitations|
|---|---|
|Enables fine-grained access control based<br>on rich context|Policies can become complex and difficult to<br>manage over time|
|Supports real-time decisions using current<br>attributes and signals|Requires consistent and accurate attribute<br>data from multiple systems|
|Decouples policy logic from application<br>code, improving maintainability|Understanding access decisions can be<br>difficult due to distributed inputs|
|Scales well across diverse teams, systems,<br>and resource types|Limited visibility into which policies affect<br>which resources without tooling|
|Flexible enough to model conditional access<br>and regulatory requirements|Performance may suffer if attribute retrieval<br>or policy evaluation is not optimized|
|Improves auditability and consistency<br>through centralized policy evaluation|Usually requires custom tooling for policy<br>management, simulation, and reporting|

Ultimately, ABAC shines when organizations need to implement nuanced, context-aware
controls across a wide range of systems and scenarios. It offers a framework for expressing

intent through policies and dynamically enforcing that intent at runtime. However, to realize
these benefits, organizations must invest in attribute quality, governance, and tools that

support the entire lifecycle of policy creation, evaluation, and auditing.

6.2.4 Where ABAC makes sense

As we’ve discussed, ABAC excels in environments where access decisions depend on

dynamic factors and fine-grained conditions. In contrast to models that rely on static
assignments or predefined relationships, ABAC shines when access needs vary based on

time, location, device state, or other runtime signals. This makes it especially useful for
enterprise systems that serve diverse functions across departments, where policies must

reflect detailed regulatory or operational requirements without constant manual updates.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

128

At ACME Corp, the identity team adopted ABAC to manage internal access in a scalable

and layered manner. A company-wide policy enforced a baseline requirement: all access to
sensitive systems must come from company-managed devices. Additionally, engineering

layered on additional policies for deploying code—engineers with high clearance could
deploy during business hours from managed devices, but outside business hours, they also

needed to be on call. Finance added policies that allowed read-only access to quarterly
reports for finance analysts, but only during active reporting windows, as shown in figure

6.4. HR enforced stricter policies on access to personnel files, combining attributes like
department, sensitivity level, and audit status. Each team retained autonomy over its

policies while inheriting shared organizational constraints, making ABAC not just flexible but
also composable and consistent across domains.

[Because ABAC separates policy from identity and data systems, it scales smoothly across](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-6?potentialInternalRefId=120---book-markup-container)
teams and tools. Attributes can be sourced from various systems—such as identity stores,

device managers, and time services—and combined at runtime without tying policy logic to
any specific application. As organizations adopt broader governance models or need to

demonstrate compliance, ABAC allows them to layer and adjust rules gradually. This makes
it a powerful fit for regulated industries, operational teams needing accuracy, and any

enterprise aiming to make real-time, context-aware access decisions without overwhelming
administrators or engineers.

6.2.5 When ABAC falls short

ABAC offers strong flexibility, but this flexibility has a cost. Since policies are written as
code, they demand a level of precision and discipline that not all teams can sustain. At

ACME Corp, the identity team started to face challenges as policies multiplied. Teams often
reused similar logic with slight differences, leading to dozens or even hundreds of

overlapping policies. Without a consistent taxonomy for attributes or clear naming
conventions, it became hard to determine which policy applied to which system or why. This

made understanding access decisions more complicated, especially for teams outside of
engineering who lacked the tools or expertise to trace how specific attributes affected

access outcomes.

ABAC also faced challenges in scenarios where access depended not just on who

someone was or what device they were using, but on how they connected with others. This
became clear in ACME’s Customer Collaboration platform. There, account managers needed

to grant temporary access to documents, customers had to invite colleagues, and support
engineers required scoped access based on account ownership. These patterns didn’t neatly

fit into attribute-driven logic and were awkward to express using policies alone. The team
designing the customer platform eventually concluded that ABAC’s ability to evaluate static

conditions at runtime wasn’t well-suited for expressing dynamic, graph-based relationships.
That’s when they started exploring ReBAC for relationship-aware authorization.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

129

Finally, ABAC’s reliance on centrally managed policies means that access control can be

highly centralized. Although attributes originated from distributed sources, only a small
group of developers or policy administrators might be employed to write or modify policies.

This bottleneck reduces agility and causes some teams to wait before implementing new
access rules. While ABAC provides precise control, it lacks the delegation and self-service

features that modern collaboration platforms increasingly need. For ACME, ABAC remained
crucial in environments with stable requirements and strict compliance, but it wasn’t a

universal solution.

[Many of ABAC’s limitations stem not from the model itself but from its implementation](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-6?potentialInternalRefId=125---book-markup-container)

and governance. Implementing clear policies, maintaining consistent attribute naming,
enforcing strong version control, and using testing and simulation tools can significantly

reduce complexity. Organizational standards and governance practices are essential for
managing policy sprawl, avoiding confusion, and keeping access decisions transparent and

auditable over time. We’ll revisit these topics in detail in chapter 19, which covers policy
governance and the operational practices needed to make models like ABAC sustainable at

scale.

#### 6.3 A hybrid approach: Policy-based access control

As ACME Corp’s authorization needs grew more complex, it became clear that no single
model—whether based on roles, relationships, or attributes—could address all use cases.

Engineers needed to enforce contextual access to production systems. Support teams
shared documents based on customer relationships. Finance required auditable, policy
driven controls to ensure regulatory compliance. Each team had unique requirements, and
each relied on a different model.

Policy-Based Authorization (PBAC) provides a unified approach to these methods under a
single framework. It externalizes access logic—moving it out of application code—and

evaluates policies at runtime using current information. In a PBAC model, policies serve as
the primary decision-making units. Some are written as rules with attributes or conditions

(like in ABAC). Others reference roles or organizational structures (as in RBAC). Still others
determine access based on relationships between people and resources (as in ReBAC).

PBAC treats these as inputs rather than as separate silos.

[This chapter has examined each of these models individually. PBAC expands on them, as](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-6?potentialInternalRefId=129---book-markup-container)

shown in table 6.6.

[Table 6.6 How PBAC incorporates and extends RBAC, ABAC, and ReBAC by treating roles, attributes, and](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-6?potentialInternalRefId=130---book-markup-container)

relationships as inputs to externalized policies evaluated at runtime

|Model|Core Concept|How PBAC Incorporates It|
|---|---|---|
|RBAC|Roles grant permissions|Roles used as input to policy decisions|
|ReBAC|Relationships define<br>access|Policies reference relationships like ownership or<br>management|
|ABAC|Attributes drive decisions|Policies written using combinations of attributes|

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

130

In PBAC, roles, attributes, and relationships are all just data, context that policies can

reference dynamically. The core idea is this: _Don’t hardcode access decisions; instead,_
_define and evaluate policies as part of a shared, external system._

Each represents a different style of externalized decision-making. In the next two
subsections, we explore both approaches, showing how PBAC provides the flexibility to

unify authorization across different domains and use cases.

6.3.1 Policy as data

In section 6.1, we saw how ReBAC expresses policies through relationship data. The rules

in a ReBAC system don’t explicitly specify every principal or resource—instead, they refer to
patterns in the graph. For example, a policy might allow access if the principal is the owner

of the resource or if they manage someone who owns it. Another might grant access if the
resource belongs to a customer the principal supports. These policies are straightforward

and static, but they create dynamic behavior because the relationship graph is always
changing.

This is what it means to treat policy as data: The policy logic remains constant, whereas
access behavior adapts to the changing state of the graph. In PBAC, this kind of dynamic

decision-making is made possible by treating relationships as structured input data. The
logic is based on a few reusable rules; however, the access outcomes shift as relationships

change. Anyone who can update the graph can affect authorization without needing to write
code.

6.3.2 Policy as code

ABAC takes a different approach. In section 6.2, we examined how ACME Corp engineers
controlled access to production tools using a set of policies that utilized contextual

attributes. These policies were implemented as code, rules evaluated by a policy engine
using current attributes as inputs. Unlike ReBAC, which grants access through relationship

data, ABAC focuses on executable policies designed for precise evaluation.

This approach represents policies as code. Policies are created using languages like

Cedar, Rego, or XACML and stored in one or more policy stores. They can be combined,
layered, and managed using version control, just like any other codebase. Although more

complex to create and maintain than relationship data, code-based policies provide
unmatched accuracy, adaptability, and auditability.

[Whether policies are implemented through relationship graphs or authored as executable](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-6?potentialInternalRefId=139---book-markup-container)
rules, PBAC offers a shared architecture for authorization across systems. The next

subsection explores how this hybrid approach is put into practice and how the models
interact.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

131

6.3.3 Beyond one-size-fits-all

Policy-based authorization provides a mental framework that helps identity teams unify the
diverse approaches to access control across their systems. Instead of choosing between

roles, attributes, or relationships, PBAC encourages teams to externalize decision logic—
regardless of form—and evaluate it dynamically at runtime. Whether policies are expressed

as structured data or executable code, they enable flexible, dynamic, and timely
authorization decisions that adapt to changing context. This shift brings consistency to

access decisions, makes policies easier to reason about, and supports better governance as
systems grow. PBAC offers a common architecture for modern, adaptable authorization.

ACME Corp’s path to mature authorization reflected the broader evolution of the identity
industry. Early on, developers used simple Access Control Lists (ACLs) to specify who could

access which resources—perfectly adequate when the team was small and access needs
were predictable. As the company expanded, the need for a structured approach grew.

Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) helped align permissions with job functions, providing
the identity team with a scalable approach to handle onboarding, offboarding, and audits.

[But growth introduced complexity. The Customer Collaboration platform, where access](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-6?potentialInternalRefId=143---book-markup-container)
depended on relationships between employees and customers, pushed ACME toward

Relationship-Based Access Control (ReBAC). Meanwhile, internal systems—like production
deployment tools and HR applications—required fine-grained, context-aware policies.

Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) allowed ACME to enforce rules based on factors
such as time of day, device posture, and clearance level. Each model added flexibility and

nuance, solving problems the previous one couldn’t.

[Table 6.7 summarizes how each model approaches authorization.](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-6?potentialInternalRefId=144---book-markup-container)

[Table 6.7 A comparison of authorization models](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-6?potentialInternalRefId=145---book-markup-container)

|Model|What Drives Access<br>Decisions|How Policies Are<br>Expressed|Key Strengths|
|---|---|---|---|
|ACL|Lists attached to each<br>resource, mapping<br>principals to actions|Data (the list itself)|Simple and<br>intuitive; fast at<br>runtime|
|RBAC|Principals are assigned to<br>roles, roles map to<br>permissions|Data (roles and role<br>assignments)|Aligns with org<br>structure; easy to<br>audit|
|ReBAC|Access depends on paths<br>through a graph of<br>relationships|Relationship data + rules|Matches human<br>concepts of<br>ownership,<br>delegation|
|ABAC|Policies use attributes of<br>principal, resource, action,<br>and environment|Policy logic evaluated at<br>runtime using contextual<br>attributes|Fine-grained,<br>contextual, scalable|

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

132

The models we’ve discussed are not mutually exclusive. Like ACME, most modern

organizations use a hybrid approach—that we’ll call Policy-Based Access Control (PBAC)—
applying RBAC for broad job responsibilities, ABAC for detailed control based on context,

and ReBAC for collaboration platforms or delegated access. Understanding each model’s
design and tradeoffs provides teams with the vocabulary and framework they need to

evaluate their systems and create access decisions that reflect real-world complexity.

In the next chapter, we focus on the fundamental components of policies. You’ve seen

policies expressed through lists, graphs, and code. Now, we’ll examine more closely how
modern systems organize policies, what they assess, how they define scope and effects,

and how they handle authorization logic within a larger system. We’ll introduce Cedar, an
open-source policy language developed by AWS, as a running example to demonstrate core

policy concepts and patterns.

#### 6.4 Summary

ACLs, RBAC, ReBAC, and ABAC each offer distinct approaches to
authorization. They differ in how access decisions are described and

enforced, ranging from simple lists to dynamic, context-aware policies.
ReBAC bases access on relationships between entities, such as ownership

or team membership. This model works especially well in collaborative
systems where access depends on organizational or social structures.

ABAC assesses policies based on attributes of the principal, resource,
action, and environment. It enables fine-grained, real-time decisions

using contextual information such as time, device, or location.
ReBAC treats policies as relationship data, with access determined by

traversing a graph. Policy rules remain the same, while changes to
relationships dynamically drive access decisions.

ABAC treats policies as code evaluated at runtime using current attribute
values. This method offers flexible and auditable control but requires

careful governance to avoid complexity.
PBAC combines RBAC, ReBAC, and ABAC by externalizing and

dynamically evaluating policy logic. Roles, attributes, and relationships
serve as policy inputs, ensuring consistent access control across different

systems.
Different models solve different problems—combining them results in

better outcomes. A hybrid approach often provides the best balance of
expressiveness, scalability, and maintainability.

## The building blocks of policy

This chapter covers

The structure of a Cedar policy: effect, scope, and conditions

The PARC model (Principal, Action, Resource, Context) for representing access
requests

How Cedar evaluates access decisions using matching, condition logic, and denyoverrides

Key features of the Cedar language, including strong typing, entity references, and

namespaces

Cedar’s design principles that enable safety, performance, and formal analysis

At ACME Corp, the identity team has just finished rolling out a new set of access policies.

Engineers can now deploy code only from company-managed devices, and only when they
are on call or during business hours. Document sharing is managed through a graph of

relationships, letting managers like Carol review their team’s work without needing explicit
access permissions. These decisions are made in real time, but behind the scenes, there

must be rules that govern access.

This chapter is about those rules. After exploring the main models for dynamic

authorization, we now focus on how policy is actually written and evaluated. What does it
mean to say “on call” or “manager” in a way that a system can understand? How does an

authorization engine decide whether to allow or deny a request?

[To answer those questions, we’ll use](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-7?potentialInternalRefId=8---book-markup-container) <u>[Cedar](https://www.cedarpolicy.com/)</u> [(https://www.​cedarpolicy.​com), a modern,](https://www.cedarpolicy.com/)

open-source policy language designed for fine-grained, real-time access decisions. Cedar
offers a clear and expressive way to define policies involving relationships, attributes, and

contextual conditions, whether we’re implementing ReBAC, ABAC, or PBAC.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

134

We’ll use ACME’s journey to illustrate key ideas. As we examine Cedar’s structure, its

underlying PARC model (Principals, Actions, Resources, Conditions), and its evaluation
logic, you’ll see how policies are created, scoped, and put into action. By the end of this

chapter, you’ll have a clear understanding of how dynamic access control is represented in
policies and a foundation for the more advanced topics to come.

#### 7.1 Introducing Cedar

Cedar is a purpose-built policy language designed for fine-grained access control. Amazon

Web Services (AWS) developed it to power services like Amazon Verified Access and
Amazon Verified Permissions (AVP), and it is now an open-source project. Unlike general
purpose languages adapted for authorization, Cedar was designed specifically to clearly and
safely express real-world access control logic.

At ACME Corp, the identity team chose Cedar for the same reasons many engineering
teams do: It offers the right balance of power, performance, and auditability. As a policy

language, Cedar has four main strengths:

**Expressive** : Cedar can model complex authorization logic using

attributes, relationships, and environmental conditions. It works well
across various policy styles, whether you’re assigning access based on

job roles, relationships within an organizational graph, or dynamic
attributes such as device trust or time of day.

**Performant** : Since access decisions often occur in the critical path of a
request, speed is vital. Cedar is optimized for real-time evaluation,

providing predictable performance that makes it suitable for large-scale
production environments.

**Analyzable** : Authorization systems must be secure, not just fast. Cedar
policies are designed to be statically analyzable, meaning you can reason

about them before they are executed. You can verify if a policy is
satisfiable, if it might grant unintended access, or if a modification causes

regressions—all without deploying it first.
**Open** : Cedar is open source and designed for embedding. You can run it

as a library within your services, integrate it into custom policy
workflows, and take advantage of tools developed by the broader

community.

While Cedar is not the only policy language available—and we will explore others in the

next chapter—it offers an excellent framework for understanding the essential components
of policy. Its core ideas align well with broader concepts in access control, making it easier

to apply what you learn here to other systems in the future.

In the following sections, we’ll examine how Cedar structures policies and models access

requests using the PARC framework, and how its evaluation engine makes decisions.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

135

#### 7.2 Policy structure: effect, scope, and conditions

Cedar policies are structured around three key elements: effect, scope, and conditions.

These elements specify what a policy does, when it applies, and under which
circumstances. Collectively, they form the foundation of policy logic in Cedar and many

other policy languages as well.

This section explains how these elements are expressed in Cedar. We won’t go into

detailed syntax yet, but we’ll introduce each part conceptually so that you can recognize
them when we look at real examples later.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

136

7.2.1 Effect: what the policy does

Every Cedar policy has an explicit effect: It either `permits` or `forbids` an action.

Most policies are written to grant access, meaning they permit access under specific

conditions. However, Cedar also supports explicit forbid policies, which let authors set rules
to deny access. A policy that forbids always overrides one that permits. This makes it

simpler to enforce constraints like “never allow access to confidential documents from
unmanaged devices,” even if a permit policy might normally apply.

[At ACME Corp, for instance, the identity team uses both types of policies:](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-7?potentialInternalRefId=33---book-markup-container)

A `permit` policy may allow engineers to deploy code from managed

devices.
A `forbid` policy might prevent deployments altogether outside of

business hours for junior engineers, even if they’re on call.

The effect is always the first thing a Cedar policy states, and it determines whether the

policy contributes a yes or a no to the overall decision.

7.2.2 Scope: when the policy applies

The scope of a policy specifies the who, what, and where of an access request:

**Principal** : who is making the request

**Action** : what operation they are trying to perform
**Resource** : which objects the action targets

In Cedar, these are included in the policy header. The engine uses them to quickly
determine which policies are relevant to a specific request.

Think about ACME’s Customer Collaboration platform. A policy might be scoped like this:

**Principal** : any employee

**Action** : “view” or “edit”
**Resource** : any document where the employee is the owner

This scoped structure allows this policy to be selected and evaluated when someone tries to
view a document they own; it doesn’t apply to unrelated actions or resources.

7.2.3 Conditions: under what circumstances

_Conditions_ are boolean expressions that must be true for the policy to apply. Conditions
further define the policy. They are optional but often necessary. They enable policies to

consider dynamic contexts, including attributes of the principal, resource, or environment.
Common examples include:

Time of day
Device trust status

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

137

Department or team membership

On-call status

In ACME’s deployment tools, conditions enable security engineers to safeguard their

applications from unauthorized deployments. For example:

The engineer must be using a company-managed device.

If it’s outside business hours, they must also be on call.
Their clearance level must be sufficient for the deployment pipeline

they’re working on.

These rules aren’t part of the scope. Instead, they exist within the condition logic, making

policies flexible without becoming unwieldy.

7.2.4 Putting it together

Effect, scope, and conditions are the foundation of a policy contract: “This principal is

permitted (or forbidden) to take this action on this resource, if these conditions are true.”

Figure 7.1 shows a complete Cedar policy that follows this structure. It permits an

employee access to any document they own, but only if they are using a managed device.

The top box states the policy’s effect: permit.

The middle box defines the scope, indicating that the policy applies to
employees performing "view" or "edit" actions on documents.

The bottom box specifies the conditions—specifically, that the resource’s
owner must match the principal and that the device must be managed.

Figure 7.1 A complete Cedar policy showing effect (top box), scope (middle box), and conditions (bottom box).

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

138

Policies like this enable ACME Corp to safeguard the Customer Collaboration platform,

ensuring that sensitive customer data is accessed only under appropriate conditions. The
structure directly mirrors the conceptual model we discussed: a clear outcome, a well
defined scope, and contextual conditions that provide flexibility to the policy.

In the next section, we will examine policy evaluation more closely using PARC—the

model Cedar employs to represent access requests at runtime. While policy structure
explains how rules are written, PARC illustrates how they are evaluated.

#### 7.3 The PARC model: understanding policy evaluation

Every access request addresses a fundamental question: Can this principal perform this

action on this resource under these conditions? This question forms the basis of Cedar’s
evaluation model, as well as most modern authorization systems. In the previous section,

we explained how policies are structured: Each policy states an effect, defines its scope
with a principal, action, and resource, and may include conditions that further restrict when

the rule applies.

Those same components also shape the structure of an access request. Cedar formalizes

them into a model we’ll refer to throughout this chapter and the rest of the book—PARC:

The _Principal_ is the entity making the request, whether it is an employee,

a service, or a delegated role.
The _Action_ is what they’re trying to do—such as “view,” “edit,” or “deploy.”

The _Resource_ is the object that is being acted upon—a document,
system, or record.

The _Conditions_ specify the context of the request—such as time of day,
device trust, or geographic location.

While the preceding section focused on policy structure—how rules are written—this section
focuses on PARC, which captures how rules are evaluated. The two perspectives mirror

each other. A policy’s scope maps to the principal, action, and resource in the request, and
its conditions are evaluated against the request’s context.

In the sections that follow, we will examine how Cedar handles each of these inputs, how
matching and evaluation are performed in practice, and what occurs when multiple policies

apply to the same request.

7.3.1 Cedar’s representation of PARC

To evaluate a policy, Cedar needs input. That input is an access request following the PARC

model: Principal, Action, Resource, and Context. These elements are provided to the Cedar
engine as structured data—usually JSON—and evaluated against the policies in a policy

store. The following JSON shows an example of such a request asking whether Bob can edit
a document from a managed device:

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

139

{

}

"principal": "Employee::\"bob\"",

"action": "Action::\"edit\"",

"resource": "Document::\"doc456\"",

"context": {

"device": {

"is_managed": true

},

"time": "2025-07-08T10:30:00Z"

}

This JSON offers a structured input to the policy engine, representing a principal, action,

resource, and context.

FROM RUNTIME TO REQUEST: MAPPING REAL-WORLD INPUTS TO CEDAR

Cedar expects each authorization request to follow the PARC model—Principal,

Action, Resource, and Context—usually represented in JSON. However, in real-world
applications, these inputs don’t always start out as JSON. They often originate from

sources such as the following:

**gRPC calls**, where caller identity and action are embedded in

metadata.
**HTTP headers**, such as bearer tokens, session information, or request

paths.
**Application context**, such as device fingerprinting, current time, or

environment variables.

In practice, these details must be extracted and normalized before they can be

evaluated. For example, a service might:

Pull the authenticated principal from a JWT in an HTTP request header

Determine the action based on the endpoint being called
Map the resource from the request body or URL path

Derive context from headers (for example, User-Agent) or internal
system state

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

140

The system invoking Cedar is responsible for constructing this request. Cedar doesn’t

specify how the data should be collected—only that, once it is, it must be organized
according to the PARC model. This flexibility allows Cedar to easily integrate with

many different architectures and protocols, without requiring a specific transport or
format.

The JSON illustrates how ACME could model an access request for its Customer
Collaboration platform. The policy shown in figure 7.1 depends on a few details about how

ACME models its data.

Principals are represented as entities in the `Employee` namespace, such

as `Employee::"bob"` .

Documents identifiers are scoped in the `Document` namespace.

As we’ve seen, ACME has an entity store represented by a relationship
graph that includes an `owner` edge linking documents to their owners.

The context of each access request includes details about the requesting
device, such as a boolean flag called `is_managed` that indicates whether

the company manages the device.

Cedar evaluates each request by comparing its input to the defined policies. Figure 7.2

shows how Bob’s request aligns with the policy from figure 7.1. The arrows indicate how
each part of the request is matched or evaluated against the corresponding part of the

policy, first by scope (principal, action, resource) and then by conditions in the when clause.

Figure 7.2 Mapping an access request to a policy. Each component of the request (left) is matched against

the corresponding part of the policy (right). Scope is matched directly; conditions are evaluated using

attributes and context.

Let’s walk through a request from Bob, an ACME employee, to edit a document in the

Customer Collaboration platform. The request contains the information needed to evaluate
the policy:

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

141

Principal: `Employee::"bob"`

Action: `Action::"edit"`

Resource: `Document::"doc456"` (which has owner: `Employee::"bob"` )

Context: `{ device: { is_managed: true } }`

When the Cedar engine receives this request, it searches for policies whose scope matches

the principal, action, and resource. The policy shown in figure 7.1 specifies the following:

```
      principal in Employee::*
      action in ["view", "edit"]
      resource in Document::*

```

That scope clearly matches Bob’s request. Next, the engine evaluates the policy’s
conditions, which specify:

`resource.owner == principal` : Bob is the owner of doc456, so this is

true.

`context.device.is_managed == true` : Bob is using a managed device,

so this is also true.

Since both the scope and conditions match, and the policy has a `permit` effect, the engine

grants a decision of `allow` .

USING THE CEDAR POLICY ENGINE

Cedar is a policy evaluation engine—it does not make access control decisions
independently. Instead, it is part of a larger system that provides the data and

context necessary to evaluate each request.

To use Cedar effectively, a developer needs to:

Construct the access request, including the principal, action, resource,
and any relevant contextual data.

Provide the relevant policies for the application.
Provide entity data representing the principals and resources involved,

including any relationships or attributes that policies depend on, such
as ownership or team membership.

The Cedar engine evaluates policies using the request and entity data and then
issues a decision: allow, deny, or no decision.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

142

In this example, the condition `resource.owner == principal` depends on data from

ACME’s internal relationship graph, not the request. Remember that the Customer
Collaboration platform uses a graph to model ownership and other relationships. An edge

labeled `owner` points from the `Document::"doc456"` entity to the `Employee::"bob"` entity,

indicating that Bob owns the document. This information is part of the entity data that the

Cedar engine references during evaluation. This setup allows policies to rely on
relationships such as ownership, membership, or management without needing those

relationships included in every request.

If Bob tries to access the document from an unmanaged device, like his personal laptop,

the scope would still match but the `is_managed` condition would fail. In that case, the policy

would not apply, and unless another permit policy applied, the request would be denied.

[This example shows how the request structure (PARC) and the policy structure (effect,](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-7?potentialInternalRefId=123---book-markup-container)
scope, conditions) work together during evaluation. In the next section, we’ll look more

closely at Cedar’s policy matching and decision semantics.

7.3.2 Evaluating policies

After receiving a request, the policy engine evaluates relevant policies to make a decision.

In a medium- or large-scale organization like ACME Corp, policy logic is rarely located in a
single place. Instead, it comes from multiple teams and systems, each with a specific

purpose and scope. For example, ACME Corp probably has several policy stores, including
the following:

Security group policies enforce organization-wide security mandates, such
as requiring managed devices or specific encryption standards.

Application-specific policies are established by teams like Finance, HR, or
Customer Collaboration to govern domain-level activities (for example,

invoice approvals or document editing).

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

143

When a request comes in—such as Bob attempting to edit a document—the authorization

layer gathers the relevant policies from these sources. Cedar treats them as a single policy
set and evaluates them in one decision cycle.

HOW CEDAR MATCHES POLICIES TO REQUESTS

Cedar evaluates each request in two distinct stages:

1. Scope Matching—Cedar first considers policies where the principal, action,

and resource match the request’s principal, action, and resource. If no
policy matches based on scope, the request is implicitly denied.

2. Condition Evaluation—Cedar then evaluates the conditions of any scopedmatching policies using attribute lookups and contextual values. Every

`when` condition must evaluate to `true` and every `unless` condition must

evaluate to `false` .

Only policies that pass both stages contribute their effect to the final decision.

DATA TYPES AND ACCESS

Cedar enforces a strongly typed, deterministic evaluation model, purpose-built for secure,

predictable authorization logic.

Every value in Cedar must have a clearly defined type. These types are declared in the

policy schema. This clarity prevents casting errors that could lead to subtle breaches. For
example, comparing `"123"` (string) to `123` (number) would be a type mismatch, not a

successful match, helping developers catch logic errors early. Cedar’s type checker can also
flag incorrect set literals (such as mixing types) before deployment, reducing surprises at

runtime.

[Cedar utilizes intuitive dot notation for accessing data fields:](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-7?potentialInternalRefId=137---book-markup-container)

principal.department

resource.owner

context.device.is_managed

This syntax mirrors how you reference object properties in everyday programming.
Whether you’re checking Bob’s department or verifying the device’s trust status, dot

notation makes the code clear and easy to understand. Cedar also supports bracket syntax,
which can be combined with dot notation. For example:

context["device"].is_managed

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

144

Cedar’s dot-notation and bracket syntax work consistently. Dot notation is cleaner, but

brackets can be helpful when attribute names include special characters or need to be
computed. In short, Cedar offers predictable, straightforward access to deeply nested data,

regardless of slight differences in how the data is modeled or represented in the entity
store or incoming request.

7.3.3 Combining results from multiple policies

Once Cedar has filtered and evaluated individual policies, it needs to combine their results
into a single decision. It does this using a simple, but powerful, deny-overrides model:

1. If any applicable policy is `forbid` → `Deny` . If even one policy with effect

`forbid` evaluates to true, Cedar immediately returns `Deny`, regardless of

any matching permit policies. This ensures that explicit denials always
take precedence.

2. If any applicable policy is a `permit` policy → `Allow` . If there are no

matching `forbids` but at least one `permit` policy evaluates to `true`,

Cedar returns `Allow` .

3. Otherwise → `Deny` by default. If no policies apply or any applicable

`permit` policies evaluate to `false`, Cedar returns `Deny` . This deny-by
default approach makes explicit permissions the only way to grant access.

This model offers important advantages:

**Safety-first defaults.** Access is granted only when explicitly allowed,

reducing exposure from missing or incomplete policies.
**Policy guardrails.** Universal deny rules like “no non-managed devices”

can always block access, even if other policies allow it.
**Order independence.** Since denials hold the ultimate authority, there's

no need to worry about policy order or priority conflicts. Cedar’s logic
stays straightforward and predictable.

Cedar’s decision model can be summarized by these three rules:

implicit `Deny` by default

explicit `permits` required

`forbids` always taking precedence

These rules ensure clear, predictable, and scalable policy evaluation that doesn’t rely on
policy order.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

145

7.3.4 PARC as the bridge

In this main section, we’ve examined Cedar’s PARC model in detail: the structure of a
request (Principal, Action, Resource, and Conditions), how policies are written to match

those elements, how the engine filters by scope, evaluates conditions, and ultimately
makes decisions using deny-overrides.

PARC is more than just a conceptual model—it’s the practical agreement Cedar expects
in every request. The same four elements determine how you create policies, how those

rules relate to real-world inputs, and how evaluation proceeds. This common language
makes Cedar easy to work with, especially when updating legacy rules or collaborating with

non-technical team members.

[PARC acts as a bridge between theory and practice. In Chapter 8, when comparing](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-7?potentialInternalRefId=159---book-markup-container)

Cedar to languages like OPA/Rego, OpenFGA, or XACML, PARC will serve as our common
reference point. Each language addresses the question “Can this principal perform this

action on this resource under these conditions?” However, they express it differently. Think
of PARC as the foundation that helps us understand other policy languages, see where they

align with PARC, and examine how their design choices influence your authorization
strategy.

#### 7.4 Cedar’s unique design

Cedar isn’t a general-purpose programming language—and that’s intentional. It
concentrates on one job: expressing authorization logic that is clear, correct, and efficient.

Its design emphasizes safety over complexity, ease of analysis over expressiveness, and
speed over generality. In this section, we’ll explore the features that make Cedar unique

and effective for building secure, real-time access control systems.

7.4.1 Strong data types

Cedar provides a variety of primitive types: booleans, strings, longs (64-bit integers), and

composite types like sets and records—along with extensions such as datetime, decimal,
duration, and ipaddr, allowing safe checks like `context.device.ip` `==`

`ip("192.168.0.10")` or conditional logic based on timestamps.

Cedar is a statically validated, strongly typed policy language. All entities, actions,

attributes, and relationships are defined in a schema, and policies are type-checked against
that schema before they can be evaluated. Strong typing prevents misuse, such as

comparing strings to numbers or mixing types in sets, catches errors at runtime, and
reduces unpredictable behavior in production.

7.4.2 Rich entity model

Cedar supports first-class entity references, meaning that principals and resources aren’t
just strings or labels—they’re structured objects. This enables natural, readable expressions

like this:

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

146

resource.owner == principal

In this case, `principal` and `resource.owner` are entity references that Cedar can reason

about, compare, and connect. Policies can express relationships (such as ownership or
team membership) without needing to pass those links in every request. Instead, Cedar

evaluates them against any entity data loaded at runtime.

This model mirrors how most real-world systems organize access: Employees own

documents, managers oversee teams, and services act on behalf of users. Cedar’s entity
model allows you to directly represent and query those relationships, making policies more

expressive, easier to maintain, and simpler to audit.

[By supporting rich entities and strong typing, Cedar promotes structure rather than ad](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-7?potentialInternalRefId=170---book-markup-container)

hoc logic, making it easier to write policies that are both correct and understandable. It also
provides a foundation for advanced analysis tools to identify coverage gaps, policy conflicts,

or unexpected grants.

7.4.3 Clear namespace and type safety

Cedar organizes all principals, resources, and actions using namespaces, which appear

before the `::` delimiter. For example:

Finance::Document

CustomerCollab::Employee

Namespaces have several benefits:

Disambiguate entities and actions—Imagine ACME manages both a
furniture inventory service and a general-purpose database system, each

having a `Table` entity type. Namespaced references like

`Furniture::Table` and `Database::Table` prevent conflicts when policies

are grouped or merged.
Organize policy domains clearly—By grouping related entities and actions

under distinct namespaces, Cedar helps teams maintain clear boundaries
between application areas more easily.

Control visibility and access — Namespaces naturally set boundaries:
Types are unqualified within their namespace but need to be fully

qualified when referenced across different namespaces. This enhances
clarity and enforces the desired access control scopes.

Namespaces also prevent incorrect attribute expressions, such as `resource.owner` . Since

each entity type is defined within a namespace, Cedar ensures that `owner` exists on that

specific type. Using `resource.owner` on an entity without that attribute results in a type

error before deployment.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

147

Likewise, namespaces ensure type-safe policy logic: You can’t mistakenly compare an

Employee to a Document or perform an IP check on a timestamp. Namespaces combined
with attribute definitions strengthen the logic, providing strong guarantees of policy

integrity and preventing subtle but dangerous authorization bugs.

7.4.4 What Cedar doesn’t include

Cedar intentionally omits certain features found in other policy or programming languages,

such as regular expressions, floating-point arithmetic, string concatenation, loops, or
external calls. These features are excluded not by mistake, but by design: Each one adds

risk to performance, complexity, or reasoning ability.

For example, regular expressions can be error-prone and susceptible to denial-of-service

attacks like catastrophic backtracking. Similarly, allowing loops or external calls could result
in unpredictable execution times and hidden side effects, violating Cedar’s core promise of

pure, deterministic evaluation with guaranteed performance limits.

[By concentrating on a limited, declarative feature set—such as booleans, strings, sets,](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-7?potentialInternalRefId=183---book-markup-container)

entity references, and basic operators—Cedar makes policies easy to read, quick to
evaluate, and suitable for formal verification, ensuring they are trustworthy and easy to

maintain at scale.

7.4.5 Minimal operators with maximum impact

Cedar provides a deliberately lean set of operators—sufficient to express powerful

authorization logic without sacrificing safety, performance, or clarity. Table 7.1 shows an
overview of Cedar’s operators.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

148

Table 7.1 Cedar’s core data types with their associated operators and functions

|Data<br>type|Operators / Functions|Example|
|---|---|---|
|Boolean|&&, ||, !|device.is_managed|| resource.category ==<br>“public”|
|String|==, !=, like|resource.category like "customer-*"|
|Long|==,<, >,<=, >=, +, -,<br>*|resource.size<= 1048576 // 1Mb|
|Datetime|==,<, <=, >, >=,<br>datetime()|context.requestTime >= datetime("2025-07-<br>01T00:00:00Z")|
|Duration|==,<, <=, >, >=,<br>duration()|context.sessionDuration< duration("8h")|
|IP<br>address|==, in, ip()|ip(context.clientIp) in ip("10.0.0.0/8")|
|Sets|in, .contains(),<br>.containsAny()|principal in Group::"acme-admins"|
|Entity<br>types|is, type qualifiers|resource is Document|
|Tags|.hasTag(),.getTag()|resource.hasTag("sensitive")|

Each operator in Cedar maps directly to real-world authorization needs. This minimal yet

expressive operator set is a key part of what makes Cedar practical and trustworthy for
real-world authorization. The next few sections discuss some of Cedar’s special operators.

WILDCARD MATCHING

While Cedar doesn’t support regular expressions, it does have wildcard matching using the
`like` operator. Here’s an example in Cedar:

context.device.name like "corp-*"

This expression returns true whenever the context includes a `device` record whose `name`

begins with `"corp-"`, providing reliable wildcard behavior despite the lack of regular

expressions.

TIME-BASED CONDITIONS

Time-based constraints are also helpful in many authorization policies for enforcing date or

duration limits on access. Here’s a policy condition using time-based criteria:

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

149

when {

context.requestTime < datetime("2025-12-31T23:59:59Z")

&& context.requestAge < duration("30d")

}

This condition requires that the request occur before the end of 2025 and within the past

30 days.

IP CONSTRAINTS

Authorization policies often assess the sources and destinations of requests, which are

identified by IP addresses. Here’s an example of a policy condition using IP operators.

when {

ip(context.clientIp) in ip("10.0.0.0/16")

}

This condition is true when the `clientIP` belongs to the 10.0.x.x internal network. Note

that the `ip()` operator constructs the range from the CIDR block specification.

7.4.6 Safe and analyzable by design

Cedar strikes a careful balance between expressiveness, speed, and auditability. Its design

emphasizes features that make it both powerful and trustworthy, starting with
performance, safety, and analyzability.

PERFORMANCE

Cedar is engineered for sub-millisecond policy evaluation—even when processing hundreds
or thousands of policies. It accomplishes this through efficient scope filtering and a compact

evaluation model that avoids costly operations. In one benchmark, Cedar consistently made
decisions in under 1ms across a large policy set.

SAFETY

Cedar avoids unsafe actions by blocking access to the file system, network calls, and other
side effects. Because developers can author policies without worrying about sandboxing,

Cedar’s evaluation engine stays reliable and secure, even with untrusted policy definitions.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

150

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

151

With SMT-based verification, your access control policies are more than code; they

become formally validated artifacts. No more guesswork. No silent mistakes. Just
proven correctness, ensuring your policies perform exactly as intended, today and in

the future.

ANALYZABILITY

Because Cedar policies utilize a limited set of types and pure expressions, they can be
analyzed statically with formal guarantees.

Symbolic encoding of policies allows SMT-based checks for invariants,
equivalence, or coverage. See the earlier sidebar “SMT analysis and why

it matters for authorization” for more details on how this works.
Cedar Analysis helps teams demonstrate that refactored policies maintain

behavior.
Policies can be checked for contradictions or unreachable rules before

they are deployed in production.

Together, these capabilities ensure teams can confirm that policy changes do not create

vulnerabilities before deployment.

WHY IT MATTERS

As shown in table 7.2, Cedar’s design provides substantial real-world benefits.

Table 7.2 Why Cedar’s design matters—a comparison of core design goals and their practical benefits to policy

|development|Col2|
|---|---|
|**Benefit**|**Impact on policy development**|
|Predictability|Pure, deterministic logic ensures the same inputs always produce the<br>same decision.|
|Trustworthiness|Explicit deny-overrides and no hidden side effects build confidence in<br>policy outcomes.|
|Auditability|Static checks and proof tools allow errors to be caught before<br>deployment.|
|Scalability|Polices remain fast and verifiable, even at enterprise scale.|

These features mean developers can trust their policies without constantly testing them in

production. Changes become deliberate, testable, and transparent, exactly what mature
security and compliance programs require.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

152

7.4.7 Clean, simple, and powerful

Cedar balances power and simplicity. It includes entities, typed values, attribute access,
and safe operators—everything you need for clear policy logic. What it doesn’t include—like

regex or loops—removes sources of error and confusion. The result is a language that’s
approachable, auditable, and high-performing, with formal reasoning benefits built in.

#### 7.5 Cedar’s distinctive strengths

Cedar combines the key elements of a strong authorization language: clarity, precision, and
performance. Earlier in this chapter, we saw how it models access decisions using PARC,

how its policies are structured around effect, scope, and conditions, and how its type
system, entity model, and evaluation semantics work together to ensure safe and efficient

decisions.

But what makes Cedar stand out isn’t just its completeness, but how each part supports

the others. Its limited but expressive operator set handles real-world use cases without
adding unnecessary complexity. Cedar’s type system catches common errors early, while its

namespace design encourages modular, conflict-free development. By omitting features like
regular expressions, loops, and external calls, Cedar keeps policies fast, easy to analyze,

and deterministic.

[These choices make Cedar approachable to developers, auditable by reviewers, and](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-7?potentialInternalRefId=236---book-markup-container)

reliable in production. The language provides enough flexibility to support various
authorization styles—from attribute-based decisions to relationship-based access—without

becoming fragile or difficult to reason about.

[In the next chapter, we will examine how other policy languages address these same](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-7?potentialInternalRefId=237---book-markup-container)

challenges. Using PARC as a reference, we will compare Cedar to alternatives like
OPA/Rego, OpenFGA, and XACML to better understand the tradeoffs and help you select the

appropriate tool for your system.

#### 7.6 Summary

_Cedar_ is a purpose-built policy language designed for real-time, finegrained authorization decisions using attributes, relationships, and

context.
Policies are organized using three elements: effect ( `permit` or `forbid` ),

scope (principal, action, resource), and conditions (contextual logic).
Access requests follow the PARC model, and Cedar evaluates them by

matching scope and evaluating conditions, using a deny-overrides
decision model.

Cedar offers a rich entity model, allowing policies to reference
relationships such as ownership or team membership through first-class

entity types and attributes.
Namespaces and type safety help prevent errors and promote modular

policy development by clearly organizing entities and enforcing strict type
rules.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

153

Cedar emphasizes safety, clarity, and analyzability by using strong typing,

simple data access, and a minimal set of operators.
Design choices such as omitting regular expressions and loops make

policies easier to audit, verify, and maintain, especially when using static
analysis tools like Cedar Analysis.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

154

## Policy languages and frameworks

This chapter covers

How XACML, OPA/Rego, OpenFGA, and AWS IAM approach authorization in modern,
large-scale systems

Using the PARC framework to analyze various policy languages

The structure of policies in each language using equivalent policy examples

Comparisons for choosing the right policy language or framework for your needs

ACME Corp wasn’t always a large company. ACME started small, and as it grew, so did the
complexity of its authorization needs. What began as a handful of internal systems quickly

turned into a sprawling network of cloud infrastructure, customer-facing platforms, and
workflows that require strict compliance. Every new system introduced additional

requirements, and often, a new approach to policy.

In the early days, ACME’s IT team adopted an off-the-shelf document management

system that used XACML for access control. The standards-based approach seemed
promising, especially for regulated workflows in HR and Finance. However, as the team

tried to adapt it to changing business needs, the issues of verbosity, complexity, and tooling
became increasingly difficult to ignore.

[When ACME’s engineering team migrated to Kubernetes and adopted microservices, they](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-8?potentialInternalRefId=7---book-markup-container)
faced a different challenge: implementing policies across a decentralized infrastructure.

They turned to the Open Policy Agent (OPA) and its Rego language, which provided the
flexibility to express complex logic and validate configurations across services. OPA was

powerful but not specifically designed for access control, and maintaining reusable,
consistent policies was difficult at scale.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

155

For ACME’s new Customer Collaboration platform, the requirements were different again.

The product team needed fine-grained access control that supported delegated permissions
and dynamic sharing between employees and customers. They chose OpenFGA, a

relationship-based authorization system inspired by Google’s Zanzibar, which provided a
clear model for managing access through a graph of relationships.

[Meanwhile, the DevOps team was all-in on AWS. They utilized AWS IAM policies to](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-8?potentialInternalRefId=9---book-markup-container)
manage access to cloud resources, including S3 buckets, EC2 instances, and Lambda

functions. IAM’s JSON-based policy language was deeply integrated into the platform, and
although it had its quirks, it provided fine-grained control through built-in support for

resource types, actions, and context-aware conditions.

[In this chapter, we’ll examine each of these policy frameworks—XACML, Rego, OpenFGA,](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-8?potentialInternalRefId=10---book-markup-container)

and AWS IAM. Along the way, we’ll apply the PARC model introduced in Chapter 7 to
understand how each language defines policy, authorizes decisions, represents resources,

and uses contextual information. We’ll conclude with a comparison that unifies these
concepts and compares all of these languages to Cedar.

#### 8.1 XACML: the first policy language standard

Before “policy as code” became a rallying cry for cloud-native developers, authorization

policies were often embedded within application logic or enforced through inflexible,
product-specific rules. The eXtensible Access Control Markup Language (XACML)

[(https://docs.​oasis-open.​org/xacml/​3.0/xacml-​3.0-core-​spec-os-en.​html),](https://docs.oasis-open.org/xacml/3.0/xacml-3.0-core-spec-os-en.html) introduced by
OASIS in 2003, was one of the first significant efforts to standardize authorization policy as

a separate, declarative language.

XACML not only defined a language for writing policies but also established a

comprehensive architecture for how decisions should be evaluated and enforced. The
authorization reference architecture introduced in chapter 4 was initially proposed as part of

the XACML standard. Recall that this included components like Policy Decision Points (PDPs)
and Policy Enforcement Points (PEPs). For a time, especially in government and regulated

enterprise settings, XACML was seen as the future of access control.

[Although it was ambitious and comprehensive, XACML struggled to gain traction in](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-8?potentialInternalRefId=14---book-markup-container)

practice. Developers found the XML syntax to be verbose and difficult to write and test.
Tooling lagged, and the runtime model was not performant enough for many real-world

applications. Still, many of its core ideas—centralized policy evaluation, structured decision
logic, separation of enforcement and decision—laid the groundwork for what came after.

8.1.1 A XACML simple example

ACME Corp has an internal document archive used by HR and finance, controlled by XACML
policies. This in prose expresses one of the rules they’d like to formalize in XACML:

Permit access to confidential documents if the requester is in the same department as
the document’s owner.

Here’s a simplified, partial XACML policy that captures this logic:

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

156

<Policy PolicyId="ConfidentialDocAccess" RuleCombiningAlgId="permit

overrides">

<Target>

<Subjects>

<AnySubject/>

</Subjects>

<Resources>

<Resource>

<Attribute AttributeId="resource:type" DataType="string">

<AttributeValue>confidential-doc</AttributeValue>

</Attribute>

</Resource>

</Resources>

</Target>

<Rule RuleId="PermitSameDept" Effect="Permit">

<Condition>

<Apply FunctionId="string-equal">

<AttributeDesignator AttributeId="subject:department"

Category="access-subject" DataType="string"/>

<AttributeDesignator AttributeId="resource:owner-department"

Category="resource" DataType="string"/>

</Apply>

</Condition>

</Rule>

</Policy>

Knowing what you already understand about policies, you can probably read this through

several times and develop a sense of its purpose. The `<Target/>` specifies the entities and

actions that the policy applies to. The `<Rule/>` defines the conditional access logic. XACML

allows a policy to have multiple rules for a given `<Target/>,` and the `RuleCombiningAlgId`

from the `<Policy/>` tag indicates how the results of the rules will be combined.

For reference, the equivalent policy in Cedar could be written as follows:

permit(principal, action, resource)

when {

resource.confidential == true &&

principal.department == resource.owner.department

};

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

157

Just like we’ve discussed for Cedar, to evaluate this XACML policy, the PEP would send a

request to the PDP, including attributes about the requester (subject), the document
(resource), the action, and any relevant environment conditions (such as time or location).

The preceding policies do not address what happens when a document is not confidential.
That would be handled by a different policy or rule that allows access to documents that are not

confidential. For the rest of this chapter, we will ignore cases where the document is not confidential
and focus only on policies for confidential documents.

8.1.2 Applying the PARC model to XACML

Let’s look at how XACML fits into the PARC model introduced in Chapter 7:

**Principal** —XACML refers to the principal as the “subject” and represents
them using attributes like username, department, and clearance. These

attributes are supplied in the access request and can be used in policy
conditions. XACML doesn’t have a first-class object model for principals;

they’re represented only by their attributes.
**Action** —XACML represents actions (such as read, write, or delete) as

string-valued attributes in the request, typically `action:id` . Policies

match actions either in the `<Target/>` element or within the

`<Condition/>` of a rule. XACML does not specify an action type system,

so consistency is left to the policy author.

**Resource** —XACML describes resources entirely through attributes such
as `resource:id`, `resource:type`, or `resource:owner-department` . There

is no native support for object hierarchies or relationships between
resources; everything is flattened into the attribute model. This

complicates the expression of fine-grained or graph-based access control.
**Context** —XACML supports rich contextual data within the “environment”

category of requests. Elements such as time of day, IP address, device
posture, or other metadata can be used in conditions. This makes it

effective in compliance or risk-sensitive environments where external
context significantly influences access decisions.

Taken together, XACML’s approach to PARC reflects its roots in attribute-based access
control: everything—principals, actions, resources, and context—is modeled as attributes

and evaluated through rule conditions. While this gives it a great deal of expressive power,
it also makes policies more challenging to write, read, and maintain. Without native support

for types, relationships, or reusable structures, policy authors are left to manage
complexity through raw XML and consistent naming conventions.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

158

The biggest barrier to adoption for XACML wasn’t the attribute model itself; it was the

overall developer experience. Writing policies in verbose XML, lacking effective tools for
testing and debugging, and integrating with heavyweight policy decision infrastructure all

made XACML feel disconnected from modern development workflows. It laid important
groundwork for separating policy from code, but ultimately highlighted the need for more

user-friendly, embeddable, and developer-friendly policy systems.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

159

8.1.3 Legacy and lessons

Although XACML is seldom used in new systems today, its influence is still felt. The
architecture it proposed—decoupling enforcement from decision logic—is reflected in policy

engines like OPA and Cedar. Its detailed approach to attribute-based logic helped shape
ABAC models, even if its syntax became a cautionary tale.

At ACME, XACML never made it out of the data center. The document archive where it
was used remains a legacy system, with the original policies largely untouched—too fragile

and obscure for most developers to safely update. But the experience shaped the
company’s thinking: centralized policy was powerful, but only if the language was

accessible and flexible.

#### 8.2 OPA and Rego: Policy for cloud-native systems

As ACME’s infrastructure evolved toward microservices and Kubernetes, the identity team

found that traditional role-based access and legacy systems like XACML couldn’t keep up.
They needed a way to enforce consistent policies across APIs, CI/CD pipelines, container

[deployments, and more. That search led them to the Open Policy Agent (OPA, https://www.​](https://www.openpolicyagent.org/)
<u>[openpolicyagent.​org)—a general-purpose policy engine—and its policy language, Rego.](https://www.openpolicyagent.org/)</u>

OPA was designed for modern, distributed systems. It provides a lightweight decision
engine that can be embedded into applications, gateways, and controllers. Rather than

focus solely on access control, OPA treats policy more broadly: it can validate Kubernetes
resources, restrict API inputs, enforce admission control, and—yes—make authorization

decisions. This flexibility made it a favorite in the cloud-native ecosystem.

[OPA evaluates policies written in Rego, a declarative, logic-based language inspired by](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-8?potentialInternalRefId=47---book-markup-container)

Datalog. Rego lets developers write rules that define what is allowed or denied, using JSON
data structures as inputs. A typical Rego policy reads more like code than configuration,

which makes it powerful but sometimes difficult to learn.

8.2.1 Rego policies example

Here’s a straightforward Rego policy that limits access to confidential documents based on

department membership, similar to the earlier XACML example.

package acme.authz

import rego.v1

default allow := false

allow if {

input.resource.confidential == true

input.principal.department == input.resource.owner.department

}

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

160

This policy returns `true` (i.e., allows access) only if the document is marked as confidential

and the requesting principal is in the same department as the owner.

The equivalent Cedar policy (from above) expresses the same logic:

permit(principal, action, resource)

when {

resource.confidential == true &&

principal.department == resource.owner.department

};

In this example, the logic is almost the same in both languages because we’re not
leveraging Cedar’s scoping features; the access decision is fully determined by the

condition block.

8.2.2 Comparing Rego with Cedar

Recall that Cedar allows you to incorporate constraints on the principal, action, and

resource in the policy’s scope, making them an integral part of the policy’s structure rather
than just its logic. For example, the following Cedar policy restricts delete actions to only

principals in the admin group.

permit(

principal in Group::"admin",

action == Action::"delete",

resource

);

This policy doesn’t just express the access logic; it explicitly limits the scope of the policy to

apply only to admins performing the delete action, regardless of what the condition states.
Rego doesn’t support this kind of structured scoping, so the corresponding policy would be

written like this:

package acme.authz

import rego.v1

default allow := false

allow if {

input.action == "delete"

input.principal.groups[_] == "admin"

}
