[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

161

While the logic is similar, the way policy intent is expressed differs significantly. In Rego, all

constraints—on the principal, action, and resource—must be written as conditions within
the rule body. This provides the policy author flexibility but also puts the burden on them to

manually manage scope and semantics. You cannot declare, for example, that a rule
applies only to specific types of users or actions; you can only require certain conditions to

be satisfied.

Cedar, in contrast, enables constraints to be declared structurally within the policy head.

This enhances clarity, minimizes the risk of unintended application, and allows for
performance optimizations. Since the Cedar engine can examine policy scope before

evaluating the condition logic, it can pre-filter policies at runtime, considering only those
relevant to the request. Figure 8.1 shows the different flows for policy evaluation in OPA

and Cedar.

Figure 8.1 OPA (left) vs Cedar (right) policy evaluation flow. OPA evaluates all policies using the full input, with

no built-in filtering based on principal, action, or resource. In contrast, Cedar policies can declare structural

scope, allowing the engine to filter policies before evaluation. This improves performance and ensures that

only relevant policies are considered.

This structural filtering is a key architectural advantage of Cedar. Because policies can
specify which principals, actions, and resources they apply to, the Cedar engine can quickly

narrow down the set of policies that must be evaluated for each request. This not only
boosts performance but also makes policy behavior more predictable and easier to audit,

especially important in systems with large, diverse policy sets. Cedar’s scoping also
supports schema validation, static analysis, and indexing, making policies not only

expressive but also safer and more efficient to evaluate.

8.2.3 Applying the PARC model to OPA and Rego

OPA and Rego are designed to be general-purpose: they can evaluate any type of

structured decision, not just access control. This flexibility is a strength, but it also means
OPA doesn’t impose a specific model for how to represent principals, actions, resources, or

context. Instead, it’s up to the policy author to define the structure of the input object and
write rules against it. Let’s see how this looks from the perspective of PARC.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

162

**Principal** —Rego does not have a built-in concept of a principal. Instead,

policies operate on a user-defined `input.principal` object—usually a

JSON structure included with the request. This may contain attributes like

identifiers, groups, or departments, but it’s up to the policy author to
define them. There’s no schema enforcement or scoping at the language

level, so all constraints need to be explicitly stated in rule bodies.
**Action** —Actions are also unconstrained; they are often just a string like

"read", "write", or "deploy" within `input.action` . Rego treats this the

same as any other data, so it’s flexible but lacks structure. Matching is

usually done with simple equality checks inside rules.
**Resource** —Similar to principals, resources are arbitrary JSON objects;

commonly under `input.resource` . Because Rego can work with deeply

nested and dynamic data, it’s powerful for evaluating real-world resource

structures. However, this also means there’s no assurance that the
resource object conforms to a known type or shape, which can cause

subtle bugs if keys are missing or misnamed.
**Context** —Context is where Rego shines. Policies can take into account

time, location, network conditions, request headers, or any other
metadata provided through input or external data sources. This makes it

especially valuable for runtime enforcement decisions that rely on
environmental or organizational state.

Overall, Rego’s approach to PARC is very flexible, but that flexibility has a cost. Without
types, scopes, or language-level structures for principals, actions, or resources, policies

need to be written carefully and tested thoroughly to ensure they are correct. This makes
Rego a strong choice for infrastructure policy—especially in complex, data-rich

environments—but it can be more demanding for teams that want to implement detailed
authorization at scale.

8.2.4 Strengths and limitations

OPA and Rego gave ACME’s DevOps team the tools they needed to secure modern
infrastructure. Policies were portable, testable, and independent of the applications they

protected. However, as the use of OPA expanded, so did concerns about complexity. Rego’s
logic programming model has a steep learning curve, and it’s easy to write policies that are

correct but difficult to read or maintain. The absence of structure or types means validation,
analysis, and testing are critical, but the language itself does not support them.

OPA is a powerful tool for infrastructure policy, and Rego provides a flexible language for
expressing logic over arbitrary data. However, when used specifically for access control,

some teams—like ACME’s product engineers—found they preferred a language designed
expressly for authorization.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

163

#### 8.3 OpenFGA

As ACME’s Customer Collaboration platform matured, so did its authorization challenges.

The platform enabled employees and customers to share documents, leave comments, and
delegate responsibilities across teams. The access rules were dynamic: some documents

were visible to collaborators, others to managers, and many required fine-grained sharing,
often with external partners. ACME needed a model that went beyond roles or attributes.

They needed a way to represent and reason about relationships.

[To facilitate this, they turned to OpenFGA (https://openfga.​dev), an open-source project](https://openfga.dev/)

inspired by Google’s Zanzibar system. Designed from the ground up for relationship-based
access control (ReBAC), OpenFGA provides a scalable way to manage permissions using a

graph of relationships between entities: users, documents, teams, roles, and more. Rather
than write imperative policies, you define types and relationships in a schema, then express

permissions as rules over those relationships. Authorization decisions are made by
traversing this relationship graph.

[For ACME, OpenFGA was a natural fit. Instead of hard-coding complex logic, the product](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-8?potentialInternalRefId=77---book-markup-container)
team could model relationships between employees, customers, and documents (like the

ones we explored in chapter 6 and modeled in figure 6.1) and let OpenFGA evaluate access
dynamically.

8.3.1 How OpenFGA works

OpenFGA is based on the idea that access control can be represented as data: instead of
writing complex policy code, you establish relationships between entities and determine

permissions based on those relationships. In OpenFGA, the data is the policy.

At the heart of OpenFGA is a schema, a declarative description of the application’s

authorization model. The schema defines types, which represent the core entities in your
system (such as user, document, or folder), and for each type, it specifies relations and

permissions.

A _type_ defines an entity and the kinds of relationships it can participate

in. For example, a document might specify `owner`, `viewer`, and `editor`

relations.

A _relation_ is a named link between two types, usually between a resource
and a principal.

A _permission_ is a logical expression involving one or more relations, using
set logic (such as `viewer` or `editor`, or `owner->manager` ).

Once you’ve defined your schema, the relationship graph is stored as tuples. Each tuple
encodes a single fact, like “Alice is a viewer of Document 123”.

document:123#viewer@user:alice

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

164

These tuples form a directed graph of relationships among all entities. When a request

comes in—such as asking, “Can Alice view Document 123?”—OpenFGA checks to see if the
requested permission (like `can_view` ) is valid, using the graph structure and the schema

rules.

Unlike OPA or Cedar, OpenFGA doesn’t evaluate conditional logic or analyze request

attributes. It responds solely by walking the graph and applying relationship-based logic.
This makes OpenFGA fast and predictable, especially in collaborative applications where

relationships determine what actions are permitted.

8.3.2 Document access example

Recall this simplified access rule from ACME’s Customer Collaboration system:

Permit access to a document if the requester is the viewer or the owner, or if they
manage someone who owns it.

Rather than encode this logic in imperative policy code, we can model it declaratively in
OpenFGA using types, relationships, and permissions. Here’s how that looks in the schema:

type user

relations

define manager: [user]

type document

relations

define viewer: [user]

define owner: [user]

define can_access as viewer or owner or owner->manager

Let’s break this down:

The `user` type defines a relationship labeled `manager` between users.

The `document` type defines two relationships: `viewer` and `owner` . These

indicate direct connections between a `document` and `users` .

The `can_access` permission is defined as a logical expression over those

relations:

A `user` has permission `can_access` if they are either a

`viewer`, an `owner`, or a `manager` of an `owner` .

The expression `owner->manager` means for each `user`

who is an `owner` of the `document`, follow the `manager`

relation on that `user` to identify additional `users` who

should have access.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

165

In OpenFGA, relationships are stored as tuples, each representing a single fact. The `#` and `@`

symbols delineate the parts of the tuple. A colon separates objects and their type. For
example:

document:doc1#owner@user:alice

user:alice#manager@user:carol

These tuples mean:

Alice, a `user`, is the owner of `doc1,` which is a `document`

Carol is Alice’s manager

Figure 8.2 shows these relationships as a graph.

Figure 8.2 Relationship-based access in OpenFGA. This example shows how OpenFGA encodes permissions as

logical paths through structured relationships, allowing for dynamic and delegatable access without altering

the underlying policy logic.

When Carol tries to access `doc1`, OpenFGA evaluates the permission check:

{

"user": "user:carol",

"relation": "can_access",

"object": "document:doc1"

}

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

166

To answer this request, OpenFGA:

1. Finds that Alice is the owner of `document:doc1`

2. Sees that Carol is Alice’s manager

3. Concludes that Carol satisfies the `owner->manager` rule

4. Returns `true`, so access is permitted

This model lets ACME support delegation without the need to update the logic each time
roles or reporting structures change. When someone becomes a manager, they

automatically receive the permissions tied to that role, as long as the relationship graph is
updated to reflect their new role. There’s no need to modify policies or update ACLs

because access is determined by the data itself.

8.3.3 Applying the PARC Model to OpenFGA

OpenFGA takes a fundamentally different approach from languages like XACML, Rego, or

Cedar. Instead of operating over attributes or evaluating logic directly, it defines
authorization through relationships between typed objects—like users, resources, groups,

and roles—represented as data in a graph. Permissions are not written as rules in code but
are declared as logical expressions over these relationships and enforced via graph

traversal. This approach makes OpenFGA especially suitable for applications like ACME’s
Customer Collaboration platform, where sharing, delegation, and organizational

relationships play a key role in access decisions.

Here’s how OpenFGA maps to the PARC model:

**Principal** —Principals in OpenFGA are usually instances of a user type,
referenced in tuples such as `document:123#viewer@user:alice` . There

are no attributes or profiles; principals are identified only by their
presence in relationships. This simplifies the model but requires identity
related logic (like group membership or department) to be explicitly
modeled in the graph.

**Action** —OpenFGA doesn’t have actions in the traditional sense. Instead,
permissions are seen as named access checks, such as `can_view`,

`can_edit`, and `can_access` . These permissions aren’t just strings in a

request payload; they are predefined in the schema as logical

combinations of relationships. This approach fits well with applications
that have fixed sets of actions and clear semantics.

**Resource** —Resources are first-class, typed entities such as a document,
folder, or report. Each resource instance has a set of relationship tuples

stored in the system, defining who can do what. The schema strictly
controls which relationships and permissions are valid for each resource

type, providing strong guarantees about how authorization logic is
implemented.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

167

**Context** —attributes like time of day, location, device security posture, or

risk score are not natively supported in OpenFGA. The system only
evaluates relationships. If you need to consider contextual information, it

must be handled externally (in application logic or middleware), with the
outcome encoded as a relationship (for example, “Alice has on-call access

to prod”) or used to determine whether an OpenFGA check should be
performed.

Taken together, OpenFGA’s approach to PARC emphasizes structure and scalability over
flexibility. It performs best when access decisions can be fully expressed by a well-designed

schema and a set of relationships that mirror the current state of the organization.

At ACME, this enabled engineers to create dynamic, delegatable access patterns within

the Customer Collaboration platform without needing constant policy updates. However, it
also meant that any logic related to external factors—such as time-based access or security

posture—had to be managed outside the system. For teams whose access rules are based
on human relationships rather than transient conditions, OpenFGA provides a clear and

efficient foundation.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

168

#### 8.4 AWS IAM

Launched in 2011, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM, <u>[https://aws.amazon.com/​](https://aws.amazon.com/iam/)</u>

<u>[iam/) is one of the most widely used authorization systems in the world. Although it’s solely](https://aws.amazon.com/iam/)</u>
connected to AWS, millions of developers use it daily to manage access to their AWS

services. If you’ve launched an EC2 instance, uploaded data to S3, or called a Lambda
function, you’ve used IAM.

Although IAM is specific to a single cloud, AWS, its longevity and scale are unmatched.
AWS has reported that its identity layer processes over half a billion API calls every second

[(https://aws.​amazon.com/​awstv/watch/​44e6f1abd16/), resulting in trillions of policy](https://aws.amazon.com/awstv/watch/44e6f1abd16/)
evaluations daily. The popularity of AWS has made IAM the first—and sometimes only—

policy language many developers encounter.

8.4.1 How IAM works

IAM policies are written in JSON and specify permissions for principals (users and roles) and

AWS resources. AWS evaluates all relevant policies, including identity-based policies,
resource-based policies, Service Control Policies (SCPs), session policies, and permission

boundaries, before deciding whether to allow or deny a request. Deny rules override allow
rules, and the evaluation order is carefully defined in AWS’s documentation.

IAM policies are specific to AWS.

Actions correspond directly to AWS API calls (such as `"s3:GetObject"` ).

Resources are AWS objects identified by Amazon Resource Names
(ARNs).

Context is derived from request metadata, AWS global condition keys,
and custom tags.

Principals include IAM users, roles, or federated identities like those from
AWS IAM Identity Center.

Because IAM policies align closely with AWS’s architecture, they feel native to anyone
building on the platform. This integration enables the language to express fine-grained

permissions with minimal ambiguity, leveraging AWS’s built-in understanding of its services,
identifiers, and context keys. While this makes IAM especially powerful within AWS, it also

confines its use to that environment, an acceptable trade-off for the millions of developers
who rely on AWS daily.

8.4.2 Example: Confidential Document Access

At ACME, all AWS access is controlled using a federation with Identity Center, which is
connected to the company’s corporate directory. This arrangement ensures that attributes

like department are automatically synchronized and appear as principal tags on each
authenticated session. ACME uses these tags in IAM policies to consistently enforce access

rules across services.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

169

When Alice uploads a document, say `arn:aws:s3:::acme-docs/report.pdf`, to the

`acme-docs` S3 bucket, an AWS Lambda function deployed by ACME automatically adds two

tags to the object.

`owner-department` —copied from Alice’s department principal tag

`confidential` —set to "true" if the document is marked confidential in

ACME’s internal document management system

Later, Dan, who works in the same department as Alice, tries to access

`arn:aws:s3:::acme-docs/report.pdf` . Since both Alice’s and Dan’s department values

come from the same authoritative source (ACME’s corporate directory via Identity Center),

IAM can compare them directly.

With these tags in place, ACME can enforce the rule:

[Permit access to confidential documents only if the requester is in the same](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-8?potentialInternalRefId=146---book-markup-container)
department as the document’s owner.

The IAM policy appears as follows:

{

"Version": "2012-10-17"

"Statement": [

{

"Effect": "Allow",

"Action": "s3:GetObject",

"Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::acme-docs/*",

"Condition": {

"StringEquals": {

"aws:PrincipalTag/department":

"${s3:ExistingObjectTag/owner-department}"

"StringEqualsIfExists": {

"s3:ExistingObjectTag/confidential": "true"

}

}

}

]

}

This policy encodes the intent of the earlier English statement in JSON, granting a read

( `s3:GetObject)` if the object’s `confidential` tag is `“true”` and the departments match.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

170

IAM’s `Condition` block is where much of its expressiveness resides; it’s the AWS

equivalent of the `when` clause in Cedar or the rule body in Rego. By leveraging Identity

Center as the authoritative identity source and IAM’s tag-based conditions, ACME can

enforce fine-grained, attribute-based access control entirely within AWS’s native
authorization system.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

171

When a request is made, IAM compares the principal’s `department` tag to the S3

object’s `owner-department` tag. If they match and all other conditions in the

statement are met, the action is allowed. Since both tags ultimately come from the

same authoritative source (ACME’s corporate directory via Identity Center), the
comparison stays consistent and doesn’t need policy updates when individuals

change departments.

8.4.3 Applying the PARC model to AWS IAM

IAM was built specifically for the AWS ecosystem, so its interpretation of Principal, Action,
Resource, and Context is closely tied to AWS services and infrastructure. Unlike general
purpose policy languages, IAM can make strong assumptions about these elements because
they directly correspond to AWS concepts.

**Principal** —Principals in IAM are AWS identities, including IAM users, IAM
roles, or federated identities from sources like Identity Center. Attributes

can be added to principals as tags, which can be referenced in policies
using `aws:PrincipalTag/<attribute-name>` . This setup allows external

identity attributes, such as those from ACME’s corporate directory, to be
incorporated directly into access decisions.

**Action** —Actions in IAM are closely linked to AWS API operations, shown
as strings like `"s3:GetObject"` or `"ec2:StartInstances` ." Each AWS

service has its own set of actions, enabling IAM policies to be very
specific about which operations are allowed or denied.

**Resource** —Resources are AWS objects identified by Amazon Resource
Names (ARNs), such as `arn:aws:s3:::acme-docs/report.pdf` . Many

services support resource-based policies, which allow permissions to be
granted directly on a resource in addition to identity-based policies

attached to principals. Resource tagging is deeply integrated into the
model and is often used for attribute-based conditions.

**Context** —IAM supports extensive context evaluation using condition
keys. These include AWS global keys (like `aws:CurrentTime` or

`aws:SourceIp` ), service-specific keys (which have a prefix like `s3:` ), and

custom principal or resource tags. Conditions are represented in JSON

within the `Condition` element of a policy statement, making context

checks a key part of policy evaluation.

Taken together, IAM’s approach to PARC reflects its domain-specific design: each element is
defined and managed by AWS, enabling deep integration and precise control but limiting

portability outside the AWS environment. For ACME, using IAM to secure S3 documents
meant they could utilize AWS-native features—like principal and resource tags from Identity

Center—to implement attribute-based access without creating a separate authorization
layer.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

172

#### 8.5 Comparing policy languages

ACME’s journey through different approaches to policy illustrates how the right

authorization system depends on the problem you’re addressing, the environment you’re
working in, and the skills of the team putting it into action. The following sections give a

clear overview of each system using the PARC model as a perspective.

8.5.1 XACML

XACML was the first widely accepted standard for externalized authorization, with strong

attribute-based logic, but uses a verbose XML syntax that limited developer adoption:

Principal: Shown as attributes in the request; no first-class identity

model.
Action: Represented as attributes, usually strings like `"read"` or `"edit"` .

Resource: Entirely described through attributes; no native object
hierarchy or relationships.

Context: Robust ABAC support with extensive environment attributes.
Strengths: Uses standards, is expressive, and clearly separates policy

from enforcement.
Limitations: Verbose XML syntax, limited modern tools, heavyweight

PDP/PEP architecture.

XACML’s attribute model works well in compliance-focused environments but seems

outdated in modern development.

8.5.2 OPA/Rego

OPA/Rego demonstrates the power of integrating a general-purpose policy engine into

modern infrastructure, but its flexibility comes with the trade-off of manual scoping and a
steeper learning curve.

Principal: User-defined `input.principal` object; unconstrained by the

language.

Action: String in input; unconstrained.
Resource: Arbitrary JSON object in input; flexible but without schema

enforcement.
Context: Very strong; any data in `input` or `data` can be used in policies.

Strengths: Very flexible, embeddable, and compatible across various
infrastructure and applications.

Limitations: Manual scoping, a steeper learning curve, and policies that
can be difficult to read and maintain.

Rego’s flexibility makes it invaluable in cloud-native applications—ranging from Kubernetes
admission control to Terraform validation and API gateway enforcement—though it lacks a

built-in structure for principals, actions, and resources.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

173

8.5.3 OpenFGA

OpenFGA makes relationship-based authorization practical and scalable.

Principal: First-class entities (for example, `user` ) in relationship tuples; no

attributes.
Action: Named permissions in schema, derived from relationships.

Resource: First-class typed objects with defined relations in a schema.
No native context; must be modeled through relationships externally.

Strengths: Perfect for ReBAC; flexible, delegable sharing; scales
effectively.

Limitations: Not well suited for fine-grained, attribute-based authorization
decisions.

OpenFGA performs well in relationship-rich applications but needs to be combined with
other systems to manage contextual decisions.

8.5.4 AWS IAM

AWS IAM remains the most widely used authorization system globally. It is deeply

integrated into the AWS ecosystem and capable of fine-grained, context-aware control, but
it is limited to AWS.

Principal: IAM users, roles, or federated identities; attributes through tags
and principal tags.

Action: AWS API operations (such as `"s3:GetObject"` ); service-specific.

Resource: AWS objects identified by ARNs; supports tagging and

resource-based policies.
Context: Extensive through global and service-specific condition keys;

tag-aware.
Strengths: Comprehensive AWS integration, fine-grained, globally

scalable, mature tooling.
Limitations: AWS-specific; not applicable outside AWS.

IAM delivers the most mature, large-scale authorization in the industry, but only inside
AWS.

8.5.5 Cedar

Cedar draws lessons from all of these: declarative policies like XACML, embedding and
developer-focused tools like OPA, dynamic relationship modeling like OpenFGA, and tight

integration like IAM, while keeping portability and a clear type system.

Principal: Typed principals with schema-validated attributes.

Action: Typed actions with schema enforcement and explicit policy
scoping.

Resource: Typed resources with schema-validated attributes.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

174

Context: Rich, strongly typed attribute support; compatible with external

data sources.
Strengths: Clear and concise syntax, structural scoping; portable, and

embeddable.
Limitations: Newer ecosystem with fewer integrations compared to OPA.

Cedar provides a unifying approach: typed principals, actions, and resources; built-in
structural scoping; and the flexibility to model attributes, relationships, and context,

making it a strong candidate for teams seeking the precision of IAM and the developer
accessibility that XACML never achieved.

8.5.6 From strengths to selection

The preceding sections provide attributes for different policy languages and frameworks,
but what do these mean when selecting an authorization system? Figure 8.3 shows a

strength map for the policy languages we’ve discussed.

Figure 8.3 Strength map comparing five policy languages and frameworks—XACML, OPA/Rego, OpenFGA,

AWS IAM, and Cedar—across the four PARC elements and portability. Darker shading indicates stronger, more

native support for that element; lighter shading indicates partial or minimal support. This visual emphasizes

how each system’s design highlights different aspects of authorization, from attribute-rich context handling to

typed principals and explicit resource modeling.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

175

When choosing among these policy languages and frameworks, organizations should begin

by identifying the types of authorization issues they most often need to address. Teams
working in AWS will almost certainly use IAM for cloud access control but will probably

require a different solution for authorization outside AWS. Applications that rely heavily on
sharing and delegation might benefit from OpenFGA’s relationship-based model, while

systems that need precise, typed schemas and structural scoping could prefer Cedar. For
cloud-native infrastructure spanning multiple platforms, OPA/Rego’s flexibility makes it a

strong choice. ALFA provides a way to use XACML without the hassle of writing policies in
XML.

To narrow the field, ask:

What’s our primary model? Roles, attributes, relationships—or a

combination?
Where does enforcement take place? Inside a single platform like AWS,

across microservices, or in a distributed environment?
How portable should policies be? Will we need them to survive a platform

change?
Who will maintain them? Will policy authors be developers, system

administrators, or domain experts who lack advanced programming
skills?

What’s our tolerance for complexity? Some frameworks offer fine-grained
control but come with steeper learning curves.

Ultimately, the best choice depends on the mix of authorization models you need, your
performance requirements, and the developer experience your team can provide. By using

the PARC model and the strength map together, you can move from abstract feature lists to
a clear, practical choice.

#### 8.6 Summary

Over the years, a variety of policy languages and frameworks have been

developed to handle different needs.
XACML pioneered standardized ABAC but saw limited adoption due to

verbosity and complexity; ALFA emerged to make it more approachable.
OPA/Rego brings flexible, general-purpose policy-as-code to cloud-native

systems, often used for Kubernetes admission control and microservice
authorization.

OpenFGA implements a relationship-based model inspired by Zanzibar,
ideal for sharing and delegation scenarios.

AWS IAM is deeply integrated with AWS services, making it the default
choice for in-cloud authorization, though it’s not portable beyond AWS.

Applying PARC reveals how each system emphasizes different aspects of
authorization, providing guidance on which might fit best in a particular

environment.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

176

Selecting an authorization framework is partly dictated by factors beyond

your control, such as the cloud vendor you use or the software you
purchase.

Most organizations will end up using a mix of authorization frameworks
and languages.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

## Implementing policies with Cedar

This chapter covers

Designing and refining a Cedar schema as the foundation for policy authoring

Writing core Cedar policies, including rules for ownership, viewers, managers, and
teams

Applying standard authorization patterns like discretionary, membership, and

relationship permissions

Enforcing global constraints and enhancing policies with templates and overrides

Mapping real-world requests to Cedar evaluation and testing policies for correctness

At ACME Corp, the identity team has just finished deploying Cedar across the company’s
Customer Collaboration platform. Chapter 7 provided the foundation: Cedar’s schema,

syntax, and the PARC model for understanding policies. Now, it’s time to move from theory
to practice.

ACME’s needs are varied. Engineers in the R&D group share design documents that must
be editable only by their owners and managers. The legal department reviews contracts

that should be visible to the entire legal team, but not to other employees. Account
managers share marketing materials with customers, sometimes granting short-term

access to external collaborators. And, in keeping with ACME’s zero-trust mandate, all access
to critical resources must come from company-managed devices, with stricter constraints

outside business hours.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

178

The identity team’s challenge is to embed all these requirements into Cedar policies that

are clear, testable, and easy to maintain. They cannot have exceptions buried in application
code or ad hoc checks scattered across services. Policies need to be unified in one place,

evaluated at runtime, and simple to modify without redeploying the entire platform.

[In this chapter, you’ll assume the role of the identity team. We’ll explore real ACME](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-9?potentialInternalRefId=9---book-markup-container)

examples, from simple “owner can view” rules to complex combinations of roles, attributes,
and relationships. You’ll learn how to implement Cedar’s common policy patterns—

discretionary, membership, and relationship permissions—and add ABAC-style constraints
to meet security and business needs. Along the way, we’ll discuss schema design, policy

organization, request mapping, testing strategies, and best practices for scaling Cedar to
production environments.

[By the end, you’ll have a toolbox of Cedar patterns that you can adapt to your own](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-9?potentialInternalRefId=10---book-markup-container)
systems. You’ll also gain a clear understanding of how a company like ACME can use Cedar

to unify its authorization logic, improve security, and stay aligned with evolving business
needs.

#### 9.1 From primer to practice

In chapter 7, you learned how Cedar’s typed schema, policy syntax, and PARC model work

together to enable detailed authorization. You created your first simple `permit` statements,

experimented with `forbid` rules, and saw how attributes and relationships can serve as

policy inputs. That chapter focused on the language and the fundamental concepts.

Now we shift from learning Cedar to applying Cedar, just as ACME Corp’s identity team

did when they chose Cedar as the main policy language for their Customer Collaboration
platform.

[In this chapter, ACME’s identity team applies Cedar in practice. They design and refine](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-9?potentialInternalRefId=14---book-markup-container)
their schema before creating any policies, then encode key rules such as granting owners

full control and allowing managers to edit subordinates' work. Cedar’s patterns—
discretionary, membership, and relationship—combine with ABAC constraints like device

trust and time of day to address real business needs. To keep policies clear and consistent,
the team uses templates, overrides, and a graph-based entity model that maintains

concise, data-driven logic.

[We’ll stay grounded in ACME’s real-world needs. Engineers in R&D share design](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-9?potentialInternalRefId=15---book-markup-container)

documents; the legal team works on contracts; account managers develop marketing
materials for customers; and every access decision follows ACME’s zero-trust policy that

critical resources can only be accessed from company-managed devices, with extra
safeguards outside business hours.

[By the end of this chapter, you’ll have the patterns, structure, and working code to move](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-9?potentialInternalRefId=16---book-markup-container)
from “we understand Cedar” to “we’re running Cedar in production.” This is the practice

phase where your policies become as essential to your system’s architecture as your APIs
and data models.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

179

WHY CEDAR FOR IMPLEMENTATION

Cedar stands out because it isn’t limited to a single authorization model. It offers the

flexibility to combine attributes, relationships, and roles within the same policy set,
without forcing a choice early on.

**ABAC flexibility** : Cedar’s `when` and `unless` clauses can reference any attributes on

principals, resources, or the request context. This makes it easy to enforce time
based access, device trust checks, clearance levels, or geographic restrictions.

**ReBAC expressiveness** : Cedar treats relationships as first-class data. Policies can

traverse the entity graph to verify relationships like “manager of an owner” or
“member of a project team.”

**RBAC simplicity** : Roles and groups can be modeled as entities and used directly in
permit statements, providing the clarity of RBAC where it makes sense.

At ACME Corp, the identity team can implement RBAC-style group checks, ReBACstyle relationship checks, and ABAC-style contextual conditions across a set of Cedar

policies. Cedar’s evaluator considers all relevant policies for a request, allowing
different patterns to work together to produce a single decision. This flexibility is

powerful because most real-world authorization requirements don’t fit neatly into
just ABAC, just ReBAC, or just RBAC, and Cedar allows you to combine them in

whatever structure makes sense for maintainability.

#### 9.2 Modeling your schema first

Before the ACME Corp identity team wrote a single policy, they developed a schema.

A Cedar _schema_ defines the shape of entities, actions, and contexts that your policies

can reference. It functions like a contract between your authorization logic and the rest of
your system: the schema specifies what’s permitted, and Cedar’s compiler ensures these

rules are followed. If a policy tries to use an attribute, action, or entity type not included in
the schema, it won’t compile.

[Without a schema, policies risk becoming inconsistent and prone to errors. With a](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-9?potentialInternalRefId=26---book-markup-container)
schema, you gain:

**Type safety** —catch mistakes before deployment.
**Precise vocabulary** —everyone uses consistent names for actions, entity

types, and attributes.
**Tooling support** —IDEs and CI/CD pipelines validate policy changes.

These benefits make the schema more than just a formality; it becomes the backbone that
keeps your Cedar policies reliable and consistent as the system evolves.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

180

9.2.1 ACME’s core entities and actions

ACME’s Customer Collaboration platform covers a few key concepts:

**Employees** —internal staff with assigned roles, departments, and

managers.
**Customers** —external individuals with limited access.

**Documents** —shared files with owners, classifications, and a delegatable
flag.

**Teams** —groups of employees assigned to projects or departments, or
customers assigned to specific clients.

They also enforce a small set of actions:

```
      doc:view
      doc:edit
      doc:share

```

Here’s the initial Cedar schema for these types and actions:

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

181

namespace ACME

entity Employee {

attributes {

department: String,

on_call: Bool,

manager: Employee,

clearance: optional { String }

}

}

entity Customer {}

entity Team {

attributes {

name: String

}

}

entity Document {

attributes {

owner: Employee,

classification: String,

delegatable: Bool,

employee_readers_team: Team,

customer_readers_team: Team

}

}

action "doc:view"

appliesTo { principal: [Employee, Customer], resource: Document }

action "doc:edit"

appliesTo { principal: Employee, resource: Document }

action "doc:share"

appliesTo { principal: Employee, resource: Document }

context {

device: { managed: Bool },

time:  { hour: Long, weekday: String }

}

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

182

This schema gives ACME’s identity team a clear, enforceable model of their authorization

environment, along with a shared vocabulary on which all policies will depend.

9.2.2 How schema shapes policies

With this schema in place:

The owner attribute of a Document must refer to an Employee.
You can’t accidentally write a policy that allows a customer to `doc:edit` .

The schema prevents it.
The `context.device.managed` attribute is included in every request,

enabling ABAC-style conditions without needing to repeat structure in
each policy.

By restricting what policies can reference, the schema ensures ACME’s authorization logic
remains aligned with real-world rules, decreasing both accidental over-permissiveness and

policy drift over time.

9.2.3 Updating schema as your system evolves

Schemas are living documents. When ACME later introduced a Folder entity to organize

documents, they first updated the schema and then created new policies. This order—
update schema → write policies → test—ensures that authorization changes stay safe and

predictable.

COMMON SCHEMA MISTAKES TO AVOID

Even with Cedar’s type safety, a poorly designed schema can lead to ongoing

problems for your authorization model. Here are some pitfalls ACME’s identity team
learned to avoid:

**Skipping action typing** —Avoid using `principal: Any` or `resource: Any` in actions

because they remove guardrails and can lead to accidental access grants. Without

specific typing, any principal or resource can match, allowing new entity types to
silently become eligible for the action. The solution involves several steps: start with

the narrowest `appliesTo` possible, enumerate types instead of using `Any`, model

separate actions for different cases, use tests to define scope precisely, and reserve

`forbid` for real guardrails rather than fix loose typing issues.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

183

**Overloading attributes** —Combining multiple concepts into one attribute (like

`"department-role": "Eng-Manager"` ) requires policies to parse strings or rely on

fragile conventions. This makes conditions more difficult to read and maintain,

increasing the risk of misinterpretation when data changes. Instead, break down
complex data into separate typed attributes or related entities ( `department:`

`String`, `role: String` ). This keeps policies simple, easier to test, and less prone to

subtle logic bugs.

**Inconsistent naming** —Using different naming styles for entity types, attributes, or
action IDs (such as using `"doc:view"` in one place and `"document-view"` in

another) causes confusion and mismatched references in policies. The schema
should be the place to establish and follow standard naming conventions: decide

early on aspects like singular versus plural, casing, separators, and namespace
prefixes, then apply them consistently. Clear naming makes onboarding new policy

authors easier and reduces the chance of hard-to-spot typos.

**Forgetting context** —Excluding request-time attributes like device trust, current

time, and geolocation from the schema forces developers to either hard-code them
into the application or skip important checks altogether. Declaring context in the

schema (such as `context.device.managed: Bool` ) makes these attributes

accessible everywhere policies are applied. It also ensures your test environment can

simulate real-world scenarios, from unmanaged device access to off-hours requests,
without extra wiring in application code.

Avoiding these mistakes early keeps your schema clean, your policies simpler, and
your authorization logic much easier to evolve as your system grows.

#### 9.3 Authoring ACME’s core policies

With ACME’s schema in place, the identity team can now write policies that are both
expressive and safe. The schema acts as a guardrail; each policy is validated against it

during compilation, preventing accidental rules that target the wrong type of principal or
resource.

Core policies set the basic rules that apply across the system. They serve as the
foundation for any decision set and tend to remain stable over time. For ACME’s Customer

Collaboration platform, three of these rules are directly based on the authorization model
discussed in Chapter 6:

Permit view if on the employee or customer document readers team
Permit all if owner.

Permit all when principal is manager of an owner

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

184

These capture the most common relationship-based access patterns in the Customer

Collaboration platform. The following sections present Cedar implementations of each
pattern.

9.3.1 Permit view if on the right team

This policy ensures that document owners can view their own documents, and that other
employees or customers in the appropriate readers team can also view them. We model

this with two policies, one for employees and another for readers:

permit(

principal is ACME::Customer,

action == ACME::Action::"doc:view",

resource is ACME::Document

)

when {

principal in resource.customer_readers_team

};

permit(

principal is ACME::Employee,

action == ACME::Action::"doc:view",

resource is ACME::Document

)

when {

principal in resource.employee_readers_team

|| resource.owner.manager == principal

};

Notice how the check links a direct relationship (owner) with team-based membership for

both internal and external readers.

WHY SEPARATE POLICIES FOR EMPLOYEES AND CUSTOMERS?

It might seem easier to combine employee and customer access into one policy. For

example, you could create a single permit that covers both groups and then use a
branch inside the `when` clause to determine which rules apply. However, Cedar

doesn’t support unions in the policy scope—you can’t specify `principal in`

`[ACME::Employee, ACME::Customer]` . To include both, you need to leave the

principal unrestricted and push the type discrimination into the `when` clause.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

185

9.3.2 Owner can do all

This policy grants owners broad rights—view, edit, and share—over their own documents:

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

186

permit(

principal in ACME::Employee,

action in [ACME:: Action::"doc:view",

ACME:: Action::"doc:edit",

ACME:: Action::"doc:share"],

resource in ACME::Document

)

when { resource.owner == principal };

Here, the schema restricts the action list, so adding a new action like `doc:delete` later

won’t automatically give the owner extra permissions.

9.3.3 Manager of owner can view and edit

This rule permits a document owner’s manager to view and edit the document, supporting

common supervisory workflows:

permit(

principal in ACME::Employee,

action in [ACME::Action::"doc:view", ACME::Action::"doc:edit"],

resource in ACME::Document

)

when { resource.owner.manager == principal };

The relationship traversal from `resource.owner` to `manager` functions because the schema

designates `manager` as an `Employee` attribute.

DENY-BY-DEFAULT IN CEDAR

Cedar evaluates each request against all applicable policies and denies it unless a

`permit` policy applies and no `forbid` policy overrides it. This deny-by-default

approach means you only need to define rules for what is allowed; everything else is

implicitly denied. Guardrails, like device security requirements, are best enforced
with explicit `forbid` rules, which override any matching `permit` .

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

187

#### 9.4 Where does Cedar find data about entities?

The _entity store_ is the data source that Cedar queries when evaluating policies. It contains

the definitions of principals, resources, and other entities, along with their attributes and
relationships. Every test, attribute reference, and relationship traversal in a policy relies on

what’s stored in the entity store. Since Cedar doesn’t specify how the store should be
implemented, you can model it in various ways, such as using a directory service, a graph

database, relational tables, or even a flat file for development and testing. Selecting the
appropriate model for your entity store is crucial for both policy expressiveness and

evaluation performance.

The Policy Decision Point (PDP) is responsible for bringing entity data together with

policy logic at evaluation time. Essentially, the PDP acts as a wrapper around the Cedar
evaluation engine, coordinating the decision process by preparing the necessary inputs—

policies, entities, and request context—and then calling Cedar to produce an `allow` or `deny`

decision. The PDP does not own the underlying business data, but it manages the decision

context, identifing which entities and relationships are needed for a specific request and
ensuring they are accessible to the policy engine in a consistent, well-structured format. In

some architectures, the PDP fetches this data directly from a relationship graph or directory
service; in others, it receives a scoped snapshot of entity data prepared upstream.

Regardless of the approach, the PDP sets the boundary between policy evaluation and data
access, guaranteeing that every authorization decision is based on a coherent, authoritative

view of the entity store, rather than on ad hoc checks scattered throughout the application.

[At ACME, the entity store for the Customer Collaboration Platform is modeled as a](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-9?potentialInternalRefId=89---book-markup-container)

relationship graph. Employees, Customers, Teams, and Documents are nodes, and edges
represent relationships such as membership and ownership (for example,

`Employee→memberOf→Team` or `Document→owner→Employee` ). A nightly process syncs HRIS

and CRM updates into this graph, so promotions, transfers, and customer roster changes

appear as new edges or attributes without requiring policy edits. Policies stay static, but the
data that informs them is dynamic; access changes are reflected through graph updates

rather than code modifications.

[Figure 9.1 shows a small part of ACME’s graph illustrating how the viewer or owner rule](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-9?potentialInternalRefId=90---book-markup-container)

is driven entirely by data.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

188

Figure 9.1 A portion of the relationship graph that makes up the entity store for AMCE’s Customer

Collaboration Platform.

When modeling relationships in the entity store, it’s almost always better to represent
group membership as relationship edges—such as `principal→memberOf→team` —rather than

embed a Set<Principal> inside a team entity. Regardless of the storage technology, the
store’s job is to answer questions like “is this principal in that team?” or “who is the

manager of this employee?” Edges allow the store to answer these questions directly, often
using indexes or ancestor caches, without loading and scanning large attributes. This keeps

evaluations fast, policies simple, and the schema clean. Updates become just changes to
the graph—adding or removing an edge—rather than rewriting entity definitions.

Using `Set<Principal>` attributes can be effective for small, static lists or special cases

like temporary whitelists, but they don’t scale well and complicate maintenance and

explanation. By maintaining membership within the relationship graph, ACME’s
authorization model remains flexible, adaptable to organizational changes, and simpler to

understand, regardless of the underlying storage technology.

TRANSITIVE RELATIONSHIPS

Cedar policies can leverage transitive relationships in the entity store. If a
relationship path connects a principal to a resource—regardless of how many edges

it involves—Cedar can follow it during evaluation.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

189

#### 9.5 Applying Cedar’s policy patterns

Cedar’s flexibility comes from its ability to express various authorization patterns and
combine them within the same policy set. The ACME identity team uses three common

patterns across the Customer Collaboration platform: discretionary permissions,
membership permissions, and relationship permissions. By mixing these where appropriate,

they can address nearly every business requirement without making policies overly
complex.

9.5.1 Discretionary permissions

_Discretionary_ permissions, often called DAC, let resource owners directly control who can
access their resources. Most ReBAC models are discretionary. For example, at ACME, an

owner can add employees to an `employee_readers_team` or customers to a

`customer_readers_team` for a document. Once a principal joins one of these teams, the

discretionary policy pattern enables them to view the document without changing the core
policy set.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

190

permit(

principal is ACME::Customer,

action == ACME::Action::"doc:view",

resource is ACME::Document

)

when {

principal in resource.customer_readers_team

};

Because team membership lives in the entity store, access updates happen instantly when

someone is added or removed from a `reader's` team; there’s no need to change policies or

redeploy services. This keeps policies simple and stable while allowing detailed, document
specific control.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

191

9.5.2 Membership permissions

Membership permissions are RBAC-style rules that grant privileges to all members of a role
or group. At ACME, the legal department has a team for contract reviewers, and all

members of that team can view and edit legal-classified documents.

permit(

principal in ACME::Team::"team:legal",

action in [ACME::"doc:view", ACME::"doc:edit"],

resource in ACME::Document

)

when { resource.classification == "Legal" };

By scoping the principal to `ACME::Team::"team:legal"`, we eliminate the need for an extra

condition in the `when` clause and make the policy’s purpose clear at a glance. This also

means the entity store only needs to answer “is this principal a member of the Legal

team?” without checking any per-document attributes.

While constructions like `principal in […]` are not allowed, using principal in

`ACME::Team::"team:legal"` is fine because `ACME::Team::"team:legal"` refers to a single

entity, not an entity union denoted by the brackets.

9.5.3 Relationship permissions

Relationship permissions (ReBAC) grant access based on the connections between
principals and resources. The “manager of owner” rule from ACME’s core policies is a

perfect example.

permit(

principal in ACME::Employee,

action in [ACME::"doc:view", ACME::"doc:edit"],

resource in ACME::Document

)

when { resource.owner.manager == principal };

This policy doesn’t mention teams at all; it relies on the manager relationship from the

entity store to determine access dynamically.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

192

9.5.4 Mixing patterns for PBAC

In practice, ACME often combines these patterns within a single policy. For example, this
policy includes a relationship check (is the employee the owner’s manager) and a

discretionary membership verification (is the principal a member of the legal team).

permit(

principal in ACME::Employee,

action == ACME::"doc:edit",

resource in ACME::Document

)

when {

resource.owner.manager == principal

|| (principal in ACME::Team::"team:legal" &&

resource.classification == "Legal")

};

This is where Cedar shines: the policy set can use attributes (ABAC), relationships (ReBAC),

and team membership (RBAC) as needed. The entity store provides the facts, and Cedar
evaluates them together in real-time.

#### 9.6 Layering global constraints

Attribute-based access control (ABAC) is how ACME enforces organization-wide rules that
span multiple products and policy patterns. Instead of duplicating checks in every

application, the identity team writes a small set of global constraints that evaluate the
request’s context—things like device posture, risk level, or location—and allow those

constraints to apply everywhere Cedar operates.

Here’s a single global rule that stops employees from taking any document actions

across Customer Collaboration when using unmanaged devices.

forbid(

principal in ACME::Employee,

action

resource in ACME::Document

)

when { context.device.managed == false };

Because `forbid` overrides any matching `permit`, this rule neatly layers on top of

discretionary, membership, and relationship policies; if the device isn’t managed, the
decision is `deny`, no matter what else matches.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

193

#### 9.7 Using policy templates and overrides

Cedar policies don’t have to be handwritten individually. Templates let the identity team

create a reusable pattern once and then instantiate it multiple times with different
parameters. This reduces repetition and keeps policies consistent across teams, products,

or customers.

9.7.1 Templates

At ACME, the identity team maintains a document access template that enforces standard

owner and viewer rules. When a new Customer Collaboration workspace is created, the
service instantiates the template to set up the workspace’s owner and reader teams,

generating a policy instance specific to that workspace.

// Template: document-view-template

permit (

principal in ?readers_team,

action == ACME::"doc:view",

resource in ACME::Document

)

when { resource.owner == ?owner };

Template parameters such as `?readers_team` and `?owner` are populated during

instantiation. The resulting policy is a standard Cedar policy, fully type-checked and
deployed alongside the rest.

Templates allow ACME’s identity team to enforce consistent Cedar policies while binding
a few variables at instantiation time—keeping logic centralized and minimizing drift. A

service or admin workflow supplies the parameters, resulting in a standard, type-checked
policy within the set.

// Template: document-view-template

permit(

principal in ?readers_team,

action == ACME::"doc:view",

resource in ACME::Document

)

when { resource.owner == ?owner };

An example template instantiation input could look like this:

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

{

}

194

"template": "document-view-template",

"params": {

"readers_team": "ACME::Team::\"team:eng-doc-readers\"",

"owner": "ACME::Employee::\"emp:alice\""

}

Use templates when you need multiple nearly identical rules that only differ by identifiers or

specific, narrow conditions, such as per-workspace reader teams, per-customer collections,
or per-environment scopes. Choose instance policies (hand-written) when a case genuinely

differs in structure, not just in values.

Here are some useful operational tips:

**Validate parameters** —ensure they exist, are the correct type, and
match tenancy before instantiation to prevent broken policies.

**Name and version** —provide templates with semantic versions and
document which instance came from which template version for audit

purposes.
**Review changes** —treat template modifications as code; run test vectors

and use staged rollouts to prevent widespread regressions.
**Split ownership** —the central identity team manages templates, and

product teams supply parameters within defined limits.
**Provide escape hatches** —combine templates with specific overrides

when a workspace or customer needs a more precise or flexible rule
without creating a separate template.

When done well, templates maintain your policy set's consistency and scalability while still
allowing for precise, auditable differences where the business truly needs them.

9.7.2 Overrides

Sometimes, the template isn’t enough for every situation. ACME uses overrides for special
cases like the following:

A customer with stricter requirements might `forbid` all sharing, even by

owners.

A project team might need to grant external contractors temporary
editing rights.

Overrides are simply additional Cedar policies added alongside the template-generated
policies. Since Cedar reviews all relevant policies together, an override can safely make

rules stricter or more lenient without changing the original template.

This differs from layering global constraints in several key ways:

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

195

**Overrides** are local exceptions—they apply to a specific resource,

workspace, or customer, and usually have a limited scope. They are often
written by delegated administrators or product teams.

**Global constraints** are organization-wide guardrails; they apply
everywhere, regardless of local policy, and are usually managed by the

central identity team.

An example where an override might be useful is when ACME needs to restrict a template

rule for a specific workspace. Imagine the `document-view-template` usually allows the

owner’s `readers` team to view any document. For a sensitive workspace, an override can

prevent all viewing unless the principal is the owner.

// added to #override document-view-template to restrict legal workspace

forbid(

principal in ACME::Employee,

action == ACME::Action::"doc:view",

resource in ACME::Document::"workspace:legal-review"

)

when { resource.owner != principal };

Here, the override acts as a local guardrail, further restricting access for a single workspace

without altering the global template. Note the comment that makes it clear this is an
override. The `#override` tag makes it easy to find overrides when searching the policy

store.

Templates promote consistency and reduce boilerplate code. Overrides let you handle

exceptions without changing the base rules. In contrast, global constraints make sure that
specific rules are never skipped anywhere in the system.

#### 9.8 Mapping requests to Cedar evaluations

For Cedar to make an authorization decision, your application or API gateway must convert

a real-world request into the three parts Cedar expects: principal, action, and resource,
along with any context. This is the role of the Policy Enforcement Point (PEP)—the

component that intercepts the request, gathers the evaluation data, and sends it to Cedar’s
decision API.

At ACME, the Customer Collaboration service’s PEP wraps each document request in a
call to Cedar. When a user clicks Share in the UI, it triggers a process similar to the one

shown in figure 9.2.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

196

Figure 9.2 The Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) in ACME’s Customer Collaboration platform translates a real
world /share request into a Cedar evaluation by combining session data (principal), entity data (resource

relationships), and context signals (environment attributes). Cedar’s is_authorized API provides an allow

or deny decision, which the PEP enforces before forwarding the request to the backend.

The PEP carries out the following tasks to make an `allow` or `deny` decision.

1. Identifies the principal from the active session or token (such as

`ACME::Employee::"emp:alice"` ).

2. Sets the action based on the operation being attempted (such as

`ACME::"doc:share"` ).

3. Resolves the resource from the target document ID (such as

`ACME::Document::"doc:Q4-plan"` ).

4. Gathers any context attributes needed by global or local ABAC rules (such

as `device.managed=true` or `timeOfDay="14:05"` ).

5. Calls Cedar’s `is_authorized` API with these values and the relevant

entity data.
6. Forwards the request to the backend if Cedar returns `allow` .

The following JSON shows an example of a request payload for Cedar:

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

{

}

197

"principal": "ACME::Employee::\"emp:alice\"",

"action": "ACME::\"doc:share\"",

"resource": "ACME::Document::\"doc:Q3-plan\"",

"context": {

"device": { "managed": true },

"timeOfDay": "14:05"

}

The PEP guarantees that each evaluation request is

Complete— all required attributes and entity references for the policies
are included.

Consistent—entity and attribute names match the Cedar schema.
Scoped—ensures the correct principal, action, or resource is used, even

when multiple options are involved.

At ACME, the PEP, which they call the _Policy Enforcement Agent,_ is part of the service’s

authorization middleware, which operates between API handlers and business logic. This
component invokes Cedar for each protected operation—whether initiated by a web

request, a scheduled job, or a service-to-service call—ensuring policies are applied
consistently.

Getting the PEP right is crucial: well-crafted policies are worthless if the evaluation
request doesn’t align with the actual operation being performed.

USING CEDAR

After authoring your schema and policies and modeling your entities, you have
options for deploying Cedar in production. Two common options are the Cedar Local

Agent and the Amazon Verified Permissions (AVP) API. Both utilize the same Cedar
evaluation logic but differ in deployment method, integration complexity, and

operational trade-offs.

**Cedar Local Agent**

Cedar Local Agent (CLA) is an open-source Rust crate that provides a customizable
cache for Cedar policies and entities. CLA can operate within or alongside your

application, often as a sidecar container or local process. Your Policy Enforcement
Point (PEP) sends evaluation requests to it over HTTP.

Pros:

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

Cons:

198

Low latency—performs a local call instead of a network hop to a

remote service.
Full control over policy and entity lifecycle; functions in any

environment.
No dependence on a public cloud; operates wherever Cedar can run.

You manage the operational workload: deploying, scaling, and

updating the agent.
Requires your own policy or entity distribution system.

**Amazon Verified Permissions**

Amazon Verified Permissions (AVP) is a fully managed AWS service that hosts Cedar

and makes it accessible through AWS APIs. Policies are stored and maintained within
the service. Entities are usually stored in a separate AWS data store. Your PEP, often

implemented as an AWS Lambda, calls the AVP API.

Pros:

No infrastructure needed; AWS handles scaling, updates, and
availability.

Integrated with other AWS services for identity, logging, and
monitoring.

Helpful for managing multi-account AWS environments.

Cons:

Network latency for each evaluation depends on your application’s
proximity to AWS.

An AWS account is required.
Policies and data are stored in AWS-managed storage, which reduces

your control over hosting.

**Hybrid deployments**

Some organizations combine both approaches: running Cedar Local Agent in their
own environment for low-latency decisions while storing and managing policies in

AVP. In this setup, AVP serves as the primary source of truth for policies and entities,
and the Local Agent periodically syncs updates. This method merges the operational

convenience of AWS-managed policy hosting with the performance and flexibility of
local evaluation.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

199

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

#### 9.9 From concept to policy

We have now progressed from the concepts of Cedar introduced earlier to the practical

work of modeling schemas, authoring policies, and conducting evaluations. We observed
how ACME’s Customer Collaboration platform integrates different authorization patterns—

ownership baselines, customer view policies, discretionary sharing, and global constraints—
into a unified framework. Along the way, we examined how the entity store and relationship

graph serve as the data sources for policies, and how requests travel through the Policy
Enforcement Point to Cedar for evaluation.

We also compared deployment methods, including running Cedar locally with the Cedar
Local Agent and using Amazon Verified Permissions as a managed service. To ensure

policies function as intended, we examined testing strategies and analysis tools that help
verify decisions before deployment.

[To see all the examples we’ve covered in this chapter connected in one flow, refer to the](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-9?potentialInternalRefId=219---book-markup-container)
appendix for a complete end-to-end walkthrough of ACME’s Customer Collaboration

platform. There, you can follow along step by step—from defining the schema to running
real is-authorized calls—and try the full scenario yourself.

[Next, we’ll step back from implementation details and focus on designing effective](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-9?potentialInternalRefId=220---book-markup-container)
authorization policies: how to consider policy as code, avoid common pitfalls, and align

policies with organizational needs.

#### 9.10 Summary

A Cedar schema provides the foundation for safe, consistent policies by
defining entity types, attributes, actions, and context.

Schema design choices—like naming conventions and typed relationships
—directly shape policy clarity and maintainability.

ACME’s core policies set the baseline: owners can act on their own
documents, readers teams can view, and managers can supervise.

The entity store, modeled as a relationship graph, provides the dynamic
data that drives Cedar’s static policy logic.

Cedar supports discretionary, membership, and relationship permissions,
providing flexibility to combine RBAC, ABAC, and ReBAC patterns.

Delegatable rights are managed explicitly, distinguishing between “using
a resource” and “granting access to a resource.”

Global constraints enforce zero-trust principles by applying organizationwide ABAC rules, such as device trust checks.

Policy templates and overrides minimize duplication, maintain
consistency, and allow for local exceptions when necessary.

The Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) translates real requests into Cedar
evaluations, making sure that each access decision is enforced

consistently.
Testing and static analysis safeguard your policy set, catching logic

errors, regressions, and contradictions before they reach production.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

Cedar’s blend of clarity, flexibility, and rigor makes it a practical language

for unifying authorization across complex systems.
Together, these lessons demonstrate how ACME and you can go beyond

theory and implement Cedar, transforming authorization from scattered
checks into a unified, strategic advantage.
