## Policy as code: Effective authorization policies

This chapter covers

How to design policies that are clear, least-privilege, and resilient to change

Why treating policies as code makes them easier to review, version, and deploy

How to manage flow from policy repositories to policy stores without confusion

Methods for testing policies with real-life scenarios to prevent bugs from entering

production

How static analysis provides a safety net by catching conflicts and gaps you might
overlook

At ACME Corp, the identity team has rolled out dynamic authorization across multiple
systems. Employees authenticate via single sign-on, and the Customer Collaboration

platform enforces ReBAC so that only project participants can access shared documents.
The engineering team uses ABAC to manage production deployments. Policies are now a

core part of how the company controls access. However, as the team increases its use of
policies, a new challenge arises: how to make these policies effective and sustainable over

time.

Writing a policy that works once is easy; creating a policy that remains relevant as

employees change roles, projects reorganize, or compliance rules evolve is more
challenging. The identity team understands that good policies are not just statements of

permission and denial; they are design artifacts that must be clear, consistent, and aligned
with organizational goals.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

203

At the same time, policies can’t stay abstract. They need to be enforced by running

systems, and ACME’s developers need a way to manage them reliably. Embedding
authorization logic in application code causes duplication and slows down updates. Instead,

the team wants policies that can be expressed in their own language, externalized from
applications but still precise enough to support real-time decisions.

[Of course, policies don’t exist in a vacuum. Deciding who writes them, who reviews](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-10?potentialInternalRefId=9---book-markup-container)
them, and how conflicts are resolved is just as important as the policies themselves. That

aspect, known as _policy governance_, is a key part of making authorization sustainable, and
we will revisit it in Chapter 14.

[This chapter presents three perspectives on authorization policy. The first is the](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-10?potentialInternalRefId=10---book-markup-container) _what:_
principles for writing clear, consistent policies that enforce least privilege and remain stable

as organizations grow. The second is the _how:_ treating policies as code so they can be
reviewed, versioned, and deployed like any other software asset. The third is _assurance:_

testing and analysis that confirm policies behave as intended and stay trustworthy over
time. Together, these perspectives ensure that authorization logic isn’t just theoretical but

can be managed, verified, and adapted in practice.

#### 10.1 Principles of effective authorization policies

As ACME’s identity team expanded its use of dynamic authorization, they realized that
writing policies is more than just encoding rules in Cedar. The real challenge is making

policies effective—clear enough for policy authors and reviewers to understand, stable
enough to withstand organizational changes, and precise enough to enforce least privilege

without getting in the way of business goals.

The following sections outline several principles that ACME found to guide its work.

10.1.1 Clarity and consistency

Policies should be clear and predictable. A policy that’s vague or that conflicts with others is
a liability. At ACME, the Customer Collaboration platform once had two policies that seemed

to conflict: one granting managers broad access and another restricting access based on
project membership. After a confusing access denial, the team standardized its approach by

always scoping policies to the project container.

BRITTLE POLICY (INCONSISTENT SCOPE)

Here’s a policy that gave ACME trouble:

permit(

principal in Team::"team:managers",

action in [Action::"doc:view"],

resource in Document

);

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

204

At first glance, this policy seems reasonable: Managers should be able to view documents.

The problem is that it defines access using a different scope than other policies. Most
policies at ACME grant access based on project membership, but this one grants it based on

organizational role. The result is a conflict: Does a manager outside Project Alpha get to
view Alpha’s documents? One policy says yes; the other says no.

IMPROVED POLICY (CONSISTENT, PROJECT-BASED)

Here’s what ACME ended up using instead:

permit(

principal,

action in [Action::"doc:view"],

resource in Document::"alpha/*"

)

when {

Project::"alpha".members.contains(principal)

};

Clear, consistent scoping prevents conflicts between policies and clearly shows who should

have access. Figure 10.1 compares ACME’s inconsistent, manager-based policy with the
better project-based approach.

To understand how a policy like this can be made more general so that we don’t have to
create one for each project, see the sidebar “How a policy template shapes tenant control” in section

13.5.7.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

205

Figure 10.1 Inconsistent versus consistent scopes. In the first case, managers outside Project Alpha gain

unintended access; in the second case, access is controlled only by project membership.

This simple change makes policies easier to understand and ensures that access aligns

clearly with the business concept of a project.

10.1.2 Least privilege

Authorization should always provide the smallest set of permissions necessary to complete

a task. ACME learned this the hard way when interns briefly gained visibility into financial
forecasts because of an overly broad “all employees” permit.

BRITTLE POLICY (OVERLY BROAD)

Here’s the policy that caused the problem:

permit(

principal in Employee,    // grants to all employees

action == Action::"doc:view",

resource in Document    // all documents

);

On the surface, this seems okay: employees should be able to view documents. However,

because it applies to all employees and all documents, it allowed access well beyond what
was intended. Interns and others had no reason to see documents outside of the ones they

needed for their work.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

206

IMPROVED POLICY (LEAST PRIVILEGE)

Here’s a version that restricts the scope to limit access:

permit(

principal,

action == Action::"doc:view",

resource in Document::"alpha/*"    // just project docs

)

when{

Project::"alpha".members.contains(principal) // only project members

};

By limiting access to the project container, only employees who genuinely need it are

granted access. Restricting policies to the smallest possible group prevents accidental
exposure and upholds the principle of least privilege.

Figure 10.2 illustrates how ACME’s initial “all employees” policy granted access too
broadly, compared to the corrected least-privilege policy.

Figure 10.2 Overly broad versus least-privilege scope. Giving all employees access to all documents exposed

sensitive financial forecasts in Project Alpha. Restricting access to only project members enforces the

principle of least privilege.

By revising the policy to apply solely to project members, ACME ensured that sensitive
documents remained accessible only to those with a legitimate need, closing the gap that

had allowed Fay to see forecasts.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

207

10.1.3 Separation of policy and data

Policies should focus on logic, not on facts. Embedding data values directly into a policy
makes it brittle and difficult to manage. At ACME, a developer once wrote a deployment

policy that listed department names explicitly. When the company reorganized and HR
renamed Engineering to Product Development, Alice suddenly couldn’t deploy her code,

even though her responsibilities remained unchanged.

BRITTLE POLICY (HARD-CODED DATA)

Here’s the problematic version:

permit(

principal,

action == Action::"deploy",

resource in DeploymentTool

)

when { principal.department in ["Engineering", "SRE"] };

At first glance, this appears to be a simple way to limit deployments: only people in

Engineering or SRE can deploy. The problem is that the policy encodes facts about the
organization. When HR renamed the department, the check failed and legitimate engineers

suddenly lost access.

IMPROVED POLICY (DATA-DRIVEN)

Here’s the approach ACME adopted instead:

permit(

principal,

action == Action::"deploy",

resource in DeploymentTool

)

when { principal in Role::"sr-engr"

|| principal in Role::"engr-mgr" };

By referencing roles dynamically pulled from ACME’s HR and identity systems, the policy
conveys the logic without including specific details that may change. This ensures the policy

remains valid even as departments and job titles change.

Figure 10.3 compares these approaches.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

208

Figure 10.3 Hard-coded versus data-driven policies. An employee can lose access when the policy checks

department names directly but keeps access when the policy references durable roles from the HR system.

Decoupling policies from unstable organizational data ensures they, along with access to
the assets they protect, remain consistent even as the organizational structure changes.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

10.1.4 Granularity and grouping

Policies are most effective when they operate at the right level of detail. Fine-grained

actions improve policy accuracy by differentiating activities such as viewing, editing, or
sharing. However, exposing every fine-grained action directly to employees or customers

can be overwhelming and hard to manage. To keep things practical, organizations often
group related actions into broader roles or bundles that are understandable to end users;

for example, offering a single collaborator role in the UI that corresponds to several
underlying capabilities.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

210

ACME reps discovered that showing detailed actions directly to customers and employees

on the Customer Collaboration platform caused confusion, so they grouped those actions
into broader roles in the UI, such as collaborator or viewer. However, behind the scenes, the

platform’s early policies used a single catch-all action, `doc:all`, which combined all

capabilities. This made writing policies easier, but it also erased important differences;

there was no way to determine if someone should be allowed to view, edit, or share a
document.

BRITTLE POLICY (BUNDLED ACTION)

Here’s the approach that caused problems at ACME: a single `doc:all` action that combined

viewing, editing, and sharing into one capability.

permit(

principal,

action == Action::"doc:all",

resource in Document::"alpha/*"

)

when {

Project::"alpha".members.contains(principal)

};

This policy seems practical because it mirrors the application’s user interface: one
`collaborator` role in the UI matches one `doc:all` action in the policy. However, by aligning

the policy language too closely with the UI, ACME blurred key distinctions. A customer with
`doc:all` rights could share documents externally when the goal was only to allow them to

view and edit.

IMPROVED POLICY (FINE-GRAINED ACTIONS)

Here’s the more precise design ACME adopted: policies that separate viewing, editing, and

sharing into distinct actions, providing finer control over who-can-do-what.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

211

// Project members can view

permit(

principal,

action == Action::"doc:view",

resource in Document::"alpha/*"

)

when { Project::"alpha".members.contains(principal) };

// Project members can edit

permit(

principal,

action == Action::"doc:edit",

resource in Document::"alpha/*"

)

when { Project::"alpha".members.contains(principal) };

// Only employees can share

permit(

principal in Employee,

action == Action::"doc:share",

resource in Document::"alpha/*"

)

when { Project::"alpha".members.contains(principal) };

Now the platform can strictly enforce each person's capabilities. All project members,

whether employees or customers, can view and edit documents. However, only employees
are allowed to share them externally. In practice, ACME still shows these three actions as a

bundled `collaborator` role in the UI, but the policies behind them remain precise.

Separating capabilities this way preserves flexibility: customers can continue

collaborating on projects while employees are responsible for sharing information outside
the project. Fine-grained rules at the policy level provide ACME with strong security

assurances, while higher-level roles in the UI keep things simple for daily use.

[Figure 10.4 compares ACME’s original bundled policy with the enhanced fine-grained](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-10?potentialInternalRefId=82---book-markup-container)

version that separates customer and employee capabilities.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

212

Figure 10.4 Bundled versus fine-grained actions. In the bundled approach, both employees and customers can

share documents, while in the fine-grained approach, only employees are able to share, giving ACME precise

control while keeping ease of use.

Separating capabilities this way restored clarity. Customers could still collaborate on project
work by viewing and editing documents, while only employees retained the ability to share

them externally. Where the bundled `doc:all` action had blurred distinctions and led to

over-permissioning, fine-grained rules clarified the boundaries. ACME could present simple

roles in the UI without sacrificing precision or security in the underlying policies.

10.1.5 Stability across change

Organizations evolve: teams reorganize, employees change roles, and projects are
launched or terminated. Policies must adapt to these changes. At ACME, a brittle policy

once linked document access strictly to an employee’s job title. Dan, who started as an
Associate Counsel, was later promoted to Senior Counsel. His responsibilities stayed the

same, but because the policy only checked for an exact title, he suddenly lost access to
legal drafts he needed to do his job.

BRITTLE POLICY (TIED TO JOB TITLE)

Here’s how ACME initially approached it:

permit(

principal,

action == Action::"doc:view",

resource in Document::"legal-drafts"

)

when { principal.title == "Associate Counsel" };

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

213

At the time, this policy seemed reasonable. The legal team was small, and the Associate

Counsel role was the only position that required access to drafts. Checking for that title
directly was an easy way to meet the requirement. But the policy depended on a volatile

attribute. As soon as Dan’s title changed to Senior Counsel, the policy no longer matched
reality. Even though his overall responsibilities had changed, he still needed access to legal

drafts.

IMPROVED POLICY (TIED TO DURABLE TEAM MEMBERSHIP)

Here’s the more stable design that ACME adopted:

permit(

principal in Team::"team:legal",

action == Action::"doc:view",

resource in Document::"legal-drafts"

);

This version links access to membership in the legal team, which is updated automatically
in the HR system. Dan keeps his access after his promotion because he remains a member

of the legal team, even though his job title has changed.

By anchoring policies to stable entities like teams or projects instead of fragile attributes

like job titles, ACME ensures that authorization decisions stay aligned with business reality
as the organization changes. Job-title checks might seem like a quick fix for small teams,

but they don’t scale well. As organizations expand and career paths become more diverse,
titles change much more frequently than team responsibilities. Creating policies based on

stable entities helps prevent unexpected failures and lowers ongoing maintenance burdens.

[Figure 10.5 shows how a brittle, title-based policy failed when Dan’s role changed, unlike](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-10?potentialInternalRefId=96---book-markup-container)

a stable team-based policy that kept functioning.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

214

Figure 10.5 Brittle versus stable policies. A title check causes Dan to lose access after a promotion, while a

team check maintains access because membership stays valid.

This example illustrates why team or project membership creates a more reliable basis for
access decisions than unstable attributes like job titles.

COMMON PITFALLS AND HOW TO AVOID THEM

Even well-meaning authorization policies can fall short in practice. Here are some

common pitfalls the ACME identity team has encountered, along with strategies to
avoid them:

**Overly broad permits**

_Pitfall:_ Creating one policy that grants access to “all employees” instead of restricting

it by role, project, or department.

_Avoid it:_ Begin with _least privilege_ . Limit conditions to the smallest group that needs

access and specify scope explicitly.

**Duplicating logic in multiple places**

_Pitfall:_ Embedding access checks across different applications, each with its own
quirks.

_Avoid it:_ Centralize your logic by externalizing it into policies as code. Reference the
same policy set across services.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

215

**Mixing policy with data**

_Pitfall:_ Embedding data values such as department names or manager relationships
directly into policy rules.

_Avoid it:_ Keep attributes and relationships within authoritative systems (such as HR
systems, identity stores, or graph databases). Policies should reference data, not

define it.

**Unclear naming**

_Pitfall:_ Using inconsistent names for actions or resources (for example, using
`editDoc` in one place and `modify_document` in another).

_Avoid it:_ Create and enforce naming conventions during reviews and with policy
schemas. Clear policies are easier to read and maintain.

**No testing or validation**

_Pitfall:_ Implementing policies that seem correct but haven’t been tested in real-world

situations.

_Avoid it:_ Validate policies against a schema, write test requests, and use automated

analysis to ensure that they enforce the intended invariants—the conditions that
must always hold true regardless of context. For example, an invariant might state

that only project members can view project documents, or that only employees can
share files externally.

At ACME, these lessons were learned the hard way: an early “all employees” permit
unintentionally allowed interns to see financial forecasts. After discovering the issue

during testing, the team adopted a stricter least-privilege approach and made
schema validation a required step in policy review.

10.1.6 From principles to practice

Taken together, these principles show that creating effective policies involves more than

just granting or denying access at a specific moment. Clear and consistent policies help
prevent conflicts. Applying least privilege minimizes overexposure. Separating policy from

data maintains the rules' resilience. Using granularity and grouping finds a balance between
security and usability. Anchoring policies to durable entities, such as teams, ensures long
term stability. By applying these lessons, ACME’s identity team develops policies that are
both secure and sustainable. In the next section, we will explore how these design

principles are implemented when policies are managed as code, versioned, and tested
alongside the software they protect.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

216

#### 10.2 Policy as code in practice

At ACME, the identity team reached a turning point when they realized that authorization

rules were spread across applications in code comments, configuration files, and even ad
hoc database queries. Each product team handled access differently. The Customer

Collaboration platform checked project membership in its database, while the engineering
group hard-coded department checks into the deployment tool. None of these methods was

easy to audit or modify. When interns unexpectedly gained access to financial forecasts, the
root cause wasn’t just a poor policy; it was the absence of a central, consistent way to

manage policies.

To address this problem, ACME adopted a policy-as-code approach. They didn’t just “put

policies in Git.” Instead, they established policy repositories as the authoritative source for
writing and reviewing Cedar policies, and they used policy stores as the places their

authorizer queried for runtime decisions. Usually, they maintained a one-to-one mapping—
one repository for one store—keeping ownership, reviews, and deployments simple.

However, they treated the two as distinct: repositories are for authoring and history, while
stores are for execution and operations.

For Customer Collaboration, ACME maintained a `collab-policy`

repository (including Cedar policies, schema, and tests) and a matching

policy store that the app queried during runtime.
For deployments, they maintained a `deploy-policy` repository and a

`Deploy` store managed by the engineering team.

Company-wide guardrails were stored in a `global-guardrails` repo and

a central `Guardrails` store managed by the identity team.

All three followed the same deployment process: _edit in repo_ _→_ _validate and test with_

_continuous integration_ _→_ _build a signed policy bundle_ _→_ _promote to the corresponding_
_store(s)_ _→_ _observe decisions and roll back if needed_ .

WHY REPOS AREN’T STORES

When ACME first adopted policy as code, it was tempting to think, “We’ll just put our

Cedar files in Git.” However, the identity team quickly realized that a policy
repository and a policy store serve different purposes.

A _policy repository_ is where policies are created, reviewed, and versioned. It’s
human-facing: Cedar files are stored alongside their schemas, test cases, and

documentation. Changes are submitted via pull requests, automatically checked by
the continuous integration process, and approved by code owners familiar with the

business rules. The repository acts as the definitive source for how authorization
logic should function.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

217

A _policy store_, on the other hand, is what the Cedar authorizer queries during

runtime. It doesn’t hold drafts or pull requests. Instead, it stores signed, versioned
policy bundles that have already passed review and testing. The store is designed for

machine use, prioritizing reliability and auditability rather than authoring. It records
decisions, enforces SLAs, and supports clean rollbacks if issues arise in production.

In Amazon Verified Permissions, for example, a policy store keeps versioned, signed
bundles generated from the repository, ensuring integrity from creation to

deployment.

Early on, an ACME engineer attempted to hotfix a production policy by editing the

store directly. The change lasted for a day, but no one could trace its origin, and the
next deployment overwrote it. Switching to signed bundles prevented this kind of

drift. From then on, the only way to modify a policy store was by way of a reviewed
pull request and a new bundle, ensuring ACME both reliability and accountability.

Keeping repositories and stores separate gave ACME the best of both worlds: Product
teams like Customer Collaboration could manage their own repositories—writing

policies they understood best—while the platform team handled the corresponding
stores that applications relied on.

10.2.1 Schemas and validation

One of the first lessons ACME learned was that policies without schemas quickly become

inconsistent. Developers on the Customer Collaboration platform had written a policy using
the action `doc:modify`, while another team used `doc:edit` . Both worked in their own code,

but when policies were combined, problems arose.

Introducing Cedar schemas resolved the issue. Every repository included a schema that

defined valid principal types, resource types, and actions. From then on, pull requests
couldn’t be merged unless policies were type-checked against the schema.

[In one memorable case, an engineer attempted to write a condition to check the](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-10?potentialInternalRefId=135---book-markup-container)
`department` attribute:

permit(

principal,

action == Action::"deploy",

resource in DeploymentTool

)

when { principal.department == "Engineering" };

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

218

The schema flagged this as invalid because `department` wasn’t a modeled attribute of

principals. Rather than silently enforce a broken rule, the error prompted a design
discussion with HR about how to represent organizational data. The corrected version relied

on roles defined in the entity store:

permit(

principal,

action == Action::"deploy",

resource in DeploymentTool

)

when {

principal in Role::"engineering-manager" ||

principal in Role::"senior-engineer"

};

Validation not only maintained policy consistency; it also revealed gaps in ACME’s data

model and encouraged the company to clearly define where attributes like `department`

belong.

10.2.2 Versioning and review

Treating policies like code also meant treating them like any other artifact in Git. Every
change was made using a pull request and was then reviewed and approved by another

engineer, resulting in a signed, versioned bundle. Developers could see exactly when and
why a policy changed, and who approved it.

This history proved invaluable when auditors asked, “Who decided customers should be
able to edit documents, and when?” The identity team didn’t have to reconstruct the

decision from memory. They pulled up a six-month-old pull request that included reviewer
comments explaining why edit rights were granted, along with a corresponding test that

confirmed customers still couldn’t share documents externally.

[Code reviews also enhanced policy quality. Reviewers didn’t just look for syntax errors —](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-10?potentialInternalRefId=143---book-markup-container)

they posed business-level questions: Does this reflect the intent? Is this scope too broad?
Over time, reviewing policy pull requests became a way for engineers, product managers,

and even lawyers like Dan to share their perspectives on authorization.

10.2.3 Operational considerations

Centralized policy stores also provided ACME with operational visibility it had never

experienced. Decision logs allowed them to finally answer the question, “Why was this
request denied?” by referring directly to the relevant policy and condition. Metrics enabled

them to measure latency and assess whether authorization was imposing unacceptable
overhead.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

219

Explainability proved to be one of the biggest wins. Before, developers would contact the

identity team whenever they encountered an access denied error. Now, decision logs
include reasons: Denied because `principal not in Project::alpha.members` . Here’s a

snippet from the logs:

decision_id=7b3f… result=DENY

reason=principal not in Project::"alpha".members for Action::"doc:edit"

on Document::"alpha/roadmap.md"

With a small internal dashboard, engineers filtered by `decision_id` or `user` and

immediately saw which policy was evaluated and why it was denied, without needing to
page the identity team.

Versioned bundles also made rollbacks easier. When a new deployment policy
accidentally blocked weekend rollouts, the engineering team didn’t panic. They simply

republished the previous bundle while debugging the change. For the first time,
authorization had the same safety nets as any other critical system at ACME.

10.2.4 Continuous integration for policies

At ACME, validating with schemas, versioning, code reviews, and operational discipline are
all integrated into their continuous integration (CI) pipeline. When Bob submits a pull

request to the policy repository, it triggers a series of automated checks: syntax and
schema validation, static analysis to find errors, and unit tests for expected behavior.

Changes can only be merged if all checks pass.

From there, the pipeline created a signed bundle of Cedar policies and published it to the

corresponding policy store. At runtime, the authorizer retrieved policies from that store to
evaluate access requests. Figure 10.6 illustrates how ACME’s CI/CD pipeline manages policy

changes from authoring to runtime.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

220

Figure 10.6 Continuous integration for policies. Bob’s pull request triggers validation, analysis, and testing.

After the checks pass, his changes are merged, bundled into a signed package, and published to a policy

store, where the authorizer uses them to evaluate requests at runtime.

This pipeline provided ACME with two key benefits. First, it identified issues early:
Misspelled action names or references to non-existent attributes were flagged before they

could cause runtime failures. Second, it established a repeatable process: every bundle was
built consistently, with the same checks, and only from reviewed code. Authorization

transitioned from being fragile “tribal knowledge" to becoming a formal part of the
company’s engineering discipline.

#### 10.3 Testing policies effectively

Even the most carefully written Cedar policies can miss subtle issues if they aren’t tested

against real-world scenarios. Authorization logic runs for every access request. Simply
verifying that policies compile isn’t enough; you need confidence that they consistently

enforce the rules you intend.

At ACME, the identity team learned this lesson the hard way. A change to project policies

once prevented managers of owners from editing documents, an edge case no one had
thought to test. The result was several days of confusion until engineers identified the gap.

Afterward, the team adopted a discipline of policy testing alongside the Customer
Collaboration platform. Every policy change now undergoes a set of tests before

deployment, just like application logic.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

221

In practice, testing works by exercising the PDP directly. Each test constructs a

representative authorization request—principal, action, resource, request context, and the
relevant slice of entity data—and submits it to the PDP for evaluation. The test then asserts

whether the resulting decision should be `allow` or `deny` . By testing policies as real

authorization requests rather than as abstract logic, the team validates the entire decision

process, including schema constraints, relationship traversal, global forbids, and
interactions between multiple policies. This approach ensures that policy changes are

verified in the same way they will be enforced in production, reducing surprises when new
rules are deployed.

[Approaches to testing include the following:](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-10?potentialInternalRefId=159---book-markup-container)

Unit tests check individual rules in isolation. An example is ensuring that

an owner can always edit their own document, or that a viewer cannot
share it.

Scenario tests run end-to-end cases involving multiple policies and
relationships. ACME performs scenarios such as “Jack (a customer)

shares the Q3 plan with Bob (his account manager)” to verify that
delegation works correctly.

Regression tests document past bugs to prevent them from happening
again. After the “manager of an owner” bug, ACME added a test to

ensure managers always inherit the correct edit permissions.
Coverage checks ensure that every major rule has at least one related

test, so no part of the policy set goes unchecked.

Because Cedar’s evaluation engine is embeddable, these tests run quickly within ACME’s CI

pipelines. Policies are just code, but they have a b _ig impact_ : a single wrong condition can
accidentally grant access to everyone or block an entire team.

Writing tests for authorization policies follows its own best practices. Unlike application
logic, policies are concise but important: One incorrect condition can accidentally grant

access or block legitimate work.

[These are some strategies for running effective tests:](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-10?potentialInternalRefId=166---book-markup-container)

Test both positive and negative cases. Every policy that allows an action
should also include a denial test to verify boundaries.

Seed entity graphs carefully. Create test fixtures that reflect production
relationships so that policies are tested in realistic situations.

Mirror the production schema. Running tests against the same schema
version as production helps prevent subtle mismatches.

Establish regressions as guardrails. Every bug fix is accompanied by a
test to prevent it from reappearing.

Automate in CI/CD. Policy tests run automatically with every pull request,
and a failing test prevents deployment until the rule is fixed.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

222

At ACME, this discipline minimized surprises in production and gave engineers the

confidence to modify schemas, refine relationships, or add global guardrails without the
fear of breaking existing access paths.

Testing provides more than confidence; it accelerates iteration. ACME’s engineers can
reliably modify schemas, improve relationship models, or add global constraints, knowing

the test suite will catch any unintended effects before deployment.

Testing policies effectively is essential; it transforms Cedar from just a policy language into

a dependable record-keeping system for authorization. By combining request-driven tests
with static analysis, ACME guarantees that its policies not only are syntactically correct but

also enforce the appropriate rules, address real-world scenarios, and stay resilient as the
organization grows. With this safety net, ACME’s engineers can refine schemas, modify

relationships, or add new guardrails, confident that any unintended effects will be caught
before reaching production.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

223

#### 10.4 Pulling it together

Authorization policies are often underestimated. On the surface, they seem minor—just a

few lines of Cedar—but they carry enormous weight. A misplaced condition or an untested
assumption can either expose sensitive data or grind a business process to a halt.

In this chapter, we’ve seen how ACME manages that risk by integrating three disciplines:

Design principles (clarity, least privilege, separation of logic and data,

fine-grained actions, stability across change) ensure that policies reflect
the correct intent.

Policy as code makes policies manageable: stored in repositories,
reviewed and versioned like any other artifact, deployed into runtime

stores with the same rigor as other software.
Testing and analysis offer reassurance: confirming expected scenarios,

preventing regressions, and thoroughly inspecting for structural conflicts
or gaps.

Together, these practices remove authorization from fragile, scattered code and place it in a
unified, reliable record system. Policies become external, transparent, and trustworthy. For

ACME, the benefit is confidence: the identity team knows that when a request is allowed or
denied, it is based on a clear, tested decision aligned with business rules.

Designing sound policies, managing them as code, and testing them effectively are the
cornerstones of dynamic authorization. With these practices in place, policies become

dependable building blocks. But policies don’t exist in isolation — they protect real services.
Nowhere is this more apparent than in APIs, which have become the front door to most

modern systems. In the next chapter, we’ll see how ACME applies Cedar to safeguard its
APIs, and how OAuth fits into the picture as a framework for delegated access.

#### 10.5 Summary

Effective policies are more than just one-off rules; they are design

artifacts that must remain clear, consistent, and aligned with business
needs over time.

Clarity and consistency help prevent conflicts. At ACME, policies defined
by project membership were more predictable than _ad hoc_ rules based on

organizational roles.
Least privilege prevents overexposure. A broad “all employees” permit

gave interns access to sensitive forecasts, but tightening policies to only
include project members closed the gap.

Separating policy from data makes rules more stable. Policies that check
durable roles or teams are better at surviving organizational change than

those that use hard-coded department names or other data that is
frequently updated.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

224

Granularity matters. Fine-grained actions like view, edit, and share offer

precision, while grouping them into higher-level roles in the UI keeps
things simple.

Policies tied to stable entities like teams or projects are resistant to
change. An employee’s promotion might violate a title-based policy, for

example, but wouldn’t affect one based on the employee’s team.
Policy repositories and policy stores serve different functions. Repos are

used for authoring, history, and review; stores are for runtime
enforcement with signed, versioned bundles.

Schemas ensure consistency. By validating policies against schemas,
ACME avoided mismatched action names and discovered missing

attributes before deployment.
Versioning and review promote accountability. Pull requests record the

reasoning for each policy change and enable reviewers to question scope
and intent.

Operational practices ensure policies are auditable. Decision logs,
explainability, and rollback features provide developers and operators

with visibility and control.
Continuous integration links these practices. Every pull request triggers

validation, analysis, and testing before bundles are published to policy
stores.

Testing is as essential for policies as it is for code. ACME employs unit,
scenario, regression, and coverage tests to prevent regressions and

confirm real-world behavior.
Static analysis complements testing. Cedar Analysis inspects the policy

set for conflicts, redundancies, and gaps, offering confidence that policies
are sound and complete.

Effective authorization relies on three key areas: principles that define
what good policies are, policy as code practices that manage and deploy

policies, and testing and analysis to ensure policies work as intended.
Key takeaway: Treat authorization policies as design artifacts, manage

them as code, and test them with the same rigor as software to
transform them from fragile one-offs into a dependable foundation for

dynamic authorization.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

## Authorization for APIs

This chapter covers

Why API authorization is difficult in a microservices environment

Three enforcement patterns for internal APIs: gateway, service mesh, and perservice proxies

How OAuth allows delegated access without sharing passwords

OAuth’s Authorization Code Grant and the Client Credentials Grant

How access tokens are integrated with Cedar for fine-grained authorization

APIs serve as the connective tissue for modern digital systems. Every mobile app, SaaS

product, and microservice relies on APIs to transfer data and initiate operations across
organizational and technical boundaries. That widespread use makes API security a critical

concern. If APIs are left too open, they become vulnerable to misuse or attack. Conversely,
if they are overly restricted, they hinder the integrations and workflows that make modern

software ecosystems possible. Authorization for APIs has to balance two requirements:

**Internal enforcement** : ensuring only authorized services and

employees can access sensitive endpoints within an organization’s own
systems

**External delegation** : providing customers with secure and managed
methods for third-party apps to access APIs on their behalf

Both are essential, but they require different methods. Internal service-to-service
interactions need runtime policy evaluation to enforce corporate rules consistently across

many APIs. Customer-driven delegation, on the other hand, relies on protocols that allow
people to grant limited access without sharing their passwords.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

226

At ACME, these two needs developed simultaneously. Inside the company, microservices

were growing rapidly. Teams had split the once-monolithic Customer Collaboration platform
into smaller services, and HR and Finance departments had done the same. However,

authorization logic was fragmented and inconsistent. The finance API should allow
managers like Carol to access payroll data for their own team but not for the entire

company. The HR API should share personal details with authorized employees but hide
them from unrelated services. Enforcing such rules across dozens of APIs had become

unmanageable.

[At the same time, ACME’s customers—Kate and Jack among them—needed to connect](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-11?potentialInternalRefId=11---book-markup-container)

the other applications their employer, CustCo, relied on to the data inside ACME’s systems,
especially the Customer Collaboration platform. Kate wanted to feed her workspace data

into CustCo’s reporting service, while Jack needed to synchronize assignments with a task
management app already used at CustCo. Allowing those applications to log in with Kate’s

or Jack’s ACME credentials would have been insecure and all-or-nothing: each app would
gain whatever access it had, with no way to limit or revoke it selectively.

[To address these challenges, ACME adopted two complementary strategies. For internal](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-11?potentialInternalRefId=12---book-markup-container)
service-to-service enforcement, they integrated Cedar with their API infrastructure to

establish a centralized, fine-grained decision point. For external delegation, they adopted
OAuth, allowing customers like Kate and Jack to delegate specific permissions to third-party

applications without sharing passwords.

[This chapter addresses those two challenges in turn. We’ll begin with internal](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-11?potentialInternalRefId=13---book-markup-container)

enforcement, where ACME realized that securing APIs is just as crucial—and often more
complicated—than protecting the user-facing application. As their systems evolved toward

microservices, each service boundary became an API surface that required protection.
Later, we’ll discuss external delegation, focusing on how customers like Kate and Jack use

OAuth to grant secure access to other applications they use.

#### 11.1 Authorization in a microservices world

For ACME, moving to microservices changed how authorization was handled. The original
Customer Collaboration platform was a single monolith, with all authorization checks hidden

neatly inside one codebase. But when teams split that system into separate services for
documents, search, and notifications, each new service boundary became an exposed API

surface. HR and Finance followed this approach, creating APIs so their data could be shared
across departments. What once felt like a single, well-guarded front door became a

neighborhood of smaller doors, each with its own lock and key.

The transition was exciting for engineers like Alice, who enjoyed the speed and

autonomy of creating new services. But it also revealed some flaws. Some APIs had strict
authorization rules, others had only basic role checks, and a few assumed their callers were

already trusted.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

227

Bob, ACME’s solutions architect, could see the bigger picture. He mapped the growing

service graph and realized that a single request—like Carol, a manager, asking for a project
report—could touch a dozen APIs. If each service were responsible for its own checks,

maintaining consistency would be impossible. “We had the classic microservices problem,”
Bob said. “Lots of flexibility, but authorization that was fragmented and brittle.”

[The identity team recognized the need for a systematic approach. They examined](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-11?potentialInternalRefId=18---book-markup-container)
architectural patterns for deploying policy enforcement in a distributed system. Three

options stood out as practical: using the API gateway as a centralized enforcement point,
implementing enforcement within a service mesh, and deploying per-service proxies in

front of critical APIs. Each option had its trade-offs, and ACME ultimately chose a
combination.

In the following examples, we will refer to the Cedar engine as the PDP used by ACME without
specifying whether it is Amazon Verified Permissions or a locally hosted Cedar runtime, since the

implementation details are not relevant to the points we are making.

11.1.1 Pattern 1: API gateway as enforcement point

The first place ACME focused on was the API gateway. It already handled every API
request, whether from employees, customer apps, or other internal systems. Bob argued

that the gateway should become the single policy enforcement point (PEP): the one location
to normalize requests into Cedar’s PARC format and consult the Cedar engine for a

decision.

Carol, for example, doesn’t access the HR API directly. She uses the Manager

Dashboard, an internal application that collects data from HR, Finance, and the Customer
Collaboration platform to give managers a single place to view their teams, budgets, and

customer assignments. When Carol clicks the View Team Salaries option, the dashboard
calls the HR API on her behalf.

[The Manager Dashboard doesn’t need to enforce authorization itself; it simply passes](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-11?potentialInternalRefId=24---book-markup-container)
along verified information about Carol as the principal. The API call specifies the action

( `view_salaries` ) and the resource (Carol’s department). The gateway intercepts the

request, constructs the complete PARC authorization request, and forwards it to Cedar.

Figure 11.1 illustrates how this functions.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

228

Figure 11.1 API Gateway as a centralized enforcement point. Carol’s request moves through the Manager

Dashboard to the HR API. The API Gateway functions as the PEP, forwarding a normalized PARC request to the

Cedar engine (PDP). The HR API receives the call only if Cedar returns an “allow” decision.

ACME wanted managers like Carol to view salaries only for their own department, not for
others. Alice’s team described this requirement as a Cedar policy.

permit(

principal,

action == Action::"view_salaries",

resource in ACME::Department

)

when {

principal.role == "manager" &&

resource.id == principal.department_id

};

With that policy in place, a typical request from the Manager Dashboard might look like
this:

Principal: Carol (employee ID, role = manager)
Action: `view_salaries`

Resource: Department(“marketing”)
Context: calling service = Manager Dashboard

Cedar returns `allow` when Carol is viewing salaries for her own department, and the

gateway forwards the call. If she tries to view another department’s salaries, Cedar returns

`deny`, and the request is blocked before it reaches the HR API.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

229

This gateway enforcement pattern provided ACME with two key advantages. First,

application developers, like the Manager Dashboard team, no longer needed to duplicate
authorization logic; they simply passed principal information and relied on the APIs to

enforce policies consistently. Second, authorization at the gateway protected ACME from
coding errors or malicious actions. Even if the dashboard UI showed actions not intended

for the current employee or if someone tried to tamper with the interface, the gateway
would block unauthorized requests before they accessed sensitive data.

[By making the gateway the universal PEP, ACME ensured that Cedar policies protected](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-11?potentialInternalRefId=35---book-markup-container)
every call in the same way, whether from the Manager Dashboard or any other system.

11.1.2 Pattern 2: Service mesh with sidecar enforcement

The API gateway solved many problems, but Bob realized it couldn’t handle everything.
Within ACME’s infrastructure, services constantly communicated with each other. For

instance, the Manager Dashboard didn’t just query the HR API; it also retrieved budget
data from Finance and project details from the Customer Collaboration platform. These

requests often triggered chains of downstream calls. The HR API might call a directory
service, or the Collaboration API might fan out to the Search service to locate documents.

Much of this _east–west traffic_ never passed through the edge gateway.

EAST–WEST AND NORTH–SOUTH TRAFFIC

In network and service-architecture diagrams, traffic is often described by its

direction. _North–south traffic_ flows into or out of a system—from an external client
or customer (north) down into the organization’s infrastructure (south). These

requests typically pass through edge components such as API gateways and firewalls
that enforce perimeter security and validate OAuth tokens. At ACME, the API

gateway mediates all north–south traffic, serving as the central enforcement point
for external API access.

_East–west traffic_, on the other hand, moves within the system—between internal
services, APIs, and databases. As ACME’s Customer Collaboration platform evolved

toward microservices, this internal traffic surged: a single customer request could
trigger dozens of service-to-service calls. Traditional perimeter controls could no

longer monitor or mediate these interactions. To secure this east–west flow, ACME
implemented Cedar-based authorization in its service mesh and local, per-service

proxies, ensuring that every internal call was evaluated against policy, just as
external calls were at the gateway.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

230

Relying solely on the gateway creates blind spots. If a bug or misconfiguration lets a service

overreach, sensitive data could leak without detection. Bob suggested adopting a service
mesh to fill this gap. With a mesh like Istio, each service-to-service call passes through a

local sidecar proxy. These proxies establish mutual TLS (mTLS) to verify the identity of each
service, and they can be configured to consult an external authorization system like Cedar

before forwarding requests.

Alice’s team integrated Cedar at this enforcement point. Each sidecar proxy became a

policy enforcement point (PEP), sending a normalized PARC request to a Cedar engine as
the policy decision point (PDP). Figure 11.2 illustrates how this worked when the Docs

service sent content to the Search service.

Figure 11.2 Service mesh enforcement with sidecars. Cedar evaluates each document sent from Docs to

Search. Documents tagged “Legal” are denied; others are allowed.

When Carol opened her Manager Dashboard and drilled into customer assignments, the
dashboard retrieved document metadata from the Collaboration platform. This, in turn,

triggered the Docs service to request indexing from Search. The Docs service fetched
documents from its repository and sent them one by one to Search for indexing. Each

outbound request went through the Docs sidecar, which built the PARC request.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

231

Alice’s team created Cedar policies to address the security concerns highlighted by the

product manager for the Docs service. For example, by default, the Docs service indexes
documents unless the document is labeled “Legal.” The policy was straightforward: a single

`permit` statement with an `unless` clause for legal documents:

permit(

principal in ACME::Service::"docs",

action == Action::"doc:index",

resource in ACME::Document

)

unless {

// exception: never index documents classified as Legal

resource.sensitivity == "Legal"

};

For ordinary documents, Cedar returned `allow`, and the indexing request was forwarded to

Search. For legal documents, Cedar returned `deny`, and the sidecar blocked the request

before it ever reached the Search service. If the Docs service product manager later

determines that documents with a sensitivity of `HighValue` should also not be indexed, that

decision can be reflected by simply updating the policy.

With that policy in place, a typical request from the Docs service might look like this:

Principal: Docs service (workload identity) acting on behalf of Carol

Action: `doc:index`

Resource: Document(“CustCo-proposal”)

Context: sensitivity = “Legal”, tenant = CustCo

Cedar evaluates this request against the policy and returns `deny` because the document’s

sensitivity is marked `Legal` . This indexing request is blocked at the proxy and never

reaches the Search service. Cedar denies `requests` for legal documents, blocking them at

the proxy. All other documents are allowed and indexed normally.

This pattern established a zero-trust baseline within the cluster. Each hop was verified

with a strong service identity, and Cedar approved every call before it was forwarded.
Developers didn’t need to add new checks to their services; enforcement was handled

automatically in the mesh. The trade-off was increased operational complexity, but for highvolume internal traffic, the advantages outweighed the drawbacks.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

11.1.3 Pattern 3: Per-service proxies

Not all ACME services were behind the API gateway or ready to be integrated into the
service mesh. Some teams operated their APIs on infrastructure that didn’t yet support the

mesh. To address these gaps, Bob suggested deploying per-service proxies. Each critical
[service would be placed behind a lightweight proxy such as Envoy (https://www.​](https://www.envoyproxy.io/)

<u>[envoyproxy.​io). The proxy would serve as a policy enforcement point (PEP): terminating](https://www.envoyproxy.io/)</u>
TLS, validating service identity, and requesting Cedar for an authorization decision before

forwarding the request to the API.

Finance was among the first teams to adopt this model. Their API provided endpoints for

retrieving cost-center data. Carol uses the Manager Dashboard to monitor her department’s
budget alongside HR data and customer assignments. When the dashboard requests data

from the Finance API, the request first passes through the Finance service proxy, as shown
in figure 11.3.

Figure 11.3 Per-service proxy enforcement. Carol’s Manager Dashboard requests cost-center data from the

Finance API. The request first passes through a proxy that verifies service identity and consults Cedar.

Managers can view their own cost centers, but requests for other departments are denied.

ACME wanted managers like Carol to view data only for their own cost centers, not for

those in other departments. Alice’s team described this requirement as a Cedar policy:

permit(

principal,

action == Action::"finance:view_costs",

resource in ACME::CostCenter

)

when {

principal.role == "manager" &&

resource.department_id == principal.department_id

};

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

233

With that policy in place, a typical request from the Manager Dashboard might look like

this:

Principal: Carol (employee ID, role = manager)

Action: `finance:view_costs`

Resource: CostCenter(“MKT-001”)

Context: calling service = Manager Dashboard

Cedar returns `allow` when Carol requests data for her own cost center, and the proxy

forwards the call to the Finance API. If she attempts to view another department’s cost
center, Cedar returns `deny`, and the proxy blocks the request before it reaches the service.

The proxy does more than just forward calls. As the policy enforcement point, it is
responsible for creating a valid Cedar authorization request by combining the API details

(which specify the principal, action, and resource) with identity information from the TLS
connection. This way, the Finance API never has to generate PARC requests itself. The

proxy ensures every call is normalized and checked against the correct policy before
reaching the service.

[This pattern allowed ACME to extend Cedar-based authorization to services outside the](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-11?potentialInternalRefId=68---book-markup-container)
gateway or mesh. It also created a smaller blast radius: if the Finance proxy failed or was

misconfigured, only the Finance API was affected, not the whole system. The trade-off was
increased operational overhead from managing and maintaining more proxies. However, for

teams not yet migrated to the mesh, per-service proxies ensured Cedar’s policies continued
to protect their APIs.

11.1.4 Comparing enforcement patterns

ACME ended up using all three enforcement patterns in different situations. The API
gateway managed edge traffic, the service mesh secured most east–west calls, and per
service proxies protected APIs that had not yet migrated into the mesh. Each pattern
offered distinct advantages and trade-offs, summarized in table 11.1.

Table 11.1 Comparison of API authorization enforcement patterns

|Pattern|Where enforced|Strengths|
|---|---|---|
|API gateway|At the edge, all incoming<br>requests funnel through the<br>gateway|Centralized enforcement,<br>consistent logs, easy to roll<br>out global rules|
|Service mesh with<br>sidecars|Between services inside the<br>cluster; each call passes<br>through local sidecars|Strong workload identity via<br>mTLS, zero-trust baseline, no<br>code changes required|
|Per-service proxies|In front of a single API; proxy<br>acts as a local PEP|Works without mesh, finer<br>blast radius, consistent policy<br>for legacy services|

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

234

Together, these three patterns gave ACME a consistent, Cedar-based authorization model

across their growing API ecosystem. Regardless of whether a request passed through the
gateway, a mesh sidecar, or a per-service proxy, the decision was always externalized to

Cedar and evaluated in the same PARC format.

11.1.5 Other enforcement patterns

The gateway, mesh, and per-service proxy patterns addressed most of ACME’s needs.

However, in certain cases, other enforcement models can also be useful. These are less
common in ACME’s story but still worth understanding.

IN-PROCESS ENFORCEMENT

Instead of routing requests through a proxy, a service can integrate the Cedar library or run
a local Cedar agent. This decreases latency and eliminates an extra network hop. It’s

especially beneficial for performance-critical services like rendering or analytics pipelines.
The trade-off is that each codebase must properly integrate Cedar and maintain consistent

request generation and policy evaluation logic. Standardized integration patterns and
libraries, shared policy stores, and caching support can mitigate this trade-off somewhat.

MTLS-ONLY AND NETWORK CONTROLS

In some cases, coarse-grained controls are enough. Services can be limited to
communicate only with specific peers using workload identity from mTLS certificates or

network rules, like Kubernetes NetworkPolicy. For example, you might allow “Docs can call
Search” but not “Search can call HR.” This method is efficient and simple, but it can’t

enforce fine-grained rules such as “Docs cannot index Legal documents.” Many
organizations set up these controls as a baseline and then layer fine-grained authorization

on top for resource-level decisions.

EVENT OR BROKER ENFORCEMENT

In asynchronous architectures, a message broker like Kafka, NATS, and SQS serves as the

natural enforcement point. Brokers can enforce coarse-grained rights such as “Service A
may publish to Topic X” or “Service B may consume from Queue Y.” For fine-grained checks

—for example, whether a specific message complies with sensitivity requirements—the
authorization engine typically operates on the consumer side. One thing to watch out for:

While brokers can prevent unauthorized producers or consumers, sensitive data may still
propagate unless consumers apply additional policy checks per message.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

235

DIRECT TOKEN EXCHANGE

Instead of relying on proxies or a mesh, a calling service can obtain a short-lived token
from a security token service (STS) and present it directly to the callee. The callee verifies

the token and consults an authorization engine before proceeding. This approach is flexible
in smaller systems, but each service must handle identity and authorization logic

consistently. This pattern is typically used for coarse-grained controls.

Each of these patterns involves a trade-off. They can lower operational complexity,

latency, or deployment overhead, but they come at the expense of consistency and
visibility. Table 11.2 compares these four methods.

[Table 11.2 Other API authorization enforcement patterns](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-11?potentialInternalRefId=84---book-markup-container)

|Pattern|Where enforced|Grain|Typical use|
|---|---|---|---|
|In-process|Inside the service code or<br>via a local Cedar agent|Fine|Low-latency, performance-<br>sensitive services|
|mTLS or<br>network<br>controls|Connection layer (certs,<br>firewall, NetworkPolicy)|Coarse|Baseline guardrails: which<br>services may talk to each<br>other|
|Event or<br>broker|Message bus (Kafka,<br>NATS, SQS)|Mostly<br>coarse|Publish/subscribe control;<br>combine with authorization<br>engine for message-level<br>checks|
|Direct token<br>exchange|Caller presents short-lived<br>STS token to callee|Usually<br>coarse|Smaller systems or when<br>proxies/mesh aren’t available|

At ACME, these additional patterns were used selectively. In-process enforcement appeared

only in performance-sensitive services where low latency was essential. mTLS and network
controls provided coarse-grained guardrails for which services could talk to each other.

Broker enforcement applied to asynchronous pipelines, controlling who could publish or
consume messages. Direct token exchange was rarely used, limited to smaller systems

outside the gateway or mesh. The common thread was that whenever fine-grained access
control was required, the decision logic was always externalized to policy in Cedar.

AUTHZEN AND STANDARDIZED AUTHORIZATION DECISIONS

The emerging AuthZen standard defines a common API for making authorization

decisions. Rather than create a new policy model or language, AuthZen concentrates
on standardizing the requests and responses between a policy enforcement point

(PEP) and a policy decision point (PDP).

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

236

In this chapter, ACME’s gateways, sidecars, and service proxies transform requests

into Cedar’s PARC format before requesting a decision. AuthZen serves a similar
purpose: It defines how a PEP asks, “May this principal perform this action on this

resource in this context?” and how the PDP responds.

Architecturally, AuthZen could sit in front of Cedar, enabling ACME to swap or

combine policy engines without altering enforcement points. In practice, many
systems today use engine-specific formats like PARC. AuthZen’s value lies in

promoting interoperability and reducing coupling between enforcement infrastructure
and decision engines.

#### 11.2 Authorization for external access to APIs

As the web became more interconnected, people increasingly wanted to link services
together. A classic example was allowing a photo-printing site to fetch your pictures from

an online photo service. In the beginning, the only way to do that was to give the printing
site your username and password for the photo service. That _password anti-pattern_ had

obvious problems: the printing site could impersonate you, it had full access to your
account instead of just the data it needed, and you had no way to revoke access without

changing your password everywhere.

[OAuth (https://oauth.​net/2/) was developed to address this problem. Instead of sharing](https://oauth.net/2/)

authentication factors like passwords, people can grant an application limited access to
their data by approving specific scopes. These scopes specify what the application is

allowed to do, such as reading contacts but not sending emails, and they can be revoked at
any time without impacting the rest of the account. OAuth allows for delegated access:

controlled, revocable, and limited to exactly what the person consents to.

All references to OAuth refer to the newer OAuth 2.0 protocol, not OAuth 1.0a. You might still

come across OAuth-1.0a-protected APIs, but OAuth 1.0a should not be used for new projects.

11.2.1 The OAuth protocol and roles

The OAuth protocol defines four main actors:

**Resource Owner** . The individual who owns the data or resources. In
ACME’s case, Kate is a resource owner; she manages documents and

workspaces on the Customer Collaboration platform.
**Client** . The application requesting access to the resource owner’s data.

Kate wants to use BI Explorer, a reporting tool, to analyze her Customer
Collaboration data. BI Explorer is the client.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

237

**Authorization Server** . The service that authenticates the resource

owner and issues tokens to the client. At ACME, this role is fulfilled by the
Customer Authentication Service, which verifies Kate’s identity and

provides OAuth tokens that encode which scopes she approved.
**Resource Server** . The API that hosts the protected resources and

responds to requests. For ACME, the Customer Collaboration API is the
resource server, providing data about Kate’s documents and workspaces.

Figure 11.4 illustrates these four roles in Kate’s scenario. Kate (the resource owner) uses BI
Explorer (the client). BI Explorer requests access through ACME’s Customer Authentication

Service (the authorization server), which issues a token if Kate consents. That token can
then be presented to the Customer Collaboration API (the resource server), which

ultimately provides data but only after evaluating Cedar policies to determine what is
permitted.

Figure 11.4 OAuth roles in action. Kate is the resource owner, BI Explorer is the client, ACME’s Customer

Authentication Service is the authorization server, and the Customer Collaboration API is the resource server.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

238

In typical OAuth discussions, the authorization server is portrayed as making authorization

decisions. However, in practice, especially at ACME, that’s only partially true. The
authorization server authenticates the user (or service), obtains consent, and issues a

token with approved scopes. Scopes specify which API surfaces can be accessed. The
actual, detailed authorization—whether this caller is permitted to perform a specific action

on a particular resource—takes place later, at the resource server, where Cedar policies are
evaluated for each API request.

This distinction is critical:

OAuth tokens and scopes control the outer perimeter of what an API call

may attempt.
Cedar policies decide the inner logic of what the caller is allowed to see or

do.

Together, OAuth and Cedar provide ACME with a layered defense. OAuth verifies who the

caller is and which parts of the API they can access, while Cedar decides whether that caller
can perform specific actions on specific resources. This separation makes the system both

flexible and secure: tokens can be widely recognized across many clients and APIs, while
Cedar policies enforce detailed business rules that adapt to ACME’s needs. Next, we’ll look

at how OAuth scopes define the broad contours of access, before turning to the ways
clients obtain tokens in practice.

OAUTH OPENS THE DOOR; POLICY DECIDES WHAT YOU SEE

When Kate connects BI Explorer to ACME using OAuth, she grants the scope
`collab:doc.read` . This scope allows BI Explorer to access the document-read

endpoints in the Customer Collaboration API. From OAuth’s point of view, the request
is valid: the token is authentic, unexpired, and has the correct scope.

But OAuth scopes only define the outer perimeter of access. When BI Explorer
requests documents, the API gateway still checks Cedar to determine what Kate is

explicitly allowed to see. For most documents in Kate’s workspaces, Cedar responds
with allow. When BI Explorer tries to access a document tagged

`sensitivity="Legal"`, Cedar responds with `deny`, and that document is blocked,

even though the OAuth token is valid.

The policy that enforces this rule is simple:

239

11.2.2 OAuth scopes

Scopes are the mechanism OAuth uses to express those broad contours of access. Instead

of granting a client full control over an account, the authorization server issues tokens with
specific scopes that specify which parts of an API the client can access. Scopes are strings

created by the API provider that represent bundles of related permissions. When a client
requests access, it asks for certain scopes, and the resource owner decides whether to

approve them.

For example, ACME’s Customer Collaboration platform specifies scopes such as these:

`collab:workspace.read` —read the list of workspaces and memberships.

`collab:doc.meta.read` —read document metadata (titles, owners, labels,

last updated), but not the full content.
`collab:doc.write` —update document titles or statuses.

`collab:task.read` and `collab:task.write` —view or update tasks

related to documents.

`collab:event.subscribe` —register for event notifications (such as

`task.created` or `document.status_changed` ).

When a token is issued, these scopes may be included directly within the token itself (as a
claim in a self-contained JWT) or stored on the server and returned during token

introspection. In ACME’s system, scopes are encoded in the access token, allowing the API
gateway to read them immediately after validating the token. In either case, scopes serve

as a broad filter: they determine which APIs a client can attempt to call. Cedar policies then
overlay this, enforcing fine-grained rules about specific resources and actions that are

permitted.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

240

11.2.3 Acquiring OAuth tokens

The core of OAuth is the grant, the process through which a client application obtains an

access token. There are several different types of grants. Each follows a slightly different
path, depending on whether a human is involved, the type of client making the request,

and the required security level. The primary method for obtaining a token is the
_Authorization Code Grant_, where a person logs in and explicitly approves the scopes of

access, and the client then exchanges that approval for a token. Other grants, like _Client_
_Credentials_, allow server-to-server applications to acquire tokens directly without user

interaction. There are also other types, such as the _Implicit Grant_ and _Resource Owner_
_Password Credentials Grant_, which are used for specific cases but are less common.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

241

AUTHORIZATION CODE GRANT

The _Authorization Code Grant_ is the most common method for a person to authorize an
application to access their data. The flow is designed to be secure: the user never shares

their password with the client application, and tokens are exchanged directly between the
client and the authorization server over a secure channel.

At ACME, Kate wanted to use BI Explorer, a reporting tool, to create dashboards using
data from the Customer Collaboration platform. BI Explorer needed to access document

metadata and workspace information, but it should do so only with Kate’s permission and
within the boundaries of her account. The Authorization Code Grant offered the right

balance of usability and security. Figure 11.5 shows the flow for the code grant.

Figure 11.5 Authorization Code Grant. The resource owner’s browser handles login and consent. ACME’s

authorization server provides a short-lived code, which the client then exchanges for an access token over a

secure back channel.

The protocol involves several steps corresponding to the arrows in figure 11.5:

1. **Client initiation** . Kate clicks “Connect to ACME” in BI Explorer (the
client).

2. **Client redirect** . The client then redirects Kate to ACME’s authorization
server, including human-readable descriptions of the requested scopes

such as `collab:workspace.read`, `collab:doc.meta.read`, and

`collab:event.subscribe` .

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

242

3. **Authentication and consent** . ACME’s authorization server authenticates

Kate using her usual credentials, then displays a consent screen showing
the scopes BI Explorer has requested. Kate reviews the request and clicks

**Allow** . Figure 11.6 shows the consent screen Kate sees when BI Explorer
requests access. The scopes she approves determine what the resulting

token can be used for.

Figure 11.6 OAuth consent screen for BI Explorer. Kate reviews the scopes requested by BI Explorer. She

grants permission to read workspace membership, view document metadata (but not content), and does not

allow BI Explorer to subscribe to updates. The token issued to BI Explorer will be limited to the scopes Kate

selected.

4. **Authorization code issued** . After consent, the authorization server

redirects Kate’s browser back to BI Explorer with a short-lived
authorization code.

5. **Token request** . BI Explorer sends the authorization code to the
authorization server directly via an HTTPS request, along with its own

client credentials.
6. **Token issuance** . The server verifies the code and returns an access

token (and often a refresh token).
