243

At this point, the client, BI Explorer, has a valid access token it can use to call ACME’s APIs.

Since access tokens are short-lived, the authorization server usually issues a refresh token
that BI Explorer can exchange later for a new access token without involving Kate again.

This way, Kate isn’t repeatedly being prompted to log in or re-consent just to keep her
dashboards updated. How the access token is validated and combined with Cedar policies is

explained in the later section on using a token.

CLIENT CREDENTIALS GRANT

The _Client Credentials Grant_ issues a token that represents an application, not an

individual. This makes it the ideal choice for headless, tenant-approved integrations that
need to operate continuously—like CustCo’s Task App that Jack relies on.

Jack’s customer success team uses a task management system—the Task App—for all
daily tasks. This is where they track assignments, set deadlines, and monitor progress.

Meanwhile, much of CustCo’s collaboration with ACME happens in the Customer
Collaboration platform, where proposals, onboarding plans, and support documents are

stored. The issue is that workflows often start in Collaboration but need to be completed in
the Task App.

[Without integration, Jack’s team must manually copy tasks between systems. Deadlines](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-11?potentialInternalRefId=146---book-markup-container)
are missed, tasks get lost, and managers cannot see a full picture of work. By connecting

the Task App with ACME’s Collaboration platform, CustCo ensures that:

When an action item is created in Collaboration, a corresponding task

automatically appears in the Task App.
When a task is finished in the Task App, the status updates in the

Collaboration workspace.
CustCo employees continue using their familiar tool, while ACME

employees stay in Collaboration—without losing context.

This type of synchronization must run 24/7, regardless of whether Jack is signed in. That’s

why CustCo can’t rely on a user token. Instead, it uses the Client Credentials Grant, where
the Task App authenticates as itself.

Before the Task App can request tokens, it must first be installed in the Customer
Collaboration platform and explicitly linked to CustCo’s tenant; this occurs once during

setup:

1. The CustCo admin installs the Task App in ACME’s Customer

Authentication service and approves narrow scopes:

collab:task.read, collab:task.write, collab:doc.meta.read, and

collab:event.subscribe.

2. ACME creates a record of the installation, linking the app to CustCo, for

example:

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

244

IntegrationInstall{id="custco-tasks", tenant="CustCo", allowed_workspaces=

["custco-sales","custco-support"]}

This installation record acts as the reference point for policy: it shows which tenant owns

the app and what resources it is authorized to access.

Once installed, the Task App can acquire tokens on its own, without any user interaction.

Figure 11.7 illustrates the flow of the credential grant:

1. The Task App authenticates to ACME’s authorization server using its

`client_id` and `client_secret` and requests the `client_credentials`

grant for the approved scopes.

2. The authorization server verifies the credentials and responds with an
access token, where the subject is the integration principal (the app), not

a user.

Figure 11.7 CustCo’s Task App authenticates to ACME’s authorization server using its client credentials and

receives an access token that represents the app (an integration principal). Admin setup and the installation

record bind the app to CustCo and specific workspaces.

By the end of this process, the Task App holds a valid access token that represents the

application itself. This token is all it needs to start making API calls on behalf of CustCo.
Since access tokens are short-lived, the app repeats this process as needed. How the token

is validated, enriched with installation details, and combined with Cedar policies is
explained in the next section on using tokens.

245

OTHER OAUTH GRANTS

OAuth specifies a few additional ways for clients to get tokens, although they are less often
recommended today. I include them here for completeness:

**Implicit Grant.** Originally intended for browser-based single-page apps,
the implicit flow bypassed the authorization code step and returned an

access token directly in the URL fragment. This saved an additional
network request but increased the risk of token leakage. Today, implicit is

considered insecure and has largely been replaced by the Authorization
Code Grant with PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange).

**Resource Owner Password Credentials Grant.** In this flow, the user
directly provides their username and password to the client application,

which exchanges them for a token. This essentially bypasses OAuth’s
protections and is safe only for first-party clients that the user already

trusts with their credentials. For third-party apps, it reintroduces the
password anti-pattern that OAuth was designed to eliminate.

These flows still exist in legacy systems, but ACME uses the Authorization Code and Client
Credentials grants for new integrations. They support both interactive user-driven access

(like Kate and BI Explorer) and long-running service-to-service integrations (such as
CustCo’s Task App).

11.2.4 Using OAuth tokens

No matter how an access token is obtained—whether through the Authorization Code

Grant, the Client Credentials Grant, or one of the secondary flows—the process of using
that token remains the same. Tokens are how a client proves it has been granted access.

Each API request includes the token, and every request is verified before it reaches the
underlying service.

At ACME, OAuth provides only the broad perimeter: a token says, for example, “this
client can read document metadata” or “this integration can write tasks.” Cedar policies

then supply the fine-grained access control, ensuring the token is applied only to the
appropriate resources under the correct conditions. That means Kate’s BI Explorer token

allows her to read metadata, but only for workspaces she belongs to. CustCo’s Task App
can use the token to write tasks only in the specific CustCo workspaces approved during

installation. Simultaneously, Cedar can enforce additional rules, such as excluding sensitive
document types or requiring user attribution for writes. Figure 11.8 illustrates how an

access token is used.

The examples in this section use an API gateway, but any of the three architectural patterns

forprotecting APIs discussed earlier in this chapter would work as well.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

246

Figure 11.8 Using an OAuth token with Cedar. The client (BI Explorer or Task App) includes an access token in

its API request. The API gateway validates the token and then creates a PARC request for Cedar. Only if Cedar

grants permission does the request proceed to the Customer Collaboration API and return data.

These are the steps shown in figure 11.8:

1. **Client presents token.** Each request to ACME’s APIs must include the
token in the HTTP header:

Authorization: Bearer <access_token>

2. **Gateway validates token.** The API gateway (acting as the policy
enforcement point) checks the token before doing anything else by

verifying the signature, issuer, and expiration. It also confirms that the
token includes the necessary scopes for the API being called. Additionally,

the gateway identifies the caller: Kate (for the BI Explorer) or the
integration principal (for the Task App).

3. **Gateway constructs a PARC request.** Next, the gateway converts the
API call into a Cedar request:

Principal: taken from the token (user or integration)
Action: inferred from the API method ( `doc.meta.read`,

`task.write` )

Resource: derived from the API path or body

( `Workspace::"custco-sales"`, `Document::"abc123"` )

Context: extra attributes like scopes, tenant, or optional

user attribution (for example, `requested_by` )

4. **Cedar evaluates policies.** The PARC request is sent to Cedar, which

evaluates the relevant policies and returns either `allow` or `deny` .

5. **Gateway enforces.** If Cedar returns `allow`, the gateway forwards the

request to the API and returns the results. If Cedar returns `deny`, the

gateway blocks the request with a 403.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

247

This layering is what makes OAuth and Cedar complementary. OAuth tokens and scopes

define the outer perimeter of what APIs a client can attempt to access, while Cedar policies
enforce the internal rules of what the caller is actually permitted to do with a particular

resource.

EXAMPLE: KATE’S BI EXPLORER (AUTHORIZATION CODE TOKEN)

When Kate connects BI Explorer to ACME, the tool acquires an access token through the

Authorization Code Grant. This token includes the scopes Kate approved
( `collab:workspace.read`, `collab:doc.meta.read`, and optionally

`collab:event.subscribe` ) and identifies Kate as the principal.

Later, BI Explorer requests a list of documents from the `custco-sales` workspace to

update Kate’s reporting dashboard. The GET request contains the bearer token in the
header:

GET /workspaces/custco-sales/documents?fields=meta

Authorization: Bearer <access_token>

At the gateway, the token is verified and then converted into a Cedar PARC request:

{

"principal": { "type": "User", "id": "kate@custco.com" },

"action": "collab:doc.meta.read",

"resource": { "type": "Workspace", "id": "custco-sales" },

"context": {

"token_scopes": ["collab:workspace.read","collab:doc.meta.read"],

"origin_service": "bi-explorer"

}

}

Cedar evaluates this request against the Customer Collaboration platform’s policy for

workspace membership:

permit(

principal in ACME::User,

action == Action::"collab:doc.meta.read",

resource in ACME::Workspace

)

when { principal in resource.members };

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

248

Because Kate is a member of the `custco-sales` workspace, Cedar returns `allow`, and the

gateway forwards the call to the Collaboration API. If BI Explorer tries to fetch documents
from a workspace Kate does not belong to, Cedar would return `deny`, and the API call would

be blocked.

This combination of OAuth scopes and Cedar policy makes sure that BI Explorer can read

only the metadata Kate has consented to and only within workspaces where she already
has access.

EXAMPLE: CUSTCO’S TASK APP (CLIENT CREDENTIALS TOKEN)

CustCo’s Task App performs a background sync that aligns tasks with ACME’s Customer
Collaboration workspaces. It uses the Client Credentials grant to authenticate itself, so the

access token’s subject is the integration principal, not a person. During setup, a CustCo
admin restricted the app to two workspaces: `custco-sales` and `custco-support` .

When the app needs to create a task for a new action item in `custco-sales`, it sends an

API request like this:

POST /tasks

Authorization: Bearer <access_token>

Body:

{

"workspace": "custco-sales",

"docId": "abc123",

"title": "Follow up with customer",

"assignee": "sam@custco.com",

"dueDate": "2025-10-15",

"requested_by": "jack@custco.com"  // attribution added by the app

}

At the gateway, the token is verified and the app’s Installation record is retrieved ( `tenant =`

`CustCo; allowed_workspaces = [custco-sales, custco-support]` ). Then the gateway

constructs a PARC request for Cedar:

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

{

}

249

"principal": {

"type": "ACME::Integration",

"id": "custco-tasks",

"attrs": {

"tenant": "CustCo",

"allowed_workspaces": ["custco-sales","custco-support"]

}

},

"action": "collab:task.write",

"resource": { "type": "ACME::Workspace", "id": "custco-sales" },

"context": {

"token_scopes": ["collab:task.write","collab:doc.meta.read"],

"requested_by": "jack@custco.com"

}

Cedar assesses the request based on integration-focused policies. The first ties the app to

CustCo and only the installed workspaces; the second is an optional guardrail that requires
human attribution on writes:

// The Task App may act only within CustCo-owned, installed workspaces

permit(

principal == ACME::Integration::"custco-tasks",

action in [Action::"collab:task.read", Action::"collab:task.write",

Action::"collab:doc.meta.read"],

resource in ACME::Workspace

)

when {

resource.owner_tenant == principal.tenant &&

resource.id in principal.allowed_workspaces

};

// Writes must carry a CustCo user attribution for audit/controls

permit(

principal == ACME::Integration::"custco-tasks",

action == Action::"collab:task.write",

resource in ACME::Workspace

)

when { context.requested_by like /@custco.com$/ };

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

250

Because the target is `custco-sales` (an approved workspace) and the request includes

`requested_by=jack@custco.com`, Cedar returns `allow`, and the gateway forwards the API

call to create the task. If the app tries to write to a workspace outside its installation (such

as `otherco-marketing` ) or omits `requested_by`, Cedar would return `deny`, and the gateway

would block the request.

This example demonstrates how Client Credentials work with Cedar to go beyond tenantlevel scoping: the gateway enriches the integration principal with installation attributes, and

policies enforce detailed constraints—such as specific workspaces, audit attribution, or
exclusions like sensitive document types—without assigning the integration to any

individual.

#### 11.3 From microservices to third parties: One policy story

In this chapter, we followed ACME through two very different authorization challenges.
Internally, microservices multiplied rapidly, and the company needed a consistent way to

ensure that each API call adhered to organizational policy. Externally, customers like Kate
and Jack wanted to connect their own tools to the Customer Collaboration platform, but

without sharing passwords or exposing more data than necessary.

The solutions appeared different on the surface. Inside ACME’s infrastructure,

authorization took place at the API gateway, within the service mesh, and through perservice proxies. Outside, access was granted via OAuth, with Kate using the Authorization

Code Grant and CustCo’s Task App employing the Client Credentials Grant. Despite these
differences, both pathways ended the same way: each API request was converted into a

PARC request and evaluated according to Cedar policies.

[That consistency is the heart of ACME’s story. OAuth tokens and scopes define the outer](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-11?potentialInternalRefId=208---book-markup-container)

boundary, specifying which APIs a client is allowed to access. Cedar handles the internal
logic, determining which actions are permitted on specific resources. By externalizing

decision-making and evaluating policies at runtime, ACME accomplishes two goals
simultaneously:

Developers no longer needed to duplicate authorization logic in each
service.

Customers can safely integrate third-party tools without granting broad or
fragile access.

From microservices to third-party integrations, ACME learned that API authorization is more
than just checking tokens or enforcing scopes. It is about integrating policy into every

request path, ensuring that the same rules apply whether the caller is a person, a service,
or an external application. With Cedar as the decision engine and OAuth as the delegation

protocol, ACME unified internal enforcement and external delegation into a single, coherent
policy story.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

251

The next chapter shifts focus from APIs to the context that policies rely on. We’ve seen

Cedar enforce rules consistently across gateways, meshes, proxies, and OAuth-protected
APIs, but what information does Cedar (or any policy engine) need to make those

decisions? We’ll examine how principals and resources are represented as entities, what
external signals influence policy evaluation, and how context can be standardized across

systems. This foundation will clarify how policies connect to the real-world actions they
oversee.

#### 11.4 Summary

ACME secures APIs on two fronts: Cedar policies safeguard internal

microservices at gateways, meshes, and proxies, while OAuth tokens—
combined with Cedar—allow safe external delegation to customer

applications.
API authorization needs to manage both internal service-to-service calls

and external third-party integrations.
ACME enforces internal policies using gateway, service mesh, and per
service proxy patterns, with Cedar serving as the decision engine.
OAuth enables delegated access without sharing passwords, with scopes

specifying which APIs a token bearer can access.
The Authorization Code Grant (Kate’s BI Explorer) and Client Credentials

Grant (CustCo’s Task App) demonstrate the two most important methods
for obtaining tokens.

Regardless of grant type, tokens are validated at the gateway and then
converted into PARC requests for Cedar, which enforces detailed access

control.

## Authorization context

This chapter covers

the three-dimensional choice space for context: which signals, how they’re
delivered, and how fresh they are

How PIPs collect signals and PDPs assemble entities for policy evaluation

Signal delivery models: tokens, queries, and hybrids using device-posture tokens at
request time

Managing freshness, caching, and revocation to balance assurance and

performance

Securing and normalizing signals using provenance, signatures, and an enterprise
PIP with a Shared Signal Framework-style eventing system

Policies alone aren’t enough to make authorization decisions; they need context to turn

abstract rules into concrete outcomes. Whether a request should be allowed depends on
not only who asks and what they want but also a surrounding set of facts: Is the device

compliant? Is the employee still active? Is the login risky? Is the customer’s account
suspended? These trust signals provide the raw material for policies to work. Without them,

even the most elegant policy language is useless.

Every authorization system must answer three questions about signals:

Which signals matter? (employment status, device trust, MFA,
geolocation, risk score, account balance)

How should those signals be delivered? (embedded in tokens, fetched
from APIs, pushed from event streams, gathered by local agents)

How fresh do they need to be? (queried live, cached briefly, or embedded
until token expiry)

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

253

Together, these questions form a three-dimensional choice space. Designing an

authorization system means choosing a position in that space for each use case.

At ACME, various contexts land at different points in this space. These different choices

are not necessarily better or worse, as long as the trade-offs are appropriate for the use
case.

**Customers on the Customer Collaboration platform** . Customers
authenticate through ACME’s customer information system, which issues

OAuth tokens. Signals like customer ID and basic role (viewer,
collaborator) are embedded in the token. Additional context—such as

account status or billing history—comes from ACME’s customer database.
For higher-value customers, the platform may also query an external

fraud detection feed before granting access.
**Employees on the Customer Collaboration platform.** Employees

authenticate through ACME’s internal identity service, not OAuth. The PDP
enhances its authentication context with HR and Finance data via internal

APIs. Device posture is confirmed by the laptop’s posture client using a
short-lived signed token that accompanies each request. Finance may

also provide spending or contract limits for employees managing
customer accounts.

**Employees on internal engineering tools.** The most demanding use
case is production deployment: The token carries employee identity and

device trust, but the PDP must also confirm in real time that the engineer
is on call by consulting PagerDuty. Here, caching is aggressive but short
lived: on-call status might be cached for minutes, while HR role data is
refreshed daily.

These examples show why context is as important as policy. The correct set of signals,
delivered in the right way and with the right freshness, makes authorization reliable. The

wrong choices—stale tokens, unverifiable claims, or missing data—leave policies toothless.
The rest of this chapter explores how organizations collect, deliver, and normalize trust

signals so that policies can do their job.

WHAT ARE TRUST SIGNALS?

At ACME, every authorization decision relies on more than just identity. A customer’s

request to view a document or an engineer’s attempt to deploy code also provides
signals that indicate the trustworthiness of that request. These trust signals give

policies the context they need to decide whether an action should be permitted.

Some signals describe who is acting—such as identity, employment status, or on-call

role. Others show what they’re using or how they’re behaving. Together, these form
a confidence profile for each request.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

254

These are some common examples:

**Device posture** —reported by an endpoint client or mobile device
manager; indicates whether the laptop is encrypted, patched, or

compliant.
**Risk score** —generated by a fraud or threat detection service that

evaluates behavior or login patterns.
**Geolocation and network context** —based on IP, GPS, or VPN data—

to flag unusual access.
**Session assurance** —indications from authentication systems showing

whether MFA was used or when a session was last validated.
**Operational status** —feeds from systems such as PagerDuty or

change management tools that reflect incident or deployment
conditions.

These signals originate from multiple sources. As we’ll see later in this chapter, some
travel with the access token—like device-posture attestations—while others come

through APIs or event streams. The Policy Information Point (PIP) collects, verifies,
and normalizes them so policies are evaluated against trustworthy, current context.

#### 12.1 Policy Information Points (PIPs)

In the abstract architecture of authorization introduced in figure 12.1, the Policy
Information Point (PIP) appeared as a neat box feeding the PDP. That diagram captured the

idea that policies rely on external data, but it concealed just how complex the real picture
is. As shown in the figure, what looks like a single component in the abstract model is, in

practice, a web of heterogeneous sources that must be integrated, secured, and kept fresh.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

255

Figure 12.1 Policy Information Points: abstract vs. reality. Left: the abstract authorization architecture shows

a single Policy Information Point (PIP) feeding data to the Policy Decision Point (PDP). Right: in practice, the

PIP represents many sources—HR, Finance, authentication systems, device posture clients, external systems,

and so on—all connected through APIs, tokens, and caches to deliver the trust signals that policies need.

Some signals come from internal systems: HR provides employment status, Finance

supplies spending authority, IT contributes device inventories, and directories list group
memberships. Others come from external providers, such as identity verification services,

fraud detection engines, or SaaS partners that share risk scores. Still others are generated
on the device itself, like a posture client that attests to whether the laptop is encrypted or

patched.

The way these sources are handled depends heavily on the use case. Returning to the

three-dimensional choice space introduced earlier, PIPs are the machinery that map those
choices into reality:

Which signals should be pulled in for this request?
How are they delivered—embedded in a token, fetched from an API,

streamed via an event bus?
How fresh do they need to be, and how long can they be cached?

At ACME, this diversity is clearly visible. The Customer Collaboration platform connects with
the customer information system to verify account status, while also consuming OAuth

tokens from the identity provider that contain customer ID and role. When employees use
the same platform, the PIP layer retrieves additional data from HR (employment status)

and Finance (authorization limits) and validates a device-posture token that accompanies
the access request, issued by the posture client on the device. In the engineering

deployment tool, the PIP must also contact PagerDuty to check if the requesting engineer is
on call.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

256

From the perspective of the PDP, all of this comes together as a coherent set of

attributes and relationships used in policy evaluation. But under the hood, the PIP is less a
single component than an ecosystem of integrations. Each contributes pieces of the context

puzzle, and the quality of authorization depends on how well those pieces are assembled,
secured, and kept fresh.

#### 12.2 Entities: principals and resources

Policy Information Points collect raw data, but policies need that data in a structured form.

To evaluate a request, a Policy Decision Point (PDP) must be able to reason about who is
acting (the principal), what they want to access (the resource), and what attributes or

relationships tie them together. These structured representations— _entities_ —are the
foundation of authorization context.

An entity is more than a record; it’s a model of a principal or resource meaningful to
policy. A principal might be an employee, customer, or service account. A resource could be

a document, project, or financial record. Each entity carries attributes such as role,
department, owner, or classification, and often relationships that link it to others: owns,

manages, collaborates with.

[Policies depend on these entities to connect rules to reality. Without a consistent](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-12?potentialInternalRefId=40---book-markup-container)

representation, signals from PIPs can’t be meaningfully combined. HR might describe an
employee as “active,” Finance as “enabled,” and IT as “provisioned.” Unless those

differences are normalized into a shared schema, the PDP can’t reliably evaluate a policy
condition like:

when { principal.employmentStatus == "active" }

In theory, the PDP is simply a decision engine that takes a request and context and returns
permit or deny. In practice, it usually includes pre-processing logic that gathers and formats

the input data.

As shown in figure 12.2, the PDP typically consists of two parts: a lightweight layer of

application logic that collects and shapes entities and a policy evaluation engine—such as
Cedar—that makes the actual decision. The preprocessing layer retrieves entities and

attributes from PIPs, transforms them into the appropriate schema for policy evaluation,
and builds the Cedar request object with the principal, action, resource, and context.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

257

Figure 12.2 Inside the Policy Decision Point. The PDP includes more than just a policy engine. At ACME, a

signal-processing layer collects data from various systems—HR, Finance, the Customer Authentication

Service, device posture clients, and external services like PagerDuty—and organizes it into well-formed

entities for evaluation by the Cedar engine. The PDP then provides a decision to the PEP after policies are

assessed against the collected context.

At ACME, this logic originally grew independently within each platform. The Customer

Collaboration platform used its own entity model for customers and employees, while the
engineering deployment tool defined a different schema optimized for operational use. Each

PDP wrapped the Cedar evaluator with custom code that translated data from internal
systems, device posture, and external service calls into its own entity structure. The

approach worked, but it required maintaining multiple, inconsistent models and writing
separate policies for each system.

These inconsistencies caused friction. A policy that depended on `resource.owner` in the

collaboration platform might use `resource.createdBy` in the deployment tool. Employees

who switched teams sometimes triggered unexpected denials because entity data was
formatted differently across systems.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

258

This experience led ACME to recognize the importance of a consistent way to represent

entities. The company started designing a normalization layer—an enterprise PIP that would
gather data from all internal and external sources, apply a unified schema, and deliver well
formed entities to each PDP. Later in this chapter, we’ll return to that decision in the section
on authorization context normalization, where we’ll see how it simplified PDP logic,

improved policy consistency, and made ACME’s overall authorization system more reliable.

#### 12.3 Signals and their delivery

Once entities are defined, the next step is gathering the data that populates them. The
signals that populate entity attributes—who someone is, what they’re trying to access, what

device they’re using, and what risk level they represent—come from many directions. These
_trust signals_ are essential for establishing the authorization context.

Different use cases draw from different combinations of signals, delivery methods, and
freshness levels. Taken together, these signals determine how the system assembles

authorization context at runtime.

12.3.1 What the signals are

At a minimum, every authorization system needs identifiers for principals and resources,

but most real systems use richer signals. Common examples include:

Identity and role details from directories or HR systems.

Device posture from endpoint clients or mobile device managers.
Account status and entitlements from customer or subscription

databases.
Environmental and risk data, such as location, time of day, or fraud

scores.
Operational status signals, such as an on-call flag or clearance level.

Which signals matter depends on the risk and the sensitivity of the decision. Viewing a
document may depend solely on role and ownership. Deploying to production may also

depend on device trust, time of day, and on-call status.

12.3.2 How signals are delivered

Signals can be transmitted through various methods, and the way they are delivered

influences both effectiveness and confidence.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

259

**Token-based signals.** Some information is transmitted within tokens.

Often in OAuth or OIDC ID tokens, but some services create custom JWTs
to convey system-specific signals. These tokens carry signed claims about

identity, device status, or authentication context. The benefit is speed:
once the token is issued, the PDP doesn’t need to query external

systems. One risk is staleness if a claim changes before the token
expires. Another is that tokens can be stolen and reused, so managing

their expiration is critical to mitigate that risk.
**Query-based signals** . Other signals are retrieved dynamically at

decision time through APIs or databases. This guarantees freshness but
introduces latency and dependencies on external systems.

**Hybrid models** . Most organizations use a combination. Tokens provide a
consistent identity and authentication context, while dynamic queries

retrieve variable data such as risk scores or operational status.

The right mix depends on the system’s requirements. Low-risk SaaS platforms usually

depend solely on tokens. High-security infrastructure generally prefers hybrids.

12.3.3 ACME’s delivery choices

At ACME, these tradeoffs are evident across its platforms:

The Customer Collaboration platform mainly depends on token-based
signals for customers. OAuth tokens from the customer authentication

service include claims for principal ID, role, and device trust (from the
embedded posture client). When the principal is a customer, extra data—

such as account status or fraud score—is fetched from ACME’s customer
database during login and stored for the duration of the token.

For employees using the same platform, the PDP enhances token data
with HR attributes (such as employment status and department) and

Finance signals (such as authorization limits). The PIP gathers this
information from internal APIs during login or periodically through

background synchronization.
The engineering deployment tool uses a hybrid approach. The token

maintains employee identity and device trust, while the PDP queries
PagerDuty in real time to verify that the engineer is currently on call. This

reduces the risk of outdated access decisions while keeping most data
local.

Each of these options represents a point in the three-dimensional space introduced earlier:

Which signals are required?

How are they delivered?
How fresh should they be?

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

260

The next section examines the third dimension in detail—freshness, caching, and revocation

—and how systems like ACME balance latency with assurance.

#### 12.4 Freshness, caching, and revocation

The third dimension in the authorization context choice space is freshness: How current a
signal needs to be when a policy decision is made. Authorization decisions are only as

reliable as the data they rely on. If a signal becomes stale, policies might grant access long
after the underlying facts have changed.

Every organization must balance latency, load, and assurance when deciding how fresh
its signals need to be. The ideal is instantaneous accuracy, but real systems must manage

performance and availability constraints.

12.4.1 The freshness spectrum

Signal freshness falls along a spectrum:

Embedded signals are fixed at the time of token issuance and valid until
the token expires. They have zero runtime latency but can grow stale

quickly.
Cached signals are fetched periodically and reused for a set interval. They

balance performance with acceptable staleness for data that rarely
changes.

Live signals are retrieved in real time for each decision, ensuring accuracy
but adding latency and dependency on the upstream system.

Each signal source and delivery method defines its own point on this spectrum. Tokens from
an identity provider might be trusted for an hour. HR data might be synced nightly. A risk

engine might provide scores that expire in minutes.

12.4.2 Caching strategies

Caching is unavoidable in distributed authorization architectures. The key question is how

long to cache and where.

**At the PDP.** Many systems cache signal values or assembled entities

within the PDP to avoid repeated lookups. This reduces latency but
requires careful invalidation logic.

**At the PIP.** Centralizing caches in PIPs lets multiple PDPs share
consistent context, but increases the blast radius if the cache is stale.

**At the edge or client.** Some applications cache tokens or context locally
for offline or low-latency operation. This can be effective for low-risk data

but introduces exposure if the device is compromised.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

261

Short cache durations improve accuracy but increase load on upstream systems. Long

durations improve performance, but risk outdated data. Systems often combine multiple
cache tiers with differing time-to-live (TTL) values.

12.4.3 Revocation and signal updates

Revocation mechanisms help shorten the window of exposure between an event and its
reflection in policy decisions. Tokens can be invalidated via revocation lists or introspection

endpoints. Dynamic signals—such as device posture or risk level—can be pushed to the PDP
or PIP through message queues or publish/subscribe systems, updating cached context

proactively.

The goal is to propagate change, not just wait for expiration. The faster an authorization

system reacts to new information, the more trustworthy its decisions.

12.4.4 ACME’s approach to freshness

ACME’s different platforms clearly illustrate these tradeoffs.

Customers on the Customer Collaboration platform authenticate through
ACME’s customer information system, which issues OAuth tokens that are

valid for one hour. Each token contains stable claims—such as customer
ID and role—while dynamic data, like account status or fraud score, is

retrieved from the customer database at login and refreshed every few
hours. This approach balances performance and reliability for daily

collaboration.
Employees on the Customer Collaboration platform authenticate through

ACME’s internal identity service rather than OAuth. The PDP enriches their
authentication context with HR and Finance data collected via internal

APIs. Device posture, however, is transmitted as a signed token issued by
the posture client on the employee’s laptop. This short-lived token asserts

that the device is compliant and up to date. It expires after fifteen
minutes and must be reissued by the client, ensuring that device trust

remains fresh even while HR and Finance data—cached daily—change far
less often. This blend provides timely assurance on device security

without overloading corporate systems.
Engineers using deployment tools face stricter checks. The engineering

environment requires the freshest signals. Employee identity and device
status are verified at login, while on-call status is checked in real time

from PagerDuty and cached for only a few minutes. If an engineer goes
off call, subsequent requests are immediately re-evaluated.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

262

Over time, ACME learned that the toughest part of maintaining freshness isn’t just setting

cache durations—it’s managing dependencies. A cached entity might combine attributes
with very different lifetimes. Employment status may change once a year, but device

posture can change hourly. ACME’s enterprise-level signal processing system, introduced
later in this chapter, handles these differences by tracking each signal’s source, TTL, and

validation method.

Freshness is never free. It involves balancing speed, reliability, and assurance. By

considering it as a key design dimension rather than an afterthought, organizations like
ACME can tune their authorization context to match the risk and performance needs of each

system.

#### 12.5 Transmission and integrity of signals

Trust signals are only as useful as they are trustworthy. Even after they’ve been gathered
from their sources, they must still travel securely from the systems that generate them to

the systems that use them. When a signal is corrupted or falsified in transit, the
consequences range from bad authorization decisions and user frustration to a direct path

for attackers to gain unauthorized access.

Signal transmission is the connective tissue of authorization context. Each hop—from the

originating system to the Policy Information Point (PIP), then to the Policy Decision Point
(PDP), and finally to the Policy Enforcement Point (PEP)—must maintain authenticity,

integrity, and confidentiality.

12.5.1 How signals move

Signals reach the PDP in several ways:

**Embedded in tokens.** Some signals, like device posture or
authentication context, are packaged as signed tokens that travel with

the access request. Their integrity is maintained through cryptographic
signatures and the verifier’s ability to validate them against a trusted

issuer.
**Queried via APIs.** Other signals are retrieved dynamically at decision

time from authoritative systems. These communications typically use TLS
for encryption and server authentication, and sometimes employ mutual

TLS for stronger assurance.
Delivered by sidecar agents or message buses. In modern microservice

environments, sidecar processes or internal message streams distribute
context updates—such as risk scores or revocation notices—to nearby

PDPs with minimal latency.

Each approach trades simplicity for greater control. Tokens are self-contained but remain

static. API calls are flexible but rely on network connectivity and upstream availability.
Streams or agents can deliver updates rapidly, but they need careful deployment and

ongoing monitoring.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

263

12.5.2 Protecting signals in transit

The security of signal transmission provides confidence in the signal's authenticity, integrity,
and confidentiality. Each system must be able to demonstrate provenance: where the signal

originated, who asserted it, and that it hasn’t been altered or exposed during transmission.

For direct, system-to-system calls within ACME, most integrations use TLS encryption for

confidentiality and mutual TLS (mTLS) where both endpoints authenticate each other.
However, mTLS isn’t always practical—especially when integrating with SaaS platforms or

OAuth-based systems that rely on bearer tokens. In those cases, signed tokens provide
verifiable provenance.

[A signed token includes a cryptographic signature from the issuing system—for example,](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-12?potentialInternalRefId=112---book-markup-container)
the posture client on an employee’s laptop or ACME’s customer authentication service.

When the Policy Decision Point (PDP) verifies this signature against a known public key, it
increases confidence in the token’s authenticity and confirms its contents haven’t been

tampered with. This reassurance enables systems to exchange context securely, even if
mutual authentication at the transport layer isn’t possible.

[The key is that the PDP can always show where each signal originated and that it arrived](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-12?potentialInternalRefId=113---book-markup-container)
unaltered. Provenance, not blind trust, is what gives the authorization system confidence in

the data it uses for policy evaluation.

12.5.3 Limiting signal scope

Preserving confidentiality means limiting how far signals travel and ensuring each system
sees only the data it needs. Currently, ACME’s various integrations each decide which

attributes to pull and store for their own purposes. The Customer Collaboration platform
requests HR and Finance data relevant to document access; the engineering deployment

tool queries PagerDuty and device posture status. ACME lacks corporate guidance on which
attributes each PDP should access. Each integration makes its own decision.

That autonomy works in the short term but introduces inconsistency and risk. Some
systems may gather more data than necessary, others less, and some may retain context

longer than intended. These differences eventually led ACME to develop a unified enterprise
PIP and normalization layer, discussed later in this chapter, to standardize which signals are

collected, how they’re transmitted, and who can access them.

[As ACME found out, signal delivery isn’t just a technical detail—it’s a crucial part of the](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-12?potentialInternalRefId=117---book-markup-container)

trust model. The authorization system must be able to verify that every piece of data used
in a decision comes from a reliable source and hasn't been changed. If policy is the logic

behind authorization, then secure transmission is its nervous system: it delivers the context
that makes authorization decisions possible.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

264

#### 12.6 Authorization context normalization

By this point, ACME had built several working authorization systems. Each had its own

custom design. The Customer Collaboration platform, the Finance tools, and the
engineering deployment environment all used Cedar for policy evaluation, but each defined

entities differently, cached signals on its own schedule, and decided independently which
attributes to fetch and store.

This worked until it didn’t. Policies that seemed similar on paper acted differently in
practice because the context behind them wasn’t consistent. For example, two systems

might both try to express the same intent: allow employees who are currently active to
access internal resources. In Cedar, that policy might look like this:

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

265

permit (

principal,

action,

resource

)

when { principal.employmentStatus == "active" };

But not every system used the same vocabulary. In one PDP, HR data represented active

employees as `active`, while another labeled them `enabled` . Even though the policy logic

was identical, its evaluation could produce different results simply because the underlying

entity data wasn’t normalized. Debugging access decisions became tedious, and engineers
spent more time reconciling data differences than writing policies.

To fix this, ACME’s identity team began designing an enterprise Policy Information Point
(PIP), a centralized signal normalization layer that would gather signals from all relevant

systems, apply a common schema, and deliver normalized entities to every PDP.

12.6.1 The normalization layer

The normalization layer performs three main functions:

1. **Collect signals from various sources.** It connects with HR, Finance,
device management, the customer information system, and external

services like PagerDuty. Each connection specifies how signals are
collected, how current they need to be, and how their authenticity and

provenance are verified.
2. **Map data into a consistent schema.** Raw attributes are converted into

standard fields— `employmentStatus`, `deviceTrustLevel`, `onCall`,

`accountTier` —ensuring that the same policy expression yields the same

result across systems.
3. Assemble entity data for policy evaluation. The normalization layer

returns normalized entities and attributes (principal record, resource
record, relationships, and derived/contextual signals) via an API. The PDP

then constructs the Cedar request—principal, action, resource identifiers,
plus the context—and passes it to the evaluator.

The result isn’t a single monolithic service but a shared context layer that uses a library and
API used across ACME’s platforms. Each PDP can request the entities it needs, confident

that the underlying data will follow the same structure and freshness rules as every other
system.

Some signals, like device posture, travel with the request as signed tokens issued by the
device itself. Others—such as HR status or account limits—flow through the enterprise PIP.

In some cases, the PIP allows ACME to simplify tokens to an identifier and scopes, with
richer attributes resolved at evaluation time. Figure 12.3 illustrates how these sources

come together in ACME’s architecture.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

266

Figure 12.3 ACME’s normalization architecture. Before normalization (top), each PDP integrated directly with

HR, Finance, authentication, and operational systems (e.g., PagerDuty, ticketing), each with custom schemas

and caches. After normalization (bottom), a shared signal-normalization layer aggregates and standardizes

those feeds, delivering consistent context to all PDPs. Device posture arrives separately as a signed token on

each access request and is verified alongside the normalized data. This hybrid model keeps tokens minimal

(identifier + scopes) while preserving rich, consistent context for authorization decisions.

This architecture marked a turning point for ACME: signal normalization changed
authorization from a collection of system-specific integrations into a unified, organization
wide service for providing trusted context.

12.6.2 Benefits of normalization

The impact was immediate. Policy authors could now reuse rules across systems because

the underlying entity structure was consistent. Caching strategies became predictable, with
time-to-live values attached to each signal type. Audit logs clearly showed where each

piece of context originated, when it was last updated, and which system asserted it.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

267

Normalization also lowered data exposure. Instead of each PDP retrieving its own set of

attributes, the enterprise PIP controlled the signal scope, providing only the data relevant
to a specific policy request. This enhanced confidentiality and removed redundant data

storage across applications.

[Normalization also enhanced signal transmission security. With a single enterprise PIP](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-12?potentialInternalRefId=142---book-markup-container)

managing all outbound and inbound context, every signal followed the same pattern of
encryption, signing, and verification. This uniformity made it easier to verify provenance,

streamlined audits, and lowered the risk of configuration drift that could expose data or
compromise integrity.

[Normalization also accelerated the adoption of fine-grained authorization across ACME.](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-12?potentialInternalRefId=143---book-markup-container)
Before the enterprise PIP, each team that wanted to implement policy-based access control

had to create its own data connectors and caching logic. With the normalization layer in
place, a shared library provided the same normalized context API to all departments. Any

system could connect with the organization’s authorization infrastructure simply by linking
the library and requesting the context it needed. This lowered development effort,

promoted consistent policy design, and helped fine-grained authorization spread rapidly
throughout ACME.

12.6.3 Extending SSF inside the organization

As ACME refined its normalization layer, the team noticed similarities between its internal
signaling issues and the aims of the Shared Signals Framework (SSF). SSF’s event-driven

approach—where systems subscribe to updates about changes instead of polling for them—
presented an appealing pattern for sharing context across ACME’s platforms.

By adopting SSF-like semantics internally, ACME could use a single library to manage
both inbound and outbound updates consistently. HR could publish employment status

changes, the device service could send posture updates, and PDPs could subscribe to the
events they care about. Each message would be signed, timestamped, and delivered

through a uniform channel, providing the same assurances of provenance and integrity that
SSF offers across organizational boundaries.

[This internal use of the SSF model further streamlined ACME’s enterprise PIP. It changed](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-12?potentialInternalRefId=147---book-markup-container)
how context is shared by using an event bus instead of custom API calls, offering a

consistent way to deliver reliable, verifiable signals wherever they are needed.

12.6.4 The broader lesson

ACME’s experience shows that normalization acts as a link between policy creation and

dependable enforcement. Policies can’t be consistent if their inputs aren’t, and they can’t
scale if each team has to build its own context system. By centralizing the work of

collecting, verifying, and structuring context, the identity team transformed authorization
data into a shared enterprise service, one that minimized engineering overhead and sped

up the adoption of fine-grained authorization across the organization.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

268

Normalization doesn’t make policies smarter; it makes them more trustworthy. A clear

schema and dependable signal processing give decision engines the ability to evaluate
policies accurately, no matter where or how they’re deployed.

#### 12.7 Putting it all together

Dynamic authorization depends on context, and context depends on signals that are

accurate, secure, and well-structured. Over the course of this chapter, we’ve seen how
ACME learned that collecting signals is only half the challenge—making them consistent,

verifiable, and usable is what turns authorization into a dependable service.

Each dimension of the three-dimensional choice space—the signals themselves, how

they’re delivered, and how fresh they are—affects the assurance and performance of every
authorization decision. Signals define what the system knows; delivery determines how

that information travels; and freshness defines how long it can be trusted.

[ACME’s systems illustrate how different contexts demand different trade-offs:](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-12?potentialInternalRefId=154---book-markup-container)

The Customer Collaboration platform relies primarily on token-based
signals, favoring performance over immediacy.

Employees on that same platform use richer context that combines
tokens, device-trust attestations, and cached internal data.

The engineering deployment tools demand the freshest context—realtime checks for on-call status, device posture, and operational readiness.

Later, in Chapter 15, we’ll revisit how an organization’s security architecture and zero-trust
strategy shape these same design choices. Assurance requirements, risk appetite, and

governance policies all influence where each system can safely operate within this threedimensional space. Table 12.1 summarizes how each of these systems occupies a distinct

point in the choice space, balancing accuracy, latency, and complexity.

#### 12.8 Summary

Policies are only as good as their signals; the three design dimensions are

what signals are used, how they are delivered, and how fresh they are.
Real-world PIPs use signals from multiple sources. PDPs feature

lightweight processing before the policy engine.
Token, query, and hybrid delivery each trade off latency, availability, and

assurance.
Freshness is a first-class design choice. Revocation and event-driven

signal delivery reduce exposure windows.
Transmission essentials: provenance, signatures, and scoped sharing

foster confidence in authenticity, integrity, and confidentiality.
Normalization (enterprise PIP + shared schema) produces consistent

decisions, safer transmission, quicker adoption, and reduced engineering
costs.

ACME’s final architecture uses a hybrid model: minimal tokens with
device-based attestations plus the normalized background context.

## Using policy engines with existing systems

This chapter covers

The evolution of ACME’s internal Customer Collaboration platform into the multitenant Customer Collaboration Cloud (C³)

How a multi-layer authorization model differentiates between platform and tenant
responsibilities

Patterns for deploying policy enforcement points at the gateway, service, and UI
levels.

How the UI uses graph queries and partial evaluation to answer “who or what can
access?” questions

Using a multi-layered policy architecture to allow secure tenant customization

Authorization rarely starts from scratch. Most organizations already have applications, APIs,
and data services with authorization embedded in their code or configuration. When

organizations adopt a policy engine, the focus isn’t on how to start but rather on how to
adapt without disrupting existing functions. Integration, rather than invention, presents the

true challenge.

ACME Corporation faced this challenge when it transformed its internal Customer

Collaboration platform into a commercial SaaS product: the Customer Collaboration Cloud
(C³). The original system was built for internal use, allowing engineers and account

managers to share project documents with trusted customers. Over time, its access
controls became scattered across controllers, stored procedures, and service endpoints,

growing organically. Each team implemented its own version of who-can-see-what, and
adding a new rule meant changing the application code in several places.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

272

[Now that ACME plans to sell the platform to external customers, these shortcuts are no](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-13?potentialInternalRefId=8---book-markup-container)

longer sufficient. Each tenant must have its own workspace, administrators, and policies for
sharing and delegation. What was once a single trusted environment must become

hundreds of isolated ones. ACME’s engineers need a way to enforce consistent, auditable
rules without rewriting every service while giving customers limited control over their

access policies.

[This chapter explores how ACME integrated a policy engine into an existing system. We’ll](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-13?potentialInternalRefId=9---book-markup-container)

follow their shift from hard-coded checks to externalized authorization, showing how Cedar
policies seamlessly fit into an architecture made up of gateways, microservices, and identity

providers. Throughout, we’ll examine practical integration patterns, multi-tenant
governance, and lessons learned from ACME’s deployment.

[By the end of the chapter, you’ll see that adopting a policy engine isn’t a switch you flip](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-13?potentialInternalRefId=10---book-markup-container)
all at once. Instead, it's a gradual process of externalizing decisions, connecting data

sources, and aligning policy with identity. ACME’s story shows how dynamic authorization
can grow within the systems you already use, one enforcement point at a time.

WE’RE NOT CHANGING HOW SHARING WORKS

Section 6.1, “Relationship-based access control,” introduced the ReBAC model ACME
used to control sharing inside the Customer Collaboration platform. That remains

unchanged.

C³’s authorization functions on two separate levels:

**1. Platform-level authorization (managed by ACME)**

This layer governs how the Customer Collaboration Cloud itself functions as a multi
tenant service. It’s responsible for enforcing tenant isolation, routing requests to the
correct entity and policy namespace, and applying global governance policies such as

device trust, compliance, and export controls.

Every authorization request passes through this layer first, ensuring that a principal

from one tenant can’t reach into another and that every decision is evaluated within
the right tenant context.

**2. Tenant-level authorization (managed by customers)**

Inside each tenant, C³ uses Relationship-Based Access Control (ReBAC) to manage

document sharing and collaboration. These rules are identical across tenants; what
differs is each tenant’s data—their relationship graph of who owns, edits, or views

what—and the templates they can choose from to adjust sharing behavior (for
example, allowing external viewers or restricting delegated access).

Here’s a simplified version of the ReBAC policy that governs sharing within a tenant:
