#### 13.1 From internal tool to external service: ACME’s next chapter

The Customer Collaboration platform began as an internal workspace where ACME’s
engineers, account managers, and customer success teams could securely share

documents with external partners. Internally, it was straightforward: every employee
authenticated through ACME’s corporate identity provider, and customers used OAuth-based

links connected to their projects. The platform’s sharing model—based on a small
relationship graph of owners, editors, and viewers—fits neatly within ACME’s internal

network and trust assumptions.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

274

As the tool gained popularity, customers started requesting more control: their own

administrators, more detailed access levels, and private workspaces separate from ACME’s
staff. The engineering leadership saw an opportunity to turn the internal tool into a

commercial product: the Customer Collaboration Cloud (C³). However, this required
rethinking the foundation. What had been a single-tenant service running under ACME’s

identity domain needed to become a multi-tenant platform capable of serving hundreds of
customer organizations, each with its own users, identity providers, and data boundaries.

[That transition forced ACME to face a truth familiar to any organization modernizing its](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-13?potentialInternalRefId=30---book-markup-container)
authorization system: what worked for a small, trusted group doesn’t scale as the group

grows. The internal version of the platform depended on implicit trust in ACME’s directory
and on informal checks scattered throughout the code. To operate as a shared cloud

service, C³ would need clear boundaries: strong separation between tenants, federated
identity for customer logins, and a common authorization layer capable of enforcing both

global and tenant-specific rules.

[C³’s engineers didn’t want to abandon the system’s successful relationship-based sharing](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-13?potentialInternalRefId=31---book-markup-container)

model. The ReBAC rules governing document sharing within each workspace still made
sense. The challenge was adding a new outer layer of authorization around that model, one

that managed multi-tenant isolation, identity federation, and policy governance. In other
words, they needed to externalize decisions into a policy engine that could enforce ACME’s

global rules while still allowing each tenant to control its own sharing relationships.

[Figure 13.1 illustrates how ACME’s authorization model developed as the Customer](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-13?potentialInternalRefId=32---book-markup-container)

Collaboration platform transformed into the multi-tenant Customer Collaboration Cloud
(C³).

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

275

Figure 13.1 Evolution of the Customer Collaboration platform: The internal Customer Collaboration Platform

(top) is compared with the multi-tenant Customer Collaboration Cloud (C³) (bottom).

The upper diagram depicts the original single-tenant setup: one identity source, embedded
authorization checks, and an in-app ReBAC engine. The lower diagram shows how C³

divides responsibilities into two layers of policy evaluation. A centralized C³ PDP manages
platform access control, while each tenant’s Sharing PDP evaluates ReBAC policies within its

own workspace.

ONE STACK OR TWO?

Readers familiar with policy engines might envision a simpler architecture than the

one shown in Figure 13.1, one with a single PEP and PDP handling all authorization
decisions across the platform. In such a design, the platform would use one policy

engine that loads data for each tenant: each tenant’s policy store and relationship
graph would be selected dynamically based on the `tenant_id` included in the

request. The PDP would evaluate both platform and tenant policies in a single call,
returning a single decision to the enforcement point.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

276

That model is entirely feasible. In fact, many production systems evolve to a unified

policy layer once the boundaries and trust assumptions are well understood. It
reduces network hops and simplifies caching because each request needs only one

evaluation.

For the Customer Collaboration Cloud, however, we’ve split the design into two

layers: a global PEP/PDP pair for ACME’s platform policies and tenant-specific
PEP/PDP pairs for ReBAC sharing. This separation makes the examples clear and

emphasizes the distinct responsibilities of each layer.

Platform authorization determines who can access the service and

enforces cross-tenant governance.
Tenant authorization specifies who can access resources within a

tenant and enforces ReBAC rules.

You can think of C³’s dual-layer model as an explanatory zoom-in: it divides what

could be one unified stack into two visible layers so that we can examine each in
detail.

#### 13.2 Understanding the starting point

The original Customer Collaboration platform worked well because everyone involved—
ACME employees and invited customers—shared a single trust boundary. Employees

authenticated through ACME’s internal identity provider, and customers logged in using
short-lived OAuth links tied to specific projects. This narrow scope kept security simple:

each request either came from an employee on a trusted device or from a preapproved
customer identity already linked to a project record.

Inside that boundary, the platform used a ReBAC engine—first introduced in Section 6.1
—to manage document sharing. Relationships such as owner, editor, and viewer were

stored as graph data and evaluated consistently by the collaboration service. Those rules
weren’t the problem; they defined how people worked together on documents and were

among the system’s best features.

[What wasn’t built for growth was the authorization system behind the platform itself: the](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-13?potentialInternalRefId=45---book-markup-container)

logic that determined who could sign in, which projects a customer could access, and what
administrative actions an employee could perform. All of that code assumed a single

organization—ACME—and was embedded in the application.

[The main way to enforce these boundaries was through the project ID. When a new](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-13?potentialInternalRefId=46---book-markup-container)

customer engagement started, ACME created a project record in its internal CRM; that
record’s auto-incrementing ID served as the link connecting everything else. Each

document, folder, and comment stored the same `project_id`, and external customer

accounts were provisioned with that ID as well. OAuth tokens for customer sessions also

carried it. In practice, `project_id` acted like a substitute for tenancy, even though it was

simply a database field shared across the system.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

277

[Authorization checks at the platform level depended solely on that value:](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-13?potentialInternalRefId=47---book-markup-container)

if request.user.company == "ACME" or request.user.project_id == project.id:

allow_access(project)

That approach worked as long as there was only one security domain. Every identity was in
ACME’s directory, every project belonged to ACME, and each customer login was ultimately

linked to an ACME account. However, it couldn’t scale beyond that boundary. Once ACME
considered turning this into a product that would onboard multiple organizations, each with

their own set of customers, those assumptions broke down:

No tenant isolation: all data resides in the same namespace.

Inflexible identity: users outside ACME’s directory needed custom
workarounds.

Duplicate logic: each service re-implemented its own boundary checks.
Opaque policy: no centralized location to audit or reason about access

decisions.

The ReBAC sharing model from Section 6.1 remains the core of collaboration within each

tenant, but the surrounding enforcement logic required a complete redesign. To turn the
Customer Collaboration platform into the Customer Collaboration Cloud (C³), ACME had to

externalize the platform-level authorization that defines its overall security boundary,
separating authentication, tenancy, and policy evaluation into distinct, composable layers.

WHY EMBEDDED CHECKS DON’T SCALE

The Customer Collaboration Platform relied on code-level checks to enforce
boundaries. Each request handler verified that a principal either belonged to ACME or

was associated with a specific, current project. The system used project IDs as a
convenient shortcut, an integer that linked employees, customer accounts, and

documents. As long as ACME ran the platform internally, that system worked: one
namespace, one database, one source of truth.

But a project ID is not the same as a tenant boundary. It is simply a shared field that
is trusted implicitly across every part of the application. There was no central

authority verifying which IDs existed, no separate policy space for each project, and
no straightforward way to isolate data or identities. The code assumed that _project_

_equality_ meant authorization, a fragile assumption that held only because everyone
operated within ACME’s trust boundary.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

278

This tight coupling between application logic and access rules made the system

brittle. Adding a new rule required modifying the application code. Supporting
federation or new customer types involved writing exceptions. Because the logic was

spread across dozens of microservices, there was no central point to observe or
analyze access decisions. Auditing access was therefore impossible.

Externalizing authorization decisions makes the process dynamic. Rather than
hardcode who can do what, the application delegates those decisions to a policy

engine that evaluates policies based on current data, identity, and context at
runtime. This method converts _ad hoc_ checks into structured rules, provides true

tenant isolation, and enables governance to evolve without altering application code.

#### 13.3 Identity and tenancy foundation for C³

When ACME began designing the Customer Collaboration Cloud (C³), the first challenge

wasn’t creating new policies. Instead, it was building the identity and tenancy framework
that those policies would depend on. The internal platform had treated “who you are” and

“which project you belong to” as properties in the same database. In a multi-tenant
environment, this connection couldn’t work. Identity had to come from outside, and

tenancy had to become a clear, enforceable boundary.

13.3.1 From project IDs to tenants

The team’s initial step was to upgrade the old project ID, which had informally signified

customer workspaces, to an official tenant entity. Each tenant now has these three
elements:

A `tenant_id` that is globally unique `and` independent of any database key

Its own namespace for entities, relationships, and policies

A record in a new tenant directory that tracks metadata about ownership,
configuration, and identity providers

In C³, the tenant became a first-class concept in the authorization model. Every principal,
resource, and policy evaluation is connected to a tenant context. The `tenant_id,` which

previously existed quietly in SQL, now appears in every authorization request, ensuring that
identity, policy, and data are all consistently scoped.

13.3.2 Unified customer identity via OIDC

ACME decided early on that all customers—large or small—would authenticate using
OpenID Connect (OIDC). This provides a consistent model for every tenant while keeping

ACME’s internal identity system completely separate.

Two connection modes encompass all scenarios:

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

279

Federated OIDC: enterprise customers link their own identity provider,

managed through metadata stored in the tenant directory.
Hosted OIDC: smaller tenants without an IdP use an ACME-hosted OIDC

instance provisioned specifically for their tenant.

Both approaches generate OIDC tokens containing a small but useful set of claims:

`sub`, `iss`, `aud`, and `tenant_id` for identity and scoping

basic attributes such as email, name, and groups, that allow policies to

resolve the subject without requiring directory synchronization
optional claims like role or department for organizations that want finer

control

These values map to Cedar entities like `ACME::Employee::"{guid}"` or

`C3::CustomerUser::"{tenant_id}:{external_id}"` .

More dynamic or high-cardinality data—data with many possible distinct values like

entitlement tiers or support status—comes from Policy Information Points (PIPs) during
evaluation, keeping tokens small and reducing replication overhead.

13.3.3 Device posture for ACME employees

C³ only uses device-posture tokens for ACME employees. Since ACME manages its own fleet
of devices, each company device can provide a signed posture token to prove compliance.

The PEP verifies the posture token, decodes it and the employee’s OIDC token, and then
determines context for policy evaluation. Rather than forward raw tokens, the PEP sends

the PDP a normalized PARC request:

`principal` : mapped Cedar entity (for example, `ACME::Employee::"`

`{guid}"` )

`tenant_id` : from the employee’s token (ACME’s tenant)

`action` : the application verb

`resource` : the target of the action

`context` : device posture, posture source, time, JWT ID, IP address, and

so on

This allows the C³ PDP to enforce ACME’s zero-trust baseline, which requires a compliant
device for admin or cross-tenant operations, without exposing raw tokens outside the

enforcement tier or requiring posture checks on customer tenants.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

280

#### 13.4 Designing for externalized authorization

With the identity and tenancy foundations in place, ACME’s next challenge was operational:

how to shift authorization decisions from code to a unified, policy-driven workflow. The goal
was to externalize authorization while keeping it invisible. Policies should decide the

outcome, but applications shouldn’t need to know anything about Cedar or policy
evaluation.

In the internal Customer Collaboration platform, every service decided access locally.
Now, in C³, the Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) acts as the broker between the application

and the policy engine. The PEP verifies incoming tokens, collects contextual data, and sends
a normalized authorization request to a Policy Decision Point (PDP).

[Each request contains four key elements—principal, action, resource, and context—the](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-13?potentialInternalRefId=90---book-markup-container)
same components introduced in the PARC model in Chapter 7. These elements together

describe the “who, what, and under what conditions” of every authorization decision.
They’re summarized in Table 13.1.

[Table 13.1 Elements of a C³ authorization request](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-13?potentialInternalRefId=91---book-markup-container)

|Element|Example|Description / Source|
|---|---|---|
|principal|C3::CustomerUser::"t-412:alex"|The identity performing the<br>action, derived from the OIDC<br>token and mapped to a Cedar<br>entity|
|action|C3::"doc:share"|The operation being attempted,<br>inferred from the API route or<br>function call|
|resource|C3::Document::"doc-981"|The target object of the request,<br>identified by its canonical ID|
|context|tenant_id: "t-412",<br>device_posture: "compliant",<br>risk_score: 0.14|Environmental information<br>assembled by the PEP, including<br>tenant, device posture (for ACME<br>employees), and other runtime<br>signals|

The PEP sends this normalized request to the C³ PDP, which evaluates global governance

policies, checking tenant isolation, data residency, and, for ACME employees, device
compliance. If the global decision is `permit`, the request is forwarded to the appropriate

tenant PDP to evaluate ReBAC sharing policies within that tenant.

13.4.1 Platform and tenant PDPs

To make this multi-tenant model work in practice, ACME adopted a two-tier authorization
architecture.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

281

The C³ PDP enforces ACME’s platform policies, which are global rules

governing the cloud service itself. These include tenant isolation, data
residency, device compliance for ACME employees, and overall

governance controls.
The tenant PDPs evaluate ReBAC policies within each tenant’s

namespace. They decide who within a tenant can view, edit, or share
resources based on that tenant’s relationship graph.

As we saw in Figure 13.1, each authorization request passes through these two layers
sequentially. The C³ PDP evaluates first; if a request violates a global rule, it is denied

before the tenant PDP reviews it. Only when the request complies with ACME’s platform
policies is it forwarded to the appropriate tenant PDP for ReBAC evaluation.

13.4.2 Deployment options for tenant PDPs

ACME offers two options for the tenant PDP layer, customized to meet the customer’s
needs.

SHARED PDP CLUSTER

Most tenants use a shared, multi-tenant PDP cluster operated by ACME. The cluster
enforces a common set of ReBAC policies—the same collaboration rules introduced in

Section 6.1—that determine ownership, editing, and viewing permissions. Each evaluation
is scoped by `tenant_id`, ensuring isolation even though all tenants share the same policy

engine and logic. The relationship graph and entity data are tenant-specific and loaded
dynamically for each request, so the PDP applies the same policies to different data for

each tenant. This design provides consistent behavior while keeping operational costs low.

DEDICATED PDP INSTANCES

Premium tenants can provision a dedicated PDP instance, deployed in their preferred region

or private environment. These instances still inherit ACME’s global schema and governance
layer but allow controlled policy customization. Tenants can extend or override the standard

ReBAC policies using approved templates, enabling customers to enforce domain-based
sharing restrictions or custom retention rules.

Dedicated PDPs offer better isolation and greater flexibility while remaining compatible
with C³’s evaluation process. They are ideal for regulated industries or large enterprise

clients who need to integrate their own compliance controls directly into their decisionmaking process.

[By organizing authorization this way, C³ maintains a consistent architectural pattern—C³](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-13?potentialInternalRefId=105---book-markup-container)
PDP for platform governance and tenant PDPs for collaboration—while allowing each tenant

to choose how much control they want over their own policy environment.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

282

13.4.3 Authorization flow request

Every authorization decision in C³ passes through two layers of evaluation. The first layer
enforces ACME’s global governance policies, which protect the platform itself. The second

layer applies each tenant’s ReBAC policies, which control collaboration within that tenant’s
namespace. Together, they ensure that system-wide compliance and tenant-level sharing

function as one smooth process.

Figure 13.2 shows this flow, tracing how a single request moves from the PEP through

both PDP layers before a final decision is returned to the application.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

283

Figure 13.2 C³ authorization flow through global and tenant PEP/PDP layers

This figure traces a single authorization request moving through the C³ platform. The

numbered circles correspond to these steps:

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

284

1. **Initial request** . A user—either an ACME employee or a tenant customer

—initiates an API call from the client. The request includes an OIDC
access token (and, for ACME employees, a device-posture token).

2. **Normalized request** . The ACME Gateway, serving as the global PEP,
verifies both tokens, extracts identity and context, and builds a PARC
structured authorization request (principal, action, resource, context).
3. **Global decision** . The normalized request is sent to the C³ PDP, which

evaluates ACME’s global governance policies for tenant isolation, data
residency, and device compliance. The PDP returns either `permit` or

`forbid` .

4. **Enforce global policy** . If the decision is `forbid`, the ACME Gateway

blocks the request. If the decision is `permit`, the gateway forwards the

normalized request to the appropriate tenant PEP, scoped to that tenant’s

namespace. The decision is recorded in global audit logs
5. **Tenant request** . The tenant PEP receives the permitted request and

makes its own policy evaluation call to the tenant’s PDP (shared or
dedicated instance).

6. **Tenant decision** . The tenant PDP evaluates the tenant’s ReBAC policies
and responds with `permit` or `forbid` .

7. **Enforce tenant policy** . The tenant PEP enforces the result locally and
records it in the tenant audit log. A `forbid` decision ends the flow; a

`permit` proceeds to resource processing.

8. **Processing** . Authorized actions run within the tenant’s workspace. The

application code can assume that access has already been verified.
9. **Response** . The service provides the application’s response to the client.

Both global and tenant layers generate audit entries, ensuring every
decision is traceable.

Together, these steps show how each authorization in C³ passes through two enforcement
layers:

Global controls enforced by ACME’s PEP/PDP ensure platform-wide
governance

Tenant-specific ReBAC controls enforced within each tenant’s environment

The flow in Figure 13.2 illustrates how every authorization decision in C³ passes through

two enforcement layers, but it shows only a single request in motion. In practice, those
enforcement points aren’t limited to one location—they are distributed throughout the

platform. Some are at the API gateway, performing coarse-grained checks before requests
reach any tenant. Others are embedded within services, enforcing fine-grained actions on

documents, folders, and workspaces. The next section examines where these Policy
Enforcement Points are situated in the C³ stack, how they vary in scope, and how each

plays a role in maintaining a consistent policy evaluation pipeline.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

285

POLICY STORES AND POLICY IDS

As we saw in Chapter 7, externalized authorization systems rely on a Policy

Administration Point (PAP), the component responsible for creating, storing, and
distributing policies to the engines that evaluate them. In C³, the PAP takes the form

of a central policy store that manages both platform-wide and tenant-specific
policies.

Policies are logically separated by `tenant_id`, and the distribution service delivers

only the relevant bundle to each PDP, whether it’s the shared multi-tenant cluster or

a tenant’s dedicated instance. This method maintains strict data isolation while
streamlining policy management and ensuring consistency across the platform.

Logical separation in the policy store ensures that, while evaluation is centralized,
accountability stays per-tenant, maintaining both operational efficiency and clear

governance boundaries.

Each policy in the store has a unique `policy_id` that tracks it throughout its entire

lifecycle—from creation to evaluation and auditing. When a PEP receives a decision
from a PDP, that ID appears in the decision log, linking every action to the specific

policy text that generated it.

#### 13.5 Policy enforcement points in the stack

The request flow in Figure 13.2 shows what happens when a single authorization is
evaluated. In practice, C³ enforces policies at multiple points within its infrastructure. Each

Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) functions at a different scope, but all share the same
purpose: to standardize requests into the PARC structure and evaluate them through the

appropriate PDP. Collectively, they create a distributed enforcement network that covers the
entire C³ platform.

13.5.1 Global enforcement: the ACME Gateway

At the outer edge of the platform, global enforcement is managed using the ACME Gateway,
a distributed network of ingress and API gateways that collectively serve as the platform’s

global PEP. Instead of a single choke point, the gateway layer consists of multiple regional
clusters deployed near customer data to minimize latency. Each gateway enforces identical

policies and follows the same evaluation workflow.

When a request enters C³—whether from an ACME employee, a customer tenant, or an

automated integration—it first arrives at the gateway in its closest region. The gateway
carries out four coordinated steps:

1. **Authenticate and verify tokens** . It validates OIDC tokens for all callers
and posture tokens for ACME employees, caching trusted issuers and

keys for improved performance.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

286

2. **Resolve tenant context** . It identifies the target tenant using the token’s

`tenant_id` claim and directs the request to that tenant’s namespace.

3. **Evaluate global policy** . It calls the C³ PDP to apply platform-wide

governance policies such as tenant isolation, rate limits, data residency,
and device compliance for ACME staff.

4. **Normalize and forward** . If the global decision is `permit`, the gateway

generates a normalized PARC request and forwards it to the tenant’s PEP

for ReBAC evaluation.

Because gateways function as a coordinated mesh, policy decisions and tenant resolution

remain consistent across regions. Each gateway stores recent policy results and PDP
connections locally, ensuring quick enforcement even under high load. This distributed

architecture prevents any request—regardless of its origin—from crossing tenant
boundaries or bypassing ACME’s governance controls.

13.5.2 Tenant-level enforcement: collaboration services

After a request passes through the global gateway, enforcement continues within the
tenant’s environment. Each tenant’s workspace is hosted across a set of microservices

along with document, folder, and workspace APIs that together form the core of C³.

Each service has its own local PEP, either as a sidecar container or a shared SDK, that

intercepts calls to protected operations. These tenant PEPs perform three coordinated
functions:

1. **Translate application actions** . They map UI or API operations—such as
view, edit, or share—to the corresponding Cedar policy actions.

2. **Consult the tenant’s PDP** . Each PEP contacts the tenant’s PDP (either a
shared cluster or a dedicated instance) to evaluate ReBAC policies for that

tenant’s namespace.
3. **Enforce results locally** . The PEP uses the decision to ensure that

business logic executes only when authorized.

Because the PEPs operate alongside or within the services that manage the data, they can

cache entity graphs and policy scopes in memory, which reduces round-trips and latency.
Each PEP updates its cache asynchronously from the tenant’s entity store, ensuring ReBAC

decisions stay current without slowing user operations.

Together, the gateway PEPs at the platform edge and the tenant PEPs inside

collaboration services create a distributed enforcement mesh. This design enables C³ to
evaluate policies near the data they protect, scale horizontally as tenants grow, and ensure

consistent semantics across every layer of the platform.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

287

13.5.3 UI and client-side enforcement

Authorization also applies to the front end. The C³ UI uses the same policies as the tenant
PDPs to hide or disable unavailable actions. This prevents users from seeing Edit or Share

buttons that would later be denied by the backend.

This doesn’t replace backend enforcement but improves user experience and decreases

unnecessary request traffic.

HOW THE UI ANSWERS “WHO OR WHAT CAN ACCESS?” WITH CEDAR

The Customer Collaboration Cloud’s user interface often needs to display visibility
information such as lists of documents a person can view or the people who have

access to a document. These are discovery questions, not enforcement checks.
Cedar itself cannot perform searches; it evaluates access requests. To efficiently

generate these UI lists, C³ combines its ReBAC graph and policy engine in a threestage process:

**1. Get candidates from the relationship graph**

Use the tenant’s ReBAC graph, which records relationships like owner, editor, viewer,

member-of-team, and team-has-access-to-folder to quickly retrieve a set of
candidate principals or resources.

To find _docs this user can access,_ start at the principal node and move
outward along relationships to identify the resources they can reach.

To find _users who can access this doc,_ start at the resource node and
move outward along inbound relationships (from the resource’s

perspective) to identify connected principals.

The direction depends on where the query begins. Both searches use the same

relationship graph. The traversal direction just reverses depending on whether you’re
starting from a user or a document.

**2. Apply a policy scope prefilter**

Some policy conditions never change at runtime, such as document labels,

classification, or the tenant a resource belongs to.

When a policy is published, C³ _partially evaluates_ it using all the information that’s

already known (such as action and tenant). The result is a simplified predicate or
scope that describes which resources or principals could ever satisfy the policy.

Partial evaluation is an experimental feature in recent Cedar versions that returns
the simplified predicate, known as a policy residual. Chapter 17 explains how

residuals can be used to precompute policy fragments.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

288

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

289

Execute multiple evaluations as a batch to reduce network overhead

between the UI service and the PDP.
Page large result sets and cache short-lived `permit` outcomes keyed by

fields like `tenant_id`, principal, action, resource, or a scope hash.

Maintain both forward (principal → resources) and reverse (resource →

principals) indexes for efficient graph traversal.
For administrative questions like “Who can access this document?”,

perform the check using a dedicated auditor context. This context
reflects current runtime conditions—such as time, tenant, and policy

inputs—so the results reflect who would be permitted right now, not
just who appears in the relationship graph.

Keep the UI and backend aligned: the same decision API that hides
unavailable buttons in the interface also manages access in the service

layer.

Together, these practices ensure that search-driven features remain responsive while

ensuring that UI results accurately reflect live policy decisions. Users see only what
they can actually open or share if they click through, and ACME avoids keeping a

separate, outdated view of access visibility.

13.5.4 Consistency through shared components

All PEPs—gateway, service, and UI—use the same decision interface and schema
definitions. Each constructs a PARC-structured request using a common SDK and forwards

it to the appropriate PDP. This consistency guarantees that:

**Decisions are consistent** . The same request always yields the same

result, no matter where it’s enforced.
**Policies are centralized** . Changes to policy logic don’t need

modifications to PEP code.
**Auditing is centralized** . Each decision is logged in a shared system,

marked with the enforcement layer that caused it.

This shared architecture gives C³ what the original Customer Collaboration platform lacked:

a single, consistent process for every authorization decision. Whether a request comes from
the API gateway, a microservice, or the UI, it is assessed using the same schema, policies,

and data sources. Consistency isn’t just a design feature; it’s what enables C³ to
confidently scale authorization across hundreds of tenants without sacrificing clarity or

control.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

13.5.5 Operational trade-offs

Different enforcement points have varying strengths and weaknesses based on their
position in the stack. Table 13.2 summarizes how gateway, service, and UI enforcement

balance context, control, and complexity.

Table 13.2 Trade-offs among C³ enforcement layers

|Enforcement<br>layer|Typical scope|Strengths|Trade-offs|
|---|---|---|---|
|Gateway PEP|Coarse-<br>grained, global|Strong isolation; central<br>visibility; early rejection<br>of invalid requests|Limited contextual<br>depth; dependent on<br>token claims|
|Service PEPs|Fine-grained,<br>per-action|Rich context; low<br>latency; close to data<br>and relationships|Requires deeper service<br>integration and careful<br>cache management|
|UI enforcement|Client-side<br>experience|Improves responsiveness<br>and prevents futile<br>requests|Not security-critical, but<br>must stay aligned with<br>backend policies for a<br>good user experience|

Together, these layers form a defense-in-depth approach: the gateway enforces global
boundaries, service PEPs enforce data-level rules, and the UI reflects those decisions to the

user. The combination provides strong security, consistent behavior, and a smoother
experience across every tenant in C³. The final part of C³’s design is the policy architecture

itself: the framework that decides how policies are written, shared, and evaluated across
tenants. Externalizing authorization pays off only when the policies behind it are clear,

consistent, and safe to extend. For ACME, this meant defining not just where decisions
happen but also which policies apply at each layer. policies apply at each layer.

13.5.6 Three layers of policy

C³ organizes authorization logic into three layers, as depicted in Figure 13.3.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

291

Figure 13.3 Concentric policy layers in the C³ authorization model. Policies in C³ are organized by scope

rather than hierarchy. System policies form the outermost layer, overseeing the entire platform and its

automation. Inside this layer, application policies govern the Customer Collaboration Cloud service itself,

managing multi-tenant governance, data residency, and compliance. At their core, tenant policies handle

collaboration within each tenant’s workspace using ReBAC and approved templates.

The layers are evaluated from the outside in. System policies set the widest trust boundary,
application policies restrict how C³ functions as a service, and tenant policies oversee

collaboration within those boundaries:

1. **System policies** . Internal rules governing operational or administrative

actions within C³
2. **Global application policies** . Created and maintained by ACME to define

the platform’s trust boundaries

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

3. **Tenant policies.** Defined within each tenant’s namespace; govern

collaboration using ReBAC

Table 13.3 presents these three layers, outlines who manages them and their scope, and

provides an example of human-readable policy.

Table 13.3 Policy layers in the C³ authorization model

|Policy layer|Managed by|Typical scope|Example|
|---|---|---|---|
|System|ACME platform<br>engineering and<br>operations<br>teams|Entire platform and<br>supporting automation|Allow scheduled backup jobs<br>to read all tenant metadata.|
|Application|ACME C³<br>product team|The C³ application<br>itself; multi-tenant<br>governance|Only ACME employees with<br>compliant devices may<br>perform cross-tenant support<br>actions.|

Together, these layers define a nested hierarchy of scope. System policies form the

outermost boundary, governing the entire C³ platform and its automation. Inside that
boundary, application policies control how the Customer Collaboration Cloud operates as a

multi-tenant service. At the center, tenant policies manage collaboration within each
tenant’s namespace. System policies are authored by ACME’s platform engineering team

under the governance of the identity team, ensuring that even automated or administrative
actions—such as backups, monitoring, or replication—follow the same authorization and

audit standards as customer-initiated requests.

13.5.7 Shared schema and type safety

All three layers use a shared Cedar schema, ensuring that each policy speaks the same

language for entities, actions, and attributes:

Entities like `C3::Tenant, C3::CustomerUser`, and `C3::Document` are

defined once, so both application and tenant policies refer to the same
canonical types.

Actions ( `doc:view`, `doc:edit`, `doc:share` ) are registered centrally, but

tenants can implement policy templates that limit or expand these actions

within their own space. (See the sidebar “How a policy template shapes
tenant control” for additional details on how this works.)

Validation occurs before deployment: policies are type-checked against
the schema and simulated with representative data to ensure they won’t

cause runtime errors or unsafe overrides.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

293

This shared schema and templates ensure that a tenant’s customization never disrupts the

platform's underlying policy logic.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

294

13.5.8 Policy lifecycle and distribution

Policies follow a clear lifecycle:

1. **Authoring** . System and application policies are developed and reviewed

by ACME’s identity team or its delegates. Tenant policies are created by

product managers and engineers on the C <sup>3</sup> team. Customers modify

them using a restricted policy-management interface that only displays
approved templates and parameters.

2. **Validation** . Each policy is compiled and tested against the shared
schema before publishing.

3. **Distribution** . Policies are stored in ACME’s policy repository and
synchronized to PDPs—whether system-, application-, or tenant-level—

using a controlled distribution service.
4. **Audit and rollback** . All policy versions are kept, enabling rollbacks or

forensic audits if necessary.

Policy changes propagate automatically, but evaluation always occurs on the latest

validated version. For tenants with dedicated PDPs, updates can be staged and deployed
independently while still enforcing ACME’s global governance layer.

13.5.9 Governance and safety

C³ follows a straightforward rule of precedence:

Application policies take precedence over tenant policies when both apply

to the same action.
Tenant policies may restrict permissions but never broaden them beyond

global constraints.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

295

Cedar’s _forbid-by-default_ principle makes this easier to enforce. This ensures that a tenant

cannot, either accidentally or deliberately, violate ACME’s compliance obligations.

To ensure tenant flexibility remains secure, ACME offers a template library of common

patterns: internal-only sharing, external sharing by domain, delegated access, or timelimited links. Tenants select and configure these templates instead of writing custom Cedar

code. The templates generate valid Cedar policies within the tenant’s namespace,
maintaining both expressiveness and control.

13.5.10 Benefits of the layered model

This architecture clearly defines ACME's lines of responsibility.

ACME-designed system policies govern their zero-trust security posture

and platform automation.
ACME product managers and engineers design policies that govern the

platform.
Tenants govern their own collaboration policies within guardrails

established by the C <sup>3</sup> product team.

Since all layers share a single schema and policy set, they can be audited collectively. Policy
logs from the C³ PDP and tenant PDPs can be correlated by `policy_id` and `tenant_id`,

resulting in a unified record of both platform and tenant decisions.

C³’s approach builds directly on the policy lifecycle practices introduced earlier, in

Chapter 10, where ACME’s engineers learned to author, validate, and test policies as code.
The same principles—schema validation, version control, and automated testing—now

extend across tenants and policy layers.

[In the next chapter, we’ll examine how this layered structure integrates into ACME’s](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-13?potentialInternalRefId=237---book-markup-container)

broader governance framework: how policies are distributed, normalized, and monitored in
production; how context freshness and assurance are maintained; and how the platform

balances flexibility with oversight at scale.

#### 13.6 Case studies inside ACME

Once C³ moved into pilot deployments, ACME used several internal scenarios to test the
two-layer authorization model in production. These case studies demonstrate how system,

application, and tenant policies interact and show how externalized authorization simplifies
what previously required custom code.

13.6.1 Case 1: Cross-tenant legal review

When ACME’s legal department needs to audit documents across multiple customers, its
employees operate outside of any single tenant boundary:

1. The request comes from an ACME employee using a compliance tool
connected to C³’s API.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

296

2. The PEP in the gateway verifies the employee’s posture and identity

before calling the C³ PDP.
3. A system policy grants access exclusively to members of the legal team

using compliant devices.
4. The application policy verifies that the request is directed at a tenant

enrolled in the compliance program and restricts access to metadata, not
document contents.

Because these checks happen entirely within policy—without requiring special application
code—the legal review system can work consistently across all tenants while respecting

each tenant’s data residency and compliance boundaries.

13.6.2 Case 2: Support escalation

ACME’s support engineers sometimes require temporary access to diagnose problems

within a customer tenant:

1. A support engineer uses the support portal to request delegated access

by specifying the target tenant and time window.
2. The support portal obtains the necessary manager approval and, if

approved, issues a short-lived credential representing the approved
escalation.

3. When the engineer later uses that credential, the PEP receives the
request, validates the token, and normalizes it into a standard PARC

authorization request.
4. System policies review the request to verify that the credential is valid,

not expired, and restricted to the approved tenant and timeframe. If
these conditions are met, the request moves on to the tenant PDP, which

applies the tenant’s usual ReBAC rules.

This pattern follows the ABAC model in practice—time-limited, attribute-based access—

while keeping all decision logic in the policy rather than in the code. When the short-lived
credential expires, access automatically ends without manual cleanup.

13.6.3 Case 3: Custom collaboration template

One large customer wanted to allow outside contractors to edit documents without granting
full tenant membership. Using ACME’s policy-template system, the tenant administrator

created a customized rule:

Permit document sharing with principals whose email domain matches

“@example.com” and whose relationship is “collaborator.”

The resulting policy can be turned into a Cedar rule evaluated by the tenant’s dedicated

PDP. ACME’s application-layer policies still apply above it, ensuring collaboration links expire
after 30 days and that audit logs record all cross-tenant activity.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

297

This example shows how tenants can safely extend collaboration within the boundaries

controlled by ACME.

13.6.4 Case 4: Automated backup verification

C³’s nightly backup service runs as a non-interactive system process. Its requests do not go

through tenant PEPs directly but still need authorization.

1. The system PEP authenticates the backup agent using a service

credential.
2. The system PDP evaluates a policy that grants read-only access to

encrypted tenant metadata for audit and restore testing.
3. Since the schema is shared, the same policy syntax and logging pipeline

apply, even though the backup process runs outside the tenant scope.

This ensures that even platform automation remains subject to the same auditing and

governance framework as human users.

13.6.5 Lessons from the pilots

Across these pilots, ACME identified three recurring patterns:

**Layered enforcement works** . Platform-wide governance can coexist
with tenant autonomy when each policy layer has a well-defined scope.

**Templates allow secure flexibility** . Tenants can customize
collaboration rules without overriding global constraints.

**Auditing ties the layers together** . Because all PDPs use the same
schema and logging format, ACME can follow any decision from a user’s

action through the tenant PDP and back to the system policy that
governed it.

These internal pilots confirmed that externalized authorization wasn’t just theoretical: it
enabled C³ to operate securely across multiple trust boundaries using a single consistent

evaluation model.

APPLYING THESE PATTERNS OUTSIDE OF SAAS

Although C³ is presented as a multi-tenant SaaS platform, the authorization patterns

in this chapter are not exclusive to SaaS systems. The main idea is layered
authorization across multiple trust boundaries, not tenancy itself. In enterprise and

zero-trust environments, those boundaries often correspond to business units,
environments, or clearance domains rather than customers.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

298

ACME encountered this firsthand when it applied the same architecture internally.

Before C³ became a product, ACME used an ABAC-style model to manage access to
deployment tools and internal systems. The “global” policy layer enforced enterprise
wide requirements such as managed devices and on-call status, while applicationlevel policies controlled access to specific tools. When ACME later introduced tenant
aware sharing through ReBAC, those new policies fit within the same structure
instead of replacing it.

In both cases, the basic process is the same: policy decisions are externalized,
evaluated by PDPs using a shared schema, and enforced by PEPs close to the

protected resources. What changes is the form of the data—attributes in an ABAC
system, relationships in a ReBAC system—not the architecture that evaluates them.

#### 13.7 Putting lessons into practice

Transforming the Customer Collaboration platform into the Customer Collaboration Cloud
taught ACME more than just how to externalize authorization; it uncovered what makes a

policy-based architecture sustainable at scale. The patterns that worked for C³ apply to
nearly any system using a policy engine.

13.7.1 Key insights

The C³ pilot gave ACME a laboratory to test ideas that initially seemed abstract on paper.
By the time the system stabilized, a few insights had surfaced, patterns that transformed

early lessons into lasting architectural practices.

**Separation brings clarity** . Splitting authorization into separate layers—

system, application, and tenant—made ownership and troubleshooting
much simpler. Each layer enforces policies suitable for its trust boundary.

**Identity is the foundation** . Federated OIDC and a consistent tenant
model provided C³ with a reliable anchor for every policy decision.

Without clear identity boundaries, even elegant policies fail.
**Context needs to stay current** . Device posture, risk scores, and other

dynamic signals quickly become outdated. The PEP’s role is not only
enforcement but also assembling context.

**UI visibility is not enforcement** . The interface may use graph queries
and partial evaluation to display what a person could access, but the

backend still makes the final decision.
**Templates make customization safe** . Providing tenants with

structured policy templates offers flexibility without losing control.
Guardrails are as important as expressiveness.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

299

Together, these insights reveal that authorization isn’t just a subsystem—it’s an ecosystem.

When policy, identity, and context develop together, externalized authorization _shifts from_
_being merely a security requirement to a strategic advantage_ .

13.7.2 Integration checklist

Teams planning to integrate a policy engine into an existing system can use the following
steps as a guide. Table 13.4 summarizes the sequence ACME followed when building the

Customer Collaboration Cloud.

Table 13.4 Integration checklist for adopting a policy engine

|Step|What to establish|Why it matters|
|---|---|---|
|1. Map boundaries|Identify system, application,<br>and tenant scopes.|Clarifies which policies run<br>where and who owns them|
|2. Define the identity<br>model|Standardize how principals,<br>tenants, and resources are<br>represented.|Ensures every PDP can reason<br>over the same entities|
|3. Externalize<br>decisions|Move allow/deny logic from<br>code to policy evaluation|Enables consistency and<br>auditability|
|4. Place enforcement<br>points|Insert PEPs at gateways,<br>services, and (optionally) the<br>UI.|Keeps policy evaluation close to<br>data while preserving<br>performance|
|5. Establish the<br>schema|Create a shared Cedar schema<br>for all policy layers.|Guarantees type safety and<br>cross-layer compatibility|
|6. Support partial<br>evaluation|Precompute scopes for fast UI<br>search and discovery.|Improves responsiveness<br>without compromising<br>correctness|
|7. Implement logging<br>and versioning|Record every decision and track<br>policy versions.|Enables rollback, audit, and<br>long-term governance|

A mature integration doesn’t end with code changes; it depends on operational discipline.

Policies need ownership, testing, and monitoring just as any other production system does.

13.7.3 Looking ahead

C³’s development from an internal tool to a multi-tenant cloud platform demonstrates what

happens when authorization becomes a first-class part of system design. By separating
policy from code, ACME gained greater flexibility, better auditability, and a structure that

can adapt as new tenants, identities, and regulations emerge.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

300

The next challenge isn’t creating more policies; it’s effectively managing them. Policies

now exist across multiple PDPs, change hands among different owners, and rely on signals
that fluctuate constantly. In the next chapter, we’ll see how ACME formalizes that

management: defining who controls each policy layer, how signals are verified and
standardized, and how policy lifecycle management turns externalized authorization into a

daily operational practice.

#### 13.8 Summary

Converting an internal application into a multi-tenant service requires
rethinking authorization boundaries and data isolation.

A layered authorization model—system, application, and tenant—clarifies
ownership and separates trust domains.

A consistent identity and tenancy foundation supports policy evaluation
across both federated and hosted tenants.

Requests pass through global and tenant PEP/PDP pairs, following the
PARC model from enforcement to decision.

Policy enforcement points can operate at different levels—gateway,
service, and UI—each enhancing security and usability.

The UI leverages graph traversal, partial evaluation, and batch PDP
checks to efficiently address visibility questions.

A layered policy architecture and template system enables tenants to
customize collaboration securely within shared constraints.

ACME’s internal case studies show the effectiveness of layered
authorization in real-world operations.

An integration checklist now guides new systems joining ACME’s policy
engine architecture.

## Policy governance

This chapter covers

How to govern policies across teams and systems

The policy management lifecycle

The roles, artifacts, and structures that make governance effective

How Identity Governance and Administration (IGA) aligns with policy governance to
ensure consistent access assurance

Using governance to meet regulatory requirements and build organizational trust in
authorization decisions

When ACME first deployed Cedar as its policy engine, the engineering team celebrated what

seemed like the end of a long journey. Policies were versioned in Git, automatically tested,
and deployed to production alongside code. The company’s Customer Collaboration

platform could finally make consistent, auditable authorization decisions across tenants and
services. For a while, that was enough.

Then the problems started to multiply, not in the code itself but in the discussions
surrounding it. Two product teams maintained nearly identical policies with subtle

differences that no one could fully explain. The compliance team found that an old datasharing policy was still active long after the retention period it referenced had expired. A

new engineer, trying to resolve a support issue, discovered a temporary policy override that
had been in place for nine months. Each incident uncovered the same core issue: ACME had

mastered policy deployment but not policy governance.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

302

The identity team recognized that policies, like identities, go through lifecycles. Each

starts with a need—a new feature, regulation, or business process—but once established,
they develop their own momentum. Without clear ownership, review schedules, and

feedback mechanisms, policies amass technical debt just as software does. Even more
concerning, since authorization is a shared service that often involves multiple teams, a

single outdated rule can quietly weaken trust throughout the entire system.

[That realization prompted ACME to develop a policy governance framework, a structured](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-14?potentialInternalRefId=9---book-markup-container)

process for authoring, reviewing, deploying, and retiring authorization policies. Governance
turned out to be more about assurance than control, making sure that policy decisions are

traceable, explainable, and aligned with the company’s goals. Just as Identity Governance
and Administration (IGA) brought order to entitlements—defining who could request,

approve, and review access—policy governance brought order to the logic that interprets
those entitlements at runtime. Together, IGA and policy governance create a complete

feedback loop for managing both the inputs and rules of dynamic authorization. We’ll
discuss IGA and policy governance later in this chapter.

[This chapter examines how organizations like ACME progress from creating policies to](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-14?potentialInternalRefId=10---book-markup-container)
governing them. It traces the lifecycle of policies in a dynamic authorization environment,

showing how governance frameworks maintain trust and accountability across teams. It
also links the operational aspect of IGA—the management of people and entitlements—with

the policy side of authorization, where access decisions are made in real time. Together,
they create a continuous feedback loop that ensures authorization aligns with business

goals, meets regulations, and adapts to change.

#### 14.1 Why governance matters for authorization

Authorization systems make decisions continuously, often thousands of times per second.
Each decision results from a complex web of policies, data, and context, reflecting what the

organization believes to be true at that moment. Governance ensures these decisions
remain legitimate. It provides the enterprise with confidence that what the system decides

aligns with the organization's intentions.

At ACME, the disconnect between intent and implementation became clear only after the

policy engine was in full production. Policies had multiplied across teams, each tailored for a
specific service or use case. Though they made sense individually, together they showed no

overarching strategy. The company’s engineers could explain what a policy did, but not
always why it existed or who was responsible for maintaining it. Governance emerged as a

way to restore intent, reconnecting the technical logic of authorization with the
organizational purpose behind it.

[Figure 14.1 shows how this drift emerges. Organizational intent exists at the enterprise](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-14?potentialInternalRefId=14---book-markup-container)
level, but without governance, it is interpreted independently by each department. Over

time, policies lose clear ownership and fall out of step with one another, some becoming
orphaned, others overly restrictive, and still others misaligned with operational practice.

Governance restores alignment by reconnecting policies to shared intent, accountability,
and review.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

303

Figure 14.1 Policy drift without governance. When authorization policies are created and maintained

independently across teams, their connection to organizational intent weakens. Policies may become

orphaned, overly restrictive, or misaligned with operational realities, even when each policy appears correct

within its local context.

Governance matters because authorization is not just a technical control but an _expression_
_of institutional will_ . Policies turn principles like least privilege, fairness, or compliance into

executable code. Without governance, those principles can drift away. Over time, policies
become inconsistent, unenforceable, or outdated. This is the authorization equivalent of

identity sprawl: Decisions that once reflected deliberate choices now persist simply because
no one is responsible for them.

But governance does more than define ownership: It also oversees the controls
themselves. Modern authorization systems treat policies as code, which means they carry

all the risks and benefits of software engineering. Policy governance sets the technical
standards for how policies are written, tested, and deployed: enforcing code reviews,

schema validation, automated testing, and continuous integration. These practices ensure
that policies are not only correct in principle but also safe in operation. In this way,

governance spans both the human and the machine, aligning human intent with automated
enforcement.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

304

A mature governance framework transforms authorization from a routine task into a

managed discipline. It clarifies roles—such as policy authors, reviewers, approvers, and
access control coordinators—and assigns accountability for each stage of the policy

lifecycle. It establishes standards for policy quality and implements regular review cycles.
Additionally, it links human judgment with automated assurance by pairing decision logs

and testing pipelines with human oversight and policy attestation. In essence, governance
ensures that each policy decision can be traced back to a business rationale, a technical

control, and a designated owner.

[Policy governance also plays a crucial role in building trust and ensuring compliance.](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-14?potentialInternalRefId=19---book-markup-container)

Regulators, auditors, and partners increasingly expect organizations to show not only that
policies exist but also that they are actively governed. Logs, version histories, and review

records provide an evidence trail that links system behavior to deliberate governance
actions. For ACME, this was more than just a compliance requirement; it became a

competitive advantage: When customers asked how ACME protected their data, the
company could demonstrate both the policies that enforced access and the governance

processes that maintained those policies.

[Ultimately,](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-14?potentialInternalRefId=20---book-markup-container) governance enables authorization to evolve safely. New features,

integrations, and regulations will always create pressure to change access rules.
Governance offers the mechanism to make those changes intentionally, balancing agility

with assurance and keeping alignment between business goals and system behavior.

#### 14.2 The policy management lifecycle

Governance provides structure to authorization, but the policy management lifecycle gives
it rhythm. Policies, like identities, move through predictable stages, each guided by a mix of

organizational oversight and technical control. Figure 14.2 shows the policy lifecycle ACME
uses to keep its authorization environment both flexible and reliable.

Figure 14.2 The policy management lifecycle. Policies go through distinct stages—creation, review and

approval, deployment and use, monitoring, and eventually retirement—with updates feeding back into the

review process. The lifecycle ensures that authorization policies remain current, coherent, and aligned with

organizational intent.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

305

14.2.1 Create

Every policy begins with intent: a new business requirement, compliance rule, or system
capability that must be expressed in authorization logic. Creation involves translating that

intent into a form the system can evaluate. As shown in figure 14.3, policy creation at
ACME unfolds as a sequence of deliberate steps—defining purpose and scope, documenting

rationale in an Architectural Decision Record (ADR), and modeling the entities and
attributes that the policy will govern.

Figure 14.3 Policy creation as a governance process. The create stage of the policy lifecycle expands into a

sequence of governance steps. Policy authors begin by identifying intent, defining purpose and scope, and

documenting rationale in an Architectural Decision Record (ADR). Only after entities and attributes are

modeled is authorization logic drafted, ensuring that every policy reflects deliberate organizational intent.

The aim is not just to write code but also to record a statement of organizational will: why
this rule exists and what principle it enforces.

14.2.2 Review and approve

Before a policy can influence real decisions, it must gain legitimacy. Governance determines
who reviews policies, what criteria they use, and how approval is documented. Reviews

include both human and automated checks: static analysis, schema validation, test-case
coverage, and peer review. Compliance officers confirm alignment with regulations, while

system administrators ensure consistency with existing policies. Approval turns a draft from
a proposal into an endorsed statement of the organization’s intent.

14.2.3 Deploy and use

Once approved, the policy is versioned, published to the PAP, and distributed to the PDPs,
where the policies become operational. This is where policy governance intersects with

policy as code: CI/CD pipelines manage deployment, change control maintains version
integrity, and automated tests verify that new policies do not disrupt existing decisions. At

this stage, governance ensures operational discipline, ensuring that policies behave as
expected in production, under real workloads.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

306

14.2.4 Monitor

Monitoring links real-world behavior back to governance. Every authorization decision is
evidence: a data point reflecting how the system interprets policy intent. Logs, metrics, and

audit trails show how often policies are evaluated, what results they generate, and whether
any decision paths are unexpected. At ACME, monitoring reports support both security

operations and policy reviews, closing the loop between design and application.

14.2.5 Update

No policy remains correct forever. Business priorities shift, new regulations emerge, and
systems evolve. Governance determines how changes are initiated, reviewed, and

approved, preventing spontaneous edits that might destabilize production. In ACME’s
framework, updates start with an issue or observation from monitoring, followed by a

structured change proposal and another review cycle. Updates are therefore both corrective
and adaptive, ensuring that the expression of institutional will remains aligned with current

reality.

14.2.6 Retire

Eventually, some policies outlive their purpose. Retiring a policy is as intentional an act as

creating one. Governance ensures deactivation is coordinated, dependencies are reviewed,
and historical context is preserved for audits. At ACME, retired policies stay archived with

metadata linking them to their successors, maintaining continuity in the organization’s
policy history.

The lifecycle ensures that every policy, from its creation to retirement, remains visible,
explainable, and accountable. Each stage has a specific role in keeping authorization a

dynamic reflection of institutional will—flexible enough to adapt to change, yet controlled
enough to build trust.

[At ACME, these lifecycle principles are reinforced by a suite of engineering tools—ADRs,](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-14?potentialInternalRefId=39---book-markup-container)
version control, CI/CD pipelines, automated log analysis, and A/B testing—that keep each

phase disciplined and auditable. Together, they ensure that governance is not just a
management process but also an operational reality (see the sidebar “ACME’s policy

governance toolkit”).

ACME’S POLICY GOVERNANCE TOOLKIT

As ACME matured its policy governance process, it realized that effective governance

relies as much on tooling as on procedures. Five complementary tools—ADRs,
version control, CI/CD pipelines, and automated log analysis—support the company’s

approach to managing the policy lifecycle.

**Architectural decision records (ADRs)**

#### 14.3 Governance frameworks for policy management

Authorization policies are evolving expressions of institutional will. Governance frameworks

ensure these expressions stay consistent, accountable, and aligned with the organization’s
values and operations over time. While the policy lifecycle describes how a policy evolves,

governance defines who is responsible, what standards are applied, and how those
standards are enforced.

At ACME, the governance framework links the three systems that influence authorization
decisions: engineering, operations, and governance itself. Engineering develops and deploys

new capabilities; operations monitors how those capabilities perform in production; and
governance reviews, interprets, and formalizes lessons learned. Without these feedback

loops, policies can drift from their original intent, incidents may recur, and institutional
knowledge can be lost.

[ACME realized this integration was crucial after a production incident—caused by an](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-14?potentialInternalRefId=56---book-markup-container)
outdated access rule—showed that policy reviews and operational data existed in separate

systems. Engineering managed policies through version control and CI/CD, while operations
tracked incidents via a ticketing system that lacked connection to governance. Connecting

these systems formed a continuous cycle: Incidents prompted reviews, reviews led to
updates, and updates were tested and deployed through the same disciplined process

described earlier. Governance became not a separate bureaucracy but a coordinating
function that united technical assurance with organizational accountability.

14.3.1 The structure of governance

A governance framework establishes the organizational structure for managing
authorization. It outlines the roles, artifacts, and processes that keep policies reliable and

understandable, ensuring that authorization stays aligned with organizational goals even as
technology and business environments change.

At ACME, governance operates under a federated model. Central standards and
templates specify how policies are created, reviewed, and tested, but daily management is

handled by individual product teams. Figure 14.4 shows how a federated governance model
addresses the policy drift illustrated earlier in figure 14.1. Rather than centralize policy

ownership, governance normalizes how intent is translated into policy through shared
standards, templates, and review processes. Teams continue to manage their own policies,

but those policies are better aligned with organizational intent.

Each team manages its own policies through the shared lifecycle: drafting new rules,

running automated tests, and submitting updates for review. The central governance group
acts as a coordinator rather than a gatekeeper, establishing conventions, resolving conflicts,

This structure relies on several key mechanisms:

Defining roles ensures accountability. Each policy has a designated owner,
reviewers, and approver.

Shared processes ensure consistency. All policies and templates undergo
the same review, testing, and deployment procedures before they can

influence production decisions.

Operational feedback fosters improvement. ACME’s incident management

and decide if new policies, updates, or training are needed.
Documentation and traceability maintain institutional memory.

Architectural Decision Records (ADRs), policy metadata, and incident

operational outcome.

This framework balances central oversight with distributed ownership. Each team can act

quickly within established boundaries, while the governance structure offers the continuity
and assurance needed to maintain the integrity of ACME’s authorization environment.

14.3.2 Roles and responsibilities

A governance framework relies on clearly defined roles. Each role at ACME carries both
technical and organizational accountability, ensuring policies align with the company’s intent

and operate safely across systems. These roles balance distributed ownership with
coordinated oversight, enabling teams to act independently within a shared governance

structure.

At ACME, the policy _owner_ and _approver_ are usually the same person: the team

manager responsible for the product or feature area. The policy _author_ is typically the
engineer with architectural responsibility for the affected component, although authorship

can be delegated to another team member. Each policy must also have at least one
_reviewer_, typically another engineer on the same team, who evaluates it through the

standard code review process. To prevent conflicts of interest, ACME’s version control
system enforces a strict rule: The reviewer cannot also be the author.

[Once a policy has been authored, reviewed, and approved, the](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-14?potentialInternalRefId=71---book-markup-container) _access control_
_coordinator_ ensures it integrates smoothly into ACME’s broader authorization system.

Coordinators come from engineering and management teams across the company and are
members of the Access Control Coordinating Council (ACCC). The council maintains policy

conventions, mediates conflicts between teams, and guarantees transparency in decisions
that affect multiple services. It also oversees the company’s policy review board, which

conducts monthly reviews of new and updated policies, templates, and relevant operational
incidents (see the sidebar “ACME’s Policy Review Board”). The council’s role is not to

centralize control but to ensure coherence, keeping local decisions aligned with
organization-wide principles.

[Finally,](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-14?potentialInternalRefId=72---book-markup-container) _auditors_ confirm that governance functions as planned. As members of ACME’s
ACCC, they are responsible for ensuring reviews happen on time, ADRs are completed, and

policy metadata is accurate. They also verify that incidents related to authorization are
properly tracked and resolved within the governance process.

ACME’S POLICY REVIEW BOARD

ACME’s Policy Review Board is operated by the Access Control Coordinating Council

and functions as the company’s official forum for reviewing authorization policies and
templates. The board meets monthly, bringing together coordinators, auditors, and

representatives from engineering, product, and operations. Its mission is twofold: to

Any suggested modifications to policy templates
ADRs related to major architectural or compliance choices

All open and recently resolved operational incidents in which access

templates have passed automated testing, code review, and approval workflows.
Incidents from the ticketing system are discussed to identify systemic patterns—such

as recurring privilege issues or drift between teams—and the board may assign
follow-up actions to update templates or implement new controls.

Board outcomes are recorded in the governance repository. Each decision is
documented as an ADR and linked to relevant policy IDs and incident tickets. This

traceability enables ACME to demonstrate not only that policies are technically
accurate but also that governance decisions are intentional, documented, and

auditable.

By integrating engineering data, operational feedback, and governance oversight,

the policy review board ensures that authorization stays consistent across the
organization.
