#### 14.4 Identity Governance and Administration (IGA) and policy governance

Policies control how access is granted; identity governance controls who can be considered

for access in the first place. Together, they form the two sides of an organization’s access
assurance system: one overseeing entitlements and the other managing authorization logic.

**Identity Governance and Administration** (IGA) refers to the processes and tools
organizations use to manage digital identities, entitlements, and access rights across

various systems. Besides controlling access, IGA also ensures that identities are properly
authenticated and maintained throughout their lifecycle, tracking credentials, enforcing

strong authentication policies, and validating identity assurance levels. IGA systems
monitor who has access to which resources, streamline access requests and approvals, and

conduct regular certifications to verify that both identity and access remain appropriate and
trustworthy over time. Modern IGA platforms also support separation of duties, policy
based approvals, and reporting for regulatory compliance. For an introduction, see the
sidebar “IGA in context.”

[At ACME, IGA was the company’s initial step toward organized access management.](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-14?potentialInternalRefId=89---book-markup-container)
Long before adopting Cedar for dynamic authorization, the IT team implemented an IGA

platform to manage joiner–mover–leaver processes, provisioning employees into systems,
and managing application access through group memberships. These workflows worked

well for internal systems, but as ACME’s Customer Collaboration platform evolved into a
multi-tenant SaaS product, the static entitlements in IGA became insufficient. Access

decisions increasingly relied on context—customer relationships, project roles, data
classifications, and device trust levels—factors that IGA alone could not assess.

[Policy governance filled that gap. Where IGA manages who can hold access, policy](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-14?potentialInternalRefId=90---book-markup-container)
governance manages how that access is evaluated at runtime. Together, they form a closed

feedback loop:

IGA defines the authoritative source of identity attributes and

entitlements.
Policy governance establishes the conditions and logic that interpret those

attributes in context.
Runtime decision logs and policy evaluations feed into IGA attestation

reports, highlighting unused, excessive, or misaligned entitlements.

This connection proved to be one of ACME’s most significant governance successes. When

the Access Control Coordinating Council started integrating data from the IGA system into
its policy review process, the company gained a clearer understanding of access intent

versus actual access. During regular access reviews, the council could now see not only
which accounts existed but also how those accounts’ attributes and entitlements interacted

with policies in real-time.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

314

For example, an audit once revealed that several contractors still held _engineering_

_collaborator_ entitlements in the IGA system even after their projects had ended. Policy logs
showed that these accounts remained authorized to access shared development

environments through inherited relationships in the policy graph. The discovery led to a
coordinated response: IGA removed outdated entitlements, and policy governance

implemented a new rule linking access validity to active project membership.

[In practice, IGA and policy governance reinforce each other:](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-14?potentialInternalRefId=96---book-markup-container)

IGA ensures that identity data, entitlements, and approvals remain
precise and are regularly reviewed.

Policy governance guarantees that authorization decisions based on that
data stay valid, explainable, and compliant.

Together, they offer end-to-end assurance: Access is justified both at the
identity level and at the decision level.

At ACME, the two systems now operate in tandem. The IGA platform produces regular
certification reports that are reviewed by the Access Control Coordinating Council, with

policy coordinators adding runtime analytics and policy metadata to those reports. This
integration links identity management and authorization governance, ensuring that every

decision—who gets access and why—is an accurate and auditable reflection of ACME’s
institutional will.

IGA IN CONTEXT

Identity Governance and Administration (IGA) appeared in the mid-2000s as
organizations struggled to manage user accounts, entitlements, and compliance

requirements across an increasing number of systems. Traditional identity
management tools could create and delete accounts, but they lacked processes for

continuous oversight, making it difficult to determine who has access to what, and
why.

IGA filled that gap by combining identity administration (the provisioning and
deprovisioning of accounts) with governance capabilities such as certification

campaigns, separation-of-duties checks, and audit reporting. Gartner popularized the
term in its early reports on identity governance frameworks, describing IGA as the

foundation for ensuring that access remains appropriate, compliant, and reviewable
throughout the identity lifecycle.

Over time, IGA evolved from a compliance function into an operational discipline.
Modern platforms like SailPoint, Saviynt, and Oracle Identity Governance automate

entitlement management, access requests, and periodic reviews across both onpremises and cloud environments. Many of these platforms align with NIST SP 800
53 controls for access management and accountability.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

315

In modern architectures, IGA operates alongside access management (authentication

and session control) and policy governance (runtime authorization):

IGA governs who can be assigned access.

Policy governance governs how access is granted or denied in real
time.

Together, they create the assurance framework that keeps authorization aligned with
organizational policy and regulatory expectations—turning identity data and access

decisions into a coherent, auditable system of control.

#### 14.5 Regulatory compliance and authorization

The same structures that align identity and authorization can also be used to fulfill external

obligations. Compliance and authorization are closely related. Every regulation that guides
how organizations handle information—whether privacy laws, financial reporting rules, or

cybersecurity standards—ultimately depends on defining who can do what, when, and
under what conditions. Policy governance provides the framework that turns those legal

and procedural requirements into practical authorization logic.

At ACME, the compliance team initially viewed authorization as an operational detail—a

matter of engineering practice rather than governance oversight. That changed when
auditors began asking for not only proof that access controls existed but also evidence

showing how those controls were governed. They wanted to see decision histories, approval
workflows, and documentation linking policy changes to regulatory requirements. The

company realized that compliance could no longer be demonstrated through spreadsheets
and attestations alone; it needed to be built directly into the authorization system.

[Governance offers that bridge. Regulations like GDPR, HIPAA, SOX, and PCI-DSS all](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-14?potentialInternalRefId=112---book-markup-container)
impose requirements that map naturally to authorization policy elements:

GDPR’s data minimization and purpose-limitation principles relate to
policies that restrict access to personal data based on role, relationship,

or purpose.
HIPAA’s requirement for least privilege maps to conditional policies that

restrict medical record access to treatment or operations contexts.
SOX and PCI-DSS require audit trails and access reviews, which

governance supplies through version control, decision logs, and policy
review schedules.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

316

Through the Access Control Coordinating Council, ACME connects its compliance obligations

to the policies and architecture decisions that carry them out. Instead of creating separate
ADRs for each regulation, policy authors include references to relevant regulatory controls

within the ADRs to support their decisions. This approach makes sure that the reasoning
behind each policy clearly states the compliance areas it covers. Each policy file also has

metadata in its comment section—tags like `sox:access-review` or `gdpr:data-access` —so

compliance reporting tools can automatically link policies to their respective controls. When

auditors ask for evidence, coordinators can provide the appropriate policies, ADRs, and
decision logs that show how those regulatory requirements are fulfilled in practice.

Automated assurance also plays an increasingly important role. ACME’s CI/CD pipeline
continuously runs policy validations against test scenarios based on compliance controls.

For instance, GDPR-related policies are tested to verify that access to data labeled as
_personal_ or _export-restricted_ always requires proper contextual justification. Violations

generate alerts and prevent policy deployment until they are resolved. This methodology
shifts compliance from being a periodic task to a continuous, testable feature of the

authorization system.

[Policy governance also improves accountability after an incident. When a privacy- or](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-14?potentialInternalRefId=118---book-markup-container)

access-control-related breach occurs, engineers commenting on the event in the incidentmanagement system reference the relevant ADRs that describe the impacted policies.

These references help investigators, coordinators, and auditors trace how authorization
decisions were made and why the underlying policy was in place. During postmortem

reviews, the governance team links runtime behavior, policy logic, and documented intent
to find any gaps in design or enforcement. This structured visibility gives ACME confidence

that its authorization system can withstand regulatory scrutiny without relying on manual
reconstruction or incomplete evidence.

[Governance thus turns compliance into a result of good engineering practice. By](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-14?potentialInternalRefId=119---book-markup-container)
integrating traceability, testing, and auditing into the policy lifecycle, ACME no longer views

compliance as an external requirement but as an essential aspect of its approach to
managing authorization. In this way, regulation becomes not a restriction but a guiding

principle, helping the organization continually refine its expression of institutional will.

ACME’S APPROACH TO REGULATORY AUDITORS

Auditors don’t just check for policies—they look for proof that those policies are

enforced, reviewed, and traceable to their intent. ACME designed its governance
framework so that this evidence naturally arises from regular operations rather than

special audit preparation.

When a regulatory audit begins, coordinators from the Access Control Coordinating

Council compile an audit package directly from the governance repository. The
package includes:

Architectural Decision Records (ADRs) documenting how each
regulatory control is implemented

The relevant policy definitions tagged with compliance metadata like

`sox:access-review` or `gdpr:data-access`

Version control history showing authorship, review, and approval

Decision logs showing how those policies perform in production
Policy review board minutes linking changes to incident reports or

access review findings

Because ACME’s governance data is continuously updated, creating the audit

During audits, ACCC coordinators and auditors hold structured review sessions.

Coordinators show how specific compliance requirements—such as least privilege or
purpose limitation—are implemented and tested automatically. Any findings or

recommendations are logged as tickets in the incident system, tracked until
resolved, and documented as new ADRs when they lead to policy changes.

This approach shifts the relationship between ACME and its regulators. Instead of
assembling static evidence for periodic audits, ACME practices ongoing compliance:

Its authorization policies, governance records, and operational logs create a living
system of accountability. Auditors see not only compliance artifacts but also an

organization actively maintaining its commitment to protect customers and fulfill its
obligations.

#### 14.6 Best practices for policy governance

Policy governance works best when it includes clear ownership, consistent processes, and
ongoing feedback. The principles guiding ACME’s mature governance model apply at any

level, whether managing a few policies or thousands across multiple systems.

14.6.1 Establish clear ownership and accountability

Every policy should have a designated owner responsible for its content and a clearly

defined approver accountable for its release. These roles ensure that policies are not just
anonymous documents but active commitments that someone maintains. Ownership should

go beyond publication; owners remain responsible for tracking policy effectiveness and
starting reviews when circumstances change.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

318

14.6.2 Use shared templates and metadata

Consistency is essential for governance at scale. A standard template for policy documents
—featuring sections for purpose, scope, ADR references, and metadata—simplifies review

and auditing processes. Metadata tags, such as creation date, owner, review cycle, and
related compliance domains, convert static text into searchable, traceable data.

14.6.3 Integrate governance into existing workflows

Governance should be integrated into the engineering process. Policies should undergo the

same pipelines and approval workflows as code: version control, code review, testing, and
deployment. Embedding governance in these steps keeps it efficient and guarantees that

quality and compliance checks happen automatically instead of after the fact.

14.6.4 Close the feedback loop

Policy governance is both proactive and reactive. Incident reports, audit findings, and

access review results should feed back into the policy lifecycle. Establish a routine for
reviewing incidents where access control was a factor, linking them to ADRs and updating

policies as needed. This feedback loop helps prevent recurring problems and shows
continuous improvement to regulators and stakeholders.

14.6.5 Align with identity governance

Policy governance and Identity Governance and Administration (IGA) support each other.
IGA supplies authoritative identity and entitlement data, while policy governance

guarantees these data are properly interpreted during runtime. Synchronizing review cycles
and sharing audit results between the IGA and policy governance teams creates a closed

loop, strengthening identity integrity and assurance of authorization.

14.6.6 Measure and iterate

Governance maturity can be quantified. Track metrics such as policy review frequency, the

number of open audit findings, and the time it takes to resolve policy-related incidents. Use
these indicators to identify gaps, prioritize improvements, and show progress over time.

Governance, like authorization itself, improves through iteration.

When governance becomes routine, authorization shifts from a set of controls to a

lasting capability, an operational discipline that consistently reflects institutional will in
every decision the system makes.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

GETTING STARTED WITH POLICY GOVERNANCE

This chapter shows ACME’s mature governance in action, but few organizations start

at that level, so don’t feel overwhelmed. Governance develops gradually as systems
and teams mature. The key is to begin small, using tools and practices that establish

visibility and accountability early on. Here are a few things you can do to get started.

**Begin with decision documentation.** If your organization hasn’t yet implemented

an IGA system or a policy engine, start with Architectural Decision Records (ADRs).
Recording the reasons behind important access or authorization choices builds a

foundation for future governance. An ADR doesn’t have to be complicated; it is
simply a _version-controlled_ document that provides a structured record of the

context, decision, and consequences. Over time, ADRs serve as the link between
intent and implementation.

**Introduce ownership and conduct reviews.** Assign ownership to each accessrelated configuration or policy. Ownership is the first step toward governance.

Schedule regular reviews—quarterly is sufficient initially—to ensure policies still meet
current business needs.

**Add version control and peer review.** Move policies and access rules into a
version-controlled repository and require at least one peer review before merging

changes. Use version control to manage ownership and policy reviews. This simple
adjustment provides traceability, accountability, and collective oversight without

adding heavy processes.

**Layer in IGA or perform identity hygiene.** When your identity environment

becomes complex enough that manual management leads to errors, adopt Identity
Governance and Administration (IGA) tools or at least implement automated

workflows for joiners, movers, and leavers. IGA offers the dependable data
foundation that policy governance relies on.

**Build on evidence, not ceremony.** Governance succeeds when it produces
evidence, not paperwork. Focus primarily on artifacts that can be inspected like

ADRs, version history, logs, and ownership records. These serve as the initial proof of
accountability that will later support compliance and assurance frameworks.

Organizations that start with small, observable practices—such as documenting
decisions, assigning ownership, and using version control—lay the foundation for

mature governance later. You don’t need ACME’s full framework to start; you just
need consistent ways to connect intention, action, and accountability.

#### 14.7 Governance as the foundation of trust

At ACME, policy governance reshaped authorization from a technical subsystem into a

management discipline that spanned the entire organization. The company’s early
experience with fragmented policies and redundant logic made it clear that access control

couldn't be fixed by better tools alone. Instead, it needed a framework for ownership,
accountability, and continuous learning. The implementation of ADRs established that

foundation. Every update to a policy or template included a clear explanation of the reason,
enabling everyone—from engineers to auditors—to understand not just what changed but

why. Over time, those ADRs evolved into a living record of ACME’s authorization intent.

The Access Control Coordinating Council provided governance with a dedicated home.

What started as an informal working group grew into a cross-functional council that
connects engineering, operations, compliance, and product leadership. The council’s

monthly policy review meetings link the proactive and reactive aspects of governance:
approving new policies, examining incidents where access control was a factor, and making

sure that every operational lesson found its way back into the design process. The outcome
is a culture where policy is not an afterthought but a core part of the engineering workflow.

[Integration with Identity Governance and Administration (IGA) unified the identity](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-14?potentialInternalRefId=157---book-markup-container)
aspect of access management. The ACCC started using IGA data to verify policy

assumptions by comparing the entitlements in IGA with the conditions outlined in policies.
This alignment created a feedback loop between identity and authorization, making sure

that both the inputs for access decisions and the logic that evaluates them adhere to the
same standards of review and accountability.

[Governance also became the language of compliance. By connecting policies and ADRs](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-14?potentialInternalRefId=158---book-markup-container)
to regulatory controls, ACME replaced manual evidence gathering with ongoing verification.

Decision logs, version control history, and audit records served as live proof of compliance,
turning external oversight into confirmation of internal discipline. Over time, governance

shifted from a defensive posture—proving compliance after the fact—to an operational
capability that continually generates assurance as a natural part of daily work.

[Together, these practices turned governance into ACME’s quiet foundation for trust. They](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-14?potentialInternalRefId=159---book-markup-container)
unified how the company expressed intent, measured assurance, and responded to change.

Governance ensured that access decisions were not only technically sound but also socially
legitimate, reflecting clear choices made openly, recorded for accountability, and reinforced

through collaboration between people and systems.

[In the next chapter, we’ll build on this foundation to examine how governance supports](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-14?potentialInternalRefId=160---book-markup-container)

the broader goals of information security, demonstrating how well-managed authorization
becomes the core principle for protecting systems, data, and the people who rely on them.

#### 14.8 Summary

Policy governance turns authorization from a technical activity into a core

organizational discipline that connects business goals to how systems
behave.

## Security, zero trust, and authorization

This chapter covers

Why Zero Trust shifts security focus from network boundaries to authorization

How PBAC enables continuous, context-aware access decisions

The roles of foundational, shared operational, and application policies in a zero-trust
architecture

How policy engines evaluate these policies together to ensure consistent access
control

Architectural and organizational metrics indicating progress toward Zero Trust

ACME’s Chief Information Security Officer, Sam, had grown weary of hearing the same
refrain. Every conference keynote, board meeting, and analyst report seemed to boil

modern security down to two words: _Zero Trust_ . The phrase was everywhere—sometimes
used thoughtfully, often as a slogan—but rarely with enough detail to help him lead

meaningful change. After one particularly pointed board meeting, Sam went back to his
security team and said, for what felt like the tenth time, “We need to get serious about

Zero Trust. What does that actually mean for us?”

The team’s early efforts yielded familiar solutions: network segmentation, VPN

tightening, endpoint monitoring, stronger passwords, and micro-perimeters. However, none
of these addressed the core issue: ACME was no longer a company with a clear perimeter

defining what was inside and what was out. The workforce was global, systems were
distributed across several different clouds, and the Customer Collaboration platform served

thousands of external customers. The security team kept circling the same conclusion: The
perimeter era was over, and no amount of firewall tuning would bring it back.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

323

During a quarterly architecture review, the authorization team discussed its latest

projects. The security team had been loosely involved in this work for months, consulting
on sensitive actions, helping classify resources, and offering guidance on how product

teams should approach risk. They understood why PBAC made things easier for developers:
It eliminated _ad hoc_ authorization code, reduced inconsistencies, and provided the product

organization with a clear way to express policies. However, the security engineers had been
treating it as an application concern rather than as a way to implement organizational

security.

[As the authorization team explained how the policy engine evaluated every request—](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-15?potentialInternalRefId=9---book-markup-container)

using a combination of identity attributes and contextual signals—something shifted for
Sam. The team wasn’t just modernizing how applications handled permissions; they were

creating the exact kind of decision framework the security group had been struggling to
envision. The realization was subtle but significant: The mechanism capable of enforcing

Zero Trust across ACME wasn’t a new security product. It was an architectural change
already taking place inside the company as part of the engineering team’s modernization

efforts.

[The next day, Sam gathered the security leads and laid it out plainly: “We’ve been](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-15?potentialInternalRefId=10---book-markup-container)

thinking about Zero Trust as a network problem. It’s not. It’s an authorization problem. And
ACME already has the beginnings of an authorization system that can support it.”

[That realization changed everything. If Zero Trust meant](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-15?potentialInternalRefId=11---book-markup-container) _authorizing every access_, then
the main component wasn’t a firewall rule or a network boundary; it was a policy engine.

PBAC wasn’t just helping product teams write cleaner code; it was providing ACME with a
consistent, scalable way to enforce security policies everywhere: across applications, APIs,

internal tools, and administrative systems. The security team started to see PBAC not just
as a convenience but also as the control plane they had been overlooking.

[This chapter explores how that recognition transformed ACME’s security strategy. We’ll](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-15?potentialInternalRefId=12---book-markup-container)
examine why Zero Trust relies on continuous, contextual authorization, how PBAC provides

the technical basis for implementing it, and what is needed to operationalize these ideas
across an enterprise. Throughout, ACME’s experience will demonstrate a key lesson: Zero

Trust isn’t a product you buy, but is instead an architectural shift that naturally occurs when
identity, policy, and context become the main tools of security.

This chapter explains how authorization provides a foundation for implementing zero trust, but
before that can occur, your organization needs a solid handle on authentication. Review chapters 2

and 3 to understand why this is necessary and see what you might be missing.

#### 15.1 Rethinking security for the Zero Trust era

Sam had spent most of his career defending a perimeter. Firewalls, network segmentation,

and VPN gateways were the tools he had relied on to keep ACME’s internal systems secure.
For years, the strategy seemed sound: Draw a clear boundary around critical resources,

funnel remote workers through a VPN. Everything outside the perimeter was untrusted, and
everything within was trusted implicitly. But by the time the board began pushing for a Zero

Trust strategy, Sam already sensed the uncomfortable truth: ACME’s environment no longer
had a true perimeter.

Figure 15.1 clearly illustrates the problem. The old security model relied on a crisp
boundary between trusted internal networks and the untrusted outside world. When

someone crossed that boundary—by joining the corporate network or connecting through
the VPN—their traffic and access requests were implicitly trusted. Lateral movement was

easy because everything inside the perimeter was considered part of the same zone of
trust.

Figure 15.1 Why the perimeter model fails in modern environments. In the traditional model (left), a firewall

defined a clear boundary, and anything inside the perimeter was implicitly trusted. In modern environments

(right), cloud services, mobile work, SaaS applications, and external collaborators eliminate the concept of a

meaningful boundary.

But ACME’s world had changed. Employees worked from anywhere. Contractors connected

to projects through other companies’ networks. Critical systems resided in cloud
environments, and entire business workflows relied on SaaS applications that sat far

outside the old perimeter. Even ACME’s Customer Collaboration platform linked thousands
of customers directly to ACME-managed systems. The perimeter was no longer a protective

wall; it was an architectural fiction.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

325

And that fiction unraveled for three interconnected reasons. First, _location was no longer_

_a reliable indicator of trust_ ; a request coming from the corporate network told Sam’s team
almost nothing about the person or device behind it. Second, _attackers increasingly_

_exploited implicit trust once they gained access_, moving laterally across internal systems
with surprising ease. Third, _users, devices, and workloads now operated from everywhere_,

making it impossible to anchor security to a single boundary. In this environment, treating
the network as a trust signal simply didn’t hold.

[Zero Trust developed as the industry’s response to this shift, not as a product category,](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-15?potentialInternalRefId=21---book-markup-container)
but as a security approach, a choice to replace inherited trust with continuous

authorization. Instead of granting broad, durable access once a principal authenticates,
Zero Trust requires that every access be evaluated in context: who is making the request,

from what device, under what conditions, and for what purpose.

[Sam had heard versions of this argument at conferences for years, but the vendor noise](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-15?potentialInternalRefId=22---book-markup-container)

often masked the core idea. Products claimed to deliver Zero Trust, but none could explain
how a device at the network's edge was supposed to fix the architectural mismatch ACME

faced. As Sam came to understand, Zero Trust can’t be achieved by simply buying a
product or tightening the perimeter, because the perimeter no longer exists.

[Zero Trust requires a different foundation. ACME needed strong authentication that](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-15?potentialInternalRefId=23---book-markup-container)
provided consistent identity signals, reliable role, attribute, and relationship data,

trustworthy device posture, and operational signals such as on-call status or recent
approvals on high-risk actions from managers or other team members. These signals

required governance to ensure they remained defined, validated, and up to date. Most
importantly, ACME needed a way to evaluate every access request against a coherent set of

policies, quickly and consistently across all systems.

[Taken together, these requirements shifted focus from network boundaries to](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-15?potentialInternalRefId=24---book-markup-container)

authorization, a decision system capable of evaluating every request based on identity,
device posture, and context. The question for ACME was whether its current authorization

framework could support this shift. The next section explores how this realization
transformed ACME’s access-decision architecture and how PBAC became the core element

of the company’s Zero Trust approach.

#### 15.2 Authorization is the foundation of Zero Trust

To support this shift, ACME needed an authorization architecture that could assess every
access request based on identity, device posture, and contextual signals, regardless of the

request’s origin.

Figure 15.2 shows how this works. Each access request, no matter where it comes from,

is ultimately assessed by a policy engine using details such as identity attributes, device
posture, operational signals like on-call status, and environmental context. The outcome of

that assessment is then enforced by the policy enforcement point (PEP) at the target
resource. As we saw in Chapter 10, ACME had already implemented several deployment

strategies for their policy decision points (PDPs) and PEPs; a zero-trust security architecture
did not require replacing them. Any of these patterns could participate, as long as they

evaluated a consistent set of policies.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

Figure 15.2 Zero Trust is enforced through continuous authorization. Every access request is evaluated by a

policy engine. Identity attributes, device posture, operational signals, and environmental context further

influence the decision. The result is enforced locally by the PEP guarding the target resource.

What changed for ACME was who authored those policies and what they expressed. Up to
this point, most of ACME’s use of policy-based access control had been driven by application

teams writing service-specific policies or by engineering teams creating policies for
deployment tools and internal APIs. Those policies governed how a particular application or

system behaved. In a zero-trust security architecture, a new category of policy emerged:
foundational security policies managed by the security and identity teams.

These foundational policies apply broadly across the entire organization. Instead of
controlling just one application or workflow, they set requirements for the entire enterprise.

They included minimum device posture, mandatory authentication levels, restrictions on
sensitive activities, and conditions for break-glass access. These policies capture decisions

that traditionally appeared in security handbooks, architecture checklists, or informal
norms, making them concrete and integrating those decisions into the real-time

authorization process.

[This approach provided ACME with two key advantages. First, it enabled the security and](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-15?potentialInternalRefId=31---book-markup-container)

identity teams to specify enterprise-wide requirements without interfering with the
independence of application teams, who continued to manage their own policies for

business logic and resource-specific rules. Second, it prevented the creation of another
standalone security mechanism. Zero Trust became a natural extension of ACME’s existing

PBAC foundation rather than yet another system sitting off to the side.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

327

What changed for application teams was how they tested and validated their own

policies. Because every access request is evaluated against both foundational security
policies and application-specific rules, teams needed to ensure their policies behaved

correctly in the presence of those broader controls. Testing now included verifying that their
application logic continued to work when device posture was absent, when authentication

sessions were expired, or when environmental context triggered an enterprise-wide
restriction. This shift wasn’t burdensome, but it did require teams to adopt a more

comprehensive testing model that accounted for the full zero-trust security architecture
rather than testing their policies in isolation.

[By grounding Zero Trust in authorization—expressed through clear, governable policies—](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-15?potentialInternalRefId=33---book-markup-container)
ACME found a way to move past vague slogans and vendor promises. Zero Trust became

tangible: a method for making better access decisions, applied consistently and adaptable
to the organization’s risk tolerance. The next section examines how ACME directly

expresses these core ideas in policy and how those policies interact with application and
engineering rules to create a cohesive zero-trust security architecture.

#### 15.3 Policies for zero trust

As ACME expanded its use of policy-based authorization, the security and identity teams

weren’t the only groups discovering the benefits of expressing rules in policies. Application
teams quickly saw the value of defining their service-specific logic in a policy store, but it

didn’t take long before other parts of the organization noticed a gap. Some rules were too
broad to belong to a single application but not universal enough to be considered

foundational security policies. These were the rules that applied to groups of systems,
departments, or cross-functional workflows.

Engineering was the first to encounter this. Various product teams had their own
deployment pipelines, but all of them wanted the same guarantees: Deploy only during

business hours, require the on-call engineer for late-night changes, and prevent releases
when incident severity was high. None of these rules were “security policies” in the

enterprise-wide sense, and they weren’t tied to the logic of a single service. They were
operational rules that spanned many systems. Rather than embed them independently into

every deployment tool, engineering chose to express them as a shared set of policies that
all pipelines could reference.

[Other groups followed. Finance established shared policies to regulate how different](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-15?potentialInternalRefId=37---book-markup-container)
categories of employees could access sensitive reports across multiple systems. Operations

outlined maintenance-window rules that applied to various internal tools. Support teams
crafted policies governing access to customer data based on role and shift. In each case,

these were neither core enterprise requirements nor single-application rules—they existed
in the space between.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

328

ACME formalized this emerging pattern into a distinct category: shared operational

policies. These policies were owned by functional groups—engineering, operations, finance,
support—and applied to specific sets of systems or workflows. They captured cross-team

operational rules without overreaching into enterprise-wide mandates or bloating individual
application policy stores. This middle layer became essential for defining responsibilities

that cut across the organization but did not fall under the security team or individual
product teams.

[Figure 15.3 shows how these policies are organized into three layers. Foundational](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-15?potentialInternalRefId=39---book-markup-container)
security policies set enterprise-wide requirements that apply to all systems, no matter who

makes the request or which service is involved. Shared operational policies include rules
that cover multiple systems or workflows and are owned by the groups responsible for

those domains—for example, deployment rules for engineering or reporting controls for
finance. Application policies define the service-specific authorization logic for individual

applications. These layers vary in scope and ownership, but they work together:
Foundational policies establish the organization’s core requirements; shared operational

policies reflect cross-system or departmental rules; and application policies control each
service's behavior.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

329

Figure 15.3 Zero-trust authorization is based on layered policies. Foundational security policies define

enterprise-wide requirements. Shared operational policies capture rules owned by functional groups and

applied across multiple systems or workflows. Application policies define service-specific authorization logic.

These layers differ in scope and ownership but are evaluated together to produce a unified authorization

decision.

The following subsections explain each layer, provide a policy example, and demonstrate

how ACME applied these layers in practice.

15.3.1 Foundational security policies

Foundational policies form the bedrock of ACME’s zero-trust security architecture. These

policies often apply no matter who the principal is, what action they want to take, or which
resource they are trying to access. In Cedar, this broad applicability is easy to recognize:

The policy does not specify a principal, action, or resource details at all. The scope is
intentionally left open, indicating that the rule applies to every request.

Foundational policies outline the minimum security requirements for the organization,
including device posture, authentication strength, or enterprise-wide restrictions on

sensitive actions. One of ACME’s earliest foundational policies enforced device posture and
authentication strength:

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

330

forbid(

principal,

action,

resource

)

unless {

context.device.posture.score >= 80 &&

context.authn.mfa_performed == true

};

This policy doesn’t specify the principal, action, or resource; it simply states that if the

device isn’t secure or the principal isn't properly authenticated, ACME won’t authorize the
request. When this policy first rolled out, Sam’s team found that several internal tools still

relied on unmanaged laptops, leading to an accelerated push for device enrollment. That
experience underscored the importance of stating fundamental requirements clearly in the

policy.

Foundational policies define ACME’s non-negotiables. They establish the baseline

conditions that every access request must meet, regardless of what other policies are
involved.

15.3.2 Shared operational policies

Shared operational policies define rules that span multiple systems, workflows, or
environments, but are not broad enough to be foundational. These policies are managed by

the functional groups responsible for the systems or workflows they govern, like
engineering, operations, finance, or support. They enable teams to articulate cross-system

operational requirements without having to embed those rules separately into each
application or tool.

These policies are particularly useful for introducing operational nuances across different
services or teams. A typical example occurs in deployment workflows. ACME’s engineering

team wanted a consistent rule for after-hours production deployments. Multiple product
groups managed their own deployment pipelines, but the requirement was the same

everywhere: Late-night deployments should be performed only by the on-call engineer.
Instead of changing each pipeline or relying on each team to apply the requirement

correctly, engineering articulated the rule as a shared operational policy that all pipelines
could reference when authorizing production changes:

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

331

forbid(

principal,

action == Pipeline::"deploy",

resource in Pipeline::"production"

)

unless {

/* During business hours */

context.time.hour >= 8 && context.time.hour < 18

||

/* After hours, only the on-call engineer may deploy */

context.oncall.current_engineer == principal

};

This forbid-unless structure clarified two concepts:

Deployment is allowed during normal business hours.
Outside those hours, deployment is allowed only for the on-call engineer.

By defining this operational rule in policy instead of code, engineering avoided the need to
change deployment scripts or add separate checkpoints in each tool. The policy engine

enforced the rule consistently across all production environments, ensuring uniform
behavior without adding operational complexity. This is exactly the kind of cross-system

requirement that shared operational policies are meant to address.

15.3.3 Application policies

Application policies represent the most specific and narrowest layer. These policies

determine how an individual service operates: which resources can be accessed, what
actions are permitted, and who has the authority to carry them out. They are managed by

the product or engineering teams responsible for the specific product or service.

Because application policies restrict authorization scope to a specific domain, they often

specify particular resource types, roles, or allowed actions. For example, ACME’s finance
reporting system uses a policy like this:

permit(

principal in Group::"Finance",

action == Report::"view",

resource in Report::"internal_financials"

);

This policy describes the business logic of the finance reporting service. It does not aim to
enforce device posture, authentication freshness, or time-based limits, since foundational

and shared operational layers already manage these.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

332

When the finance reporting team began defining its access rules in policy, this division of

responsibility proved helpful. The operations team responsible for the finance system could
focus on accurate domain rules without worrying about organization-wide controls.

Meanwhile, Sam’s team continued to specify the security guarantees ACME required
everywhere.

15.3.4 Putting the layers together

These three layers—foundational security policies, shared operational policies, and
application policies—work together to create a flexible framework for expressing a zero
trust security architecture. A single access request is assessed once using policies pulled
from multiple policy stores that correspond to each layer. By applying all relevant policies

across these stores, the policy engine determines the full set of conditions necessary for the
decision. Foundational requirements, shared operational rules, and service-specific logic are

all taken into account to produce one unified authorization decision.

This layered approach distributes policy ownership across the organization without

fragmenting decision logic. Security and identity teams handle enterprise-wide
requirements; functional groups like engineering, operations, or finance define shared

operational rules; and product teams set the behavior of their own services. The result is an
authorization system that stays consistent and enforceable while allowing the different

teams to fulfill their responsibilities. It makes Zero Trust both practical and sustainable,
giving each group a clear way to express its intent while making sure that every request is

checked against the organization’s full set of expectations.

WHY FORBID-OVERRIDES-PERMIT SEMANTICS MATTER

One of the most important and sometimes surprising aspects of Cedar’s evaluation

model is that a `forbid` always overrides a `permit` . This rule is essential in a layered

policy architecture, where foundational, shared operational, and application policies

are assessed together. Without a clear and predictable override rule, combining
policies from multiple stores could quickly lead to ambiguous or inconsistent results.

Consider what happens when an application policy permits an action, but a
foundational policy enforces a security requirement that the request does not satisfy.

If the application’s permit could override the foundational restriction, the entire zerotrust model would fall apart. By prioritizing forbid rules, the policy engine guarantees

that security-critical constraints stay in place, no matter how many application-level
permissions are granted.

This behavior also enhances authorization safety during failures. If required context,
such as device posture or authentication freshness, is missing or outdated, a

foundational policy that relies on that context issues a forbid, causing the system to
deny access. In a zero-trust architecture, this _fail-closed_ behavior is a feature, not a

flaw.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

333

Practically speaking, forbid-overrides-permit means:

Foundational security rules, written as `forbid` policies, are always

enforced, even if application logic would otherwise allow an action.

Shared operational rules are consistently applied across systems
without depending on developers to add extra checks.

Application policies remain focused on business logic, trusting
foundational and operational layers to manage broader concerns.

A layered policy system only works when the evaluation model is predictable. Forbidoverrides-permit semantics provides that predictability, ensuring that combining

policies from multiple stores results in a single, consistent, and secure decision every
time.

#### 15.4 Using policy to control access

As ACME expanded its use of policy-based access control, policies shifted from being
internal implementation details to becoming the main way the company managed access.

Instead of relying on network location, ACME now enforces access by evaluating each
request against policies that specify expectations for devices, identity, and application

behavior.

Figure 15.4 refines figure 15.2 by illustrating the complete process of an access decision.

When a principal tries to perform an action, the request is initially handled by the policy
enforcement point at the target resource. The PEP gathers relevant context—such as the

authentication session and device posture—and constructs a normalized request that it
forwards to the policy engine. Instead of evaluating policies from only one source, the

policy engine creates an effective policy set by selecting applicable policies from the
foundational, shared operational, and application policy stores. It then evaluates the

normalized request against this combined set, yielding a unified authorization decision. This
decision is subsequently returned to the PEP, which enforces it at the target resource.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

334

Figure 15.4 Access control in a zero-trust security architecture. The policy enforcement point (PEP) collects

authentication context, device posture, and other request information to create a normalized request for the

policy engine. The policy engine forms an effective policy set by selecting relevant foundational, shared

operational, and application policies, then evaluates the normalized request once to make a unified

authorization decision. The PEP then enforces that decision at the target resource.

This approach allowed ACME to enforce its core requirements across all applications

consistently. Device posture checks, authentication-strength criteria, and other
organization-wide rules were evaluated alongside application and shared operational

policies for every request. For example, if Alice tried to view a finance report from a laptop
that didn’t meet the foundational device-posture requirement described in section 15.3.1,

the device policy resulted in a `forbid` . Even if the finance application’s own policies would

otherwise permit access, Cedar’s “forbid overrides permit” semantics mean the overall

decision is still `deny` . These core requirements ensured that common security standards

were upheld everywhere, across all applications and services.

rule from section 15.3.2 is automatically enforced whenever a deployment request is

[Application policies provided the final layer of decision-making. These policies articulated](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-15?potentialInternalRefId=80---book-markup-container)
the business logic of each service, specifying which principals could access specific

resources and under what conditions. For example, the finance reporting policies from

foundational and shared operational checks before access is granted. This application policy
managed the service’s own requirements, but it did so in coordination with the foundational

and shared operational layers. A finance employee could view a report only if their device
met security standards and if no shared operational rule restricted access based on time,

location, or workflow state.

[Together, these policies established a unified access-control model that aligned with](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-15?potentialInternalRefId=81---book-markup-container)

ACME’s zero-trust security architecture. Application teams retained control over their own
logic, but foundational and shared operational policies enabled security and cross-team

organizations to articulate requirements without altering application code. Since the policy
engine evaluated all relevant policies collectively, each decision reflected both ACME’s

enterprise-wide requirements and the specific rules of the service being accessed.

[This structure gave ACME a consistent and scalable way to manage access across the](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-15?potentialInternalRefId=82---book-markup-container)

company. It prevented duplication of logic across applications, reduced the risk of policy
drift over time, and aligned authorization with the organization’s structure and governance

model. With foundational, shared operational, and application policies working together,
Zero Trust evolved from simply an architectural strategy to the everyday practice of how

ACME protected its systems.

TESTING DECISIONS IN A LAYERED POLICY ARCHITECTURE

As organizations adopt a layered policy approach, testing becomes essential not just

for individual policies but also for how those policies interact. In a zero-trust security
architecture, each access request is evaluated against an effective policy set drawn

from multiple stores. This means a policy that works in isolation may behave
differently when foundational or shared operational rules are present.

Three kinds of testing become important:

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

336

**Foundational policy testing** : These policies set organization-wide requirements, so

any change needs to be validated against a representative sample of requests from
various systems. A new device-posture rule, for example, should be tested against

shared operational and application policies to ensure it doesn’t unintentionally block
expected access.

**Shared operational policy testing** : Since these policies apply across multiple
systems or workflows, tests should verify not only the policy’s logic but also how it

interacts with different applications. For example, an after-hours deployment rule
should be tested with pipelines from various teams to ensure consistent behavior.

**Application policy testing** : Teams must verify that service-specific rules function
correctly when foundational and shared operational requirements are present.

Application policy tests should simulate scenarios with missing posture signals,
expired authentication sessions, or conflicting operational conditions.

Comprehensive testing ensures that changes in one layer do not produce unintended
consequences in another. In a layered Zero Trust architecture, correctness is about

more than just creating policies; it’s about verifying decisions against the entire set
of rules the organization depends on.

#### 15.5 Measuring progress toward zero trust

As ACME moved toward a zero-trust security architecture, Sam faced a familiar question:
How would the company know it was making progress? Zero Trust had long been discussed

in broad terms; sometimes as a goal, often as a slogan, but rarely as something that could
be assessed in concrete, architectural terms. Sam wanted a method to measure

improvement without falling into the trap of vendor-defined maturity ladders or artificial
stages.

The solution was to evaluate the quality of authorization decisions. If Zero Trust is
defined by assessing each access in context—using identity, device posture, operational

signals, and policy—then progress is demonstrated by improving the inputs that inform
those decisions and by making sure they are applied consistently. ACME identified several

independent dimensions that together showed the health of its zero-trust architecture.

[Figure 15.5 depicts these as parallel, non-sequential indicators radiating from the same](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-15?potentialInternalRefId=93---book-markup-container)

central goal. No single dimension defines Zero Trust, and none must be “completed” before
another begins.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

337

Figure 15.5 Independent dimensions of progress toward Zero Trust. Instead of following a maturity ladder,

ACME evaluated its Zero Trust progress across several architectural dimensions: policy coverage, signal

quality, decision consistency, reduced reliance on perimeter-based trust, and fewer authorization exceptions.

Each highlights an area where architectural improvements enhance ACME’s authorization
decisions, making them more reliable, contextual, and aligned with organizational intent.

15.5.1 Policy coverage

The first dimension was the breadth of systems using PBAC. As more applications, APIs,

and internal tools adopted policy engines and began evaluating requests against
foundational, shared operational, and application-specific rules, ACME could enforce

consistent requirements across more of its environment. Growth in policy coverage
indicated that Zero Trust was penetrating deeper into the organization’s systems.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

338

In practice, ACME measured policy coverage by tracking which systems made

authorization decisions through a policy engine and which still relied on embedded or ad
hoc logic. The security and platform teams maintained an inventory of services and tools,

noting whether each one enforced access using PBAC, partially delegated authorization to
policy, or bypassed policy entirely. This inventory was reviewed regularly and used to

identify gaps.

[For example, early in the transition, ACME discovered that while most customer-facing](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-15?potentialInternalRefId=99---book-markup-container)

services evaluated requests through a policy engine, several internal administrative tools
still relied on hard-coded role checks and network-based trust. By migrating those tools to

use the same foundational and shared operational policies as other systems, ACME
significantly increased policy coverage without rewriting business logic. Over time, the

percentage of access decisions evaluated by a policy engine became a leading indicator of
Zero Trust adoption.

15.5.2 Signal quality

High-quality signals were equally important. Device posture, authentication freshness,
principal attributes, and operational context needed to be accurate, timely, and governed. If

these inputs were incomplete, stale, or inconsistent, even well-written policies could
produce unreliable decisions.

ACME assessed signal quality by checking if data feeding its policy engine met defined
expectations for freshness, completeness, and consistency. For each major signal type, the

security and identity teams defined service-level indicators: how recently the signal was
updated, how often it was missing when needed, and whether it followed agreed-upon

schemas. Signals that arrived late frequently, were unavailable, or required fallback
assumptions were identified as reducing the accuracy of authorization decisions.

[For example, ACME found that device posture signals for managed laptops were not](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-15?potentialInternalRefId=103---book-markup-container)
always up to date. Some devices only reported posture at login, which meant a device

could become non-compliant hours later without the policy engine noticing. By tightening
posture refresh intervals and enforcing expiration rules on outdated signals, ACME

improved the reliability of its device-trust data. Similar updates were made for
authentication freshness and operational signals, such as on-call status and approval

records.

[As signal quality improved, the policy engine could make more accurate decisions with](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-15?potentialInternalRefId=104---book-markup-container)

fewer false denials and exceptions. High-quality signals reduced the need for conservative
fallback rules and helped ensure that access decisions truly reflected ACME’s intent rather

than compensating for missing or unreliable data.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

339

15.5.3 Decision consistency

Decision consistency reflects whether authorization behaves predictably across systems
when the same conditions apply. Before adopting PBAC, ACME often saw identical requests

produce different outcomes depending on which application processed them. Each system
encoded its own assumptions about roles, risk, and trust, sometimes in configuration files,

sometimes directly in code. Consequently, a principal could be granted access in one
system and denied in another, even if nothing about the identity, device posture, or context

changed.

ACME assessed decision consistency by running standardized authorization scenarios

across multiple systems and comparing outcomes. The authorization team crafted a set of
canonical test requests—combinations of principal identity, attributes, device posture, time

of day, and operational context—and examined how various applications responded to these
requests. Early results showed notable variation, particularly in systems that still depended

on embedded authorization logic or network-based shortcuts.

[As foundational and shared operational policies became more widely adopted, these](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-15?potentialInternalRefId=108---book-markup-container)

discrepancies began to disappear. For example, ACME tested a scenario where Alice, a
finance employee using a managed device with current MFA, attempted to view an internal

financial report across several reporting tools. With foundational and shared operational
policies in place, each system returned the same decision: access permitted. When Alice

repeated the request from an unmanaged device, all systems denied access for the same
reason—the foundational device-posture policy—rather than for application-specific quirks.

[Over time, Sam’s team tracked the percentage of tested scenarios that yielded identical](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-15?potentialInternalRefId=109---book-markup-container)
authorization outcomes across participating systems. An increase in consistent decisions

indicated that ACME’s zero-trust architecture was becoming cohesive: policies were
assessed uniformly, signals were interpreted consistently, and trust decisions no longer

depended on which system received the request. Decision consistency became a practical
sign that Zero Trust was functioning as a shared architectural reality.

15.5.4 Reduced perimeter reliance

Reducing reliance on network-based trust signals was another key indicator of ACME’s

progress toward Zero Trust. Historically, many systems made implicit assumptions based on
network location, VPN membership, or IP address ranges. Requests coming from “inside”

the network were often trusted by default, while those from elsewhere were blocked or
needed special handling. These perimeter-based shortcuts made access decisions brittle

and inconsistent.

ACME measured reduced reliance on perimeter security by tracking how often access

decisions depended on network-derived signals versus identity- and context-based signals.
The security team inventoried firewall rules, VPN exceptions, and IP allowlists that were still

necessary for application access and monitored if these controls were shrinking over time.
A decline in new network exceptions—and the retirement of existing ones—indicated that

systems relied more on policy-based authorization rather than location.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

340

For example, ACME identified two internal reporting tools that still required users to be

on a corporate VPN to access sensitive dashboards, even though the same identity and
device-posture checks were already enforced elsewhere. By removing the VPN requirement

and establishing those constraints as core, shared operational policies, ACME ensured
consistent access decisions regardless of where the request originated. Users with the

correct identity, device posture, and context could access the tools from anywhere, while
unauthorized access was blocked even from inside the network.

[Over time, the security team noticed a steady decrease in VPN-only access paths, IP-](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-15?potentialInternalRefId=114---book-markup-container)
based allowlists, and special-case firewall rules. This trend showed that trust was no longer

based on network location but on evaluated context. Reducing reliance on the perimeter
didn't mean removing network controls entirely; it meant moving them from primary

gatekeepers to supporting signals. This change clearly indicated that ACME’s zero-trust
architecture was becoming both stronger and more adaptable across services.

15.5.5 Decline in authorization exceptions

Authorization exceptions often indicate that the access-control model cannot fully represent
the organization’s actual needs. Before PBAC, ACME frequently managed edge cases with

one-off rules: hard-coded role checks in application code, special VPN groups, IP allowlists,
or temporary flags that bypassed standard authorization logic. These exceptions solved

immediate problems but accumulated over time, making access behavior more difficult to
understand, test, and audit.

Sam’s team started measuring how often these exceptions occurred as ACME
implemented a zero-trust architecture. They monitored several indicators: the number of

code changes that added custom authorization logic, the use of emergency bypass flags,
the amount of access granted through special-case configurations, and how often manual

approvals were needed to override normal controls. Early metrics revealed that many
exceptions existed simply because no shared policy could fully express the intended rule.

[As foundational and shared operational policies expanded, these exceptions became less](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-15?potentialInternalRefId=118---book-markup-container)
necessary. For example, engineering teams previously used manual overrides to allow

after-hours deployments during incidents. Once the on-call deployment rule was expressed
as a shared operational policy, those overrides were eliminated entirely. Similarly, finance

teams removed special access lists after shared policies captured reporting access rules
across systems.

[Over time, ACME tracked progress by observing a steady decline in exception-related](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-15?potentialInternalRefId=119---book-markup-container)
changes and emergency access procedures. Fewer one-off rules led to fewer surprises in

authorization behavior and reduced opportunities for policy drift. For Sam, this decrease
was one of the clearest signs that Zero Trust had moved beyond just theory. Instead of

depending on fragile, undocumented workarounds, ACME’s teams increasingly trusted the
policy system to accurately reflect and enforce the access decisions the organization

genuinely needed.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

341

As figure 15.5 illustrates, progress toward Zero Trust isn’t a ladder to climb but a set of

architectural dimensions to develop over time. By improving policy coverage, signal quality,
and decision consistency, reducing reliance on the perimeter, and eliminating ad hoc

authorization exceptions, ACME built a security architecture where Zero Trust was not just a
goal but an actionable strategy based on greater reliance on policy-based access decisions.

#### 15.6 Beyond security: the organizational payoff

As ACME’s zero-trust security architecture took shape, Sam expected enhancements in

access control, auditability, and incident response. What he hadn’t fully anticipated was how
far the benefits would extend beyond the security team. By basing access control on clear

policies assessed against high-quality signals, ACME not only boosted its defenses but also
improved its operational, collaborative, and innovative capabilities. Zero Trust evolved into

more than just a security strategy; it became a foundational architecture that enhanced the
way the entire company worked.

15.6.1 Better alignment between teams

One of the earliest benefits was a change in how teams worked together. Before PBAC,
authorization logic was spread across applications, CI/CD pipelines, and operations tools,

leading to minor differences in how systems handled roles, permissions, and risk. With
policies stored in shared repositories and consistently evaluated everywhere, teams began

to speak the same language. Product teams could create resource-specific rules without
having to reinvent authentication, device posture, or contextual checks. Security teams

could set up guardrails without blocking development. Operations teams could define
workflow requirements—such as on-call status, approval processes, or emergency

procedures—without embedding logic in scripts or dashboards.

The effect was a measurable decrease in architectural friction. Instead of focusing on

implementation details, teams talked about policy semantics and organizational goals. The
discussions became more effective because the authorization layer made security

requirements clear, testable, and easy to review.

15.6.2 Improved auditability and incident response

Zero Trust also made ACME’s systems easier to audit and investigate. Because every access

decision passed through a policy engine and was based on clearly defined policies and
signals, security analysts no longer needed to piece together application-specific logic

scattered across codebases. They could understand why a decision was allowed or denied
simply by examining the relevant policies and the request’s context.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

342

This clarity made incident response faster and more precise. When unusual access

occurred, analysts could determine whether it was allowed by policy, whether a shared
operational condition had been met, or whether an outdated signal had influenced the

decision. In several early cases, core policies uncovered misconfigurations in device
management or authentication systems that previously would have gone unnoticed. The

zero-trust architecture didn’t just prevent incidents; it revealed dependencies that needed
strengthening.

15.6.3 Greater agility for product development

ACME also found that Zero Trust increased developer velocity. By moving enterprise-wide
requirements into core and shared operational policies, application teams no longer needed

to create their own versions of these controls. They could focus on domain logic—what their
service should allow—while trusting other policy layers to handle posture checks,

authentication strength, and operational constraints.

This separation of concerns made the authorization model more flexible. As the security

team introduced new foundational requirements, applications automatically adopted them
without needing code changes or redeployments. Conversely, when product teams added

new actions or resources, those updates integrated smoothly into the policy structure
without reopening security reviews or refactoring authentication flows. PBAC became

shared authorization infrastructure, providing developers with a stable platform to build on.

15.6.4 Improved governance and transparency

As ACME’s policy ecosystem matured, governance became more organized and transparent.

The security and identity teams handled core policies; operations groups took charge of
shared ones; product teams set application policies. This clear division of responsibilities

made policy review more predictable, enabled delegated accountability, and created a more
open approval process.

Perhaps most importantly, the policy architecture made governance practical. Instead of
treating governance as just a documentation task, the organization conveyed governance

directly through executable policy. The rules that defined how ACME wanted to operate
were the same rules enforced at runtime.

15.6.5 A more resilient security posture

Finally, Zero Trust made ACME more resilient. Because authorization decisions no longer
depended on network boundaries or implicit trust, the company’s exposure to lateral

movement, credential misuse, and device compromise decreased. Strong authentication
became standard; device posture signals became a regular part of decision-making; and

contextual conditions prevented routine access from turning into high-risk access.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

343

Even when components failed or signals degraded, the architecture remained

predictable. Policies that required specific context simply denied access when that context
wasn’t available. This _fail-closed_ approach gave Sam confidence that the system would

degrade safely under load or during outages, something ACME’s old perimeter model had
never guaranteed.

15.6.6 More reliable access for legitimate users

One unexpected benefit of ACME’s zero-trust architecture was how much it enhanced
access for people who needed to do their work. Under the old, perimeter-centric model,

access was often inconsistent: Some systems relied on VPN membership, others on IP
ranges, and some on hard-coded role checks embedded in application logic. The result was

frustration. Employees submitted access tickets for tools they needed to perform their jobs.
Vendors had difficulty reaching the systems ACME expected them to use. Customers

occasionally encountered confusing permission errors that reflected outdated assumptions
rather than current business needs, leading to costly support calls.

By evaluating foundational, shared operational, and application policies together, access
became more accurate and predictable. When a principal’s identity attributes, device

posture, and contextual signals aligned with policy, access simply worked—regardless of the
system they aimed to reach. If something went wrong, the cause was clear and could be

diagnosed by reviewing the relevant policies and signals. This approach reduced the time
employees waited for approvals, decreased troubleshooting time for teams, and minimized

the friction of cross-organizational collaboration.

[This change was more than just a convenience. It boosted ACME's productivity. By](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-15?potentialInternalRefId=141---book-markup-container)

ensuring the right people had access to resources at the right time, using reliable, up-todate context, the zero-trust architecture helped the organization run more smoothly with

fewer delays. The authorization layer didn’t just block unauthorized users; it consistently
allowed the right ones in.

defensive posture; it improved how teams collaborated, how systems operated, and how

quickly the organization could adapt. By treating authorization as a shared, policy-driven
capability, ACME gained a foundation that supported both security and day-to-day
