## Using verifiable credentials for authorization

This chapter covers

Why traditional account-based and federated identity models face challenges when
authority exists outside the organization

How verifiable credentials enable portable, cryptographically verifiable claims for
authorization decisions

How organizations can build trust and confidence in credential-based attributes

How credential presentations are used in policy evaluation

Patterns for integrating verifiable credentials with policy-based authorization
models, including attribute- and relationship-based methods.

As ACME’s collaboration platforms expanded—including the legacy Customer Collaboration
system and the newer multi-tenant Customer Collaboration Cloud (C³)—they came to

support several closely related service areas: the traditional customer and project work, a
portal that manufacturers use for managing suppliers, a clinic-integration API and

management system branded ACME Health, and a platform that ACME provides to other
companies for supporting their service technicians in the field. These are not standalone

products so much as different expressions of the same platform. Each one depends on
authorization decisions that must be made quickly and consistently with high assurance,

even when the people involved have no accounts in ACME’s internal identity systems.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

347

For internal employees, ACME’s identity system works well. Accounts are provisioned in

the corporate directory, roles and attributes flow into the authorization layer, and lifecycle
events are tied to HR systems. The issues occur when ACME needs to give access to non
employees. Contractors, independent auditors, partner-clinic staff, supplier representatives,
and field technicians all require controlled access, but none of them belong in ACME’s

internal directory. Creating accounts for these groups is costly and challenging to manage
at scale.

[To address some of these needs, ACME experimented with federation. Several large](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-16?potentialInternalRefId=8---book-markup-container)
suppliers and clinic networks were onboarded through SAML or OIDC connections, which

worked adequately when both organizations had the technical maturity and ongoing
interest to manage a bilateral relationship. However, the limitations soon became clear.

Federation requires each partner to operate an identity provider. It also requires ACME to
configure that provider, manage metadata, coordinate attribute mappings, and troubleshoot

failures that occur outside its administrative boundary. More importantly, federation does
not work for many of the organizations ACME interacts with. Small contractors, regional

clinics, and field-service companies often lack the infrastructure or motivation to support it.

[At the same time, ACME’s authorization requirements need more flexibility. Decisions](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-16?potentialInternalRefId=9---book-markup-container)

increasingly rely on information from outside ACME’s systems: professional certifications,
clinical affiliations, project-specific delegations, and supplier relationships, to name a few.

These are authoritative statements, but ACME is not the authority that can issue or
maintain them. The company needs a way to trust information held by customers, partners,

licensing agencies, and other external organizations without importing all that identity data
into its own systems.

[ACME also faces a growing lifecycle burden. Temporary accounts have multiplied. Short-](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-16?potentialInternalRefId=10---book-markup-container)
term access often lasts longer than planned because deprovisioning depends on manual

signals from partners about when work is done or personnel changes. These signals often
arrive late or not at all. ACME cannot query a partner’s HR system to know if a contractor

has left or a technician has changed roles, so temporary access often exceeds the
circumstances that justified it.

[This chapter introduces a different approach. As we discussed in chapter 2, decentralized](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-16?potentialInternalRefId=11---book-markup-container)
identity models shift trust to the parties who can legitimately assert these facts, rather than

force everything through a central directory or federated identity provider. ACME has built
its authorization engine to use attributes provided by verifiable credentials. _Verifiable_

credentials are portable, cryptographically verifiable attestations issued by entities that
actually know the facts: employers, certification bodies, customers, clinics, manufacturers,

and others. Rather than ask whether ACME has a record for a specific person, the
authorization system asks whether trusted issuers attest that the person has the attributes

needed for the action they are attempting.

[With this shift, ACME can grant access to contractors without creating new accounts,](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-16?potentialInternalRefId=12---book-markup-container)

trust suppliers without setting up IdP integrations, recognize professional authority without
maintaining directories of external certifications, and handle emergency access in a way

that remains governed and auditable. The rest of this chapter explores how verifiable
credentials work in practice and how they integrate with ACME’s policy-based authorization

architecture.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

348

#### 16.1 Why authorization needs verifiable credentials

As we discussed in chapter 12, reliable authorization depends on knowing who is taking an

action, what they are permitted to do, and under what circumstances the action should be
allowed. For internal users, ACME can draw these facts from authoritative internal systems

such as HR records and the corporate directory. However, as ACME’s collaboration platform
has expanded, more and more authorization decisions involve people who have no accounts

in these systems. Contractors, auditors, supplier representatives, clinicians, and field
technicians all need controlled access to ACME’s services. ACME does not employ these

people, cannot manage their lifecycle events, and lacks authoritative knowledge of their
roles and qualifications.

This reality challenges traditional approaches. Account-based models require every
external person to be added to ACME’s directory, even if they work for a different

organization. This leads to identity records that ACME cannot verify and lifecycle
responsibilities it cannot realistically manage. Federation solves part of the problem when

both parties have the necessary infrastructure, but many of ACME’s partners do not. Even
when federation is feasible, it creates a fixed, bilateral relationship that is hard to scale

across hundreds of partners and often breaks when roles, attributes, or organizational
structures change.

[Just as chapter 12 emphasized the importance of trustworthy context in authorization](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-16?potentialInternalRefId=16---book-markup-container)
decisions, a similar need exists here. Context isn't limited to device posture, session details,

or environmental factors. It also includes organizational roles, professional licenses, clinical
affiliations, supplier relationships, and project-specific delegations. These are forms of

context that ACME cannot generate or maintain on its own, yet they can be just as vital as
device or session attributes when assessing an access request. Viewing verifiable

credentials as another category of trusted signals highlights an important idea: external
attestations can be integrated into the authorization engine using the same architectural

model and policy-driven approach described earlier.

[Verifiable credentials offer a structured way to gather external context in a trustworthy](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-16?potentialInternalRefId=17---book-markup-container)

and verifiable format. Instead of relying on internal accounts or federated assertions,
ACME’s authorization system can assess credentials issued by organizations that possess

the relevant facts. These credentials represent roles, qualifications, delegations, and
relationships as portable, cryptographically verifiable statements. They naturally integrate

into ACME’s existing context model because they serve as another type of trustworthy
signal that the authorization engine can use to make decisions.

[The rest of this chapter explains how verifiable credentials are organized, how ACME can](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-16?potentialInternalRefId=18---book-markup-container)
decide whether to trust an issuer, and how these credentials can provide reliable signals to

support authorization decisions across the collaboration platform.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

349

#### 16.2 How verifiable credentials work

Verifiable credentials package identity attributes into cryptographically secured claims that

people can carry on their own devices and present when required. Some people are
surprised that this could work. We’ve been trained to believe that identity information must

stay on a central server or flow directly between organizations. The idea that someone can
carry authoritative attributes on their own device and reliably present them may seem

counterintuitive at first. However, this approach isn't as unusual as it might seem.

ACME already depends on context signals that originate from devices employees use in

various locations and on untrusted networks. While ACME controls and manages these
devices, the employees hold and operate them. An example of this is _device posture_

_attestation,_ where the device assesses its own security status and sends a signed token to
ACME when the employee accesses ACME systems. As discussed in chapter 2, ACME’s

confidence in this signal comes from cryptographic protections that prevent tampering and
enable ACME to verify that the token was generated by trusted hardware or software. Trust,

on the other hand, is placed in the organization that developed the attestation software and
on ACME’s own processes for installing, configuring, and managing it on employee devices.

Verifiable credentials follow the same principle: a holder can store and present a credential,
but ACME’s confidence in the credential stems from the issuer’s signature and cryptographic

protocols, while its trust is based on the issuer’s authority to make the claims it contains.

[A verifiable credential is best understood as a cryptographic container for attributes. The](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-16?potentialInternalRefId=22---book-markup-container)

issuer writes a set of claims about a subject, such as employment status, a professional
license, or authorization to act on behalf of a company. These claims are assembled into a

credential, signed by the issuer, and given to the subject to hold. The subject can present
this credential to ACME when requesting access. ACME can verify the signature to ensure

that the claims have not been changed and that they were issued by an authorized entity.
In this way, attributes travel with the person yet remain linked to the issuer’s authority.

I use the terms claims and attributes interchangeably when describing the data in verifiable
credentials. The W3C specification uses the word claim to emphasize that the issuer is asserting

something about the holder. In the context of authorization, these claims serve as attributes that the
policy engine can use to inform its authorization decision. You can think of claims as the attributes

contained in the credential, and we will use whichever term is most natural in a given context.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

350

16.2.1 Credential presentation

The trust triangle in figure 16.1 shows how verifiable credentials work in practice. A trusted
issuer makes claims about a holder and signs them so they can be verified by a relying

party. When a holder presents a credential, the verifier can use cryptography to confirm
four things: who the issuer is, that the credential has not been tampered with, that it was

issued to the wallet presenting it, and that it has not been revoked. The holder transports
and presents the credential, but is not the source of trust. When ACME verifies a credential

during an access request, the key question is not whether the holder is honest. Instead, the
question is whether the issuer signed the credential and whether the claims meet the

policy’s requirements.

The previous paragraph was careful to specify that cryptography guarantees the credential

was issued to a specific wallet, not a person. The link between the wallet and the person presenting
it is established outside the credential itself. Most wallets rely on the device’s biometric unlock, such

as a fingerprint or face scan, to ensure that only the device’s rightful controller can present a
credential. Issuers also help reinforce this link by performing identity proofing when issuing the

credential, confirming that the claims in the credential belong to the person who controls the wallet
it is linked to.

Figure 16.1 The verifiable credential trust triangle. The issuer, AuditsRUs, creates and signs the credential.

The holder, Angela, carries and presents it. ACME verifies the signature and uses the data in the credential as

context when it evaluates policy.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

351

This approach allows attributes to move across organizational boundaries without the need

for synchronization, federation, or prior relationships. Employers, certification bodies,
clinics, regulators, suppliers, and manufacturers can all issue credentials that verify facts

within their authority. ACME doesn’t have to maintain directories for each partner or
integrate with each partner’s identity system. Cryptography separates the process of

transmitting the credential from the act of trusting it. As shown in the figure, the holder
does not merely send the credential. Instead, they generate a presentation based on it,

which the verifier can validate independently.

Because verifiable credentials present structured claims that can be validated, checked

for freshness, and normalized, they integrate naturally into ACME’s context model. From
the authorization engine’s perspective, they are simply another trustworthy signal that

accompanies the access request. Once a credential has been verified, the policy engine can
assess its contents just as it would evaluate internal attributes, environmental context, or

device posture signals.

16.2.2 Example: Contractor access using verifiable credentials

To understand how ACME interprets these attributes in real-world scenarios, consider the

case of a short-term contractor who needs limited, time-bounded access to audit logs. A
simple set of credentials, issued by her employer and certification authority, provides

exactly the context ACME needs to make an informed authorization decision.

Angela, a short-term contractor, is assigned to conduct a two-day audit of ACME’s legacy

Customer Collaboration platform. She is employed by AuditsRUs, a boutique securityauditing firm that ACME occasionally hires for specialized review projects. Angela also holds

a CISA-R certification issued by the National Institute for Security Accreditation (NISA), a
credential ACME considers authoritative for security audit qualifications.

Both the NISA and CISA-R certifications are fictional.

When Angela requests access to ACME’s audit interface, her wallet creates a presentation

using two credentials that state:

1. Angela is employed at AuditsRUs.

2. She holds a CISA-R certification, issued by the National Institute for
Security Accreditation (NISA).

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

352

The PEP controlling access verifies that the presentation is properly signed, checks that

neither credential is expired or revoked, and confirms that NISA is an issuer of security
certifications that ACME has recognized for this purpose. It also verifies that the credentials

were issued to Angela, the presenter. The PDP then uses the claims to evaluate policies that
ensure Angela works for a firm that ACME routinely uses for audit work, and she holds the

necessary certification. The policies also ensure that the requested access is within the time
window specified for this engagement.

If all conditions are satisfied, ACME grants Angela limited access to view the relevant
logs during her audit. No account setup is necessary, and no lingering access remains after

the contract ends. This approach also makes it easy for AuditsRUs to assign additional
auditors to the project or replace Angela if circumstances change, without creating new

accounts or coordinating manual onboarding steps with ACME. The verifiable credentials
provide the context ACME needs to make a confident authorization decision without directly

managing the identities of external personnel.

#### 16.3 Trusting credential issuers

Verifiable credentials give ACME a way to incorporate authoritative external claims into
policy decisions, but only if ACME trusts the issuers of those claims. Trust is not established

by the holder or by cryptography. As discussed in chapter 2, cryptography gives ACME
confidence that a credential is genuine and unaltered, but trust is based on the authority

behind the claim. ACME must evaluate whether an issuer is qualified to make a particular
type of claim and whether the issuer operates within a governance framework that ACME

considers trustworthy.

Figure 16.2 shows the trust diamond, which extends the trust triangle introduced in

figure 16.1. Along with the holder, issuer, and verifier, the diamond adds a governance
authority that defines the processes for evaluating issuers and the criteria they must meet

to participate. As we discussed in chapter 14, governance is the foundation of trust. The
governance authority publishes a governance framework that documents its governance

processes and decisions. Verifiers use the framework to understand how issuers are vetted,
supervised, and held accountable.

[In our example, NISA fulfills this role. NISA establishes the requirements for becoming](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-16?potentialInternalRefId=45---book-markup-container)
an accredited security auditor, evaluates and certifies organizations that meet its standards,

and documents the procedures for issuing, renewing, suspending, or revoking
accreditations. ACME relies on this framework to determine whether a credential issuer is

accredited by NISA and can be trusted.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

353

Figure 16.2 The trust diamond. The governance authority (NISA) establishes the rules for issuing and verifying

security-auditor credentials. NISA grants an accreditation credential to AuditsRUs and publishes a

governance framework. ACME consults that framework to decide which issuers it should trust and for which

purposes. The verifier’s trust in the issuer is based on the governance authority’s rules, not in the credential

holder.

Establishing trust in issuers is a core part of ACME's internal governance. Before a

credential is used in policy evaluation, someone within ACME must verify that the issuer is
trusted for the claims it makes. This verification happens before presentation, as part of the

identity team’s ongoing management of external vendors.

16.3.1 Example: ACME onboards AuditsRUs as a trusted issuer

Several months before Angela’s audit, ACME’s security auditing team began evaluating
potential external audit firms. Tim, a senior member of ACME’s security team, was tasked

with deciding whether AuditsRUs should be added to ACME’s list of trusted auditors. To do
this, Tim reviewed the NISA governance framework, which details the requirements for

becoming an accredited security auditing firm and the steps organizations must follow to
maintain that status. The framework also describes how NISA assesses and certifies

individual auditors, including the issuance of the CISA-R credential that Angela holds. These
procedures helped Tim understand both the organizational accreditation for AuditsRUs and

the asserted qualifications of the auditors it employs.

As part of the review, Tim examined the accreditation credential issued to AuditsRUs by

NISA. The credential verified that AuditsRUs met NISA’s standards and was authorized to
issue employment and role credentials for security auditors working under its supervision.

Tim verified the credential’s signature, checked its validity period, and confirmed that it had
not been revoked. He also confirmed that the credential identified AuditsRUs as the

accredited organization by comparing the legal name, organizational identifier, and public
key in the credential with the information NISA publishes in its governance framework and

with the materials AuditsRUs had provided during his review.

[Satisfied that AuditsRUs was a legitimate NISA-accredited auditor, Tim added AuditsRUs](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-16?potentialInternalRefId=51---book-markup-container)

to ACME’s internal registry of issuers. Importantly, ACME did not just trust AuditsRUs for
audit work; it also trusted AuditsRUs to issue any credentials that NISA’s governance

framework allowed them to, such as verifying employment, role assignments, and audit
qualifications of their staff. By recording this in ACME’s governance system, the trust

relationship was formalized and made available in ACME’s trust store (described in the next
section).

[This onboarding step meant that when Angela later presented her employment](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-16?potentialInternalRefId=52---book-markup-container)
credential from AuditsRUs and her CISA-R certification credential from NISA, ACME already

knew how to evaluate them. The cryptography provided confidence that the credentials
were genuine and linked to Angela’s wallet, while ACME’s trust in NISA and AuditsRUs,

established earlier by Tim, provided assurance that the claims were authoritative.

16.3.2 Building and maintaining ACME’s trust store

Once ACME determines that an issuer is trustworthy for a specific set of credential types,
the identity team records that decision in ACME’s trust store. The _trust store_ is a registry of

issuers that ACME depends on, along with the credential types it accepts for each vendor.
This is not simply a list of public keys; it is a governance artifact that captures ACME’s

decision that an issuer is authoritative for certain credential types and outlines the scope of
that trust.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

355

For example, after reviewing NISA’s governance framework and the accreditation

credential issued to AuditsRUs, Tim added AuditsRUs to the trust store as an issuer ACME
recognizes for employment and role credential types. He also added NISA as a trusted

issuer for the CISA-R certification credential type. These trust decisions are scoped. ACME
does not trust AuditsRUs to issue certification credentials, nor does it trust NISA for

employment credentials. By scoping trust this way, ACME protects the security of its
processes and ensures that each external organization can only assert the credential types

within its recognized authority. This prevents vendors from exceeding their intended role
and keeps ACME’s authorization decisions grounded in well-defined sources of authority.

[Maintaining the trust store is an ongoing responsibility, but it does not require ACME to](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-16?potentialInternalRefId=56---book-markup-container)
monitor the ongoing performance or compliance of each credential issuer. ACME trusts NISA

because Tim conducted a thorough evaluation of NISA’s governance framework and
concluded that NISA’s accreditation process is reliable. That evaluation gives ACME

significant leverage: any firm or individual auditor accredited by NISA can now be trusted
without repeating the analysis. ACME’s role is simply to ensure that the accreditation

credentials on which its trust decisions rely remain valid and have not been revoked. If
NISA were to revoke AuditsRUs’s accreditation, ACME would update its trust store

accordingly. These updates might happen automatically either through periodic checks that
ACME’s infrastructure makes or via a subscription to NISA’s trust registry. If this were to

happen, future credentials from AuditsRUs would no longer satisfy policies requiring work
by accredited auditors. This change would also impact individuals. If Brian, another auditor

at AuditsRUs, tried to access ACME systems after such a change, his employment credential
would no longer meet policy requirements, even if it remained cryptographically valid.

[These trust-store entries become part of ACME’s governance layer and are distributed](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-16?potentialInternalRefId=57---book-markup-container)
using ACME’s policy information points (PIPs) that we discussed in chapter 12. PIPs expose

trust decisions as structured signals that PEPs and PDPs can rely on during request
assembly and policy evaluation. This allows the authorization system to depend on

verifiable credentials without embedding issuer lists into policies or spreading trust
decisions across multiple systems. The trust store consolidates ACME's determinations

about which claims from specific issuers should be accepted and for what purposes.

#### 16.4 Credential freshness, revocation, and assurance

Trusting an issuer is only the first step. ACME must also verify that the credentials it
assesses reflect the current state of the world. As discussed in chapter 12, authorization

depends not only on the accuracy of each signal but also on its freshness and assurance
level. These principles directly apply to verifiable credentials. A credential can be

cryptographically valid and still no longer represent an accurate fact if the holder’s
employment has ended, the issuer has lost its accreditation, or the credential has been

revoked. Therefore, ACME must include mechanisms to validate the current status of
credentials each time they are presented.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

356

Most verifiable credentials include an expiration date that limits how long they remain

valid. This provides a basic level of freshness. AuditsRUs might issue Angela an
employment credential valid for a fixed term, such as one year, which must then be

reissued using normal HR procedures. Similarly, NISA might issue a CISA-R certification
credential with a renewal cycle defined in its governance framework. While expiration dates

set predictable limits on each credential's use, they don’t cover cases where a credential
becomes invalid unexpectedly, such as when someone leaves a company or loses their

certification. For such situations, ACME depends on revocation information published by the
issuer or its governance authority.

[Revocation mechanisms vary. Some issuers offer a real-time status endpoint, while](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-16?potentialInternalRefId=61---book-markup-container)
others publish a signed revocation list that ACME can check locally. In either case, the

authorization engine must verify that the credential has not been revoked before using its
claims. Since ACME already trusts NISA’s governance framework and the software

implementing its revocation processes, it has confidence that the revocation information is
accurate and can be used safely in high-assurance decisions.

[These checks can have operational consequences. Suppose that Brian, another auditor](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-16?potentialInternalRefId=62---book-markup-container)
at AuditsRUs, tries to access ACME’s systems after his employment ends. His employment

credential might still be cryptographically valid, but AuditsRUs would have revoked it. When
Brian presents his credentials, ACME verifies their signatures, confirms their issuer, and

then retrieves or validates their revocation status. Since Brian’s credential is no longer
valid, ACME automatically denies access. This process eliminates the need for manual

deprovisioning and prevents outdated accounts from remaining in ACME’s identity systems.

[Verifiable credentials give ACME a scalable way to incorporate authoritative external](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-16?potentialInternalRefId=63---book-markup-container)

context in authorization decisions without expanding its identity systems or creating fragile
integrations. The trust store specifies which issuers ACME depends on and for which

credential types, enabling ACME to reuse those trust decisions across many products and
use cases. Freshness and revocation checks verify that the information from those issuers

stays current, accurate, and safe to use. Collectively, these mechanisms allow ACME to
make high-confidence, real-time authorization decisions based on data it does not maintain

while reducing administrative overhead and enhancing the security of its overall process.

#### 16.5 Requesting verifiable credential presentations

When ACME needs attributes from an external party, it does not request a specific
credential. Instead, it requests the claims necessary to make a particular authorization

decision. The holder responds by creating a credential presentation, which may include
claims from one or more credentials. This indirection is important because it allows ACME to

request only the attributes relevant to a specific policy while giving the holder control over
which credentials to use and how to disclose them.

Figure 16.3 illustrates this step in isolation. This is the final part of the flow in the trust
triangle from figure 16.1: the holder presenting verifiable claims to the verifier. Here, we

focus only on that step, showing how the PEP sends an attribute query, the holder’s wallet
assembles an appropriate presentation based on the user’s request, and the PEP receives

the resulting claims for policy evaluation.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

357

Figure 16.3 Claim-based credential presentation. Upon receiving an access request, the PEP requests

specific attributes it needs for the authorization decision. The holder’s wallet receives the attribute query,

selects the necessary claims from one or more credentials, and assembles a signed presentation. The PEP

verifies the presentation and prepares the claims for policy evaluation.

The attribute query identifies the claims that the PEP needs. The holder’s wallet reviews its

credentials, finds those with the necessary claims, and creates a signed presentation
containing only the required information. The presentation is not the credential itself;

rather, it is a derivative object specifically generated for the request, enabling selective
disclosure and the combination of claims from multiple sources.

This mechanism offers ACME flexibility that isn't possible with federation or static
directory synchronization. When Angela logs in to systems that keep audit-related

documents and logs, the PEPs for those systems check the metadata of the policies that
apply to her request to decide which attributes are needed. Based on this analysis, the PEP

sends an attribute query to her wallet asking for two types of claims: her employer and her
CISA-R certification status. Angela’s wallet replies by assembling a presentation that

includes the necessary claims from two different credentials: her employment credential
from AuditsRUs and her certification credential from NISA. Cryptography ensures each

claim remains bound to its original issuer and confirms both credentials were issued to
Angela’s wallet. From ACME’s point of view, it receives a single presentation with the

attributes required to assess the relevant policies.

[Requesting specific attributes rather than credentials offers additional benefits. It keeps](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-16?potentialInternalRefId=70---book-markup-container)

ACME from depending on issuer-specific credential formats. It allows ACME to evolve its
policies without coordinating changes with external organizations. It also protects holders

by minimizing unnecessary disclosure. The wallet discloses only the claims required, even if
the underlying credentials contain more information.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

358

This presentation model is essential for supporting ACME’s wider product ecosystem.

Different workflows require various attributes. A clinic workflow may request professional
affiliation and licensing information. A supplier portal might ask for employment and

delegation information. A system for managing field technicians could request role
assignments and scope-of-work details. In each instance, the verifier requests the

attributes it needs, and the holder assembles an appropriate presentation from whatever
credentials they have.

[Together, these mechanisms provide ACME with a flexible, privacy-respecting way to](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-16?potentialInternalRefId=72---book-markup-container)
gather the contextual information it needs without taking responsibility for issuing, storing,

or interpreting raw identity data. ACME has outsourced those tasks to organizations better
equipped to handle them.

#### 16.6 Using verifiable credentials with policies

Once the PEP verifies a credential presentation and extracts the relevant claims, those

claims become part of the context that the PDP uses during policy evaluation. The policy
engine doesn’t see the presentation itself; it only sees the structured attributes that ACME

has chosen to model, such as the holder’s employer, certification status, or project role.
This separation keeps policies simple and allows ACME to manage its trust mechanisms

independently of its authorization logic.

Before evaluation, the PEP normalizes the extracted claims into an internal attribute

schema. This reflects the approach described in earlier chapters for device posture and
other contextual signals. A claim such as `employer=AuditsRUs` or `certification=CISA-R`

becomes an attribute on the principal. The responsibility for verifying credential signatures,
checking issuer trust, and ensuring that the claims come from authorized sources lies with

the PEP and the mapping layer that prepares the request the PDP receives.

[Policies can then reference these attributes in the same way they reference any other](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-16?potentialInternalRefId=76---book-markup-container)

contextual information. A policy might require that the principal’s employer be on the list of
trusted auditing firms or that the principal hold a specific certification issued by an

accredited authority. More complex policies may combine credential-derived attributes with
session information, environmental conditions, or resource metadata. The key point is that

verifiable credentials integrate seamlessly into ACME’s policy model because the claims they
contain become attributes evaluated at decision time.

[When Angela accesses the systems where the audit-relevant documents and logs are](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-16?potentialInternalRefId=77---book-markup-container)
stored, the PEP extracts the claims from her presentation, normalizes them, and evaluates

policies like those shown in the following examples. The policies do not need to know how
those claims were obtained or which credentials were combined to produce them.

16.6.1 Allow access only to auditors from accredited firms

This policy illustrates how ACME ensures that only auditors employed by recognized firms
and holding the proper certification can access audit logs. It relies on two VC-derived

attributes: the principal’s employer and their certification status.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

359

permit(

principal,

action == Audit::"view-log",

resource in Audit::Log

)

when {

principal.employer in context.trusted_auditor_firms

&& principal.certification == "CISA-R"

};

Note that the list of trusted auditor firms is stored in ACME’s trust store, not in the policy,

and reflects Tim’s earlier assessment of NISA and AuditsRUs. The certification attribute is
from a credential issued by NISA. The policy remains unchanged even if ACME hires

additional NISA-accredited firms or if NISA updates its credentialing procedures.

16.6.2 Require current certification from an accredited authority

Some audit actions require increased assurance. This policy ensures that sensitive

documents are accessible only to individuals with a current certification issued by an
approved authority:

permit (

principal,

action == Document::"view",

resource

)

when {

resource.hasTag("SensitiveDocument")

&& principal.certification.type == "CISA-R"

&& principal.certification.issuer in context.trusted_certification_bodies

&& principal.certification.expiry > context.now

};

This policy checks to ensure that:

The principal holds the required certification.

The issuer of that certification is a trusted certification body.
The credential has not expired.

These checks depend on ACME’s trust store and mapping rules, not on any issuer-specific
details embedded in the policy. If ACME later trusts additional certification bodies accredited

by NISA, this policy remains unchanged.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

360

This model provides ACME with the advantages of externalized authorization without

involving policies in the details of credential verification. If ACME later adds another
accredited auditing firm, no policies need to change. If NISA updates its certification

program, only the trust store and mapping rules require adjustments. The policies that
govern access stay consistent because they rely on attributes, not on how those attributes

were obtained.

HOW TO AVOID HARDCODING ISSUERS OR CREDENTIAL FORMATS IN POLICIES

Policy authors are sometimes tempted to embed issuer identifiers, credential

schemas, or claim names directly in policies. This creates fragile authorization logic
that depends heavily on specific external organizations or credential formats. ACME

prevents this by using its trust store and signal platform to keep policy logic separate
from the details of credential verification.

As noted, ACME depends on the Policy Information Point (PIP) introduced in earlier
chapters to do this effectively. The PIP integrates with ACME’s trust store, which

records the issuers ACME trusts and the types of credentials they issue. The PIP
provides this information to PEPs and PDPs so that policies don’t need to include

issuer knowledge. The PEP uses the trust store data when verifying presentations,
checking signatures, and confirming that the credential was issued by an authorized

issuer. After verifying and normalizing the claims, the PEP sends only the resulting
attributes to the PDP. The PDP evaluates policies based on these attributes and

information in the PIP without needing to know anything about credentials issuers,
formats, or revocation details.

To keep policy logic clean and stable:

1. **Keep issuer trust in the trust store, not in policy.** Policies should

reference information managed by the PIP, such as
`context.trusted_certification_bodies` . The PIP maintains this

information; PDPs only consume it.
2. **Normalize all credentials before policy evaluation.** The PEP and

PIP convert raw VC claim names into stable internal attributes. Policies
reference attributes such as `principal.certification` rather than

schema-dependent fields.
3. **Express semantics, not formats.** A policy should require an

accredited auditing firm rather than encoding a specific issuer name or
credential structure. Semantics remain stable even when schemas

evolve.
4. Use indirect references for claim sources. If different credential types

can provide the same attribute, map them into a single normalized
form. This helps the PDP focus on evaluating attributes rather than

determining their origins.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

361

5. **Let the PIP and PEP handle credential validity concerns.**

Revocation checks, issuer validations, and signature verification belong
in the enforcement pipeline, not in policy logic. Policies evaluate

attributes, not cryptographic proofs. Note, for example, that the policy
shown in the preceding section did not reference details like whether

credentials were revoked or expired.

By centralizing issuer trust and credential interpretation in the PIP and PEP, ACME

keeps policies simple, strong, and protected from ecosystem changes. This enables
ACME to increase the number and types of credential issuers it collaborates with

while keeping its authorization logic both stable and easy to understand.

#### 16.7 Protocols and ecosystem integration

The mechanics of verifiable credentials involve more than just the credential itself. A

functioning ecosystem relies on three interconnected layers: issuance protocols that
describe how credentials are created and delivered to holders, presentation protocols that

control how holders respond to attribute requests from verifiers, and wallet standards that
specify how credentials are stored, protected, and managed on the holder’s device. These

layers differ in how they handle discovery, transport, and user interaction, but they all
support the same authorization pattern shown in figure 16.3: The PEP requests attributes,

the holder assembles a presentation, and the PDP evaluates normalized claims that the PEP
has already verified.

Two protocol families dominate current deployments. The first follows the W3C Verifiable
[Credentials Data Model (https://www.​w3.org/TR/​vc-data-model-​2.0/), where issuers use](https://www.w3.org/TR/vc-data-model-2.0/)

DID-based identifiers and sign credentials that wallets store. Holders respond directly to a
verifier’s request with a signed presentation that the verifier checks using issuer keys

discovered through DID resolution to discover information about the DID identifier. The
second family builds on existing web identity infrastructure through OpenID for Verifiable

[Credentials (https://openid.​net/sg/openid4vc/), including both the issuance protocol](https://openid.net/sg/openid4vc/)
(OpenID4VCI) and the presentation protocol (OpenID4VP). These protocols reuse OAuth

and OpenID Connect conventions for transport, discovery, and authentication flows, making
them appealing because of their familiarity to developers.

This section touches on topics, like DID-based identifiers and OpenID4VC, that are complex
and worthy of more discussion. I cover all of this in depth in my earlier book Learning Digital Identity

(2023, O’Reilly Media).

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

362

Despite their differences, these protocols achieve the same authorization outcome: a signed

presentation containing claims that can be verified using issuer keys and signatures.
ACME’s has chosen to ensure its verification process is able to accept and validate

presentations delivered through various protocols. Nevertheless, the verification steps stay
the same. The PEP verifies that claims come from trusted issuers listed in ACME’s trust

store, checks expiration and revocation status, and then passes normalized attributes to
the PDP. The PEP enforces issuer trust during request assembly, but policies may still

reference issuer sets when different actions require different trust scopes. From the PDP’s
perspective, it does not matter whether the credential was issued using a DID-based

protocol, retrieved via an OpenID4VCI flow, or presented using OpenID4VP. Policies focus
only on the attributes, not the specific protocol used to deliver them. (See the sidebar for

how ACME maintains protocol flexibility in its verification layer.)

Different parts of ACME’s ecosystem may rely on different combinations of issuance and

presentation protocols. Credentials issued by ACME to its employees and long-term
partners use the `did:scid` method [(https://lf-​toip.atlassian.​net/wiki/​spaces/HOME/​](https://lf-toip.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/HOME/pages/88572360/DID+SCID+Method+Specification)

<u>[pages/88572360/​DID+SCID+​Method+Specification), which seamlessly integrates with](https://lf-toip.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/HOME/pages/88572360/DID+SCID+Method+Specification)</u>
ACME’s web infrastructure and key management practices. External auditors, on the other

hand, might receive their employment and certification credentials through OpenID4VC
flows, supported by their employers and industry associations. Clinicians accessing ACME

Health systems may use mobile wallets that support either DID-based credentials or
OpenID4VC-based credentials, responding to presentation requests via QR codes or

browser redirects, depending on their workflow. ACME’s verification layer is designed to
accept all these inputs. What changes is the user experience and transport mechanism, not

the structure or meaning of the claims or their role in policy evaluation.

ACME’S ECUMENICAL STANCE ON CREDENTIAL PROTOCOLS

Even though ACME issues credentials using the `did:scid` method, it designed its

credential verification layer to support presentations delivered through different
protocol families and a variety of DID methods. This ensures that ACME can

collaborate with partners, suppliers, clinicians, and auditors, whether they use DIDbased infrastructure, OpenID4VC tools, or wallet software that supports both.

At the heart of this strategy is a flexible verification service that can adapt to
different protocols. This component operates within ACME’s PEP layer and handles

receiving presentations, validating signatures, verifying issuer trust, and checking
revocation status. The verification service provides a consistent interface to the rest

of ACME’s authorization pipeline, even when presentations arrive through various
transport methods and interaction patterns. Supporting a new VC protocol requires

updating this service; it does not require rewriting policies, changing the PDP, or
modifying application logic.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

363

The trust store and issuer governance information managed by the PIP are

integrated into this verification layer to ensure that protocol differences do not leak
into policy. A credential presented using a DID-based method and one using an

OpenID4VC flow both produce the same outcome: a set of trusted, normalized
attributes that the PDP can evaluate. Policies remain centered on business meaning,

not on protocol specifics.

By maintaining a protocol-neutral verification layer, ACME avoids locking itself or its

partners into any single ecosystem. This flexibility enables ACME to adapt as the
verifiable credential landscape changes, while maintaining a consistent and reliable

authorization workflow across all its products.

#### 16.8 Applying verifiable credentials across ACME’s products

The examples in earlier sections focused on an external auditor, but the same patterns

naturally extend to ACME’s other authorization needs. In each case, verifiable credentials
provide trusted context that ACME’s policy engine can evaluate without requiring ACME to

create or manage accounts for every external participant. The PEP requests the attributes
needed for policy evaluation, the holder responds with a presentation assembled from one

or more credentials, and the PDP makes a decision using those normalized claims. The
underlying issuance or presentation protocol may differ across ACME’s ecosystem, but the

authorization flow stays consistent.

16.8.1 Supplier portal: Representing supplier authority across multi-tier
relationships

ACME’s supplier portal enables manufacturers to manage contracts, purchase orders,

invoices, and shipment records across their supply chains. These supply chains often
involve multiple tiers: ACME provides a service platform to manufacturers, manufacturers

manage on suppliers, and suppliers employ workers who need secure access to shared
records. In the past, granting this access usually meant manufacturers had to create and

manage accounts for each supplier’s workers, even though those workers weren't part of
the manufacturer’s organization. This led to the familiar security problems of lingering

accounts, inconsistent deprovisioning, and fragile onboarding processes as workers cycled
through projects or changed employers. Verifiable credentials made this much simpler.

When a supplier employee signs in, ACME’s PEP sends an attribute query requesting
claims to confirm the employee's employment at the supplier organization and their

delegated authority for a particular contract or customer account. Most suppliers issue
these credentials using OpenID4VCI, and employees present them through OpenID4VP

flows.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

364

The PEP verifies the credentials, confirms that the supplier is approved by the

manufacturer, and forwards normalized attributes to the PDP. The combination of
presentation verification by the PEP and policy enforcement at the PDP ensures that a

supplier employee can view or update a purchase order only if all these conditions are true:

The employee works for the supplier listed on the order.

The supplier has delegated authority for the relevant contract.
The delegation credential has not expired or been revoked.

With this model, authorization follows the natural hierarchy of the business relationship:
manufacturer → supplier → supplier employee. ACME no longer needs to manage identities

or roles for individuals working several tiers away in the supply chain. Authority flows
through verifiable credentials, not through manual account creation or fragile directory

integrations. Access automatically updates as delegations and employment relationships
change, reducing the administrative burden and security risks of outdated accounts.

16.8.2 Clinic integration: Clinicians from external organizations

ACME Health works with clinics that are not included in the platform’s internal identity
system. Physicians, nurses, and administrative staff often need temporary or conditional

access to patient data, test results, and appointment information. Originally, this was
handled through federation agreements or manually created accounts, but verifiable

credentials offer a cleaner, more flexible solution.

In this model, clinicians possess credentials issued by their licensing authorities and their

employing clinic. When a clinician tries to access ACME Health systems, the PEP requests
attributes describing these factors:

The clinician’s professional license
Their affiliation with a specific clinic

The clinician’s relationship to the patient or care team

ACME verifies the presentation using the protocol-flexible verification layer described earlier

and establishes trust in issuers through jurisdiction-specific accreditation frameworks for
clinical organizations and medical licensing boards.

Policies can then require these conditions, for example:

The clinician is licensed in the relevant jurisdiction.

The employing clinic has a valid business relationship with ACME Health.
The clinician is assigned to the patient’s care team.

No long-term accounts are needed, and access automatically aligns with current licensure,
employment, and patient assignments.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

365

16.8.3 Field technicians: Employer-issued scope-of-work credentials

ACME offers operational tools for companies that dispatch technicians to the field for
installation, maintenance, and repair work. These technicians are employed by service

partners, not by ACME, and their authority depends on their employer, role, training, and
assigned service area.

Service partners issue credentials that detail a technician’s employment, role, and
authorized service scope. When a technician logs into ACME’s service (often from a mobile

device), the PEP requests the attributes needed by policy: role, region, product
certifications, and employer.

[The verification layer validates the credentials, and the PDP evaluates policies such as:](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-16?potentialInternalRefId=138---book-markup-container)

Technicians may only access documentation or configuration tools for the

product lines they are certified to service.
Technicians may only initiate work orders within their assigned region.

Certain high-risk operations require both employer authorization and
recent completion of a safety-training credential.

This allows ACME’s platform to support flexible, widely spread field operations for its
customers without maintaining its own technician directory of technicians.

16.8.4 Customer Collaboration Cloud (C³): Project-scoped roles in a multi-tenant
platform

The Customer Collaboration Cloud (C³), introduced in chapter 13, is ACME’s multi-tenant
service that allows its tenants—customers of ACME—to collaborate directly with their

customers on shared projects. Each tenant manages its own collaboration spaces, invites its
own partners and clients, and sets project roles based on their business processes. ACME

does not oversee these project roles, nor is it involved in the identity management between
a tenant and its customers. Team composition changes as projects progress, and access

requirements vary across project stages, departments, and stakeholder groups.

Instead of requiring tenants to create and manage accounts in C³, tenant organizations

issue project-role credentials to participants they invite. These credentials include the
tenant identifier, the project identifier, and the participant’s role, such as project owner,

contributor, reviewer, or finance approver. Many tenants distribute these credentials using
OpenID4VC flows from their existing identity, CRM, or project management systems.

Participants then present these credentials from their wallets when accessing C³.

[When a participant opens a C³ project space, the PEP for the C³ service sends an](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-16?potentialInternalRefId=146---book-markup-container)

attribute query requesting the necessary claims for policy evaluation: the tenant, project,
and role. The verification layer confirms that the credential was issued by the correct tenant

for that specific project, checks expiration and revocation status, and forwards normalized
attributes to the PDP.

[Policies in C³ can then enforce rules such as these:](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-16?potentialInternalRefId=147---book-markup-container)

Project owners may manage workspace configuration and membership.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

366

Contributors may create and edit project artifacts.

Reviewers may comment but not alter documents.
Finance approvers may view budget and billing information but not

modify project settings.

Since project roles are provided as verifiable credentials, C³ does not need to maintain a

role directory or account store for each tenant’s customers and partners. The role lifecycle
remains under the tenant’s control. When a participant’s assignment changes or the project

ends, the tenant updates or revokes the credential, and C³ automatically reflects those
changes. This enables ACME to provide a secure, flexible collaboration environment without

involving itself in every tenant’s identity and access management processes.

#### 16.9 Operational and governance considerations

Integrating verifiable credentials into authorization involves more than just protocol support
or policy design. It requires operational discipline and governance structures that ensure

the system behaves predictably as issuers, credentials, and workflows evolve. The same
principles that guided ACME’s use of contextual signals in chapter 12, such as freshness,

trust, confidence, and controlled distribution, are also applicable here. Verifiable credentials
broaden ACME’s context surface, and with that expansion comes the need to carefully

manage how issuers are assessed, how credentials are verified, and how exceptions are
handled.

16.9.1 Deciding when to use verifiable credentials

Verifiable credentials aren't necessarily a substitute for every type of identity integration.
They are most effective when any of the following apply:

**Authority resides outside ACME.** When another organization is the
primary authority for employment, licensure, delegation, or certification

VCs make the most sense.
**Participants change frequently.** Short-lived collaborations, rotating

teams, and external contractors benefit most from credential-based
access.

**Cross-organization access is the norm.** Federation works well with a
small number of partners; VCs scale to many.

**Assurance matters.** When ACME needs to trust not just an identity but
the source and integrity of specific attributes, VCs can provide strong

assurance through both technical methods and governance.
**Multiple authoritative sources are needed in a single decision.**

Some policy decisions require claims from several independent
organizations—such as employers, certifiers, regulators, or tenants—

making VCs an effective way to combine these attributes at decision time.
**Directory synchronization becomes brittle.** VCs eliminate the need to

constantly mirror external data structures inside ACME.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

367

In contrast, long-term internal employees with consistent access patterns may continue to

use ACME’s traditional account lifecycle. The aim is not uniformity; it is selecting the
appropriate tool for each trust model.

16.9.2 Failure modes and fallback paths

Credential-based access introduces new failure modes that ACME must handle gracefully.
Most are expected. Here are some of the most common:

**The holder cannot present the required credential.** Their wallet is
offline, unconfigured, or missing the claims needed for the request.

**A credential has expired or been revoked, and access is denied.**
This is the assurance model working as intended. However, from the

user’s perspective, it may feel like an error, especially if they believe they
still hold the relevant role or relationship. In these cases, ACME’s

workflow should guide the user toward resolution. For example, it might
direct them to renew a certification, request an updated delegation from

their organization, or contact the issuer responsible for the attribute that
no longer meets policy.

**The issuer is no longer trusted.** A governance update or revocation of
issuer accreditation could suddenly invalidate credentials that were

previously considered acceptable.
**Presentation flows fail.** Network interruptions, unsupported wallet

features, or browser restrictions can disrupt an otherwise valid session.

ACME must establish fallback workflows for these and similar situations. As discussed in

chapter 12, this generally involves exception-based access such as temporary permits,
break-glass procedures with rigorous auditing, or manual verification by an authorized

reviewer. These exceptions should be infrequent, limited in duration, and thoroughly logged
for future review.

16.9.3 Governance responsibilities

Governance determines who ACME trusts, for what purposes, and under which conditions.
As chapter 14 emphasized, separating policy from governance maintains consistent

authorization while allowing the trust framework to evolve.

Several responsibilities fall naturally into place:

**Identity team:** Assesses governance frameworks and issuer
accreditation models, manages the trust store, sets assurance levels, and

determines acceptable credential types for various access decisions.
**Integration and signals team (responsible for the PIP):** Maintains

issuer metadata, revocation endpoints, schema mappings, and the
normalized attribute definitions that policies depend on. This team

ensures that trust and confidence information flows smoothly into the
enforcement pipeline.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

368

**Authorization platform teams (responsible for the PEPs): Operate**

**the systems that understand and respond to credential**
**presentation protocols supported by ACME. This team makes sure**

**the correct claims are requested during access, validates the**
**resulting presentations, checks signatures and revocation status,**

**enforces freshness requirements, and normalizes verified**
**attributes before passing them to the PDP for policy evaluation.**

**Policy engineering team:** Expresses business requirements in terms of
normalized attributes instead of issuer identifiers, protocol constructs, or

credential schemas. This approach maintains the stability of policy logic
even as the ecosystem of issuers and credential types expands.

Governance ensures that ACME can adopt new issuers or credential types without rewriting
policies or changing application code. It also provides the formal framework needed to

review these trust decisions over time.

16.9.4 Rolling out verifiable credentials incrementally

Like any change in identity architecture, a gradual rollout is most effective. ACME used this

incremental approach:

1. **Begin with a narrow use case.** External auditors are ideal: a well
defined group, clear policies, and strong external authorities (NISA).
2. **Stabilize verification processes.** Test presentation flows, revocation

endpoints, and issuer trust rules across various devices and wallets.
3. **Expand to adjacent use cases.** Supplier delegations, clinician access,

and field technicians become easier after the verification service and trust
store are mature.

4. **Monitor policy outcomes.** Telemetry and decision logs help confirm that
credential-based attributes function correctly in production.

5. **Iterate governance rules.** As issuers evolve, assurance levels and
trust-store entries can be updated without altering policy logic.

This gradual adoption enabled ACME to expand credential-based authorization where it
adds the most value while ensuring continuity in existing systems.

#### 16.10 Summary

Verifiable credentials offer portable, cryptographically verifiable claims

that serve as trusted context in authorization decisions.
Credential verification establishes _confidence_ through cryptographic

proofs and _trust_ through evaluation of issuer authority and governance
frameworks.

Presentation protocols enable holders to respond selectively to attribute
requests, supporting privacy-preserving access decisions.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

369

The trust triangle and trust diamond models explain how issuers, holders,

verifiers, and governance authorities create end-to-end assurance.
Trust stores track which issuers are recognized for specific credential

types, distinguishing governance from policy logic.
Revocation and expiration checks ensure that credential-based attributes

stay current and valid when making decisions.
Verification services can be built to accept presentations from various

credential protocols and wallet types.
Normalizing credential claims into consistent attributes simplifies

authorization policies and decoupled from credential formats.
Policies evaluate attributes, not credentials, enabling new issuers or

credential types to be added without modifying policy logic.
Credential-based access is particularly useful when authority resides

outside the relying system or when participants frequently change.
Exception workflows can allow controlled access when presentations are

incomplete or credential requirements are not met.
Incremental adoption, beginning with narrow, well-governed use cases,

reduces operational risk and builds confidence in credential-based
authorization.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

370

## AI in policy practice

This chapter covers

Why AI systems must not act as authorization decision-makers

How AI assists policy authoring and design without becoming authoritative

Using AI in runtime analysis to compare design-time intent with observed behavior

Enforcing authorization before retrieval in RAG systems

How architecture enables accountability and governance in AI-enabled systems

As AI systems become part of daily life, they play a bigger and bigger role in key decisions.

These include what data is displayed, what actions are allowed, and who is accountable if
something goes wrong. As a result, many teams are tempted to delegate authorization

decisions to AI. That idea seems reasonable, but it’s usually a mistake.

Authorization exists to enforce the intent behind access decisions. It relies on

determinism, explainability, auditability, and predictable failure modes. AI systems excel at
many tasks, such as interpretation, synthesis, and exploration. When these strengths are

applied appropriately, AI can significantly enhance the design, understanding, testing, and
governance of policies without becoming the component responsible for access

determination.

[When ACME Corp started experimenting with AI tools, authorization was not the main](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-17?potentialInternalRefId=8---book-markup-container)

focus. Teams around the company explored AI for various reasons: improving developer
productivity, automating customer support, searching documents, analyzing data, and

conducting initial tests with conversational interfaces. As these tools were integrated into
existing systems, they began to interact with authorization in ways that were initially

unclear.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

371

As we’ve seen in earlier chapters, ACME already relied on policy-based authorization to

control access across its Customer Collaboration platform, internal systems, and APIs.
Policies were evaluated by shared policy engines at runtime and managed through review

and testing. Still, policy work remained challenging. Engineers found it hard to understand
the impacts of policy changes. Policy owners wanted clearer explanations of why access

was allowed or denied. Security reviews often revealed edge cases that no one had
predicted.

[Early experiments with AI showed promise. Teams asked AI tools to explain policies,](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-17?potentialInternalRefId=10---book-markup-container)
summarize rules, and explore hypothetical access situations. This chapter explores how

ACME reshaped its approach. We look at how AI supports policy creation and analysis
without influencing enforcement, how AI can show what policies actually do in practice, and

how authorization must be applied to AI-powered systems like retrieval-augmented
generation (RAG). The main idea is simple. AI should be part of the policy process, not the

final decision point. When used this way, it enhances security, boosts policy quality, and
increases accountability.

#### 17.1 AI is not your policy engine

Once AI tools became part of ACME’s daily workflows, it was only a matter of time before

someone asked the obvious question: if an AI system can explain policies, summarize
rules, and reason about access scenarios, why not let it make authorization decisions

directly?

The idea appeared in several places. One prototype support chatbot embedded access

rules directly into its prompt, instructing the AI to decide whether to display internal
documents based on conversational context and a textual description of company policy.

Another internal tool tested prompting an AI assistant to determine whether an engineer’s
request “seemed reasonable,” given a summary of their role and recent activity. In each

case, the goal was efficiency. If AI could reason about intent from context and instructions,
maybe it could make enforcement simpler.

[In these early prototypes, access was no longer controlled by policy but inferred from](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-17?potentialInternalRefId=14---book-markup-container)
text embedded in prompts. This method quickly encountered significant limitations. As

shown in Figure 17.1, embedding access intent in prompts can lead to nondeterministic
outcomes. Even when the request, context, and prompt stay the same, an AI system may

produce different authorization decisions, each backed by a plausible explanation. Without
deterministic evaluation based on policy and data, these decisions cannot be trusted for

enforcement.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

372

Figure 17.1 Nondeterministic AI authorization. When authorization intent is embedded in prompts and inferred

by an AI system, identical requests with the same context can result in different outcomes. In this example,

the same access request and prompt lead to both permit and deny decisions, each with a plausible

explanation. Since the reasoning is inferred rather than evaluated as policy, the results are not repeatable and

cannot be used as a reliable basis for access enforcement.

Authorization decisions must be consistent and reproducible. The same request, evaluated

under identical conditions, should always produce the same result. They must also be
explainable in clear terms. When access is denied, the system should be able to reference a

specific policy, rule, or condition. When access is granted, the organization must be able to
demonstrate why the decision was permitted and identify the source of intent behind it.

These qualities are essential for security reviews, audits, incident response, and regulatory
compliance.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

373

AI systems do not provide these guarantees. Given the same input, they can produce

different outputs. Their explanations might be fluent but incomplete or even wrong. They
infer intent instead of enforcing it. These traits are strengths in many situations, but they

are liabilities in authorization.

[At ACME, this distinction became clear during a design review. An engineer asked an AI](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-17?potentialInternalRefId=18---book-markup-container)

tool to explain why a particular document access request was allowed. The explanation
sounded correct and matched the policy engine's decision. However, when the team

compared it to the actual policy evaluation trace, they discovered that the AI had not
described the evaluation at all. The AI had inferred intent from the policy structure instead

of analyzing the actual authorization logic. The mistake was caught during the review, but it
revealed a deeper problem. Plausible explanations are not the same as correct decisions,

and authorization can’t rely on interpretation alone.

[That experience clarified an architectural boundary that ACME now treats as non-](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-17?potentialInternalRefId=19---book-markup-container)

negotiable. Authorization decisions and their authoritative explanations come from the
policy engine, which evaluates policies as code and data against clearly defined inputs and

current system state. Given the same request and context, it produces the same result
every time and can show exactly which rules were applied. AI systems operate differently,

excelling at inference, summarization, and exploration. At ACME, AI is allowed to assist
humans in understanding policies and decisions, but it is never allowed to substitute for

policy evaluation or serve as the source of truth for why access was granted or denied.

[Figure 17.2 shows the conceptual architecture ACME ultimately adopted to keep AI out](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-17?potentialInternalRefId=20---book-markup-container)

of the authorization decision loop. In this architecture, authorization is done first, using
policy and the current system state to determine what data and actions are permitted. That

decision produces an authorized context, which is then used to construct prompts for the
language model. The AI system never evaluates access rules and never directly queries

sensitive data. Its role is limited to operating within the boundaries already established by
authorization.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

374

Figure 17.2 AI-assisted request handling. In this architecture, authorization is evaluated before any AI

interaction. The authorization system determines the scope of access and produces an authorized context,

which is then used to construct prompts for the language model. Sensitive data is never accessed directly by

the AI. This separation ensures that access decisions remain deterministic and enforceable while still

allowing AI systems to operate on authorized inputs.

This separation illustrates a broader principle in system design. Enforcement paths should

be predictable and limited. Exploratory and interpretive tools must remain outside those
paths. By excluding AI from the enforcement loop, ACME preserved the properties that

ensure trustworthiness in authorization while still utilizing AI’s strengths elsewhere.

The rest of this chapter builds on that boundary. Instead of asking how AI can decide

access, we ask more productive questions. How can AI assist authors in creating better
policies? How can it identify gaps and unintended consequences? How can it help teams

understand what their authorization systems are really doing in production? How can
authorization limit AI-enabled systems to ensure safety by construction?

#### 17.2 Policy authoring and analysis with AI

Once ACME defined a clear boundary between authorization enforcement and AI-assisted
workflows, focus shifted to where AI could deliver the most value. One answer was policy

authoring and analysis. These activities are clearly outside the enforcement path, yet they
have a significant impact on the quality, accuracy, and maintainability of authorization

systems.

Authorization policies must represent organizational intent in a precise, unambiguous,

and deterministic manner. Converting that intent into executable policy is often challenging,
especially as policy sets grow and interact in complex ways. Even experienced engineers

can find it hard to predict the effects of small changes or to explain why a request is
allowed or denied.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

375

[ACME discovered that AI tools are well-suited for these design-time tasks. When used](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-17?potentialInternalRefId=27---book-markup-container)

[carefully, they can help draft candidate policies, clarify policy logic in plain language, and](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-17?potentialInternalRefId=27---book-markup-container)
identify edge cases that might otherwise be overlooked. None of these places AI in the

enforcement path. The policy engine remains the ultimate authority, with AI serving as an
assistant to the humans responsible for policy design.

This section explains how ACME uses AI tools to help with policy authoring and analysis at a
conceptual level. Appendix B provides a practical, step-by-step walkthrough of this workflow using

the ACME Cedar model and an AI-enabled editor. Readers interested in concrete examples, prompts,
and policy files can refer to that appendix while reading this section.

17.2.1 Explaining existing behavior

One of the earliest uses of AI at ACME was explaining why a specific authorization request

led to a particular outcome. For example, an engineer working on access control for the
Customer Collaboration platform might ask:

“Why is Kate allowed to view the Q3 plan document?”

With access to the Cedar schema, the relevant policies, and the entity relationships, the AI

could respond by pointing to a specific `permit` policy and explaining that Kate was a

member of the document’s reader relationship. This type of explanation helps engineers

and policy owners quickly verify whether the system’s behavior matches the intended
design.

These explanations were never regarded as authoritative. Engineers routinely checked
them against the actual policy evaluation trace. When the AI’s explanation was vague or

surprising, it prompted a closer inspection of the policy. In several instances, this revealed
policies that were technically correct but poorly expressed, making them difficult to

understand.

17.2.2 Exploring alternative expressions of intent

ACME also used AI to explore various methods of expressing the same authorization intent.
Suppose a product owner requested a change such as:

“Deny Kate access to this document, but don’t affect other customers.”

Instead of immediately editing policies, an engineer would ask the AI how to achieve the

desired outcome. The AI might suggest creating a new `forbid` policy targeting that specific
