principal and resource. When asked for alternatives, it might instead recommend narrowing

an existing `permit` policy or adding an `unless` clause to carve out the exception.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

376

Each option was syntactically valid and produced the same result for the immediate

request. However, they differed from a design perspective. A new `forbid` policy made the

exception explicit but created a narrow exception by increasing the number of policies. A

narrower `permit` reduced scope but made the original rule more complex. An `unless` clause

kept the general rule intact while clearly documenting the exception.

[The AI’s role was to quickly surface these alternatives. Choosing among them required](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-17?potentialInternalRefId=40---book-markup-container)
human judgment regarding clarity, maintainability, and how authority should be expressed.

The AI sped up exploration without determining which policy best aligned with ACME’s
intent and style.

17.2.3 Using concrete requests to ground analysis

ACME learned early that AI-assisted policy analysis works best when it’s based on concrete
examples instead of abstract descriptions. Rather than asking broad questions like “Who

can see customer documents?”, engineers focus discussions on specific requests and the
expected results.

For example, a team might ask:

[“What would change if this request were made outside business hours?”](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-17?potentialInternalRefId=44---book-markup-container)

“Which policy is responsible for denying access when the requester is not a workspace
member?”

By tying analysis to real requests, the AI was forced to reason within the limits of the actual
model. When responses included entities, actions, or attributes that were not present in the

schema, it was immediately obvious that the analysis had strayed. Concrete examples kept
both the AI and the human reviewer aligned with the actual system.

17.2.4 Human judgment remains central

Throughout this process, ACME treated AI output as advisory. The AI could explain
behaviors, suggest changes, and refactor policy expressions, but it could not decide which

policies to accept. That responsibility stayed with the human author, who was accountable
for understanding and defending the resulting behavior.

This distinction mattered in practice. Many policy changes that are functionally correct
still poorly communicate authority. Some obscure intent. Others introduce future risk by

overfitting to a single case. Recognizing these issues requires understanding organizational
norms, risk tolerance, and potential future developments. These judgments cannot be

delegated to an AI language model.

[The common thread in these examples is that AI accelerates understanding. It assists](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-17?potentialInternalRefId=50---book-markup-container)

teams in explaining existing behavior, exploring alternatives, and reasoning about the
effects of change. What it cannot do is determine which policy best aligns with

organizational intent.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

377

By keeping AI within the design-time workflow and outside the enforcement path, ACME

was able to enhance policy quality without compromising the guarantees that authorization
systems must ensure. Policies remained deterministic, explainable, and auditable, while

engineers received quicker feedback and better tools for expressing intent.

#### 17.3 What AI can tell you about your authorization policies

Writing a policy expresses intent; authorization systems enforce behavior. The distinction
between the two often only becomes clear at runtime, when policies are evaluated against

actual data, relationships, and context. As ACME increased its use of policy-based
authorization across systems, this gap between design-time intent and runtime reality grew

more evident.

Figure 17.3 illustrates this difference. On the left, policies are written to reflect

organizational intent, often with AI assistance to draft, explain, or refine rules. On the right,
authorization outcomes from production are recorded in decision logs and reviewed

alongside the relevant policies. AI-assisted analysis helps teams compare what happened at
runtime with what the policies were intended to express, surfacing gaps, surprises, and

edge cases. Although AI is used in both scenarios, the inputs and objectives differ, as does
the AI’s role. At design time, AI helps articulate intent. At runtime, it analyzes the results.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

378

Figure 17.3 Design-time intent versus runtime reality. Authorization policies are created to express intent at

design time, while their effects are revealed through observed decisions at runtime. Comparing these two

perspectives—how policies were intended to work and how they actually behave in production—helps teams

identify mismatches, unexpected outcomes, and areas that need governance review.

The remainder of this section examines how AI-assisted analysis reveals that reality and

how these insights contribute to clearer, more accountable policy design.

17.3.1 Seeing what policies really do

At ACME, policy owners often had a clear mental model of what a policy was supposed to

do. For example, a statement like “support agents can view customer documents” sounded
straightforward and aligned with business expectations. However, once deployed, that

intent was influenced by various factors: workspace membership, document ownership,
delegated roles, time-based conditions, and device posture.

By examining decision logs, teams could view the tangible outcomes of these
interactions. AI tools proved helpful in summarizing and analyzing this data. Instead of

manually reviewing thousands of authorization decisions, engineers could ask questions
such as:

“Who has accessed the Q3 plan in the last 30 days?”
“Which policy most often permits access to customer documents?”

“Are there principals who can access documents we did not expect them
to see?”

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

379

Because these questions were answered on the basis of observed decisions rather than

inferred intent, they often revealed surprises. In some cases, access was wider than
expected due to overlapping policies. In other cases, legitimate access was blocked because

a required relationship was missing or misconfigured.

17.3.2 Identifying gaps and edge cases

A common pattern at ACME was the discovery of edge cases that were technically correct

but operationally surprising. For instance, a policy might permit managers of a customer
account to access a document, even if they had never directly interacted with that

customer. The policy outlined the intended hierarchy accurately, but the runtime behavior
raised questions about whether that access was appropriate in all situations.

AI-assisted analysis helped teams quickly identify these scenarios. By clustering
decisions and highlighting outliers, AI tools could draw attention to rare permits or

unexpected denials. These findings did not automatically indicate a bug. Instead, they
prompted a review to see if the original intent still aligned with current expectations.

[In several instances, ACME used this insight to improve policies, clarify documentation,](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-17?potentialInternalRefId=67---book-markup-container)
or add tests that explicitly covered edge cases revealed by the process. The key point was

that runtime analysis guided design-time decisions, completing the loop between intent and
behavior.

17.3.3 Asking better questions

As teams grew more confident with this approach, the type of questions they asked
evolved. Instead of solely inquiring if a specific request was permitted, they started posing

more general questions about policy behavior:

“What is the effective audience for this document type?”

“How often do exceptions override general rules?”
“Which policies are responsible for most access decisions in this service?”

These questions were difficult to answer solely by reading policies. They required
aggregating and interpreting runtime data. AI was well-suited for this because it could help

people examine large amounts of information and find patterns worth exploring.

17.3.4 From observation to accountability

Understanding runtime behavior also played a key role in accountability. When access

decisions were challenged, ACME could present concrete evidence: the policies in effect at
the time, the data used during evaluation, and the decision that was made. AI-assisted

analysis facilitated the collection, interpretation, and explanation of this evidence,
particularly for non-technical stakeholders.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

380

Authorization decisions still originated from the policy engine, based on policy and data.

But AI assisted in explaining and analyzing those decisions afterward. This maintained the
determinism and auditability needed for authorization while increasing the system’s

transparency and clarity.

[By using AI to bridge the gap between design-time intent and runtime reality, ACME](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-17?potentialInternalRefId=77---book-markup-container)

gained a clearer understanding of how its authorization system actually functioned. That
insight made policies easier to update, defend, and align with organizational goals. Next,

we’ll see how these same principles apply when authorization is combined with retrievalaugmented generation systems, where enforcing access before retrieval becomes crucial.

#### 17.4 Authorization before retrieval: making RAG safe by construction

As ACME began experimenting with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems, the

architectural boundary that ensured authorization decisions are made by the policy engine
and not by the AI became an important safety requirement.

RAG systems combine a language model with external data sources to retrieve
documents or records, grounding generated responses in enterprise data. While this

approach can dramatically improve the relevance and usefulness of responses, it also
introduces a subtle but serious risk. RAG makes retrieval the point where context enters

the model. If retrieval is not constrained by authorization, unauthorized data can be put in
the prompt before any safeguards apply.

[ACME learned that the only reliable way to prevent this class of failure is to enforce](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-17?potentialInternalRefId=81---book-markup-container)
authorization before retrieval. Instead of asking the language model to decide what

information is appropriate, the system must first determine which data is allowed to be
retrieved at all. Only authorized data is ever placed into the model’s context. This makes

the system safe by construction, eliminating reliance on prompt discipline or model
behavior.

17.4.1 A quick review of how RAG works

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) provides a language model with application- or
domain-specific documents and data. Rather than relying solely on the model’s internal

parameters, a RAG system retrieves relevant information at runtime and injects it into the
prompt used to generate a response.

In a RAG architecture

Application- or domain-specific and data documents are broken into

chunks and converted into vector embeddings.
Those chunks are stored in a vector database, typically alongside

metadata such as document identifiers, ownership, classification, or
tenancy.

When a user submits a query, the system first _embeds_ it, converting the
text into a numerical vector that represents its semantic meaning.

The system uses the query embedding to retrieve the most relevant
chunks from the vector database.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

381

Those retrieved chunks are inserted into the prompt as additional

context.
The language model generates a response using both the user’s

instruction and the retrieved material.

This pattern is well documented and widely implemented; canonical descriptions can be

found in documentation from OpenAI, Amazon Web Services, and LangChain. From an
authorization perspective, however, one detail matters more than all others: RAG adds

system-selected context to the user-provided context. The RAG application determines
which information is retrieved and presented to the AI. That decision point is exactly where

authorization must be enforced.

17.4.2 Retrieval is the enforcement boundary

In traditional applications, authorization controls what data a requester can access directly.

In a RAG system, retrieval serves a similar purpose. Retrieved documents become part of
the model’s working context, influencing not only what it can state explicitly but also what

it can infer implicitly when generating a response.

Many early RAG implementations tried to control access at the prompt or response level.

Prompts contained instructions like “do not reveal sensitive information,” or responses were
edited afterward to remove unwanted content. These methods view the language model as

a tool for enforcement.

[ACME considered this approach to be inherently unsafe. Language models infer intent](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-17?potentialInternalRefId=95---book-markup-container)

from context, respond based on probabilities, and lack an understanding of policy, scope, or
accountability. Once unauthorized data enters the model’s context window, it can subtly

influence the output in ways that are hard to detect or audit, even if the final response
seems compliant.

[The key point is that retrieval is the last step where access control can be enforced](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-17?potentialInternalRefId=96---book-markup-container)
reliably. If unauthorized data is never accessed, it cannot be leaked, summarized, or

analyzed by the model. Authorization after retrieval is already too late. This leads directly
to the architectural principle that governs ACME’s RAG systems: _authorization must occur_

_before retrieval, not after generation_ .

17.4.3 From architectural principle to concrete flow

Figure 17.4 illustrates how ACME applied the architectural boundary introduced earlier in

Figure 17.2 to a retrieval-augmented generation system. The overall service structure
remains the same: the application receives a request, builds context, calls on an LLM, and

returns a response. The key change is where and how authorization impacts retrieval.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

382

Figure 17.4 Authorization before retrieval in RAG systems. Authorization constrains retrieval rather than

generated output. By enforcing access before data is retrieved, the system ensures that the language model

operates only on authorized inputs, making information leakage structurally impossible rather than merely

discouraged.

In this design, the application logic first uses a request constructor to build a structured
authorization request from user information, including the principal and the requested

action. That request is then passed to the Cedar component (see the sidebar to this section
for more on this), which evaluates the relevant policies using TPE (typed partial evaluation).

Instead of returning a simple `allow` or `deny` decision, Cedar TPE produces a policy residual

that shows the remaining constraints under which access would be allowed.

The policy residual is then passed to a component that converts it into a query filter that
represents concrete constraints that can be applied during retrieval. Each chunk in the

vector database is stored with metadata that captures relevant attributes, such as tenant,
ownership, or classification. The query filter is applied to this metadata when retrieving

results, ensuring that only chunks within the authorized scope are considered. For example,
in a multi-tenant system, the filter might restrict retrieval to chunks associated with a

specific tenant.

[The retrieved results constitute authorized additional context. This context flows into a](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-17?potentialInternalRefId=102---book-markup-container)

prompt constructor, where it is combined with the user’s instruction to form the final
prompt sent to the LLM. Because retrieval itself is constrained by policy, the language

model never sees unauthorized data. Its role is limited to generating output based on
inputs that have already been vetted by authorization.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

383

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

384

In a production system, this constraint could be used to search a vector database;

however, in this demonstration, we simply translate the residual into the filter.

**Why this matters**

This example demonstrates the main point of this section: authorization-beforeretrieval is not just a quick fix or a recommended practice. Instead, it is a design

pattern that prevents certain types of failures. By integrating access control into the
retrieval process and basing it on policy evaluation, systems can securely combine

AI-driven interactions with sensitive enterprise data.

Readers interested in exploring the mechanics more deeply can use the notebook to

experiment with different authorization scenarios and observe how policy changes
influence retrieval behavior. The notebook is meant to be exploratory rather than

prescriptive, emphasizing that enforcement remains deterministic while AI functions
as an assistant rather than an authority.

17.4.4 Safe by construction, not safe by instruction

This architecture shifts responsibility for access control from prompts and model behavior

to system design. Prompts still influence quality, tone, and task framing, but they no longer
bear the responsibility of enforcing access boundaries. These boundaries are enforced

structurally before any data retrieval.

For ACME, this distinction was crucial. Requiring authorization before retrieval prevented

numerous failure modes and made governance easier. When questions arose about what an
AI system could see or explain, the answer always traced back to policy and authorized

scope, not prompt wording or model behavior.

[By embedding authorization into the retrieval path, ACME made its RAG systems safe by](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-17?potentialInternalRefId=124---book-markup-container)

construction rather than relying on best-effort controls. As AI systems advance beyond
retrieval to autonomous action and delegation, this same principle becomes even more

vital, creating a foundation for accountability in increasingly agent-driven architectures.
We’ll explore this more in the next chapter.

#### 17.5 From architecture to accountability: how AI helps policy become practice

Earlier in this chapter, we discussed architectural boundaries: where AI belongs, where it
doesn't, and how authorization limits what AI systems can access and do. Those boundaries

are necessary but not sufficient. Authorization only gains meaning when decisions can be
understood, explained, and acted upon over time. That is the purpose of accountability.

Figure 17.3 visually introduced this concept. Figure 17.5 reproduces the right side of
that figure.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

385

Figure 17.5 Runtime analysis and governance loop. Authorization outcomes captured in decision logs are

analyzed with AI assistance and surfaced as questions, patterns, and reports. These insights feed into

governance processes, where humans interpret the evidence and decide whether policy changes are needed.

The flow makes authorization behavior observable and actionable without placing AI in the enforcement path.

On the right side of the figure, authorization outcomes are recorded in decision logs,

analyzed with AI support, and fed into governance processes, which, in turn, affect policies.
This section elaborates on that flow. It explains how observed authorization behavior

becomes evidence, how that evidence guides review and oversight, and how AI helps close
the loop between architectural intent and organizational responsibility.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

386

At ACME, the shift to policy-based authorization laid a foundation for consistent decision
making, but it didn't automatically bring clarity. As policies increased in number and
complexity, teams faced practical questions that were hard to answer by inspection: Who

can access this resource today? Why was one request granted while another was denied?
Which policies dominate outcomes in practice?

17.5.1 Accountability starts with observable decisions

Accountability goes beyond having well-written policies. It also requires evidence. As we
discussed earlier, that evidence comes from authorization decisions recorded at runtime,

linked to the policies and data that generated them. These decision logs provided a factual
record of what the system allowed and denied, regardless of what anyone believed the

policies were meant to do.

AI-assisted analysis made this record useful. By summarizing patterns in decision logs,

highlighting outliers, and linking outcomes to specific policies, AI tools help teams turn
anecdotes into evidence-based observations. Questions like “Who can actually access this

resource?” or “Why did this decision happen?” can be examined directly through observed
behavior.

[This is the initial step in the governance process depicted in figure 17.5. The aim is not](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-17?potentialInternalRefId=134---book-markup-container)
to automate judgment but to uncover information that would otherwise be hidden in logs.

17.5.2 Turning reports into responsibility

Once authorization outcomes become visible, responsibility is easier to identify. When
authorization logic is embedded in application code or spread across multiple systems, it’s

often unclear who is responsible for a specific decision. In contrast, policy-based
authorization produces decisions that can be traced to specific policies and, consequently,

to their owners.

AI-assisted analysis helps make these connections explicit. It can identify which policies

are most frequently used, which ones lead to unexpected outcomes, and where exceptions
override general rules. These reports do not make decisions, but they shape the questions

governance bodies need to answer.

[At ACME, this shifted governance conversations away from abstract discussions and](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-17?potentialInternalRefId=138---book-markup-container)

toward concrete behavior. Instead of questioning whether a policy appeared reasonable,
reviewers could assess if actual outcomes still aligned with organizational goals.

Responsibility shifted from interpretation to accountability.

17.5.3 Closing the feedback loop

Figure 17.3 shows two feedback loops. The design-time loop refines policy intent through

authoring and review. The runtime loop uses observed outcomes to inform governance
processes.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

387

Here we’re focusing on the runtime loop, shown in figure 17.5, where AI supports

analysis and reporting while humans make governance decisions. It helps summarize what
happened, highlight what is unusual, and connect outcomes back to the policies that

produced them. What it does not do is decide whether those outcomes are acceptable. That
decision remains with humans in ACME’s policy governance process, guided by evidence

rather than intuition.

[When governance determines that a policy no longer reflects desired behavior, changes](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-17?potentialInternalRefId=142---book-markup-container)

are made intentionally and re-enter the design-time cycle. In this way, architecture,
analysis, and governance support each other without collapsing into automated

enforcement.

17.5.4 Why architecture makes accountability possible

None of this works without the architectural constraints outlined earlier in the chapter. If AI

systems are allowed to infer access from prompts, retrieve data without permission, or act
independently without policy review, the reports supporting governance lose their

significance. Decisions become hard to explain and even harder to defend.

In contrast, architectures establish stable points of control when they restrict AI to

assisting and analyzing require authorization before retrieval, and log decisions
consistently. They ensure that access decisions are observable, attributable, and

reviewable.

[This is how architecture supports accountability. It doesn’t ensure sound decisions, but it](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-17?potentialInternalRefId=146---book-markup-container)

clarifies responsibility and makes governance practical.

17.5.5 Policy as practice

Figure 17.5 clearly illustrates one last point: Policy is not a static artifact. It is a practice.

Policies are written, evaluated, observed, questioned, revised, and managed over time. AI
can support every stage of this process without replacing the systems that implement

policy or the individuals responsible for its outcomes.

At ACME, this distinction proved crucial. AI enhanced the creation, analysis, and review

of policies. Authorization limited what AI systems could access and perform. Governance
procedures ensured that observed behavior stayed aligned with intent. Together, these

elements transformed policy from a specification into an operational discipline. _This is how_
_policy becomes practice._

#### 17.6 Summary

Authorization needs predictability, transparency, and traceability, which AI

systems cannot deliver.
AI works best when it is limited to assistance roles such as drafting,

explaining, and analyzing.
Embedding authorization logic within prompts as text results in

unpredictable and unsafe outcomes.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

388

Clear architectural boundaries stop AI systems from turning into implicit

enforcement tools.
Design-time intent and runtime behavior frequently differ, especially in

complex policy systems.
Decision logs offer the evidence necessary to understand how

authorization behaves in practice.
AI-assisted analysis helps reveal unexpected outcomes, edge cases, and

policy interactions.
Governance relies on observable actions, not guessed intentions or likely

explanations.
In retrieval-augmented generation systems, retrieval serves as the proper

enforcement point.
Authorizing before retrieval prevents unauthorized data from ever

entering an AI model’s context.
Policy residuals can be utilized to convert authorization results into

retrieval constraints.
Architecture, not prompts, determines whether AI-enabled systems are

safe by construction.
Accountability emerges when decisions are traceable from outcomes back

to policy and ownership.
Policy becomes a practice when authoring, observation, and governance

form a continuous loop.
