## Authorization for AI agents

This chapter covers

Why authorization becomes the hardest problem in agentic AI systems

How AI agents interact with enterprise systems and their authorization
requirements

Policy-aware agent loops and runtime authorization checks

Using policies to guide agent behavior, not simply to deny actions

Delegation and subagent authority in agentic systems

A year after launching the Customer Collaboration platform, ACME started experimenting

with a new class of tools powered by artificial intelligence (AI). What began as a few
internal prototypes quickly spread throughout the organization. Engineers used agents to

analyze logs and troubleshoot deployments. Sales teams utilized them to prepare account
briefings. Customer support tested agents that could summarize cases and suggest

responses.

The early results were impressive. Tasks that once took hours of manual effort could now

be done in minutes. The engineering team developed integrations that let agents access
internal systems, retrieve documents, and carry out routine operational tasks. The

company started to envision an AI-enabled workforce where software agents worked
alongside employees.

[To coordinate these efforts, ACME hired Trudy, a seasoned technology leader, as Senior](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-18?potentialInternalRefId=8---book-markup-container)
Director for AI. Trudy’s mandate was simple in principle but ambitious in scope: help ACME

deploy AI agents safely and effectively across the enterprise.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

390

In her first weeks, Trudy met with teams across the company to understand how they

were using these new tools. The conversations were lively. Teams described agents that
could read documents, analyze customer data, prepare reports, and even trigger

workflows.

[But one pattern quickly caught her attention. Most of these systems focused on what](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-18?potentialInternalRefId=10---book-markup-container)

agents could do, but almost none of them clearly defined what agents should be allowed to
do. During a meeting with ACME’s identity team, Trudy asked a simple question.

[“What exactly are these agents authorized to do in our systems?”](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-18?potentialInternalRefId=11---book-markup-container)

[The room went quiet.](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-18?potentialInternalRefId=12---book-markup-container)

[The engineers explained that agents accessed internal APIs using the same mechanisms](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-18?potentialInternalRefId=13---book-markup-container)
used by applications and employees. Authentication verified that requests came from the

correct service or account. But beyond that, authorization decisions were often implicit. If
an agent could reach a tool or API, it could usually use it.

[Trudy immediately saw the problem. Traditional software follows predictable code paths,](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-18?potentialInternalRefId=14---book-markup-container)
so authorization rules can be written with confidence, knowing how the application will

behave. Agents are different. They plan actions dynamically, choose tools at runtime, and
revise their strategies as they gather new information. In systems like this, authorization

can't simply act as a gate at the system's edge. It must become part of the agent’s ongoing
decision-making process.

[This flexibility to replan is what makes agentic systems powerful. It is also what makes](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-18?potentialInternalRefId=15---book-markup-container)
them hard to control. Trudy summarized the problem during a follow-up discussion with the

engineering team: “Authentication tells us who is making a request,” she said. “But agents
introduce a new problem. We also need to govern how they behave.”

[That realization led ACME to a greater challenge. If agents could dynamically plan](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-18?potentialInternalRefId=16---book-markup-container)
actions and invoke tools throughout the enterprise, then authorization could no longer be

seen as a static barrier at the system's edge. It had to become an ongoing part of the
agent’s decision-making process. In other words, authorization was no longer just about

controlling access; it became about shaping how agents interact with surrounding systems.

[Here we will examine how ACME addressed that challenge. We analyze why traditional](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-18?potentialInternalRefId=17---book-markup-container)

authorization models have difficulty with agentic systems, how policy-aware agent
architectures can establish safe boundaries, and how techniques like policy constraints and

delegated authority can influence agent behavior.

[Along the way, we will see how ACME incorporated authorization directly into the agent's](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-18?potentialInternalRefId=18---book-markup-container)

execution loop and how policies written in Cedar became a crucial part of governing agent
activity. AI agents may represent a new class of actors in software systems, but the

principles of effective authorization architecture still apply. If anything, they are more
important than ever.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

391

#### 18.1 Why authorization is the hard problem in agentic AI

In the weeks after her arrival at ACME, Trudy started reviewing the company’s early AI

experiments. Engineers integrated language models with internal tools. Sales teams used
agents to prepare account briefings. Operations teams tested agents that could diagnose

infrastructure issues and trigger automated workflows.

Most of these systems followed a similar pattern. A language model was wrapped in an

agent framework that allowed it to interact with enterprise systems using various tools.
These tools provided functions such as retrieving documents, querying databases, and

calling internal APIs.

[The architecture worked well technically. Agents could reason about problems, select](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-18?potentialInternalRefId=22---book-markup-container)

tools, and combine their outputs to achieve complex goals. But as Trudy spoke with the
teams developing these systems, she noticed that most conversations focused on what

agents could do. Very few discussed what agents should be allowed to do.

[Traditional authorization models assume software behaves predictably. As Trudy](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-18?potentialInternalRefId=23---book-markup-container)

observed, that assumption no longer holds for agentic systems. Agents plan their actions
dynamically. Given a goal, an agent can explore multiple strategies, use different tools, and

adapt its plan as it acquires new information. The sequence of actions may differ from one
execution to another. This flexibility is what makes agents powerful, but it also makes them

difficult to govern. Three characteristics of agentic systems create this challenge:

**Dynamic planning** —agents decide which actions to take at runtime.

**Tool-based execution** —agents rely on external tools that may access
sensitive data or systems.

**Adaptive behavior** —agents revise their plans as they gather new
information.

These are not edge cases. They are defining properties of agentic systems. Together, these
characteristics mean that authorization can no longer rely on static assumptions about how

software will operate. Each action must be evaluated in the context in which it occurs.

In this sense, authorization in agentic systems becomes a natural extension of Zero

Trust principles. Instead of assuming an application will behave as intended, the system
continuously evaluates each action the agent proposes, verifying that it complies with policy

under current conditions.

[At ACME, this led to a shift from treating authorization as a gate at the edge of an](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-18?potentialInternalRefId=29---book-markup-container)

application to embedding it directly into the agent’s runtime decision-making process.
Before invoking a tool or accessing data, the agent constructs a request describing the

action it plans to take, which ACME’s policy engine evaluates using the same enterprise
policy infrastructure that governs the rest of its systems.

[Agents did not receive their own authorization system. Instead, they operated under the](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-18?potentialInternalRefId=30---book-markup-container)
same policy architecture that governed the rest of ACME’s software systems. While the

governance process and tooling were the same, the policies were adapted to control agent
behavior, emphasizing tool use, delegation, and runtime constraints instead of the static

workflows common in traditional applications.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

392

[Trudy summarized the change like this: “In traditional systems, authorization answers](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-18?potentialInternalRefId=31---book-markup-container)

the question Can this application access this resource? With agents, the question becomes
Is this action safe for the agent to perform right now?” In other words, agentic systems

turn authorization from a static configuration problem into a continuous governance
challenge.

#### 18.2 How agents interact with external systems

As Trudy and the engineering team examined ACME’s early agent deployments, another

architectural pattern quickly became evident. Agents rarely work alone. To perform useful
tasks, they need to communicate with other systems.

In most agent frameworks, these interactions happen through some type of tool
invocation. A tool might retrieve documents, query a database, call an internal API, or

trigger an automated workflow. The agent decides which tools to use as it works toward a
goal.

[Different systems present these capabilities in various ways. Some use structured tool](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-18?potentialInternalRefId=35---book-markup-container)
interfaces where available operations are clearly described and accessed through defined

schemas. Others enable agents to interact with systems via command-line interfaces or
scripted environments. In both cases, the fundamental pattern remains the same: the

agent requests to perform some operation outside the model itself.

[From an authorization perspective, this pattern is essential. Every time an agent invokes](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-18?potentialInternalRefId=36---book-markup-container)

a tool or executes a command, it is trying to perform an action on a resource. Conceptually,
these requests follow the same _PARC model_ introduced earlier in the book. Each request

specifies the _principal_ making the request, the _action_ it plans to take, the affected _resource_,
and the _context_ in which it occurs.

[The key difference is in how often they occur. Traditional applications usually follow](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-18?potentialInternalRefId=37---book-markup-container)
predictable workflows, leading to a few authorization checks during a transaction. Agents,

on the other hand, might try many actions while testing different strategies to solve a
problem.

[This means authorization decisions are no longer occasional checkpoints in a workflow.](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-18?potentialInternalRefId=38---book-markup-container)
They become a continuous part of the interaction between the agent and the surrounding

systems.

[Figure 18.1 illustrates this relationship. An agent chooses a tool or command to invoke,](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-18?potentialInternalRefId=39---book-markup-container)

submits a request describing the intended operation, and the policy engine evaluates the
request before executing the action.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

393

Figure 18.1 Authorization during agent tool invocation. When an agent invokes a tool or command, the

request passes through a policy enforcement point. The enforcement point asks the policy decision point

whether the action is permitted before the tool executes.

For ACME, this architecture reinforced Trudy’s earlier conclusion: authorization could not

simply sit at the edge of the system. It had to be embedded in the interaction between
agents and the tools they use.

Next, we will explore how ACME integrated policy evaluation directly into the agent’s
execution loop.

WHY AUTHENTICATION ISN’T ENOUGH FOR AGENTS

Authentication answers a simple question: Who is making this request?

In traditional software systems, that answer is often enough. Once an application or
user is authenticated, authorization policies can grant access based on predefined

roles or permissions. Because the application's behavior is predictable, those policies
can be written confidently with respect to how the system will operate. _Agentic_

_systems break that assumption._

An agent can use various tools, access different data, and try different strategies

each time it attempts to achieve a goal. Knowing who the agent is doesn’t reveal
what actions it might take next.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

394

For this reason, agent systems cannot depend solely on authentication. Each action

proposed by the agent must be assessed against policy in real-time. Authorization
acts as the mechanism that limits the agent’s behavior, making sure that even

dynamically planned actions stay within safe limits.

#### 18.3 A policy-aware agent loop

The interaction shown in figure 18.1 does not occur just once. As an agent works toward a

goal, it repeatedly plans, acts, evaluates results, and revises its strategy. Each step may
involve invoking tools, accessing data, or triggering workflows.

In traditional applications, authorization checks are placed at specific points in a
predefined workflow. With agents, there is no fixed sequence of steps. The path to

completing a task emerges dynamically as the agent explores different strategies. This
means authorization decisions can no longer be treated as occasional checkpoints. They

must be integrated into the agent’s ongoing execution loop.

[ACME addressed this challenge by embedding policy evaluation directly into the agent’s](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-18?potentialInternalRefId=51---book-markup-container)

runtime behavior. Rather than allowing the agent to invoke tools freely, every attempted
action passes through a policy enforcement point (PEP) before execution. Figure 18.2

illustrates this architecture.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

395

Figure 18.2 A policy-aware agent loop. An agent iteratively plans and executes actions while a policy

enforcement point evaluates each proposed action before execution. Authorization decisions become part of

the agent’s feedback loop, allowing it to revise its plan when actions are denied.

Each time the agent proposes an action—such as reading a document or calling an API—the

request is intercepted by the PEP. The enforcement point then constructs an authorization
request using the familiar PARC model:

**principal** —the agent invoking the tool
**action** —the operation requested (for example, `documents.read` )

**resource** —the target system or data
**context** —task-specific information such as the customer, file path, or

environment

This request is sent to the policy decision point (PDP), where Cedar evaluates it against the

relevant policies. If the decision is `permit`, the tool executes. If the decision is `deny`, the

action is blocked, and the agent must revise its plan.

Conceptually, the flow looks like this:

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

396

build authorization request

send request to policy engine

if decision == permit:

execute tool

else:

return denial to agent and replan

This pattern transforms authorization from a static gate into a continuous control loop.

Every action the agent attempts is evaluated in context, ensuring that dynamically
generated behavior stays within defined boundaries.

Appendix C provides hands-on demonstrations of the authorization patterns described in this
chapter. Section C.3 shows the reactive authorization model in action, illustrating how each tool

invocation is evaluated by a policy enforcement point and how permit or deny decisions feed back
into the agent’s execution loop.

18.3.1 Authorization as part of the feedback loop

Besides preventing unsafe actions, embedding authorization in the agent loop also changes

the agent’s behavior.

When a traditional application encounters an authorization failure, it typically returns an

error to the caller. In an agent system, a denial serves as input to the agent’s reasoning
process. The agent interprets the failure, updates its understanding of the environment,

and attempts an alternative strategy.

[For example, consider an agent tasked with retrieving information from a protected](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-18?potentialInternalRefId=67---book-markup-container)

directory. If the agent attempts to read a file outside its authorized scope, the PEP blocks
the request and returns a denial. The agent then revises its plan, perhaps selecting a

different data source or narrowing its query.

[This interaction creates a feedback loop:](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-18?potentialInternalRefId=68---book-markup-container)

1. The agent proposes an action.
2. The policy system evaluates the action.

3. The result influences the agent’s next step.

Authorization decisions, therefore, serve as signals that guide the agent’s behavior, not

merely controls that block it.

18.3.2 Defining operational boundaries with policy

The policies that govern agent behavior are often straightforward. Some restrict which
actions the agent can perform, while others limit the resources it can access.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

397

For example, ACME allows agents to work with customer documents but restricts access

to those owned by the customer associated with the current task:

permit (

principal,

action in [

Action::"documents.search",

Action::"documents.read",

Action::"documents.summarize"

],

resource in Entity::CustomerDocument

)

when {

resource.customerId == context.customerId

};

This policy sets a clear boundary. The agent can explore different strategies for completing

its task, but every action must remain within the scope of the current customer.

Other policies restrict entire categories of actions. For instance, agents may be allowed

to trigger workflows but not to modify them:

forbid (

principal in Agent,

action in [

Action::"automation.create",

Action::"automation.update",

Action::"automation.delete"

],

resource in Entity::Automation

);

This distinction between operational and control-plane actions is critical. Agents can carry

out useful work, but they cannot alter the systems that define that work. In effect, the
policy system “childproofs” the environment, enabling safe interaction while protecting

critical controls.

18.3.3 From predefined workflows to governed behavior

The policy-aware loop marks a fundamental shift in how systems are designed. In

traditional software, developers define workflows and insert authorization checks at
predetermined points. The system’s behavior is predictable, and policies are written with

that predictability in mind.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

398

In agentic systems, behavior is not predefined. The agent determines its own sequence

of actions based on its goals and the information it gathers. This makes static authorization
models insufficient.

[By integrating policy evaluation into the execution loop, ACME ensured that every action](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-18?potentialInternalRefId=84---book-markup-container)
—regardless of how it was generated—would be assessed against the same set of rules.

Policies no longer require knowing the application’s overall behavior in advance. Instead,
they evaluate each action as it occurs.

[This approach aligns naturally with Zero Trust principles. Rather than assuming a system](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-18?potentialInternalRefId=85---book-markup-container)
will behave as expected, each action is verified in real time based on current conditions.

18.3.4 Practical implications

In practice, embedding authorization in the agent loop has several important effects:

**Continuous enforcement** —Every action is checked before it executes,

not just at system entry points.
**Dynamic adaptability** —Policies apply even when the agent’s behavior

changes from one execution to another.
**Clear operational boundaries** —Agents can explore freely within

defined limits but cannot exceed them.
**Behavioral feedback** —Denials inform the agent’s planning process,

shaping its approach to a task.

These properties enable safe deployment of agents in environments where they interact

with sensitive data and critical systems.

At ACME, this architecture enabled agents to access enterprise tools, analyze data, and

automate workflows while remaining subject to the same policy framework that governed
employees and applications. Agents were not treated as a special case. They became

another class of principal operating within the organization’s authorization system.

[The result is a system where flexibility and control coexist. Agents retain the ability to](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-18?potentialInternalRefId=94---book-markup-container)

plan and adapt, but every action they take is constrained by policy. Authorization is integral
to the agent's operation, not merely an external safeguard.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

399

AgentCore Policy uses the Cedar policy language to specify what tools an agent can

invoke and under which conditions. These policies are assessed outside the agent’s
runtime, usually at an enforcement gateway that controls access to external

systems. This design enables organizations to externalize decision logic, maintain
centralized governance, and ensure uniform enforcement across multiple agents and

applications.

For example, an enterprise might allow a customer-support agent to retrieve account

information but prohibit it from starting financial transactions. Another policy might
permit a procurement agent to submit purchase requests only within specified

spending limits. Because these policies are expressed declaratively and evaluated at
runtime, they can adapt flexibly to changing contexts such as user identity,

delegation relationships, or operational constraints.

AgentCore Policy marks a significant shift in how AI systems are built. Instead of

embedding behavioral rules directly into agent code or prompts, organizations are
now starting to treat agent authorization as a primary architectural concern. This

change is in line with the larger move toward policy-based access control for
dynamic systems, where decisions are handled externally and assessed on an

ongoing basis.

As agent ecosystems become more complex—with agents calling on other agents,

acting for humans, and engaging with sensitive enterprise systems—formal
authorization methods like Cedar-based policy evaluation will play an increasingly

important role in ensuring trust, safety, and operational accuracy.

#### 18.4 Beyond denial: guiding agent behavior with policy constraints

When ACME first implemented the policy-aware loop described in the previous section, the

system behaved much like a traditional authorization system. Each time the agent
attempted to invoke a tool, the policy engine evaluated the request and either permitted or

denied it. This approach was correct, but it revealed a practical limitation.

Agents do not follow a single path to a solution. They explore multiple strategies, trying

different actions as they work toward a goal. When an action is denied, the agent revises
its plan and tries something else. In some cases, the agent might repeatedly attempt

actions that the policy would never allow.

[From the policy system's perspective, everything was working as intended. From the](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-18?potentialInternalRefId=104---book-markup-container)

agent's perspective, however, the system provided very little guidance. The agent learned
what not to do by trial and error.

[ACME’s engineers realized that denial alone was not enough. If policy was going to](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-18?potentialInternalRefId=105---book-markup-container)
govern agent behavior effectively, it needed to do more than block unsafe actions. It

needed to help the agent understand which actions were possible before it attempted them.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

400

Appendix C.4 provides a working demonstration of this pattern. The constraint-aware planning

demo shows how partial requests produce policy residuals that the agent can use to guide its
planning before executing actions.

18.4.1 From reactive enforcement to constraint-aware planning

To address this, ACME extended the role of the policy system. Instead of only using it to

evaluate fully specified authorization requests, they enabled the agent to query the policy
system during planning.

The key idea is simple: rather than just asking “is this action allowed?”, the agent can
ask broader questions like:

Given my identity and the current context, which actions am I allowed to
perform?

For a given action, which resources can I access?

This shift transforms the policy system from a simple gate into a constraint system that

actively guides planning.

ACME implemented this capability using Cedar’s Typed Partial Evaluation (TPE). As

discussed in chapter 17, TPE enables the policy engine to evaluate policies even when part
of the request is unspecified. By leaving one element of the PARC model open—such as the

action or the resource—the policy engine can return the conditions under which a request
would succeed. Figure 18.3 illustrates how this capability extends the policy-aware agent

loop.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

401

Figure 18.3 Policy constraints guiding agent planning. During planning, the agent queries the policy system

with a partial request. The policy engine returns constraints—such as permitted actions or accessible

resources—that the agent incorporates into its plan. Each action is still evaluated at execution time to ensure

consistent enforcement.

Instead of proposing actions blindly, the agent now directly incorporates policy-derived
constraints into its reasoning. During planning, it can submit a partial authorization request

—for example, specifying the principal, resource, and context while leaving the action
unspecified.

Rather than simply returning permit or deny decisions, the policy engine produces a
structured result that specifies which actions satisfy the policy conditions. Conceptually, the

response might look like this:

principal: Agent::"acme_assist"

resource: CustomerDocument::"custco-briefing"

permitted_actions:

 - documents.search

 - documents.read

 - documents.summarize

The agent can then construct a plan using only actions that are likely to succeed.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

402

18.4.2 Integrating constraints into the planning loop

ACME integrated this capability by adding a constraint-query interface to the existing
authorization check.

During planning, the agent:

1. Identifies a potential action or resource.

2. Queries the policy system with a partial request.
3. Receives policy-derived constraints in the form of a policy residual.

4. Develops a plan within those constraints.

Later, during execution, each action still flows through the policy-aware loop described in

section 18.3. The constraint query does not replace enforcement. It complements it.

This distinction is essential:

Constraint queries guide planning.
Authorization checks enforce decisions.

The policy engine is the authoritative source of truth in both cases.

18.4.3 Reducing trial and error

Consider an agent attempting to access a restricted directory containing credential files. In
a purely reactive system, the agent may explore different ways to access the files—

effectively probing for a path that works—only to discover through repeated denials that
access is not permitted. Each denial forces the agent to revise its plan, resulting in

repeated failures.

With constraint-aware planning, the agent queries the policy system first. A policy that

restricts access to credential files returns a result indicating that such operations are not
permitted. The agent incorporates this constraint into its reasoning and avoids attempting

the operation entirely.

[This reduces trial-and-error behavior and improves both efficiency and safety. The agent](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-18?potentialInternalRefId=135---book-markup-container)

spends less time exploring invalid paths and is less likely to generate unnecessary or risky
requests.

18.4.4 Policy as a source of guidance

This approach changes the role of policy in the system. In traditional authorization models,
policy primarily serves as a gate. It evaluates requests and blocks those that violate

defined rules. In a constraint-aware model, policy also serves as a guide.

Table 18.1 compares the reactive and constraint-aware approaches.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

403

Table 18.1 Reactive authorization versus constraint-aware authorization in agent planning

|Reactive authorization model|Constraint-aware authorization model|
|---|---|
|Agent proposes writing to any path|Agent queries allowed write paths first|
|PDP denies disallowed paths at runtime|PDP returns allowed path constraints during<br>planning|
|Denial triggers replanning|Plan is formed within defined constraints|
|Higher frequency of runtime denials|Fewer runtime denials|
|Policy acts primarily as a gate|Policy acts as both boundary definition and<br>gate|

By exposing policy constraints during planning, the system enables the agent to reason

within the boundaries defined by policy rather than discovering those boundaries through
failure.

18.4.5 From control to collaboration

Constraint-aware authorization marks a shift from controlling agent behavior to
collaborating with it. Instead of simply blocking unsafe actions, the policy system provides

information that helps the agent make better decisions. The agent remains flexible and
adaptive, yet its behavior is shaped by the same policy framework that governs the rest of

the system.

At ACME, this approach improved both efficiency and predictability. Agents generated

fewer failed requests, completed tasks more directly, and operated more consistently within
defined boundaries.

[More importantly, it highlighted a key architectural principle for agentic systems:](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-18?potentialInternalRefId=144---book-markup-container)
authorization is not just about preventing actions. It is about shaping behavior. By making

policy both a boundary and a source of guidance, ACME enabled its agents to operate safely
while fully leveraging their ability to plan and adapt.

SEQUENCING AGENT BEHAVIOR WITH POLICY

The examples in this section illustrate how policy can guide an agent’s behavior by

specifying which actions are permitted. In many real-world scenarios, however, it is
not enough to control _what_ an agent can do. We must also control _when it can do it_ .

Agents typically execute tasks as a sequence of steps. As they progress, they gather
information, produce intermediate results, and sometimes gain access to additional

capabilities. A permission that is safe at one stage of a task may be unsafe at
another. For example, an agent that is allowed to send email might need to

summarize documents first. Allowing access to email too early could expose sensitive
information from the agent’s working context.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

404

#### 18.5 Childproofing the control plane

As ACME’s engineers refined their agent architecture, Trudy raised another concern. The

new systems were becoming more capable. Agents could retrieve data, call APIs, and
trigger automated workflows across the company’s systems.

That capability raised an obvious question: what would prevent an agent from modifying
the systems that governed those actions?

[In many modern platforms, the same APIs used to perform operational tasks can also](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-18?potentialInternalRefId=158---book-markup-container)
alter the system's configuration. These operations make up the system’s control plane, the

set of tools used to define workflows, manage infrastructure, and configure policies.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

405

[If an agent were permitted to freely modify these components, it could potentially](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-18?potentialInternalRefId=159---book-markup-container)

weaken the safeguards designed to constrain it.

[Trudy emphasized that ACME’s engineers should treat the control plane differently from](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-18?potentialInternalRefId=160---book-markup-container)

normal operational tools. “We should assume agents will eventually try everything they
can,” she told the team. “So we need to make sure the important knobs are out of reach.”

[The engineers responded by implementing strict policy controls on any operation capable](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-18?potentialInternalRefId=161---book-markup-container)
of modifying the system’s configuration. Tools that created or updated workflows, changed

infrastructure settings, or altered authorization policies were restricted to only authorized
principals. Agents acting under delegated authority were permitted to perform operational

tasks, but they were explicitly forbidden from modifying the control plane.

[For example, ACME’s internal automation platform allows users and services to trigger](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-18?potentialInternalRefId=162---book-markup-container)

predefined workflows. Agents can start existing workflows as part of their tasks but cannot
create new workflows or modify existing ones. A Cedar policy enforcing this rule might look

like the following:

forbid (

principal in Agent,

action in [

Action::"automation.create",

Action::"automation.update",

Action::"automation.delete"

],

resource in Entity::Automation

);

This policy prevents any agent principal from modifying automation definitions while still

allowing agents to trigger approved workflows.

This approach effectively childproofed the system. Agents could interact with enterprise

systems and carry out useful work, but the mechanisms that defined policy and governance
remained protected.

[As ACME gained more experience with agent behavior and the policies that govern it, the](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-18?potentialInternalRefId=166---book-markup-container)
engineers were able to refine these restrictions. Some operations that were initially blocked

could be safely delegated once the team understood the risks and implemented suitable
safeguards. The core control-plane protections remained in place, but the operational

boundaries around agents gradually expanded as the policy system and governance
processes matured.

[In practice, this meant defining two categories of actions:](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-18?potentialInternalRefId=167---book-markup-container)

**operational actions**, which agents might perform as part of their tasks

**control-plane actions**, which were reserved for trusted administrative
principals

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

406

Policies enforced this separation, ensuring that even a powerful agent operating under

delegated authority could not alter the rules that governed its behavior.

#### 18.6 Delegation and subagents

As ACME’s engineers grew more comfortable with their agent architecture, they began
exploring more complex tasks that involved multiple agents working together. A common

pattern quickly emerged: a primary agent would break a task into smaller pieces and
assign them to specialized subagents.

For example, when an employee asks the ACME Assist agent to prepare a customer
briefing, the agent might break the work into distinct steps. One subagent retrieves

relevant documents, another analyzes recent customer activity, and a third combines and
summarizes the results. Each subagent focuses on a specific part of the task.

[This pattern raises an important authorization question: under whose authority are these](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-18?potentialInternalRefId=174---book-markup-container)
subagents operating?

[In traditional systems, delegation is often implicit. A service calls another service, and](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-18?potentialInternalRefId=175---book-markup-container)
trust is assumed based on identity or configuration. In agent systems, that approach is

insufficient. Because agents plan and act dynamically, implicit delegation risks expanding
authority beyond what was intended. ACME addressed this by making delegation explicit

and treating it as structured data that policies can evaluate.

Appendix C.6 provides a working demonstration of this pattern. The delegation demo shows

how a main agent creates a delegation record for a subagent and how the policy enforcement point
and Cedar policies enforce those constraints on every action the subagent attempts.

18.6.1 Delegation as data

When treating delegation as data, a primary agent delegates work by creating a delegation
record that defines the scope of the authority being transferred. This record specifies:

the delegating agent (delegator)
the receiving subagent (delegate)

the actions the subagent may perform
the resources it may access

the conditions under which the delegation is valid, including an expiration

A simplified delegation record might look like this:

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

407

delegation_id: "d-1027"

delegator: Agent::"acme_assist"

delegate: Agent::"research_agent"

delegatedActions: [

Action::"documents.search",

Action::"documents.read",

Action::"documents.summarize"

]

resourceScope: CustomerDocs::"CustCo"

expires: "2026-03-31T18:00Z"

This record does not grant authority on its own. Instead, it provides additional context that

the policy system evaluates at runtime. This distinction is critical. Delegation does not
bypass policy. It becomes an input to policy.

DELEGATION THROUGH ATTACHED POLICY SETS

The delegation model presented here considers delegated authority as structured
data stored in a delegation record. Policies evaluate this data at runtime to

determine if a subagent is allowed to act within the delegated scope. In this way,
delegation is expressed through _policy as data_ : the authority being transferred is

represented by attributes that policies interpret.

Other delegation models represent delegated authority directly through _policy as_

_code_ .

In these systems, delegation happens when a trusted component creates or attaches

policies that specify what a subagent is allowed to do. Instead of recording that one
agent has delegated particular permissions to another, the system grants authority

by linking a set of policies to the subagent or to a role it assumes. This method is
similar to that used by cloud platforms like Amazon Web Services, in which

permissions are granted by attaching identity-based or resource-based policies to
roles and service principals.

This model generally assumes a default posture in which all actions are forbidden
unless explicitly allowed. Delegated authority is added by attaching narrowly scoped

policy statements that allow specific operations. These policies can be temporary,
contextual, or dynamically created during task execution.

Both methods make authority transparent and enable easier delegation. Delegation
as data allows flexible, task-specific authorization because policies assess contextual

attributes during execution. Delegation with attached policy sets helps clarify
permissions by making authority clear through explicit policy artifacts.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

408

In practice, systems might combine these approaches by using policy attachment for

coarse-grained delegation and structured delegation data for dynamic, fine-grained
control.

18.6.2 Enforcing delegation at runtime

When a subagent attempts to invoke a tool, the request still flows through the policy-aware

loop described earlier. The difference is that the policy enforcement point (PEP) now
enriches the authorization request with delegation information. Figure 18.4 illustrates this

interaction.

Figure 18.4 Policy enforcement for delegated agents. When a primary agent delegates work, a delegation

record defines the scope of authority. When a subagent invokes a tool, the policy enforcement point includes

the delegation data in the authorization request. The policy engine evaluates both the request and the

delegation constraints before returning a decision.

At runtime, the process looks like this:

1. The subagent proposes an action.
2. The PEP retrieves the relevant delegation record.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

409

3. The PEP constructs an authorization request that includes delegation data

in the context.
4. The policy engine evaluates the request using both the base policies and

the delegation constraints.
5. The action is permitted or denied.

Conceptually, the request now includes an additional layer of context:

**principal** —the subagent

**action** —the requested operation
**resource** —the target system or data

**context** —task state, environment, _and delegation data_

This ensures that every action taken by a subagent is evaluated not only against general

policy rules, but also against the specific limits of the delegated authority.

18.6.3 Policies that enforce delegation

Because delegation is represented as data, policies can enforce its constraints directly. A

foundational policy ensures that the subagent is acting within the delegated identity:

permit (

principal,

action,

resource

)

when {

principal == context.delegation.delegate

};

Additional policies enforce the scope of the delegation itself:

permit (

principal,

action,

resource

)

when {

action in context.delegation.delegatedActions

&& resource in context.delegation.resourceScope

&& context.currentTime < context.delegation.expires

};

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

410

These policies ensure that:

the subagent can perform only the actions explicitly delegated
the subagent can access only the specified resources

the delegation is valid only within its defined time window

If any of these conditions are not satisfied, the request is denied.

18.6.4 Allowed and denied behavior

This model makes delegation behavior explicit and verifiable.

If a subagent performs an action within the delegated scope—for

example, reading documents for the specified customer—the policy
engine issues a permit decision, and the action proceeds.

If the subagent attempts to exceed its authority—for example, by
accessing documents for another customer or performing an unapproved

action—the policy engine returns a deny decision. The action is blocked,
and the agent must revise its plan.

Because the delegation constraints are included in every authorization request, the policy
decision reflects both the subagent's identity and the limits of the authority it was granted.

18.6.5 Delegation as constrained authority

This approach reinforces a key principle: agents cannot delegate authority they do not
have, nor can they expand authority through delegation.

Delegation does not create new permissions. It narrows existing permissions to a
specific, task-bound scope. Policies remain the ultimate authority, and delegation data

defines the boundaries within which those policies apply.

[In this model, delegation is a controlled and auditable mechanism for distributing work](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-18?potentialInternalRefId=228---book-markup-container)

across agents. Each action taken by a subagent is evaluated in context, ensuring that
responsibility can be shared without sacrificing control.

18.6.6 Extending the policy-aware architecture

Delegation builds directly on the policy-aware architecture introduced earlier in this chapter.

In section 18.3, authorization was integrated into the agent’s execution

loop.
In section 18.4, policy constraints were used to guide planning.

Here, delegation extends the model by allowing authority to be distributed across agents
while preserving enforcement. The same policy engine evaluates all decisions. The only

difference is the information provided as input.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

411

At ACME, this approach enabled agents to collaborate on complex tasks without

establishing implicit trust relationships. Subagents could operate independently, but every
action they took remained bounded by explicit, policy-enforced constraints.

[As one of the engineers summarized during an architecture review: agents can help each](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-18?potentialInternalRefId=235---book-markup-container)
other, but they cannot grant powers they do not already have. Delegation is therefore a

natural extension of policy-based authorization. It enables flexible cooperation while
maintaining strict control over how authority is used.

#### 18.7 Cross-domain delegation among agents

Delegation becomes more complex when it crosses organizational boundaries. The model

described in the previous section assumes a shared policy environment in which every
request is evaluated by the same policy engine, using common enforcement points and

governance processes. Within ACME, this allows delegation to be tightly controlled and
consistently enforced. But when authority moves between organizations, that shared

control is lost. The delegating system cannot directly enforce how the receiving agent acts.

Situations like this illustrate the idea that I call a _society of agents_ . A society of agents

does not emerge simply because agents interact. It emerges when shared rules, protocols,
and governance mechanisms allow independent systems to cooperate reliably.

[ACME faced this situation when the finance team started preparing to launch a new](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-18?potentialInternalRefId=239---book-markup-container)
service to automate reimbursements for small contractors. The team wanted to use an AI

assistant to help review routine reimbursement requests and initiate payments through a
financial partner that provided a payment-agent service.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

412

In the reimbursement example in this section, ACME and its financial partner operate

under legal agreements that define their business relationship. These agreements
outline responsibilities, liabilities, and audit requirements. In addition, each

organization agrees to specific protocols, schema, and other technical standards.
Within this framework, the software agents representing each organization make

more specific operational commitments. For instance, the partner’s payment agent
may promise to process only reimbursements below a certain threshold, require

receipts for each payment, and return signed records documenting every
transaction.

These promises are significant because they are based on policies that limit the
agent’s behavior within its own domain. The partner’s Cedar policies guarantee that

the payment agent cannot exceed the limits specified in its promise, while ACME’s
policies specify when it is appropriate to delegate authority.

Over time, each organization observes whether the other’s agents keep their
promises. The results of these interactions build a reputation database that affects

future delegation choices. An agent that consistently fulfills its commitments
becomes a more trusted partner, while one that violates expectations quickly loses

the ability to receive delegated authority.

Policies define the boundaries of behavior, promises communicate intent across

different domains, and reputation tracks the results of those interactions. Together,
these mechanisms allow independent systems—like ACME and its payment partner—

to operate as a society of agents while still enforcing their own local policies.

Many contractor reimbursements were straightforward: a mileage claim, a reimbursable

meal during travel, or a small software subscription approved for project work. Automating
these transactions could greatly reduce manual effort. However, once authority moved from

ACME’s environment into the partner’s payment system, ACME needed assurance that the
partner’s agent would operate within acceptable limits.

Trudy had already seen how quickly agent capabilities could expand inside ACME’s
systems. Past experiments demonstrated that agents might attempt unexpected actions

unless their behavior was carefully constrained by policy. These lessons made her wary of
granting authority outside the company’s boundaries. If ACME was to let an external

payment agent initiate reimbursements, she wanted assurance that the agent’s actions
would be governed by policies as strict as those used by ACME.

[The partner’s payment agent was also governed by Cedar policies. A simplified policy in](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-18?potentialInternalRefId=248---book-markup-container)
the partner’s domain might look like this:

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

413

permit (

principal,

action == Action::"reimbursement.pay",

resource

)

when {

context.delegation.capability == "contractor.reimbursement.pay"

&& context.payment.amount <= context.delegation.constraints.max_amount

&& context.payment.currency == context.delegation.constraints.currency

&& context.payment.receipt_present == true

&& context.currentTime < context.delegation.constraints.expires

};

This policy ensures that payments are only issued when the request complies with the

delegation limits: the reimbursement amount must stay below the authorized threshold, a
receipt must be provided, and the delegation must still be valid.

Because the partner’s agent is constrained by policy, it can make structured promises
about how it will behave. These promises describe how the agent will act if authority is

delegated to it. For example, the partner’s payment agent might offer a promise derived
from its policy configuration:

{

"agent": "did:web:agents.partnerpay.example:reimbursement-agent",

"promise": {

"action": "contractor.reimbursement.pay",

"constraints": {

"max_amount": 250,

"currency": "USD",

"requires_receipt": true,

"purpose": "process contractor reimbursements"

},

"audit": "signed payment receipt returned",

"policy_framework": "cedar"

}

}

A promise does not grant authority; instead, it communicates how the receiving agent’s
internal policies constrain its actions when authority is delegated. Figure 18.6 shows the

resulting interaction pattern. The partner’s agent first presents its promise. ACME’s
reimbursement agent assesses the promise using its local policies and the information

stored in its reputation database, then decides whether to delegate authority to the
partner’s agent.

414

Figure 18.5 Cross-domain delegation in a society of agents. Two policy-limited agents collaborate across

different domains. The receiving agent makes promises about its future behavior, the requesting agent

assesses those promises and the partner’s reputation, and then grants authority using a credential. The

receiving agent operates under its own policies, and both domains log the outcome for future decisions.

Once ACME accepts the partner’s promise, it delegates authority using a verifiable
credential, following the pattern introduced in chapter 16. The credential transports the

delegated authority across the organizational boundary so the partner’s policy system can
assess it. A credential issued by ACME’s finance system might look like this:

The credential carries the delegation across domains but does not decide if a payment is

permitted. The partner’s Cedar policies still review each request using the credential’s
claims as inputs.

If the payment is processed successfully, the partner returns a signed receipt to ACME.
Both systems record the result, updating their internal reputation databases. Over time,

these interactions help each side evaluate if the other agent consistently keeps its
promises.

[Cross-domain delegation relies on more than just credentials. It emerges from the](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-18?potentialInternalRefId=259---book-markup-container)
interaction of policies that constrain behavior, promises that communicate intent, and

reputations that serve as records of past interactions’ outcomes. Together, these
mechanisms allow independent domains to cooperate while still enforcing their own

authorization boundaries. In this way, authorization architecture becomes one of the core
mechanisms that makes a practical society of agents possible.

#### 18.8 Summary

AI agents introduce a new authorization challenge because they

dynamically plan actions and interact with many systems during
execution.

Authentication alone cannot govern agent behavior because it verifies
identity but does not constrain what actions an agent may attempt.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

416

Policy-aware agent loops integrate authorization directly into the agent’s

planning and execution cycle, ensuring that each action is evaluated
against policy at runtime.

Policies can serve not only as enforcement gates but also as constraint
systems that guide agent planning using techniques such as Cedar’s

typed partial evaluation.
Separating operational actions from control-plane operations helps

protect the systems that define workflows, infrastructure, and
authorization rules.

Delegation allows agents to distribute work among specialized subagents
while policies ensure that delegated authority remains within defined

limits.
Cross-domain delegation requires additional mechanisms—policies,

promises, credentials, and reputation—to enable cooperation between
independent systems.

Verifiable credentials can transport delegated authority across
organizational boundaries while local policies still determine whether

specific actions are permitted.
A society of agents emerges when independent systems interact under

shared agreements, using policies to enforce behavior, promises to
communicate intent, and reputation to evaluate past outcomes.

## Authorization as strategy

This chapter covers

How small advances in authorization can develop into a strategic ability

Why growing systems create authorization pressure that constrains scale and
innovation

The architecture and governance patterns that enable consistent, real-time
decisions

How to evaluate authorization maturity and take effective next steps

Why the future of digital systems depends on continuous, policy-driven authorization

When ACME’s engineering team first started working on what would eventually become the

Customer Collaboration platform, authorization was already part of the conversation.

The initial goal was modest. Teams needed a better way to share documents with

customers. Existing tools were slow, confusing, and hard to secure. Alice, as a senior
engineer leading the early design effort, worked to make access controls clear and

predictable. Bob, as a solutions architect, focused on integrating the new system with
ACME’s identity services. Managers like Carol stressed the importance of enabling

collaboration without adding unnecessary risks. From the start, the team understood that
safely sharing information was key to the platform’s value.

[Authorization was never ignored. It evolved alongside the system. Each improvement](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-19?potentialInternalRefId=8---book-markup-container)
addressed a specific need. Engineers adjusted policies when inconsistencies appeared.

Security reviews prompted architectural changes. Product teams learned to more carefully
consider how access decisions affected user experience. Over time, ACME developed both

stronger technical capabilities and a deeper institutional understanding of managing trust in
software systems.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

418

As the platform grew, the role of authorization grew as well. Access decisions were no

longer limited to simple role checks at the edge of an application. They increasingly
depended on relationships, attributes, and real-time context, and were evaluated as part of

how systems operated. What had once been a localized concern began to shape behavior
across services, teams, and customer interactions.

[What they did not initially realize was how crucial authorization would become to the](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-19?potentialInternalRefId=10---book-markup-container)
company’s future or how costly it would be to let decision logic evolve in isolation across

teams and systems. Authorization was more than a feature of the platform. It had become
part of ACME’s operating model. And the drawbacks of a piecemeal approach were starting

to impact revenue, reputation, and the company’s ability to scale.

[This realization did not come all at once but developed gradually, as leaders across](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-19?potentialInternalRefId=11---book-markup-container)

engineering, security, and the business started to notice recurring decision patterns
everywhere. Choices about who or what could act were shaping product design, partnership

strategy, and risk posture. The infrastructure supporting those decisions had grown
incrementally, but its significance had increased more quickly.

[By the time ACME recognized authorization as a strategic concern, it had already taken](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-19?potentialInternalRefId=12---book-markup-container)
many steps to manage it effectively. What changed wasn't their commitment to improving

access control, but their understanding that authorization was not just something to
implement well; it had become something the organization had to design and rely upon to

scale.

#### 19.1 When authorization became the hard problem

Initially, the issues seemed unrelated. A product launch slipped because partner access
rules behaved differently across environments. A major customer raised concerns about

inconsistent permission failures during a critical deployment. Engineering teams spent
weeks resolving policy differences between services that had developed independently.

Security reviews revealed delegation paths that were technically correct but hard to
understand. Each incident was investigated, addressed, and eventually closed.

In most cases, ACME responded by improving the system in targeted ways. Policies were
clarified, enforcement logic was consolidated, and new governance checkpoints were added.

These changes provided real benefits. Teams learned from each experience, strengthening
both their technical approach and their understanding of how access decisions shaped user

outcomes. Individually, none of these events seemed existential. But when viewed together,
they began to reveal a pattern.

[As Customer Collaboration expanded, ACME’s](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-19?potentialInternalRefId=16---book-markup-container) _decision surface_, the total set of situations
in which access must be evaluated, grew faster than its decision infrastructure. More

employees were interacting with more customers across more systems. Automation
reduced the need for human intervention but increased the number of actions performed.

Contextual signals such as device posture, location, and workload status started influencing
outcomes in ways that were hard to test thoroughly. Decisions were no longer evaluated

only at the boundaries of applications, but increasingly as part of how systems operated in
real time. The organization’s ability to explain how access decisions were made lagged

behind its capacity to implement new features.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

419

[The company continued to invest in targeted improvements. Shared policy services were](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-19?potentialInternalRefId=17---book-markup-container)

introduced to reduce duplication. Relationship-based models replaced rigid role hierarchies
in key workflows. Attribute-driven controls improved assurance in high-risk scenarios. Each

step made the platform more coherent and more adaptable. Yet each step also expanded
expectations about what the system could support.

[As shown in Figure 19.1, the gap between the decision surface and decision](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-19?potentialInternalRefId=18---book-markup-container)
infrastructure created _authorization pressure_ —the increasing difficulty of making decisions

consistently, explaining outcomes, and maintaining control as systems scale—resulting in
both operational friction and strategic uncertainty. Product leaders had to balance trade-offs

between feature speed and consistent performance. Sales teams found it difficult to
reassure potential partners that complex collaboration scenarios could be managed without

custom engineering. Security teams identified risks resulting from the accumulation of
implicit trust relationships embedded in code and configuration.

Figure 19.1 Decision surface and decision infrastructure. As systems grow, the decision surface—the set of

situations where access must be evaluated—expands faster than the infrastructure that governs those

decisions. This gap creates authorization pressure: the growing difficulty of making decisions consistently,

explaining outcomes, and maintaining control. Incremental architectural investments can close this gap,

enabling organizations to manage trust reliably as complexity grows.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

420

Authorization was no longer just a technical issue. It had become a constraint on ACME's

ability to grow quickly. The turning point did not come from a single crisis. Instead, it
emerged as leaders across disciplines began describing the same problem in their own

words. Engineers talked about duplicated logic and brittle integrations. Security teams
focused on limited delegation and decision visibility. Executives worried about stalled

partnerships and inconsistent customer experiences. What linked these concerns was that
access decisions were being made everywhere but governed nowhere.

When authorization finally became a regular topic in executive reviews, it was not
because ACME had failed to act. It was because the organization had gradually come to

realize that improving local access control was no longer enough. Their ambitions now
depended on treating authorization as shared infrastructure. Authorization had become the

hard problem because ACME’s ambitions had outgrown the assumptions on which its earlier
solutions were built.

#### 19.2 The architecture ACME built

By the time the organization recognized authorization as a strategic concern, ACME had

already built most of the components of a modern decision infrastructure. ACME’s decision
infrastructure was not built as a single initiative, but instead emerged through a series of

deliberate improvements, each addressing a specific limitation in how access decisions were
made or enforced.

Early investments were aimed at reducing duplication and inconsistency. Teams
externalized decision logic from application code when local solutions started to diverge (as

discussed in chapter 6 on dynamic authorization models). Shared evaluation services were
introduced where coordination was needed. As collaboration patterns grew more complex,

relationship-based models were deliberately adopted to support controlled sharing (see
section 6.1 on ReBAC). Attribute-driven controls were added to address access

requirements that static roles could no longer fulfill (see section 6.2 on attribute-based
access control).

[These changes were incremental but not accidental. Engineers and security leaders](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-19?potentialInternalRefId=25---book-markup-container)
increasingly identified recurring decision patterns across systems. Architectural discussions

started to explicitly consider how authority should flow through the platform. Over time,
authorization ceased being treated as just a feature-level concern and became integral to

how new capabilities were designed.

[The architecture ACME designed was a direct response to this pressure. Rather than](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-19?potentialInternalRefId=26---book-markup-container)

attempting to limit the growth of the decision surface, the company focused on
strengthening the infrastructure that supports it. Shared policy services, contextual signals,

and governance mechanisms were developed to ensure that decisions could be made
consistently, even as systems grew more complex.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

421

At the core of this system was a shared policy decision capability in the form of a

common policy decision layer responsible for evaluating access decisions consistently
across applications (building on the PARC model introduced in section 7.3). Rather than

embedding access logic directly in application code, ACME’s services increasingly relied on
this common policy layer. Product teams created policies that aligned with business goals,

while foundational policies, written by the identity and security teams, ensured consistent
enforcement throughout the organization. Decisions were made at runtime, using

relationships, attributes, and contextual signals to determine which actions could move
forward (as explored in Chapter 12 on authorization context).

[This shift changed how authority moved through ACME’s platform. Relationship-based](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-19?potentialInternalRefId=28---book-markup-container)
models enabled collaboration patterns that previously needed manual effort. Attribute
driven policies let high-security controls be applied dynamically rather than through strict
process gates. Delegation mechanisms allowed both people and systems to act within

clearly defined boundaries. Automation increased, but within decision frameworks that
stayed visible and explainable.

[Equally important was the governance that developed alongside the technology (see](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-19?potentialInternalRefId=29---book-markup-container)
chapter 14 to read more about policy governance). ACME invested in defining ownership for

decision signals, establishing expectations for freshness and assurance (building on the PIP
model described in section 12.1), and creating review processes for policy changes.

Decision logs became a source for operational insights (as discussed in section 17.3 on AI
and policy analysis), allowing teams to understand not only what actions occurred but also

why they were permitted or denied. This made it possible to identify inconsistencies, audit
behavior, and improve policies based on real system outcomes. Over time, authorization

moved from being an implementation detail to a managed capability that could be improved
deliberately rather than rediscovered repeatedly.

[As the decision surface expanded, testing and validation grew more complex and more](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-19?potentialInternalRefId=30---book-markup-container)
critical. Decisions were no longer isolated in individual features or services. A change to a

policy or signal could affect behavior across multiple systems, users, and contexts.
Traditional testing approaches, which focused on individual code paths, were no longer

sufficient to ensure consistent outcomes.

[In response, ACME invested in policy-aware testing practices (as discussed in chapter](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-19?potentialInternalRefId=31---book-markup-container)

14). Policy changes were evaluated using representative scenarios and historical decision
data to assess their impact before deployment. Simulation and staged rollouts were

introduced to reduce risk, allowing teams to observe how decisions performed under realworld conditions. These practices did not eliminate uncertainty, but they helped manage

authorization pressure by making changes safer, more predictable, and easier to reason
about.

[None of these elements eliminated complexity. ACME’s ecosystem continued to grow.](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-19?potentialInternalRefId=32---book-markup-container)
New partnership models introduced new forms of delegation. Agent-assisted workflows

created new categories of risk. But the organization now had an architecture capable of
adapting to these changes. Authorization was no longer a collection of local solutions; it had

become a shared foundation for building new capabilities.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

422

What began as incremental responses to immediate needs had produced something

more powerful: a shared capability for controlling how people, services, and agents act
across the company’s systems.

#### 19.3 When the CIO and CISO finally agreed

The quarterly board meeting had already run long. Financial performance was strong. The

Customer Collaboration platform continued to grow at a faster pace than forecast. ACME’s
expansion into partner-led distribution had opened new markets, and the early

deployments of agent-assisted workflows were showing measurable gains in productivity.
The discussion had moved past revenue and product plans and into a topic that, not long

ago, would never have appeared on the board agenda: _operational trust, security, and risk_ .

Elena, ACME’s CEO, leaned forward slightly as Ravi, the company’s CIO, finished his

update. “Before we move on,” she said, “I’d like Sam, our CISO, to walk us through how
we’re managing risk as more decisions move out of human workflows and into automated

systems.”

[Sam nodded. A year earlier, the request might have been framed very differently, as a](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-19?potentialInternalRefId=37---book-markup-container)

security review or a compliance check. Now the board expected a broader answer. “What’s
changed,” Sam began, “is that we no longer treat authorization as something embedded in

individual systems. Decisions about who or what can act are evaluated consistently, using
shared policies and real-time signals. That gives us visibility we simply didn’t have before.”

[One board member frowned slightly. “Visibility is good,” he said, “but does it mean we’re](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-19?potentialInternalRefId=38---book-markup-container)
taking on more risk? You’re delegating more authority to partners and software agents.

Isn’t that inherently dangerous?”

[Sam glanced briefly at Ravi before answering. “We are taking on more responsibility,” he](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-19?potentialInternalRefId=39---book-markup-container)

said. “But the risk is bounded. Delegation is explicit now. Every decision is constrained by
policy. We can see how authority flows across teams, across customers, even across

systems. That allows us to take risks intentionally rather than discovering them after the
fact.”

[Ravi picked up the thread. “From the platform side,” he said, “this has been](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-19?potentialInternalRefId=40---book-markup-container)
transformative. We used to spend enormous effort trying to make access decisions

consistent across services. Each product team solved the problem differently. That slowed
delivery and created unpredictable behavior for customers. Now decision logic is

externalized. Teams build against shared policy infrastructure. We move faster because the
rules are clear.”

[Another board member leaned forward. “So you’re saying this is both a security](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-19?potentialInternalRefId=41---book-markup-container)
improvement and an operational improvement?”

[“It’s more than that,” Ravi replied. “It’s architectural. We’ve effectively built a decision](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-19?potentialInternalRefId=42---book-markup-container)
layer for the company. Whether an employee shares a document, a partner invokes an API,

or an agent executes a workflow, the question of authorization is answered using the same
policy framework. That consistency lets us scale.”
