#### 19.4 What changed inside ACME

The most significant changes at ACME were not just technical. They were shifts in how
people thought about decisions, responsibility, and trust in response to the growing decision

surface and the authorization pressure it created.

Engineers experienced a shift from implementing authorization as logic inside feature

code to designing it as part of system architecture. Instead of embedding access checks
wherever functionality required them, teams began identifying decision points explicitly and

relying on shared policy infrastructure to ensure consistent outcomes across the expanding
decision surface. Authorization became something to model and reason about, not just

something to code.

[Product managers shifted from treating access control as a constraint to recognizing it as](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-19?potentialInternalRefId=51---book-markup-container)

part of the product. As the decision surface expanded, decisions about delegation,
collaboration boundaries, and contextual behavior were considered earlier in the design

process. Policy flexibility became a tool for enabling new capabilities rather than an obstacle
to delivering them.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

424

Within the identity and security teams, there was a shift from review and enforcement

toward stewardship. Their governance efforts increasingly focused on signal quality, policy
lifecycle, and decision transparency. Instead of trying to prevent every risky action through

manual processes like approvals and reviews, these teams focused on managing
authorization pressure through infrastructure. Within those boundaries, actions could

proceed without additional friction. This enabled the organization to move faster while
ensuring that decisions remained controlled, observable, and consistent.

[These shifts enabled new organizational capabilities. ACME could expand its decision](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-19?potentialInternalRefId=53---book-markup-container)
surface—supporting more complex collaboration, delegation, and automation—without

losing control. Partner onboarding accelerated as delegation models became easier to
understand and implement. Automation expanded because its behavior could be

constrained predictably. When decisions were challenged, the company could explain not
only what happened, but why. _Authorization had not become simpler. But it had become_

_deliberate._

#### 19.5 Where most organizations are today

Most organizations are still in the early stages of their journey toward strategic
authorization. Authorization decisions are often embedded inside individual systems,

shaped by the immediate needs of product teams and the limitations of current platforms.
Role models evolve over time as new use cases arise. Contextual signals are added

selectively to address specific risks. Governance practices develop unevenly across
domains. These approaches are rarely due to neglect; instead, they reflect the reality that

software systems grow incrementally and that access decisions must be made long before a
comprehensive strategy is in place.

As organizations expand their digital ecosystems, the limitations of this localized
approach become more obvious.

**Employees face inconsistent behavior across products and**
**services** —an engineer might be able to deploy code through one service

but be blocked in another because each system enforces access rules
differently.

**Customers encounter confusing permission failures or delayed**
**onboarding** —customers invited to collaborate on a document are able to

view it but not comment or share it, with no clear explanation why.
**Partners need custom integration work to achieve controlled**

**delegation** —a partner integrating with an API may require custom logic
to ensure it can act on behalf of a customer without being over
permissioned.
**Automation initiatives reveal gaps in how authority is defined and**

**limited** —an automated workflow might be able to trigger actions across
systems but lack clear constraints on when or how those actions should

be allowed.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

425

These challenges often seem unrelated at first, but they share a common root: the surface

area of authorization decisions has grown faster than the infrastructure used to manage
them.

Figure 19.2 illustrates a common progression in how organizations respond to this
pressure. Early efforts focus on embedding access logic directly within applications. As

complexity grows, teams start to externalize decision logic to improve consistency and
incorporate richer context signals. Over time, some organizations realize that authorization

should be treated as a shared decision infrastructure that serves as a strategic capability to
support delegation, automation, and ecosystem collaboration.

Figure 19.2 Authorization maturity spectrum. Organizations usually evolve from embedding access decisions

within individual systems to developing shared decision-making infrastructure. Incremental investments in

policy externalization, contextual signals, delegation models, and governance support more consistent

automation, collaboration within ecosystems, and strategic trust management.

Many organizations today are in the _Coordinated_ stage. They have introduced policy
services for specific use cases, started including contextual attributes into access decisions,

and set up governance practices to lower risk. These efforts bring meaningful
improvements, but decision models often remain fragmented. Different teams may use

different methods for policy definition or delegation, making it hard to reason about
authority consistently across the organization.

Progress beyond this stage doesn't require a wholesale transformation. Instead, it
involves a consistent focus on already emerging patterns. By continuing to externalize

decision logic, unify policy models, and enhance signal governance, organizations can
incrementally develop the infrastructure needed to manage trust intentionally. As ACME’s

experience shows, strategic authorization capability is rarely developed all at once. It is
built through incremental choices that align architecture, governance, and organizational

understanding.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

426

#### 19.6 A practical path forward

By the time organizations recognize authorization as a growth constraint, they often have

already started improving it. Policies are externalized in some systems. Contextual signals
are being incorporated into decision-making. Governance practices are emerging in

response to risk and operational needs.

In most cases, the challenge is not knowing where to start. It’s how to move forward

thoughtfully without causing unnecessary disruptions. The best approach is to build on what
already exists, beginning with a single, clear access problem that is already causing visible

friction for employees, customers, or partners. This might be a document-sharing rule, a
partner API permission, or an internal approval workflow that is hard to change or explain.

Externalizing that decision into a shared policy service provides immediate value while
developing skills, establishing patterns, and creating practices that can be reused

elsewhere.

[Instead of trying a complete redesign, organizations should focus on targeted](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-19?potentialInternalRefId=69---book-markup-container)

improvements that address urgent needs while also enhancing the underlying decisionmaking infrastructure. Throughout these efforts, a consistent set of practices emerges:

Make authorization decisions observable.
Externalize a meaningful policy domain by moving a coherent set of

related decisions (such as document sharing or API access) into a shared
set of policies.

Unify policy language and evaluation.
Invest in the governance of signals and delegation.

Design systems assuming that authorization decisions will be made at
runtime.

These are not phases to finish in sequence, but practices to adopt and revisit as systems
evolve. Each step reduces inconsistency, enhances visibility, and expands the ability to

manage delegation and context more deliberately.

Table 19.1 shows common situations and corresponding next steps. These examples

illustrate how the practices given above can be used in real-world scenarios. They are not a
checklist; they are practical actions organizations can take depending on their current

situation. Most teams will recognize multiple rows that are relevant to their current state.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

427

Table 19.1 Incremental steps toward strategic authorization. Organizations can enhance authorization

capabilities by making targeted changes to address immediate challenges. Each step builds on existing

practices, gradually strengthening decision infrastructure and governance without requiring a complete

|overhaul.|Col2|Col3|
|---|---|---|
|**If you are here**|**You’re likely seeing**|**A practical next step**|
|Authorization logic<br>embedded in<br>applications|Inconsistent behavior across<br>systems, hard-to-change<br>rules|Externalize one high-value<br>decision into a shared policy<br>service|
|Multiple policy<br>mechanisms across<br>teams|Duplicate logic, outcomes<br>that are difficult to reason<br>about|Standardize on a common<br>policy model and evaluation<br>approach|

The steps in table 19.1 are intentionally modest. None requires a complete transformation.

Instead, transformation begins with small architectural moves that make decisions visible,
externalize policy, and strengthen how authority is defined and governed. Each reflects a

pattern that organizations already encounter as their systems evolve. The goal is not to
eliminate complexity, but to manage it more deliberately by making decisions visible,

consistent, and adaptable.

As ACME’s experience shows, progress in authorization results from aligning

architecture, governance, and organizational understanding. The earlier this alignment
starts, the easier it becomes to support new capabilities without creating friction or risk.

The work is ongoing, but also cumulative. Each small improvement strengthens the
foundation for the next.

#### 19.7 The next era of digital trust

The challenges ACME faced are not unique. They are early signs of a wider shift that is

already happening. As digital solutions are applied to more and more domains, the number
and complexity of authorization decisions will continue to grow. The use of AI to develop

applications is likely to accelerate this trend. More interactions will cross organizational
boundaries. More actions will be performed by services and agents instead of people. More

decisions will rely on real-time context, including signals about device posture,
environment, and operational state. Authorization’s surface area will not stabilize. It will

expand.

Organizations relying on static models and embedded decision logic will encounter the

same issues ACME did: inconsistent behavior across systems, friction in collaboration, and
growing difficulty in explaining or controlling how authority is exercised. These challenges

will not emerge all at once but develop gradually as systems evolve and expectations rise.
But they will appear. In this environment, _dynamic authorization is no longer a luxury. It's_

_essential_ .

[The practices we've discussed in this book—externalizing policy, incorporating context,](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-19?potentialInternalRefId=83---book-markup-container)

governing signals, and evaluating decisions at runtime—are not tied to any specific
technology stack or moment in time. They represent fundamental shifts in how software

systems operate. As these systems become more distributed, automated, and
interconnected, the demand for consistent, explainable decision-making will only grow.

[This is especially true as agents become more capable and autonomous. Systems that](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-19?potentialInternalRefId=84---book-markup-container)
plan and act over time require adaptable authorization models that can change with

conditions. Decisions must be evaluated continuously rather than assumed. Delegation
must be explicit and bounded. Trust must be enforced through policy, not inferred from

static configuration.

[The ideas in this book are not a snapshot of current practice. They serve as a foundation](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-19?potentialInternalRefId=85---book-markup-container)

for what comes next. What ACME experienced as a gradual realization will become more
immediate for others. The gap between decision surface and decision infrastructure,

illustrated in figure 19.1, will appear earlier and grow more quickly. Organizations that
recognize this shift will be positioned to respond intentionally. Those who do not will find

that complexity overwhelms them.

ACME did not set out to build a strategic authorization capability. Instead, it evolved
gradually, influenced by the needs of the systems they created and the relationships those

systems fostered. By the time the organization recognized its significance, authorization
had already become part of how ACME operated. That realization changed what came next.

#### 19.9 Deciding continuously

Throughout this book, we have explored how authorization decisions are made: who can

act, what they can do, and under what conditions. In many systems, these decisions are
considered static. They are defined once, embedded in code or configuration, and assumed

to remain unchanged until someone updates them. _That assumption no longer applies._

As systems become more distributed, automated, and interconnected, authorization

decisions need to be made continuously. They must consider changing relationships,
shifting context, and actions taken by people, services, and agents. Access is no longer

something that can be granted once and left unchanged. It must be evaluated every time it
matters.

[This shift may seem large, but you don't need to start with a complete transformation.](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-19?potentialInternalRefId=98---book-markup-container)
You can make meaningful progress through small, intentional changes. Make your

authorization decisions visible. Externalize a policy domain. Introduce consistent evaluation.
Strengthen governance of signals and delegation. Design your systems so decisions can be

made at runtime.

[You can start by tackling one access problem that’s causing friction or is the source of](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-19?potentialInternalRefId=99---book-markup-container)

security problems. Identify a rule or permission that is hard to explain, change, or enforce
consistently. Make it visible. Integrate it into a shared policy. Evaluate it using real-world

context that reflects how your system actually operates. Learn from the outcomes. Then,
apply the same approach to the next decision.

[Over time, these changes accumulate. Decisions become simpler to make. Behavior](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-19?potentialInternalRefId=100---book-markup-container)
becomes more consistent. Introducing new capabilities becomes easier without raising risk.

What starts as a local improvement eventually becomes part of how your systems function.

[As we’ve seen, the future of access control is not defined by roles or rules alone. Rather,](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/chapter-19?potentialInternalRefId=101---book-markup-container)

it’s defined by the ability to make decisions continuously, based on policy and context, as
conditions change. _You do not have to build that future all at once. But you can begin_

_building it now._

#### 19.10 Summary

Authorization typically starts as a local implementation issue but grows
into a system-wide limitation as complexity increases.

Incremental improvements to access control accumulate over time,
influencing how systems develop and how organizations function.

Inconsistent authorization logic causes fragmented user experiences,
operational friction, and missed opportunities.

As systems grow, the decision surface—the set of situations in which
access must be evaluated—expands rapidly across people, services, and

contexts.
When the decision surface outpaces the infrastructure used to govern it,

organizations experience authorization pressure, leading to inconsistent
decisions, reduced visibility, and increased operational risk.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

431

Treating authorization as shared infrastructure allows for more consistent

and predictable behavior across systems.
Externalizing decision logic reduces duplication and enables policies to be

evaluated consistently at runtime.
Managing authorization pressure requires strengthening decision

infrastructure so access can be evaluated consistently, explained clearly,
and adapted as systems evolve.

Relationship-based, attribute-based, role-based, and delegation models
can be combined to support complex, real-world scenarios.

Governance is crucial for maintaining the trustworthiness and
effectiveness of signals, policies, and delegation mechanisms.

Decision visibility, including logs and analysis, helps organizations
understand and enhance how authorization functions.

Authorization maturity develops incrementally through deliberate
architectural and governance choices.

Beginning with a clear, straightforward access problem offers a practical
way to start improving.

Standardizing policy language and evaluation enables teams to make
consistent decisions across systems.

Designing systems for runtime evaluation enables authorization to adapt
to changing contexts and conditions.

As systems grow more distributed and automated, ongoing decisionmaking becomes essential.

Authorization is becoming the primary control plane for managing trust
among people, services, and agents.

## Appendix A. End-to-end example with Amazon Verified Permissions

To run the ACME “Customer Collaboration” example introduced in Chapter 9 on Amazon

Verified Permissions (AVP, at <u>[https://aws.amazon.com/​verified-​permissions/), follow the](https://aws.amazon.com/verified-permissions/)</u>
instructions in this appendix. They will help you create a policy store, load a Cedar schema,

add policies, and call `is-authorized` to determine `allow` or `deny` decisions. You only need

the AWS CLI (v2) and an AWS account.

AVP is a fully managed authorization service that evaluates Cedar policies in the cloud.
Instead of hosting our own policy engine, we upload a schema and policies to an AVP policy

store and then send authorization requests through an API. AVP verifies policies against the
schema in strict mode, evaluates requests in real time, and returns a single allow or deny

decision along with the policies that caused it. This simplifies experimenting with Cedar and
running production workloads without needing to set up infrastructure, while still using the

same policy language and models discussed throughout the book.

The schema and policies used here are available as a GitHub repository at <u>[https://github.​](https://github.com/windley/acme-cedar-demo)</u>

<u>[com/windley/​acme-cedar-​demo. The repository also includes a Jupyter Notebook for running through](https://github.com/windley/acme-cedar-demo)</u>
the examples in this appendix.

#### A.1 Prerequisites

We’ll use the AWS command line tool to interact with AVP. It’s also possible to perform
these examples through the AVP console, if you prefer. The following prerequisites are

assumed in the examples that follow:

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

433

AWS CLI v2 is installed and configured. You can check the installed

version by running `aws –version` .

You must choose a region where AVP is available. You can set your region

to `us-east-1` using the CLI tool: `aws configure set region us-east-`

`1` .

JSON tools are also helpful. For instance, we’ll use `jq -Rs` to wrap the

Cedar schema string.

Once these are configured, we can begin by setting up a policy store.

[To install the AWS CLI, see “Getting started with the AWS CLI” (https://docs.​aws.amazon.​](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/cli-chap-getting-started.html)

<u>[com/cli/latest/​userguide/​cli-chap-​getting-started.​html). The documentation for the AVP CLI](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/cli-chap-getting-started.html)</u>
commands can be found here: <u>[https://docs.​aws.amazon.​com/cli/latest/​userguide/​](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/cli_verifiedpermissions_code_examples.html)</u>

<u>[cli_verifiedpermissions_​code_examples.​html.](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/cli_verifiedpermissions_code_examples.html)</u>

#### A.2 Create a policy store

The initial step is to create a new policy store in AVP. This serves as the container for your

schema, policies, and entities. You can do this either through the AWS Console or using the
AWS CLI. For example, the command creates a policy store and puts the ID in the variable

`STORE_ID` :

STORE_ID=$(

aws verifiedpermissions create-policy-store \

--validation-settings "mode=STRICT" \

--query policyStoreId --output text

)

echo "$STORE_ID"

Using `strict` mode causes AVP to enforce type checks against our schema and prevents us

from uploading malformed policies.

#### A.3 Upload the Cedar schema

Next, tell AVP about the shape of your world. The schema defines entity types (Employees,
Customers, Teams, Documents), key attributes (owner, readers teams), and the actions

supported by the app ( `doc:view`, `doc:edit`, `doc:share` ).

Here is the schema we used in chapter 9:

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

434

namespace ACME

entity Employee {

attributes {

department: String,

on_call: Bool,

manager: Employee

}

}

entity Customer {}

entity Team {

attributes {

name: String

}

}

entity Document {

attributes {

owner: Employee,

classification: String,

delegatable: Bool,

employee_readers_team: Team,

customer_readers_team: Team

}

}

action "doc:view"

appliesTo { principal: [Employee, Customer], resource: Document }

action "doc:edit"

appliesTo { principal: Employee, resource: Document }

action "doc:share"

appliesTo { principal: Employee, resource: Document }

context {

device: { managed: Bool },

time:  { hour: Long, weekday: String }

}

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

435

[The Cedar CLI (https://github.​com/cedar-​policy/cedar) offers an automated way to do this,](https://github.com/cedar-policy/cedar)
but for this example, we’ll manually translate it:

If you compare this with the earlier schema file, you can see the pattern of the JSON

representation of the schema.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

438

The AVP `put-schema` API expects this JSON object to be the value of another JSON and

stored in the `cedarJson` field as an escaped string. To do this, we use `jq` to convert the

JSON to a string by escaping all embedded quotation marks with a backslash and

combining all lines into a single line with no line breaks:

jq -Rs '{cedarJson: .}' acme.cedarschema.json > schema-definition.json

Once we have the schema as a JSON object, we can upload the schema to our policy store

using the following command:

aws verifiedpermissions put-schema \

--policy-store-id "$STORE_ID" \

--definition file://schema-definition.json

If everything is correct, you’ll receive a JSON response showing the policy store ID, the

namespaces within it, and the creation and update dates. The namespace should match the
one in the schema you just uploaded to the policy store. In our case, it’s `ACME` .

#### A.4 Uploading policies to AVP

With the schema in place, ACME Corp can now upload Cedar policies that define how access

decisions are made. In AVP, each policy is created using the `create-policy` command. AVP

validates each policy against the schema before storing it, ensuring that errors are caught

early.

We’ll begin with the core “view” policies and then add edit, share, and global guardrail

rules. Consider this as gradually building the access model, layer by layer.

The policies shown here may be slightly modified from those in chapter 9 to consolidate

various ideas discussed in that chapter.

A.4.1 View policies

The simplest rule involves who can view a document. We have two policies: one for

customers and one for employees.

CUSTOMERS

This is the policy that allows viewing a document if the customer is part of the customer

reader team:

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

439

permit(

principal is ACME::Customer,

action == ACME::Action::"doc:view",

resource is ACME::Document

)

when {

principal in resource.customer_readers_team

};

When uploading to AVP, we store the policy as a JSON object. Unlike the `put-schema`, the

`create-policy` API accepts the policy in Cedar format, so there’s no need to convert it to

JSON within the string.

If we save this policy as `policy-view.cedar`, we can convert it into the proper format

for the AWS CLI call using the following `jq` command:

jq -Rs --arg desc "Customer view policy" \

'{static: {description: $desc, statement: .}}' \

policy-customer-view.cedar > policy-customer-view.json

Now we can upload this policy to the policy store using the following call to the `create-`

`policy` API:

aws verifiedpermissions create-policy \

--policy-store-id $STORE_ID \

--definition file://policy-customer-view.json

This returns a JSON object that provides its policy ID, type ( `STATIC` in this case), actions,

effect, and timestamps for creation and last update.

EMPLOYEES

The following policy permits employees to view a document if they are on the employee
readers team for it or if they are the manager of the owner:

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

440

permit(

principal is ACME::Employee,

action == ACME::Action::"doc:view",

resource is ACME::Document

)

when {

principal in resource.employee_readers_team

|| resource.owner.manager == principal

};

We can apply the same formatting we did to the policy for customers viewing documents

and then upload it to the policy store:

jq -Rs --arg desc "Employee view policy" \

'{static: {description: $desc, statement: .}}' \

policy-employee-view.cedar > policy-employee-view.json

aws verifiedpermissions create-policy \

--policy-store-id $STORE_ID \

--definition file://policy-employee-view.json

Like before, you should get back a JSON message confirming that the policy has been

successfully added to the policy store and providing the relevant information about it.

A.4.2 Owner can do everything policy

The most fundamental policy in ACME’s system is the owner baseline. Each document has

exactly one owner, and by default, that owner should be able to perform any action the
schema allows on that document. Instead of adding special-case rules throughout the

system, ACME encodes this as a single policy. This ensures that no matter how other
policies evolve—whether granting view access to customers or layering global constraints—

owners always maintain full control of their documents:

permit(

principal is ACME::Employee,

action in [ ACME::Action::"doc:view",

ACME::Action::"doc:edit",

ACME::Action::"doc:share" ],

resource is ACME::Document

)

when { resource.owner == principal };

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

441

Recall that we list all the actions to make them explicit and keep the “all” limited to the

actions the schema defines for `Document` .

Like before, we can apply the formatting and use the AWS CLI to upload this policy to

the policy store:

jq -Rs --arg desc "Owner baseline: all actions on owned docs" \

'{static:{description:$desc,statement:.}}' \

policy-owner-all.cedar > policy-owner-all.json

aws verifiedpermissions create-policy \

--policy-store-id $STORE_ID \

--definition file://policy-owner-all.json

You should receive the same type of JSON response you received for the policies regarding

viewing documents.

A.4.3 Employees can share documents that are delegatable

Not every permission at ACME is absolute. Some documents are marked as `delegatable`,

meaning the owner can empower others to act on their behalf. Importantly, this doesn’t
mean anyone can grant access; delegation is tightly scoped. Only employees who are

already members of a document’s readers team are allowed to share it further, and even
then, only if the document has been explicitly flagged as delegatable. This separation

between using a document and granting access to it helps ACME maintain strong controls
while still supporting collaboration. The following policy enforces that principle:

permit(

principal is ACME::Employee,

action == ACME::Action::"doc:share",

resource is ACME::Document

)

when {

resource.delegatable == true

&& principal in resource.employee_readers_team

};

Again, we upload this document by first wrapping it in the proper JSON and then uploading
it through the CLI:

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

442

jq -Rs --arg desc "Employees can share if delegatable" \

'{static: {description: $desc, statement: .}}' \

policy-share.cedar > policy-share.json

aws verifiedpermissions create-policy \

--policy-store-id $STORE_ID \

--definition file://policy-share.json

And the response tells us whether this was successful.

A.4.4 Forbid access from unmanaged devices

So far, our policies have provided access under specific conditions. However, ACME also
enforces global constraints that apply across all applications. One key restriction is device

security: No matter your role or the document you need, if you are an employee accessing
from an unmanaged device, the request must be denied. This policy doesn’t target a

particular action or resource; instead, it functions as a broad rule layered over all others,
ensuring every authorization decision aligns with ACME’s zero-trust device posture:

forbid(

principal is ACME::Employee,

action,

resource is ACME::Document

)

when { context.device.managed == false };

Note that this policy uses ALL for the action instead of listing them individually. This
guarantees that the forbid applies to any new document actions ACME might add in the

future, preventing gaps or drift if policies aren’t updated alongside the schema.

We can encode this policy and upload it to the policy store as before:

jq -Rs --arg desc "Global forbid for unmanaged devices" \

'{static: {description: $desc, statement: .}}' \

policy-managed-device.cedar > policy-managed-device.json

aws verifiedpermissions create-policy \

--policy-store-id $STORE_ID \

--definition file://policy-managed-device.json

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

443

For this example, we uploaded this policy to the same policy store as the others. At ACME,

the previous policies were uploaded to the policy store for the Customer Collaboration
platform, managed by the team responsible for building it. The policy that forbids employee

access on unmanaged devices was placed in a separate policy store managed by the
security team.

#### A.5 Defining entities

Next, we’ll upload entities to test policies and see how they work. In a real application, this

data would come from a relationship graph stored in a database. But for this example, we’ll
just upload them directly.

A.5.1 Employees

We begin by creating the ACME employees, who are the principal members of the
organization. These include Alice and Bob, both engineers who report to Carol; Carol

herself, who oversees Engineering; and Dan, who works in Legal and has no manager. By
defining the reporting structure here, we ensure that policies depending on hierarchical

relationships (such as manager access) can be evaluated accurately:

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

[

]

{

},

{

},

{

},

{

}

444

"identifier": { "entityType": "ACME::Employee",

"entityId": "alice" },

"attributes": {

"department": { "string": "Engineering" },

"on_call": { "boolean": true },

"manager": { "entityIdentifier": { "entityType": "ACME::Employee",

"entityId": "carol" } }

}

"identifier": { "entityType": "ACME::Employee", "entityId": "bob" },

"attributes": {

"department": { "string": "Engineering" },

"on_call": { "boolean": false },

"manager": { "entityIdentifier": { "entityType": "ACME::Employee",

"entityId": "carol" } }

},

"parents": [

{ "entityType": "ACME::Team", "entityId": "doc-q3-employee-readers" }

]

"identifier": { "entityType": "ACME::Employee",

"entityId": "carol" },

"attributes": {

"department": { "string": "Engineering" },

"on_call": { "boolean": false }

}

"identifier": { "entityType": "ACME::Employee", "entityId": "dan" },

"attributes": {

"department": { "string": "Legal" },

"on_call": { "boolean": false }

}

In this simple example, Carol and Dan don’t have managers. Note that we’ve also made

Alice on-call.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

445

A.5.2 Customers

Next, we define CustCo employees Kate and Jack. They are the external principals who will
access documents in ACME’s Customer Collaboration platform. Separating customers from

employees keeps their roles clear in the policies and allows us to show how crossorganizational access is managed:

[

{

"identifier": { "entityType": "ACME::Customer", "entityId": "kate" },

"parents": [

{ "entityType": "ACME::Team", "entityId": "custco-readers" }

]

},

{

"identifier": { "entityType": "ACME::Customer", "entityId": "jack" },

"parents": [

{ "entityType": "ACME::Team", "entityId": "custco-readers" }

]

]

These are fairly simple because we’re not using any customer attributes in our policies, but
a real-life system would likely allow customers to store other profile information as well as

internal attributes to guide policies.

A.5.3 Teams

After defining the individuals, we create teams that group them together. Teams make it
easier to manage access at scale, since policies can refer to a team rather than to each

individual member. Here, we have an employee readers team for the Q3 plan document for
ACME employees and a CustCo readers team for customers:

[

{

"identifier": { "entityType": "ACME::Team",

"entityId": "doc-q3-employee-readers" },

"attributes": { "name": "Q3 Plan Employee Readers" }

}

{

"identifier": { "entityType": "ACME::Team", "entityId": "custco" },

"attributes": { "name": "CustCo Readers" }

}

]

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

446

Notably, while the employee reader team supports the Q3 plan, the CustCo reader team is

not identified as supporting any specific document. This isn’t a security issue, as we’ll see in
the next section.

A.5.4 Document

Finally, we define the document itself, the resource to which access decisions will apply. In
this example, the Q3 plan is owned by Alice, marked as confidential, and designated as

delegatable. Its employee readers are members of the `doc-q3-employee-readers` team,

and its customer readers are CustCo employees Kate and Jack:

{

"identifier": { "entityType": "ACME::Document", "entityId": "q3-plan" },

"attributes": {

"owner": { "entityIdentifier": { "entityType": "ACME::Employee",

"entityId": "alice" } },

"classification": { "string": "confidential" },

"delegatable": { "boolean": true },

"employee_readers_team": {

"entityIdentifier": { "entityType": "ACME::Team",

"entityId": "doc-q3-employee-readers" }

},

"customer_readers_team": {

"entityIdentifier": { "entityType": "ACME::Team",

"entityId": "custco-readers" }

}

}

}

By defining both an employee readers team and a customer readers team for each
document, ACME ensures that only the designated groups can access it. In this case, there

is a dedicated `doc-q3-employee-readers` team but only a general `custco` readers team.

This suggests that ACME creates a unique employee readers team for each document while

reusing a single readers team for each customer. If ACME chose to structure the
relationships differently, the policies would not need to change—only how the entities are

related.

A.5.5 Using the entity definitions

At ACME, the identity team doesn’t manage static JSON files of employees, customers, and

documents. Instead, they manage a live relationship graph of entities and edges that acts
as the single source of truth. Each authorization decision pulls just the slice of that graph

that’s relevant to the request. In AVP terms, this relationship graph is called the _entity_
_store_ .

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

447

In this example, we’re taking a simpler approach. Instead of integrating with a graph

service, we provide an `entities.json` file with each request to AVP. This shows how

policies and data can be integrated easily without needing ACME’s full infrastructure.

Usually, you would generate these JSON snippets dynamically—one for each request—by
querying the relationship graph, not by editing files manually.

#### A.6 Evaluating authorization requests

Once the schema, policies, and entities are set up, the authorization system can then

answer real questions. In Cedar and AVP, this is done via the `is-authorized` API. Each call

provides three inputs: the principal (who is making the request), the action they want to

perform, and the resource involved. Additionally, a context object can be included to
represent environment attributes, such as the device used or the time of day. The policy

engine assesses these inputs against the stored policies and entities and returns either
`allow` or `deny` .

A.6.1 Owner actions

Since Alice is the document owner, the owner-baseline policy applies to all document
actions, not just viewing. Whether the request is to view, edit, or share, the policy checks

`if resource.owner == principal` and allows the action. This highlights one of the main

benefits of writing a baseline policy for owners: It prevents duplicate logic across separate

view/edit/share policies and ensures consistency in how ownership is enforced:

aws verifiedpermissions is-authorized \

--policy-store-id "$STORE_ID" \

--principal entityType=ACME::Employee,entityId=alice \

--action actionType=ACME::Action,actionId=doc:view \

--resource entityType=ACME::Document,entityId=q3-plan \

--context '{"contextMap":

{"device":{"record":{"managed":{"boolean":true}}}}}' \

--entities file://acme-entities.json

The result of this call is the following JSON:

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

{

}

448

"decision": "ALLOW",

"determiningPolicies": [

{

// polic-owner-all.cedar

"policyId": "WkMiyXxTtteMcTm24mWsam"

}

],

"errors": []

Since Alice owns the document, the owner-baseline policy allows her to edit it without any

additional conditions. This shows how a single owner rule can consistently cover multiple
actions.

A.6.2 Customer viewing

Our next test involves Kate, who works for CustCo. As a customer, Kate should be able to
view documents that ACME has explicitly shared with her company. In our entity setup,

Kate is a member of the CustCo readers team, and that team has been granted reader
access to the Q3 plan. Since customers aren’t subject to the device-management

constraints that ACME employees are, we don’t need to pass any device context for this
request:

aws verifiedpermissions is-authorized \

--policy-store-id "$STORE_ID" \

--principal entityType=ACME::Customer,entityId=kate \

--action actionType=ACME::Action,actionId=doc:view \

--resource entityType=ACME::Document,entityId=q3-plan \

--entities file://acme-entities.json

The result of this call is the following JSON:

{

"decision": "ALLOW",

"determiningPolicies": [

{

// policy-customer-view.cedar

"policyId": "GuNiYfTkyWyEqB7RDwgk7s"

}

],

"errors": []

}

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

449

The result is an `allow` decision. The determining policy is the customer view policy, which

checks for customer principals in the appropriate reader team. Notice that this call to `is-`

`authorized` didn’t include context about whether Kate was using a managed device. This

confirms that CustCo employees can successfully see shared documents without triggering
employee-specific constraints.

A.6.3 Employee sharing

Our next check looks at Bob, an ACME employee who has been added to the doc-q3employee-readers team for the Q3 plan. Unlike Kate, Bob is an employee rather than a

customer, so his requests are also governed by ACME’s device-management restrictions.
Additionally, the share action has an extra condition: the document must be marked as

delegatable before non-owners can transfer access:

aws verifiedpermissions is-authorized \

--policy-store-id "$STORE_ID" \

--principal entityType=ACME::Employee,entityId=bob \

--action actionType=ACME::Action,actionId=doc:share \

--resource entityType=ACME::Document,entityId=q3-plan \

--context '{"contextMap":

{"device":{"record":{"managed":

{"boolean":true}}}}}' \

--entities file://acme-entities.json

The result of this call is the following JSON:

{

"decision": "ALLOW",

"determiningPolicies": [

{

// policy-share.cedar

"policyId": "gEqePQqFosaYTX4cZ1fcf"

}

],

"errors": []

}

This request returns the result `allow` . The policy used is the delegatable share policy, which

verifies that the document is marked `delegatable == true` and that the principal is part of

the employee readers team. Since Bob meets both conditions and is using a managed
device, the system approves his attempt to share the Q3 plan.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

450

A.6.4 Unmanaged devices

Finally, we test what happens when an ACME employee tries to access a document outside
company controls. Bob is still part of the doc-q3-employee-readers team, so under normal

conditions, he should be able to view the Q3 plan. But this time, we’ll simulate him
connecting from a laptop that isn’t enrolled in ACME’s management system:

aws verifiedpermissions is-authorized \

--policy-store-id "$STORE_ID" \

--principal entityType=ACME::Employee,entityId=bob \

--action actionType=ACME::Action,actionId=doc:view \

--resource entityType=ACME::Document,entityId=q3-plan \

--context '{"contextMap":

{"device":{"record":{"managed":

{"boolean":false}}}}}' \

--entities file://acme-entities.json

The result of this call is the following JSON:

{

"decision": "DENY",

"determiningPolicies": [

{

// policy-managed-device.cedar

"policyId": "PKtu1UHcdrHYRmmDMEmfzD"

}

],

"errors": []

}

The decision here is `deny` . Although Bob qualifies under the employee view policy, the

global forbid policy takes precedence: It denies all employee actions when the device is
unmanaged. This demonstrates how ABAC-style global constraints can override more

specific relationship- or role-based rules to enforce organizational security requirements.

#### A.7 Wrapping up the end-to-end example

With these tests, we’ve observed authorization scenarios for ACME’s Customer Collaboration

platform in action. Alice, as the owner, can edit the Q3 plan without restrictions. Kate,
representing CustCo, can view the document through her customer readers team. Bob, as

an ACME employee, can share the document when it is delegatable and he is on a managed
device, but the global forbid policy prevents him from viewing it when he connects from an

unmanaged laptop.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

451

Taken together, these scenarios show how Cedar policies combine various authorization

patterns: ownership baselines, customer sharing, discretionary delegation, and global
ABAC-style constraints. Each policy is quite simple on its own, but when combined, they

create rich, context-aware authorization behavior. In a real-life deployment, ACME wouldn’t
be uploading static entities from a file for each request; instead, the Customer

Collaboration platform would read them dynamically from its relationship graph.

[With schema, policies, entities, and requests in hand, we now have a complete picture of](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/appendix-a?potentialInternalRefId=121---book-markup-container)

how Cedar can enforce fine-grained, dynamic authorization for ACME’s Customer
Collaboration platform.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

## Appendix B. Step-by-step AI- assisted policy authoring

This appendix provides a hands-on, step-by-step walkthrough for using AI-assisted
development tools to help author and review authorization policies. It is intended to be

used alongside a code editor, following the examples in the companion repository as you
read.

This appendix focuses on how to apply AI assistance in practice. It does not explain why
AI can be useful for policy authoring or what role authorization plays in AI-enabled

systems. Those topics are covered in chapter 17. It also does not introduce Cedar syntax or
policy fundamentals, which are covered earlier in the book.

[Readers should approach this appendix with the companion repository open in an AI-](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/appendix-b?potentialInternalRefId=3---book-markup-container)
enabled editor such as Cursor. The steps are designed to be followed in order, with short

pauses to interact with the tools and review results.

The examples in this appendix make use of Cursor and the GitHub repository `acme-cedar-`

`ai-authoring` [(https://github.​com/windley/​acme-cedar-​ai-authoring).](https://github.com/windley/acme-cedar-ai-authoring)

#### B.1 Why AI assistance is useful in policy authoring

Authorization policies encode intent in a form that must be precise, unambiguous, and

deterministic. Translating business intent into executable policy is often difficult and errorprone, particularly as policies grow in number and complexity.

AI-assisted tools can help at this stage by drafting candidate policies, explaining existing
logic, and surfacing edge cases that might otherwise be missed. Used correctly, they can

improve clarity and reduce iteration time without changing how authorization decisions are
evaluated or enforced.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

453

[This appendix assumes that authorization decisions remain deterministic and are always](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/appendix-b?potentialInternalRefId=9---book-markup-container)

evaluated by a policy engine. AI assistance is limited to design-time activities such as
authoring, review, and testing. For a deeper discussion of why this separation matters, see

Chapter 17.

#### B.2 Recap: the ACME policy environment

This appendix builds directly on the ACME Cedar schema and policy examples introduced in
Appendix A. Readers should already be familiar with the ACME domain model, including the

core entity types, actions, and relationships used in the policies.

The companion repository reused here contains the same schema and policy files shown

in Appendix A. No new entities, actions, or attributes are introduced in this appendix, and
the underlying model is not modified.

[For a full description of the ACME policy model, refer to appendix A. For a refresher on](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/appendix-b?potentialInternalRefId=13---book-markup-container)
Cedar policy structure and semantics, see chapter 9. For details on policy evaluation and

tooling, see chapter 10.

#### B.3 Getting set up: the companion repository and Cursor

As noted above, this appendix uses a companion GitHub repository, `acme-cedar-ai-`

`authoring`, to demonstrate AI-assisted policy authoring in practice. The repository reuses

the ACME Cedar schema and policy files from appendix A and adds a small amount of
tooling and example material to support hands-on exploration.

Begin by cloning the repository and opening it in an AI-enabled editor such as Cursor. If
you use Emacs-style key bindings, enable them in Cursor’s settings before continuing.

[The repository is organized into a small number of directories:](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/appendix-b?potentialInternalRefId=17---book-markup-container)

`cedar/` contains the Cedar schema, entity data, and policy files reused

from Appendix A. These files are the source of truth for all examples in
this appendix.

`examples/` contains representative authorization requests used to

illustrate policy behavior.

`tests/` contains expected decisions associated with those requests.

`ai/cursor/` contains tool-specific guidance for using Cursor safely,

including a starter prompt and human review guidelines.

Before proceeding, read the files in `ai/cursor/`, starting with the `README`, followed by

`starter-prompt.md` and `authoring-guidelines.md` . These documents describe how AI

assistance is intended to be used in this repository and the constraints that apply to all AI
generated output.

You do not need to modify any files yet. The goal in this section is simply to become

familiar with the structure of the repository and to ensure that Cursor can see the schema
and policy files together.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

454

#### B.4 Providing the right context to the AI

AI-assisted policy authoring works best when the model has access to the same artifacts a

human reviewer would use. Before asking the AI to draft or modify a policy, make sure it
can see the schema, the existing policies, and at least one concrete example of policy

behavior.

Begin by opening the following files in your editor:

```
      cedar/acme.cedarschema
```

All policy files under `cedar/policies/`
```
      examples/sample-request.json
      tests/expected-decisions.json

```

In Cursor, add these files to the AI context before issuing any prompts. You can do this by
opening the files in the editor, by referencing them directly in the prompt using Cursor’s

file-context feature, or by selecting them from the context panel so the AI can read their
contents. Including these files ensures that any proposed policy changes are grounded in

the actual ACME model and prevents the AI from inventing entities, actions, or attributes.

Next, open `ai/cursor/starter-prompt.md` . Use the base prompt in that file to initialize

the AI session. This prompt establishes the constraints under which AI assistance is
allowed, including the requirement to propose test cases and explain policy intent in plain

language.

[At this point, you can verify that the AI has sufficient context by asking a simple, non-](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/appendix-b?potentialInternalRefId=33---book-markup-container)

destructive question, such as:

[“Explain why the sample request results in its expected decision.”](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/appendix-b?potentialInternalRefId=34---book-markup-container)

The response should reference the relevant policy files and conditions rather than restating
the request in generic terms. If the response introduces entities, actions, or attributes that

do not exist in `acme.cedarschema`, stop and recheck which files are included as context.

Providing concrete examples is especially important. Small, representative requests help

the AI reason about scope and intent far more effectively than long textual descriptions. For
this reason, every policy change discussed in this appendix is grounded in an explicit

request and an expected decision.

#### B.5 A human-in-the-loop authoring workflow

With the repository open and the sample request in place, you can now walk through a
complete, _human-in-the-loop policy authoring_ workflow. The goal in this section is not to

change policy behavior yet, but to see how AI assistance fits into the normal review and
iteration process.

Begin by asking the AI to explain the system's current behavior. With the schema,
policies, entities, and sample request included as context, ask a question such as:

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

455

“Which policy or policies permit this request, and what relationship on the resource

makes that true?”

Review the response carefully. A good answer should reference a specific policy file and

point to a concrete condition, such as membership in a reader relationship on the
document. If the response is vague, or if it invents attributes or relationships that do not

exist in the schema, stop and correct the context before proceeding.

Next, ask the AI to restate the authorization logic in plain language. For example:

[“Ex plain this authorization decision as if you were describing it to a product manager.”](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/appendix-b?potentialInternalRefId=43---book-markup-container)

This step is important because it tests whether the policy logic aligns with human intent. If

the explanation surprises you, that is a signal to review the policy more closely.

Now introduce a small hypothetical change. Without modifying any files yet, ask the AI

something like:

[“ What change would be required to deny this request while leaving other customer](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/appendix-b?potentialInternalRefId=46---book-markup-container)

access unchanged?”

The AI may respond in various ways. One typical response is to suggest adding a new

`forbid` policy that explicitly denies this request. That approach can be valid in some cases,

but it is not the only option, and it is often worth exploring alternatives before introducing

additional policies.

You can then ask a follow-up question, such as:

[“What if instead of adding a new policy, we wanted to modify one of the existing](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/appendix-b?potentialInternalRefId=49---book-markup-container)
policies to do this?”

In this case, the AI may suggest modifying an existing permit policy such as `policy-`

`customer-view.cedar` by adding an additional condition to the `when` clause that explicitly

excludes this principal and document. This typically appears as an extra conjunct that
narrows the circumstances under which the permit applies.

At this point, you might further refine the discussion by asking:

[“What if I wanted to do this by adding an unless clause instead of putting a](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/appendix-b?potentialInternalRefId=52---book-markup-container)

conjunction in the when clause?”

The AI may then refactor the proposed change to use an `unless` clause that cleanly

expresses the exception. This version often reads more clearly, especially when the intent is
to describe a general rule with a specific carve-out.

Each of these alternatives may be syntactically valid and semantically equivalent, but
they are not interchangeable from a design perspective. Choosing between a new `forbid`

policy, a narrower `when` clause, or a more readable `unless` clause is ultimately a human

judgment about clarity, intent, and long-term maintainability. These are decisions about

how authority should be expressed, not questions a language model can answer on its own.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

456

This is the core of a human-in-the-loop workflow. The AI can generate options, surface

trade-offs, and refactor logic, but it does not decide which policy best reflects organizational
intent. The final responsibility for authorization behavior remains with the human reviewer,

who must understand and accept the consequences of each change before it is applied.

#### B.6 Steps for modifying a policy set to achieve a specific outcome

Policy changes should begin with an intended outcome, not with code. In this section, you
will follow a structured approach for modifying a policy set to achieve a narrowly defined

authorization result, using AI assistance to explore options while keeping decision-making
under human control.

Step 1: Establish the current behavior

Start with a concrete request whose behavior you understand. In this appendix, the request
is:

{

"principal": "User::\"kate\"",

"action": "Action::\"view\"",

"resource": "Document::\"q3-plan\""

}

Confirm that the request is currently permitted and ask the AI to explain why. The
explanation should reference a specific policy and identify the relationship or condition that

makes the request valid. This step ensures that any change is grounded in a correct
understanding of the existing policy behavior.

Step 2: State the desired outcome precisely

Next, articulate the change in intent as clearly as possible. For example, the desired
outcome here is not “change access to the document,” but “deny this specific request while

leaving other customer access unchanged.”

Precision matters. Vague intent leads to overly broad policy changes and unintended side

effects.

Step 3: Ask the AI to explore implementation options

With intent clearly stated, ask the AI how the desired outcome could be achieved.

Encourage it to propose multiple approaches rather than a single solution.

At this stage, the AI may suggest introducing a new forbid policy, narrowing an existing

permit policy, or refactoring logic using an unless clause. Treat these as alternative
expressions of the same intent, not as recommendations.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

457

Step 4: Evaluate options as a human reviewer

Review the proposed alternatives with an eye toward clarity, scope, and long-term
maintainability. Ask questions such as:

Which option communicates intent most clearly?
Which minimizes the risk of unintended access?

Which will be easiest to understand and modify later?

Although the alternatives may be functionally equivalent, they are not equivalent from a

design perspective. Choosing between them is a human judgment, not a mechanical
decision.

Step 5: Apply the change deliberately

Select one approach and apply it manually to the policy set. Update or add test cases to

reflect the new behavior and re-evaluate the original request to confirm that the outcome
now matches the stated intent.

If the result is surprising, revisit the policy change before proceeding. Unexpected
outcomes are a signal to slow down, not to add more conditions.

Step 6: Reflect on the change

Finally, consider whether the modified policy still reads as a coherent statement of
authority. A good policy change should be explainable in plain language and defensible in

an audit.

This structured approach keeps AI assistance focused on exploration and drafting while

ensuring that responsibility for authorization behavior remains firmly with the human
reviewer.

Things to try

Once you are comfortable with this process, try applying it to a few small variations. Each
of these exercises is intentionally narrow and can be reversed easily.

1. **Introduce a temporary exception.** Modify the policy set so that the
request is denied only under a specific condition, such as a particular

document attribute or time window. Ask the AI to propose multiple ways
to express the exception and compare their clarity and scope.

2. **Generalize the exception.** Instead of denying access for a single
principal, explore how the same approach would apply to a small group.

Use the AI to surface where additional relationships or attributes would
be required, and decide whether that added complexity is justified.

3. **Revert and explain.** Restore the original policy behavior and ask the AI
to explain the difference between the original and modified versions in

plain language. This is a useful way to validate that the change was truly
minimal and that its intent is easy to articulate.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

458

These exercises reinforce the habit of starting from intent, exploring alternatives, and

making deliberate, reviewable changes, rather than accumulating policy complexity through
trial and error.

#### B.7 Guardrails and review checklist

The starter prompt that we loaded as part of getting set up is the foundation for how the AI

interprets context, constraints, and its own role in the policy authoring process. It shapes
not only what the AI can see, but how it reasons about policy, authority, and responsibility.

Because of that, the prompt deserves careful attention—it encodes guardrails just as
deliberately as the policies themselves.

The starter prompt used in this appendix includes several intentional constraints:

**Use the schema and existing policies as the source of truth.** This

ensures that AI suggestions are grounded in the actual authorization
model. Any policy proposal that invents entities, actions, or attributes is

incorrect by definition.
**Do not invent new entities, actions, or attributes.** Schema changes

are architectural decisions. Keeping them out of AI-assisted policy
drafting prevents accidental expansion of the authorization model.

**Prefer least-privilege outcomes by default.** This biases AI
suggestions toward narrower grants, reducing the risk of unintended

access.
**Provide example requests and expected outcomes** . Requiring

examples forces proposed changes to be evaluated in concrete terms
rather than accepted as abstract logic.

**AI output is advisory and will be reviewed by a human.** This
explicitly reinforces accountability. The AI is a drafting assistant, not a

decision-maker.

Taken together, these constraints shape the AI’s behavior toward exploration and

explanation rather than authority. They are not optional, and they should not be removed
lightly.

The prompt establishes how the AI operates within defined boundaries. Humans use the
following checklist to evaluate and accept or reject the output.

[✅ Confirm intent](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/appendix-b?potentialInternalRefId=96---book-markup-container)

Can you explain the policy change in one or two plain-language

sentences?
Does the change do exactly what was intended, and nothing more?

Would another reviewer reach the same conclusion after reading the
policy?

✅ Check scope

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

459

Is access limited to the smallest set of principals, actions, and resources?

Are there any new conditions or relationships that could grant unintended
access?

Does the change interact with other policies in unexpected ways?

✅ Review structure

Is the choice between a new forbid policy, a narrower when clause, or an
unless clause deliberate?

Does the policy read clearly, or is intent obscured by complexity?
Will this policy still make sense to someone who was not involved in the

change?

✅ Validate behavior

Are there test cases that demonstrate both intended permit and deny
outcomes?

Do the tests reflect intent, not just syntax?
Does the evaluated result match what you would expect to explain during

an audit?

✅ Reaffirm accountability

AI suggestions are advisory, not authoritative.
The policy engine evaluates decisions, but humans remain accountable

for what those decisions allow or deny.
If you cannot confidently defend the change, do not accept it.

Starting with the prompt and ending with human accountability reinforces the central
lesson of this appendix: guardrails are not something you add after using AI—they are what

make AI assistance safe to use in the first place.

#### B.8 Key takeaways

This appendix has shown a practical, step-by-step approach to using AI tools to assist with
authorization policy authoring. The focus was not on automating decisions, but on

improving the quality and clarity of human-authored policies.

The key lessons are straightforward:

AI is most effective during design-time activities such as drafting,
refactoring, and explanation.

Authorization decisions remain deterministic and are evaluated by a
policy engine, not by an AI system.

Clear intent, narrow scope, and deliberate structure matter more than
syntactic elegance.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

460

Guardrails in prompts and disciplined human review are what make AI

assistance safe and useful.
Final responsibility for authorization behavior always rests with the

human author.

For a deeper discussion of why these boundaries matter, see chapter 17. For a contrast with

systems that delegate authority to AI agents, see chapter 18.
