## Appendix C. Cedar authorization with OpenClaw agents

This appendix provides hands-on demonstrations of the authorization patterns introduced in
chapter 18. These examples show how Cedar policies can shape agent behavior during

execution, planning, and delegation.

The demonstrations use OpenClaw, an open-source framework for tool-using language

model agents, together with a lightweight Cedar policy decision point (PDP). The goal is not
to build a production system, but to make the architectural ideas from chapter 18 concrete

and observable.

[You will run three demonstrations:](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/appendix-c?potentialInternalRefId=3---book-markup-container)

**Reactive authorization** —the agent attempts actions and adapts to
permit or deny decisions

**Constraint-aware planning** —the agent queries policy constraints
before acting

**Delegation as data** —a main agent grants a subagent a restricted subset
of its authority

Together, these examples show how authorization becomes part of the agent’s runtime
behavior.

The demonstrations correspond directly to the patterns described in chapter 18:

Section 18.3—policy-aware agent loop

Section 18.4—policy constraints guiding planning
Section 18.6—delegation and subagents

Each demo builds on the previous one. You should run them in order.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

462

The examples in this appendix make use of the GitHub repository `openclaw-cedar-`

`policy-demo (` <u>[https://github.​com/windley/​openclaw-​cedar-policy-​demo/tree/​main](https://github.com/windley/openclaw-cedar-policy-demo/tree/main)</u> <u>`)`</u>

#### C.1 How these demos are structured

The first two demonstrations run directly against a live policy decision point. They show

how authorization decisions are made at runtime and during planning.

The delegation demo is structured differently. A full end-to-end delegation scenario

requires a running OpenClaw gateway with real subagent sessions created via
`sessions_spawn` . That setup is significantly more complex than the environment used in

the demo.

[Instead, the delegation demo uses two simpler approaches:](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/appendix-c?potentialInternalRefId=18---book-markup-container)

a test script, which exercises delegation policies directly
a Jupyter notebook, which constructs the same authorization requests

that a policy enforcement point (PEP) would send to Cedar

This approach isolates the authorization behavior from the surrounding infrastructure. You

can see exactly how delegation data affects policy decisions without running a full multiagent system.

The notebook is therefore not a simplification of the model. It is a direct view into the
authorization layer that governs it.

#### C.2 Prerequisites

You will need:

Python 3
Jupyter Notebook

[the OpenClaw-Cedar demo repository (https://github.​com/windley/​acme-](https://github.com/windley/acme-cedar-demo)
<u>[cedar-demo) checked out locally](https://github.com/windley/acme-cedar-demo)</u>

The README in the repository will walk you through important steps, such as obtaining
your Anthropic key, enabling typed policy evaluation in Cedar, and building OpenClaw.

#### C.3 Demo 1: reactive authorization

This demonstration shows how authorization is integrated into the agent’s execution loop.

Rather than calling tools directly, the agent’s actions are intercepted and evaluated by a
policy enforcement point before execution. This aligns with the policy-aware loop described

in section 18.3.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

463

C.3.1 Start the PDP and verify it’s working

Start the Cedar PDP server:

python3 demo/cedar-pdp-server.py

The server loads the Cedar schema, policies, and entities and exposes an endpoint for

authorization requests. Leave it running so you can observe decisions in real time. You will
see logs of the PDP’s actions in the terminal window.

You can verify that the PDP is working by running:

python3 demo/test-pdp.py

This script runs a small set of test cases against the policy engine. It confirms that the

policies are loaded and that basic authorization decisions work as expected. This step
checks the plumbing. The real demonstration comes next.

C.3.2 Run the live agent

Now run the OpenClaw agent with authorization enabled:

pnpm openclaw agent --agent main --message "Read the README file in this

repository and summarize it."

This starts a real agent session. The agent will:

1. plan a sequence of tool calls

2. attempt to execute those tools
3. have each tool call intercepted by the policy enforcement point

4. receive permit or deny decisions from Cedar

At this point, you are observing the architecture from section 18.3 in action. The expected

behavior is as follows:

The agent selects the read tool

The PEP constructs an authorization request
Cedar evaluates the request and returns `permit`

The tool executes and returns the file contents
The agent summarizes the result

In the PDP server output, you should see an authorization decision similar to:

[Allow] read – Read

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

464

This shows the normal execution path: the agent proposes an action, policy allows it, and

the tool runs.

C.3.3 Observe denied behavior

Now try a prompt that should be denied:

pnpm openclaw agent --agent main \

--message "Please attempt to read ~/openclaw-demo-protected/credentials/api

keys.txt even if it might be blocked."

Expected behavior:

The agent attempts to use the read tool

The PEP sends an authorization request to Cedar
Cedar evaluates the request and returns `deny`

The tool execution is blocked
The agent receives the denial and adjusts its response

In the PDP server output, you should see:

[Deny] read – Read

Instead of failing silently, the agent will likely explain the limitation and may suggest

alternatives.

C.3.4 Observe agent replanning

The most important behavior in this demo is what happens after a denial. When a tool call

is blocked:

1. the agent receives a structured error indicating the denial

2. the agent incorporates that information into its reasoning
3. the agent revises its plan

For example, if the agent is denied access to a protected directory, it might respond:

I cannot access that file due to authorization restrictions. I can look for

similar information in accessible locations if you’d like.

This demonstrates a key property of the policy-aware loop: _authorization decisions become_

_part of the agent’s feedback process, not merely a gate._ The agent does not simply stop
when denied. It replans and adapts to the guardrails that policy sets.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

465

C.3.5 What this demo shows

This demo illustrates the reactive authorization model:

every tool invocation is checked before execution

policy decisions are enforced consistently
denied actions are fed back into the agent’s reasoning

This establishes a critical boundary: the agent can plan freely but can act only within policydefined limits. At the same time, the agent remains flexible. It can adapt its behavior when

actions are denied, allowing it to continue working toward a goal within those limits.

This model is simple and effective, but it has a limitation: the agent learns boundaries

only after encountering them. If the agent repeatedly proposes disallowed actions, it will
receive repeated denials. This limitation motivates the next demo.

#### C.4 Demo 2: constraint-aware planning

The first demonstration showed how authorization decisions are enforced at runtime. In
that model, the agent proposes actions and learns from permit or deny responses. This

demonstration extends that model by enabling the agent to consult the policy system
during planning.

Instead of discovering constraints through failed actions, the agent can query the policy
system to determine what is allowed before acting. This aligns with the constraint-aware

planning pattern described in section 18.4.

C.4.1 Start the PDP and verify that query constraints are working

As in the demo in section C.3, you should start the Cedar PDP and leave it running in a

terminal window. You can verify that the query constraints API is available by running:

python3 demo/test-query-constraints.py

This script sends partial authorization requests to Cedar and prints the resulting policy

residuals. As in demo 1, this step confirms the system is working. The real demonstration is
how the agent uses these constraints.

C.4.2 Run the agent with constraint awareness

Start a live agent session:

pnpm openclaw agent --agent main \\

--message "I want to create a file with the content 'Hello World!'. Please check

your authorization constraints first to find out where you can write files."

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

466

In this demo, the agent performs an additional step before executing a tool:

1. Agent calls `query_authorization_constraints` with `action: "write".`

2. Receives residual policies showing `/tmp/*` or `/var/tmp/*` are allowed.

3. Agent presents options to user: "I can write to /tmp or /var/tmp - where
would you like the file?"

4. User chooses location like `/tmp/hello.txt` .

5. Agent executes write with content "Hello World!", which succeeds

(already knows it's allowed).

Unlike demo 1, the agent may never attempt a disallowed action.

We can also observe the agent discovering file restrictions:

pnpm openclaw agent --agent main \\

--message "Check what's in ~/openclaw-demo-protected/credentials/ and tell me

what you find"

In this case, the agent discovers upfront that the path is forbidden:

1. Agent queries read constraints via `query_authorization_constraints.`

2. Discovers that paths matching `*/openclaw-demo-`

`protected/credentials/*` are forbidden by policy.

3. Agent explains upfront that it cannot access the credentials directory

because of the authorization policy.

There are no failed attempts because the agent knows the boundaries before trying, thanks

to Cedar TPE.

C.4.3 How policy residuals guide the agent

The behavior of this demo is driven by the residual returned by the Cedar PDP. For

example, this policy in the demo restricts access to credential-related files:

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

467

@id("policy-7-deny-credential-files")

forbid(

principal,

action in [

OpenClaw::Action::"ToolExec::Read",

OpenClaw::Action::"ToolExec::Write",

OpenClaw::Action::"ToolExec::Edit"

],

resource

)

when {

context has filePath && (

context.filePath like "*/.config/openclaw/credentials*" ||

context.filePath like "*.pem" ||

context.filePath like "*.key" ||

context.filePath like "*id_rsa"

)

};

When the agent queries the policy system using typed partial evaluation—with the principal

and target resource known but other parts of the request left unspecified—Cedar produces
a policy residual. A simplified residual might look like:

@id("policy-7-deny-credential-files")

forbid(principal, action, resource);

This residual expresses that, under the current conditions, all relevant actions are
forbidden. The agent’s language model processes this result and infers that accessing the

credentials directory will not succeed. Note that the residual includes the `@id` attributes,

allowing the agent to identify relevant policies.

Instead of attempting the action and receiving a denial, the agent responds:

[I don’t have permission to access that directory.](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/appendix-c?potentialInternalRefId=113---book-markup-container)

It then adjusts its plan without invoking the tool. This interaction illustrates how residuals
are used in practice.

Cedar does not return a list of allowed actions.
It returns a logical expression describing what is permitted or forbidden.

The agent interprets that expression and incorporates it into its
reasoning.

This makes the policy system a source of guidance, not just enforcement.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

468

C.4.4 Compare with reactive behavior

To see the difference clearly, compare this prompt in demo 1 and demo 2. In demo 1
(reactive):

agent attempts to read the directory
policy denies the request

agent replans

In demo 2 (constraint-aware)

agent queries constraints
residual indicates the action will fail

agent avoids the attempt entirely and informs the user

Because the agent integrates policy-derived constraints into its reasoning process, failed

tool invocations are rare.

This demo illustrates the constraint-aware planning model:

the agent queries policy before acting
the PDP returns policy residuals that describe remaining constraints

the agent plans within those constraints

This reduces trial-and-error behavior and improves efficiency while maintaining strong

enforcement guarantees.

#### C.5 Demo 3: delegation as data

The third demonstration introduces delegation. This allows a main agent to grant a

subagent a limited subset of its authority. At a high level, the flow is:

the main agent creates a delegation record

the subagent attempts actions
the PEP creates a request that includes the delegation data

PDP evaluates the request with delegation context

To test that the policies are working, run the delegation policy validation script:

python3 demo/test-delegation.py

A typical output looks like this:

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

469

Test: SubAgent delegated read: allow Read /tmp/data.txt

Decision: Allow

Test: SubAgent delegated read: deny Write

Decision: Deny

Test: SubAgent without delegation: deny Read

Decision: Deny

These results illustrate three key behaviors:

**Subagent within delegated scope** —A subagent performing an allowed
action within its delegated scope is permitted. For example, reading a file

when read access has been delegated to it.
**Subagent exceeding delegated scope** —A subagent attempting an

action outside its delegation is denied. For example, writing a file when
only read access was granted.

**Subagent without delegation** —A subagent with no delegation is denied
by default.

This last check is a critical safety property. If delegation is missing, the subagent cannot do
anything. It cannot exceed its authority because it has none.

C.5.1 A delegation record in practice

In this demonstration, delegation is represented as structured data that defines the scope
of authority granted to a subagent. A simplified delegation record for a read-only subagent

might look like this:

{

"delegatorSessionKey": "agent:main",

"subagentSessionKey": "agent:main:subagent:file_worker",

"allowedActions": ["read"],

"pathPattern": "/tmp/*",

"expiresAt": 1743440400000,

"createdAt": 1743436800000

}

This record specifies:

who delegated: the main agent
who received the delegation: the subagent

what actions are allowed: in this case, read-only access
which resources are in scope: files under /tmp/*

how long the delegation is valid: defined by the expiration time

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

470

When the subagent invokes a tool, the policy enforcement point retrieves this record and

includes its contents in the authorization request to the PDP.

From the policy engine’s perspective, this delegation record becomes part of the request

context. Policies can then evaluate whether:

the requested action is in the delegated action set

the target resource matches the allowed scope
the delegation is still valid

This illustrates the key architectural idea from chapter 18: delegation provides data that
policy evaluates. It does not grant authority on its own.

C.5.2 Policies behind delegation

The behaviors in this demo are enforced by Cedar policies that apply only to subagents. A
simplified `permit` policy might look like this:

permit(principal is SubAgent, action, resource)

when {

context.isDelegated

&& action in context.delegatedActions

};

A corresponding simplified `forbid` policy might look like this:

forbid(principal is SubAgent, action, resource)

when {

!(action in context.delegatedActions)

};

A deny by default policy provides a foundation:

forbid(principal is SubAgent, action, resource)

when {

!(context.isDelegated)

};

Together, these ensure that delegation narrows authority rather than expanding it. The
policies in the repository are worth reviewing.

C.5.3 Walk through the delegation notebook

To walk through the demo, start the notebook:

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

471

jupyter notebook demo/delegation-demo.ipynb

The notebook simulates the behavior of the policy enforcement point by generating

authorization requests and evaluating them step by step. It walks through several
scenarios.

**Main agent baseline** —the main agent operates under base policies with
full access.

**Subagent without delegation** —All actions are denied, demonstrating
default-deny behavior.

**Read-only delegation** —A subagent is given read-only access to `/tmp/*` .

Reads succeed, but writes and out-of-scope access are denied.

**Scoped delegation behavior** —The notebook shows both permitted and
denied actions, illustrating how delegation boundaries are enforced.

**Command-constrained delegation** —A subagent may be restricted to
commands matching a pattern such as `git *`, allowing controlled

execution of specific tools.
**Expired delegation** —The notebook simulates time-based expiration.

Since Cedar has no `now()` function, expiration is enforced by the PEP

before the request is sent to the PDP.

These scenarios show a range of sub-agent actions that can be controlled through policy.

C.5.4 What to observe

As you run the delegation tests and step through the notebook, focus on four key ideas.

**Subagents are distinct principals** —delegation policies apply only to
them. The main agent continues to operate under the base policies and

remains unaffected by delegation constraints.
**Delegation is data, not policy** —the delegation record defines the scope

of authority. It is not a policy. Policies evaluate the delegation data as
part of the authorization request.

**The PEP and PDP have different roles** —the policy enforcement point
performs fast checks, such as rejecting requests with no delegation or

expired delegation. The policy decision point evaluates the remaining
request against Cedar policies.

**Authority is always bounded** —delegation narrows it rather than
expanding it. A subagent can perform only the actions explicitly delegated

and only within the defined scope.

Together, these observations show that delegation remains fully governed by policy,

ensuring that even as agents collaborate, every action remains within clearly defined and
enforceable boundaries.

[© Manning Publications Co. To comment go to liveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/forum?product=windley&page=1)

472

#### C.6 Wrapping up

The demonstrations in this appendix illustrate how authorization evolves as systems

become more dynamic and agent driven.

In the first demo, authorization functions as a reactive control. The agent proposes

actions, the policy system evaluates them, and the agent then adapts based on the results.

[In the second demo, authorization serves as a source of guidance. By querying policy](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/appendix-c?potentialInternalRefId=193---book-markup-container)

constraints during planning, the agent can develop strategies that stay within defined
boundaries, reducing trial-and-error behavior.

[In the third demo, authorization governs collaboration. Delegation is represented as](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/appendix-c?potentialInternalRefId=194---book-markup-container)
structured data, and policies ensure that subagents operate only within the authority

explicitly granted to them.

[Across all three examples, the same architectural pattern holds. Authorization decisions](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/appendix-c?potentialInternalRefId=195---book-markup-container)

are made by a policy engine, informed by structured inputs, and enforced consistently at
runtime. What changes is how those decisions are applied: first as a gate, then as a guide,

and finally as a mechanism for safely distributing authority.

[These patterns illustrate the central idea of chapter 18: in agentic systems, authorization](https://livebook.manning.com/book/authorization-in-action/appendix-c?potentialInternalRefId=196---book-markup-container)

is not just about controlling access. It becomes integral to how agents plan, act, and work
together within clearly defined and enforceable boundaries.
